en: Oṃ.
The Saṃhitā of the Ṛgveda, together with the commentary composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya;
now begins the second Maṇḍala.
The first maṇḍala, consisting of the Śatarcins, has been explained. Now the second maṇḍala, belonging to Gṛtsamada, is being explained.
This second maṇḍala begins with the hymn: “O Agni, you [with] the days” (*tvam agne dyubhiḥ*).
There are four sections (anuvākas). In the first section, there are eleven hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of sixteen verses, begins with "tvam agne dyubhiḥ."
Gṛtsamada, the seer, is the beholder of the maṇḍala. Formerly, being the son of Śunahotra in the lineage of Aṅgiras, he was seized by the asuras at the time of a sacrifice and liberated by Indra.
Subsequently, by that very word [of Indra], he became known by the name Gṛtsamada, the son of Śunaka, in the lineage of Bhṛgu.

And so says the *Anukramaṇikā*: “He who, having been Gṛtsamada of the lineage of Aṅgiras and Śaunahotra, became Śaunaka of the lineage of Bhṛgu, he beheld the second maṇḍala. Likewise, there is the statement of that very Śaunaka in the *Ṛṣyanukramaṇī*: “In the hymn beginning with ‘tvam agne,’ Gṛtsamada—Śaunaka, who attained the state of a Bhṛgu—is the seer; he was originally Śaunahotra, who is said to belong to the lineage of Aṅgiras.”
Therefore, the seer (ṛṣi) of this maṇḍala is Śaunaka Gṛtsamada; the metre (chandas) is Jagatī;
and by the conventional definition of the beginning of a maṇḍala, it belongs to Agni.
The table of contents here is: ‘O Agni, you [are addressed] in the Jāgata [meter].’

The application of these two initial hymns occurs within the *Jagatī* metre during the *Prātaranuvāka* and the *Āśvina-śastra*, because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "In the hymn beginning with 'tvam agne dyubhiḥ'... (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.13).
In the rites of *upākaraṇa* and *utsarjana* as well, the first [verse] is employed.

O Agni, you are born from the heavens; you are the one who desires to blaze; you are the Aṅgiras; you are born from the stone. You are born from the forests, you are born from the plants, and you, O Lord of men, are born pure among men.
O Agni, you are born with the days; you, O seeker of light; you, O Aṅgiras; you from the stone; you from the forests; you from the plants; you, O Lord of men, are born pure. 1.
O Agni, distinguished by qualities such as being the leader (*agraṇī*), O Lord of men (*nṛpate*)!
Among men (*nṛṇām*), you are the special protector of those who are men and performers of sacrifice (*yaṣṭāraḥ*).
Alternatively, by both words [the terms *nṛṇām* and *nṛpate*], plurality and eternal lordship are respectively expressed.
The meaning is that he is the eternal protector of all men as well.
The absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) in the word *nṛṇām* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

O such a god, you are born through the "days"—that is, through the sacrificial days which serve as the instrumental cause; the meaning is that you are produced by means of churning for the sake of the sacrifice.
Or rather, you are born together with such days.
The meaning is that you become well-known on the various days of sacrifice.
Likewise, "you, the Āśuśukṣaṇi (the one who desires to burn swiftly), are born everywhere.
1. ṇa-ṇa-na-va- nu | 2. ma-upākarmotsarjanayorāpi | 3. ṇa-pratipadyate | 4. ṇa-ma- manthanena | 5. ka-jha-ma-pravṛddhaḥ |
You are shining brightly.
This is a Vedic form of the root *śuc* meaning "to shine," preceded by the prefix *āṅ* and followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*).
Alternatively,
it means that he is served because he is radiant (*śuci*), shining quickly (*āśu*).
He is called *āśuśukṣaṇi* because he quickly (*āśu*) bestows (*sanoti*) or gives (*dadāti*) grief (*śucam*, i.e., sorrow) to his enemies by means of burning and other such afflictions.
Such you become.

In this manner, the phrase "you are born" (*jāyase*) should be applied to every specific attribute. O Agni, you are born from the waters—that is, from the waters of rain—in the form of lightning or as the submarine fire (*vāḍava*) from the waters of the ocean.
You are born from the stone, from the cloud, or from the rock;
for there is another mantra: "He who generated fire between the two stones" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.12.3).
[You are born] from the forests, that is, from the multitudes of trees and such, in the form of forest fire.
"From the plants, you [are born] in the form of Vaiśvānara.
The meaning is that you, being thus possessed of great majesty, having been produced by friction, become the self of all;
you are born indeed as pure.
Alternatively, "śuciḥ" means having the form of the sun; that is, he is the most excellent.
In this regard, the *Nirukta* passage beginning with "thou, O Agni, by days and nights" (*Nirukta* 6.1) should be consulted.
O Agni, yours is the office of the Hotṛ; yours is the office of the Potṛ at the appointed time; yours is the office of the Neṣṭṛ; you are the Agnīdh for the one who bestows gifts.
You are the Praśāstṛ; you act as the Adhvaryu; you are both the Brahman and the Gṛhapati in our home.

Thine is the office of the Hotṛ, O Agni; thine is the office of the Potṛ according to the season; thine is the office of the Neṣṭṛ. Thou art the Agnīdh for the one who follows the Truth; thine is the office of the Praśāstṛ. Thou performest the duties of the Adhvaryu; thou art both the Brahman and the Lord of the House within our home. 2.

O Agni, that which is the office of the Hotṛ—the performance of the ritual, the recitation of the *śastra*, the eating of the first portion, and so forth—that too is yours alone; the meaning is that it is for your own sake. Likewise, that which is the office of the Potṛ—the performance of the Potṛ’s duty—that too is yours alone.
Similarly, the priestly function (*ṛtviya*) performed at the appropriate time is yours alone.
The office of the *neṣṭṛ*, consisting of the duties such as offering the *prasthitayājyā* and so forth, is yours;
O Agni, you alone are the *agnidh*.
Likewise, for you who desire the sacrifice (*ṛtāyat*), that which is the work of the *praśāstṛ*—namely, the ritual actions of the *praśāstṛ* and the *maitrāvaruṇa*—is yours alone.
O Agni, you act as the officiant (*adhvarīyasi*); that is, you desire the sacrifice (*adhvara*), the ritual;
the meaning is that you become the *adhvaryu*.
This is because of the etymological derivation of the word *adhvaryu* in that manner.
"For 'Adhvaryu' means one who desires the sacrifice" (Nirukta 1.8); thus it is said in the Nirukta.
Likewise, you are the Brahmā and also the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin;
likewise, you are the Gṛhapati in our house—that is, in our sacrificial hall.
O Agni, you are Indra, the bull among the virtuous; you are Viṣṇu, the wide-striding one, worthy of homage.
You are the Brahman, the finder of wealth, O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati); you are the upholder, united with the wisdom of the city-fortress.

O Agni, you are Indra, the bull among the virtuous; you are Viṣṇu, the wide-striding, worthy of homage. You are the Brahman, the winner of wealth, O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati); you, O Sustainer, are accompanied by wisdom. You are the Brahman, the winner of wealth, O Lord of Prayer; you, O Sustainer, are accompanied by wisdom. 3.
O Agni, since you are the bull, the showerer [of benefits], for those who exist, therefore you are Indra; or rather,
you are Indra for the virtuous, the good.
You are the showerer of desires;
you are Viṣṇu,
because you are the wide-striding one who is praised by many and worthy of salutation.

O Brahmaṇaspati, protector of the ritual action and the mantra of the sovereign, since you are the possessor of wealth (rayivit) through the form of Vaiśvānara [manifested] from the *ka*, *ja*, *ña*, *ma*, *tra*, *ī*, and so forth,
and through the form of Āditya [manifested] from the *ta*, *ma*, *va*, and so forth.
3 ka-ṇa-1-na-va: [ma. 2. a. 1, sū. 1] "brahmāṇam api chandasi" (Pāṇini 6.4.17).
Second Aṣṭaka: 3. You are the *brahmán* because you know that which begins with the cow (*gavādi*). Thus, you are the *brahmán*.
O Vidhartṛ, you who perform manifold deeds, you always abide together with the Purandhi—the wisdom of many kinds; that is to say, O Agni, you ever delight in wisdom.

O Agni, you are King Varuṇa, the upholder of sacred vows; you become Mitra, the wondrous one worthy of praise. You are Aryaman, the lord of the righteous, whose enjoyment is shared; O God, you are Aṃśa, the distributor of portions at the sacrifice.

O Agni, you are King Varuṇa, whose laws are firm; you become Mitra, the wondrous one worthy of praise; you are Aryaman, the lord of the virtuous, whose enjoyment is shared; O God, in the assembly, you are Aṃśa, the distributor of portions. 4.
O Agni, since you are one whose vows are firm and whose actions are sustained, therefore you are Varuṇa, the King.
Since you are a *dasma*, a destroyer of enemies, and worthy of praise and hymns, therefore you are Mitra, the deity so named.
Since you are the Lord of the Good (*satpati*), protecting them by bestowing what they desire, therefore you become Aryaman.
Generosity is the characteristic mark of Aryaman;
they call him Aryaman who gives.
He is Aryaman whose gift is "saṃbhujam"—that is, enjoyed together, enjoyed constantly, and all-pervading.
Or alternatively:
he whose wealth is "saṃbhujam," meaning perfectly suitable for the enjoyment of those who receive it;
likewise, you are his "aṃśa," a deity of this name who exists within the orb of the sun.

O such a God, in our sacrificial assembly, you are the one who distributes—that is, the bringer and bestower—of fruits. O Agni, you are Tvaṣṭṛ; you grant great heroic power to the worshipper. You, O Mitra-mahas, are the kinsman of the pressing-stones. Through you, these swift horses of ours have been granted; you possess excellent steeds. You are the host of men, the possessor of abundant wealth.

O Agni, you are Tvaṣṭṛ; you bestow great heroic power upon the worshipper. In you, O Mitra-like one, the pressing-stones find kinship. You, the swift impeller, grant us excellent horses. You are the host of men, possessing abundant wealth. ||5||

O Agni, you are Tvaṣṭṛ, the perfect accomplisher of the fruit; for the person who serves and honors you, you are the cause of that excellent heroic strength and wealth. Those words of praise which exist are yours by nature.

"O you of great glory, born of beneficent action, resort to our kinsman of the same lineage"—this is the meaning. O Agni, swift impeller, you grant the fruit consisting of a noble team of horses (*svaśvya*).
O Agni, possessor of abundant wealth, you are the strength (*śardhaḥ*) of men, acting as their support.
O Agni, you are Rudra, the Asura of the great heaven; you rule over the host of Maruts and over nourishment.
You travel with the ruddy winds as the bringer of bliss; you, as Pūṣan, protect those who serve you by your own power.

O Agni, you are Rudra, the Asura of the great heaven; you are the host of the Maruts; you rule over nourishment. You travel with the ruddy winds for the sake of happiness; as Pūṣan, you yourself protect those who worship you.

1. *va*—having many offspring as its characteristic; 2. *tha*—pervading the shared [space]; *ka*, *ma*, *va*—constantly pervading the arms; *ṇa*, *na*—constantly pervading the arms. O Agni, you [come] from the great heaven, the vast celestial world.
This is an elliptical expression [meaning] "from the three worlds.
You are Rudra, the one who casts down the enemies, the Asuras.
*Ruhaḥ* means either space (*kha*) or the cause of suffering, such as sin (*pāpa*).
You are the deity named the *drāvayitṛ* (the one who causes to flow away or dissolve) of that.
This is because Agni is designated by the word *rudra* in passages such as, "Agni, indeed, is this Rudra" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.3.1).
Or alternatively:
you are Rudra;
he is called Rudra because he cries out, "Alas, men will fall into sufferings if they do not worship me."
Such are you.
For the Nirukta states: "Rudra is so called because he roars" (Nirukta 10.5).
Likewise, you are the Asura belonging to the great, vast world of heaven (dyuloka).
It is the strength of the Asuras;
you are its giver and you possess the form of Āditya.
The asura-nature of Agni in relation to the heavenly world is seen in such passages as, "Or rather, the thought of the heavenly Asura" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.41.3).
Likewise, O Māruta, you are a host (*śardhaḥ*), meaning you are a force in the form of the Maruts;
the sense is that you are also in the form of Vāyu. Thus, you are in the form of Agni, Āditya, and Vāyu.
O Vṛkṣa, you are the lord (īśiṣe), the sovereign, of Agni, who is characterized by the oblation (havi-lakṣaṇa).

Since this is so, being a true self (tattvam), you—being a dwelling place (āvāsa-bhūta) in the form of a house of bliss (aṅgayaḥ)—go to, that is, reach, the sacrificial hall (yāga-gṛha) with the reddish-colored (aruṇa) horses that are like the winds (vātaiḥ).
Or alternatively:
Driven by the ruddy, ever-moving winds, you indeed course through the forest;
likewise, being the nourisher (Pūpā) of all, you swiftly protect with your own breath—the very nature of your favor—and through your own intelligence, the sacrificers who perform your service.
O Agni, you are the giver of wealth to the one who serves you; you are the god Savitṛ, the bestower of jewels.
You, O lord of men, rule over splendor and riches; you are the protector for him who has devoted himself to your dwelling.

O Agni, you are the giver of wealth to him who has prepared the offering; you are the god Savitṛ, the bestower of jewels. You, O lord of men, are the splendor and you rule over all riches; you are the protector in the home for him who has worshipped you. 7.
O Agni, you are the giver of wealth (*draviṇodāḥ*), the bestower of gold, to the sacrificer who adorns you and makes you ready.
You, the radiant god Savitṛ, the impeller of all toward virtuous deeds, are the possessor of jewels (*ratnadhāḥ*), the holder of delightful riches such as gems and necklaces.
Likewise, O Lord of men (*nṛpati*), O Agni who protects humanity, being worthy of worship (*bhagaḥ*), you are the master (*īśiṣe*) of wealth (*vasvaḥ*); you are capable of bestowing it.
O you, you are the protector and guardian of that sacrificer who serves and attends upon you in his own home, the sacrificial hall.
O Agni, the clans honor you as the lord of the household within the home; they honor you, the king, the one who finds great wealth.
O god of radiant countenance, you rule over all things; you are equal to ten hundred thousand.

O Agni, enter this house as the lord of the people; toward you, the benevolent king, the clans turn themselves. O you of beautiful countenance, you rule over all things; you are equal to ten hundred thousand. 8.
O Agni, the subjects—the sacrificers—settle you, the lord of the people and protector of the sacrificers, within their own home, the sacrificial hall.
Due to the influence of a prefix, there is the ellipsis of the action of conjunction.
Having done so, they honor and propitiate you—the radiant king, of excellent insight and beautiful wisdom, whose mind is well-disposed toward us, the one of good fortune.
1. *Ṛñjati* means "to adorn" (according to Yāska).

2. *Ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *ma*, *tra*, *poṣaṇaḥ*. 3. *Ka*, *ma*, [it is] by right understanding alone. 4. *Ka*, *jha*, *pāsa*, you protect. 5. *Tha*, *ba*, giver of gold. 6. *Ma*, Savitṛ, the impeller of all (Yāska).
Since this is so, therefore, O *svanika*—you who possess a host of beautiful flames—you [consume] all, that is, all the oblations; this is the ellipsis.
The accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
You become the master (īśvara) of all oblations, such as clarified butter, Soma, sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa), and so forth.
This refers to lordship, because it is listed among its names in the statement: "He rules; he goes" (Nirukta 2.21.2).
Or rather, you act as a substitute;
you, however, are a representative for "thousands," that is, for "hundreds," and "ten"—
meaning you are the equivalent of these numbers of desired means of accomplishment.
By the rule *pratiḥ pratinidhipratidānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.92), *prati* functions as a *karmapravacanīya*. The meaning is: "Whatever fruit results from those [actions], that is obtained by you."
O Agni, we seek you as a father with our sacrifices; you, for the sake of our kinsman, shine forth with your body through our labor.
You become a son to him who honors you; you are a most gracious friend, protecting us from the unassailable foe.

O Agni, we [approach] you as a father with our sacrifices; we [approach] you for protection, you whose body shines through our labor. You become a son to him who honors you; you, as a most gracious friend, protect him from the assailant. 9.
O Agni, the leaders—the sacrificers—worship you, the protector (pitaram), with *iṣṭis*, that is, with sacrifices which are the means of attainment;
the sense is that they worship for the sake of protection (*pitṛt*).

Likewise, for the sake of kinship (*ātrāya*), meaning for brotherhood (*saubhrātrāya*), [they worship] you, who shine upon the body (*tanūrucam*), illuminating the bodies by means of the Vaiśvānara fire, with the sacrificial pin (*śamyā*).
This is a name derived from its function.
The ellipsis is "they worship through ritual action" (*karmaṇā yajante*).
Alternatively,
in both cases, there is a connection with the word "did not know" (*avidhat*), which will be mentioned later.
O Agni, he who serves you—that man—you become his son; that is, you become his protector like a son.
Likewise, you are his friend, acting for his benefit as a companion, and you are most gracious.
"Śevam" is a name for happiness.

Being one who brings about excellent happiness, you protect against those who desire to assail; you protect as a father for one who desires a father, as a brother for one who desires a brother, and as a son for one who desires a son—
meaning that you protect in these three ways.
O Agni, you are the Ribhu to be honored in the assembly; you are the lord of food and of wealth that brings strength.
You shine forth for the granting of gifts; you are the one who, as the son of the people, extends the sacrifice.

O Agni, you are the Rbhu, to be honored nearby; you are the lord of strength and of wealth accompanied by food. You shine forth; you burn along for the sake of giving. You are the one who sharpens the people, the spreader of the sacrifice. 10.
O Agni, you are the Ṛbhu—
one who shines widely or one who is wise.
You are to be honored with reverence (namasyaḥ), that is, worthy of salutation, even in our very presence (āke).
The meaning is "worthy of praise.
The sense is that you are not merely worthy of praise through a form mediated by a mantra like other deities, but rather you are directly perceptible.
Likewise, you *īśiṣe*—you are the lord—of *vāja*, food that is accompanied by sound (*kṣumataḥ*) and heard everywhere, as well as of *rāyaḥ*, wealth.
Therefore, the meaning is "come here.
O Agni, you shine forth; you blaze intensely for that purpose.
1. By means of *ta-vā-śeva*;
2. for one desiring a son through *ṇa-ta-na*;
3. by means of the form of the mantra to be imparted by *ka-la-ca-kṣa-ṇa*.

You burn, you consume wood and other materials in due order; this is the form of the root *dah* in the present indicative (*laṭ*) with the suffix *sip*. The absence of the substitution of *bha* in the *saṃhitā* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). For what purpose? For the purpose of driving away or cutting through darkness; or else, for the sake of the sacrificer who offers the oblation (*havis*). Furthermore, you are one who instructs—that is, one who specifically teaches and perfects—the sacrifice (*yajña*). The genitive case is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyaya* (Pāṇini 2.3.69). Likewise, you are the spreader, the one who extends the fruit in every direction. || 18 ||
O Agni, you are Aditi, O God, for the donor; you, as Hotrā Bhāratī, grow strong through our song.
You are Iḷā, the giver of a hundred winters, for skillful action; you, O Lord of Wealth, are Vṛtra-slayer Sarasvatī.

O Agni, you are Aditi, O God, for the one who offers oblations; you, as Hotrā Bhāratī, grow strong through our song of praise. You are Iḷā, providing a hundred winters for skillful action; you, O Lord of Wealth, are Sarasvatī, the slayer of Vṛtra. 11.
O Agni, you are Aditi— the unimpeded protector— for the donor, the sacrificer who has offered the oblation;
or rather,
you are the undepressed earth.

Furthermore, as *hotrā*, the performer of the oblation, you are *bhāratī*—belonging to *bharata*, the Āditya—and existing in the form of his rays; thus, through *girā*, praise, you grow and become magnified.
Moreover, you are *śatahimā*;
the word *hima* here indicates time.
You are the eternal Iḷā, the earth of immeasurable duration;
being such, you are capable of bestowing gifts.
Because it is the subsequent [element], there is no loss of accent (anighāta).

Likewise, O Lord of Wealth (*vasupati*), protector of riches, slayer of Vṛtra—that is, destroyer of the body of evil—you are Sarasvatī, the one who possesses movement, namely Vāyu. You are that which is connected to them, the controller thereof, the goddess of the middle region (*mādhyamikā*).
The meaning is that you alone are those three goddesses known as Bhāratī, Īlā, and Sarasvatī, who are connected to Āditya, Agni, and Vāyu respectively.
O Agni, you are well-maintained, the highest vital power; you are splendor in the form of a beautiful appearance, visible to the eye.
You are the victorious strength that carries us forward, the lofty one; you are abundant wealth, wide-reaching on every side.

O Agni, you are well-sustained, the highest vital power; you are the protector in the assembly, the mark of splendor. You are the great, far-reaching prize of victory; you are abundant wealth, wide on every side. 12.
O Agni, you, being well-sustained and well-nourished, are that which possesses supreme, unsurpassed *vayas*—meaning food or vital energy—and you are the one who brings it about; this is the sense.

Likewise, in your desirable color, characterized by red, white, and so forth, which is beautiful to behold, the glories (*śriyaḥ*)—meaning sovereign powers or splendors—abide, having taken their resort therein.
Because of the hearing of a prefix, there is the ellipsis of a verb expressing connection.
Furthermore, you are *vāja*, which means food; because you are the means of accomplishing that, you are *śraddha*.
The meaning is: "the accomplisher of food."
One who carries across, a deliverer from evil.
Therefore, you are *bṛhan*, great;
likewise, you are *rayi*, consisting of wealth.
You are *bahula*, endowed with abundance in all respects, and *viśvataḥ pṛthuḥ*, vast and renowned in every direction—this is the meaning.

1. *ta* refers to wood and so forth; *tha* refers to desire and so forth. 2. *ma* means one who instructs or purifies; *ṇa* and *na* mean one who casts away or accomplishes; *va* means one who diminishes or accomplishes. 3.
*ka* and *ma* are related to the sun (*āditya*).
4. *kha* and *ma* mean incapable.
5. From the falling of the *tathana* (the sacrificial grass).

6. *Jha*: from all sides, from everywhere. O Agni, the Ādityas have made you their mouth; O Sage, the pure ones have made you their tongue. Those who seek delight have followed you at the sacrifices; in you, the gods eat the offered oblation. 13. tsām | agne | ādityasaḥ | āsyam | tvām | jihvām | śucayaḥ | cakrire | kave | tsām | rati'sācaḥ | adhvareṣu | saścire | tve iti | devāḥ | haviḥ | adanti | ā'hutam ||13||
"O Agni, the Ādityas—the sons of Aditi, Indra and the others—have made you their own mouth," meaning their instrument for eating, drinking, and so forth; this is the connection with what follows.
Likewise, "O Kavi (wise one) of far-reaching intellect, the pure, bright, or radiant gods have made you their tongue," meaning your own tongue as their instrument for tasting.
The sense is that they eat through your very mouth and taste through your very tongue.
Likewise: "Thee alone as the lord of delight. Delight is giving; the wealth given consists of oblations and the like.
(Ṛgveda, Aṣṭaka 2, Adhyāya 5, Varga 20).
O Agni, you unite with those well-known gods through your majman— your power—
and you remain joined with them; likewise,
you are also present for me.

You are distinct from each of them, or rather, you are their representative; the meaning is that at the time of each individual reception, you are both united with them and yet separate from them. O *sujāta*, one of auspicious birth!
Because the fire is produced by churning accompanied by mantras, it possesses a noble birth (*sujanmatva*).
O such Fire, O God, you are *pra-ricyase*—you are preeminent;
you become superior through their power.
He states the reason for the abundance:
*yat* because, *atra* in this sacrifice, *pṛkṣaḥ* all food; the plural number is used by way of emphasis (*vyatyayena*).
Right there, it becomes threefold; it becomes capable through its greatness (*mahiman*), that is, by virtue of its majesty.
Since such greatness exists, for that reason—this is the meaning. Where? That is stated as follows:
"Following both Rodasī," that is, both Heaven and Earth, whose inherent nature is to cause all things to resound;
"toward them," meaning it is pervaded within the space between those two.
The meaning is that the oblation, offered with the cry of *svadhā*, has pervaded the three worlds by its own greatness.

Those wise ones (*sūrayaḥ*) who bestow upon the singers a gift consisting of cattle, villages, horses, and beautiful ornaments—lead both us and them toward greater prosperity. May we, possessing heroic sons, sing aloud at the assembly (*vidatha*).
O Agni, those wise patrons who bestow upon the singers a gift with cattle as its foremost part and horses as its ornament— lead both them and us toward greater prosperity and high exaltation.
May we speak at the assembly,
possessing excellent heroes.
By means of this [verse], the Hotṛ, under the guise of praise and citation, invokes a blessing:

"O Agni! May the *sūrayaḥ*—the wise ones or the instigators, namely the sacrificers—[grant] to the *stotṛbhyaḥ*, the singers of praise, [a gift] having cows as its foremost part (*goagrām*), meaning that which has cows as its leaders, and having horses as its ornament (*aśvapeśasam*). *Peśaḥ* is a name for form."
It is to be determined by means of the horse.
This pair [of cow and horse] is intended to indicate preeminence,
because among the enumerations of sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), the cow and the horse occupy the first place— as in "the cow, the horse, and the goats."
They bestow—that is, they grant—such a gift.
You indeed lead—that is, you lead forth with excellence—to a better, more excellent, and most sublime state such as heaven, both those sacrificers and us, the officiating priests;
this is the meaning.
The particle *hi* signifies well-known fact.
And we, being *suvīrāḥ*—possessing excellent sons and so forth—shall *vadema*, that is, utter or praise, the *bṛhat* great collection of mantras at the *vidathe*, the sacrifice. This is the meaning.
The second hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "yajñena rādha," is the *ārṣa* (seer's composition) of Samada, the son of Maṇḍūka.
According to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "the hymns beginning the *maṇḍalas* are dedicated to Agni," this hymn belongs to Agni.
Because it contains the imitation of the word "nu," this hymn is also composed in the *jagatī* meter.
"yajñena sasanā" is the heading [of the hymn].
Its application is in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra* when the meter is the *jagatī*.
However, the ritual rule (*sūtra*) has already been stated in the preceding hymn.

Likewise, this Jātavedasya Nivid is to be used at the third pressing in the twenty-four-day rite (*cāturviṃśika*), because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "With the words ‘yajñena vardhata’ and ‘āprīmāratam’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4). Furthermore, this Jātavedasya Nivid is also used on the second day of both the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* six-day periods.
"The third pressing consists of twenty-four [verses]," thus he prescribed the *caturviṃśa* and the other [stomas].
1. *ma-stutiṃ nigamam atha*;
2. *ma-pra ṇeṣi hi*; *kha-ga 1-na-va-pra hi ṇeṣi*; *na-pra ṇiha ṣi*; *ka-praṇeṣi*.
3. *ṇa-na-ma* are the *anividāna*. 4. *kha-ga* are the *anividānīya*.
"Increase through sacrifice; worship Agni Jātavedas with oblation and with continuous song."
To him who is kindled, well-provided with sacrificial food, the bearer of light, the celestial Hotṛ-priest, bold in the assemblies.

Grow by means of sacrifice; worship Agni Jātavedas with oblation and with continuous song—him who is kindled, well-nourished, the bringer of light, celestial, the invoker, and bold among the people. 1.

O you who are either the sacrificers or the officiating priests, do you increase—cause to grow—the Agni known as Jātavedas, the knower of all that is born, or the possessor of innate wealth and innate wisdom, by means of the sacrifice (yāga).
Having stated this in general terms, he speaks specifically:
"Worship him with oblation (havis), such as cooked rice (caru) and sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), and with extensive speech (tanā girā), that is, with praise; honor him."
Of what nature is he?
"Kindled" (samidhānam), meaning being ignited; "well-provided with food" (suprayasam), meaning possessing excellent nourishment.
"Belonging to one for whom the sacrificers are to be led to *svarbharasvarga* (the heaven that supports the sun); or rather, *svar* is a synonym for all [heavenly realms].
The leaders of praises are the chanters (*stotṛ*)."
The meaning is "one who has many praises. "Dyukṣam" means radiant or dwelling in heaven. "Hotāram" means the performer of the oblation.
"In the settlements and in the armies" means "the invincible one, the maker of strength.
It is well known that when there is intensity of fire, bodily strength arises.
The nights and the dawns have lowed toward you, like milch-cows in their stalls toward their calves;
O possessor of many boons, from heaven alone your radiance shines throughout the human generations and the continuous succession of nights.

Toward you, O Agni, the nights and the dawns have lowed, as milch-cows toward their calf in the stalls. Like the messenger of heaven, you shine through the human generations, O possessor of many boons, throughout the continuous nights.
"O Agni, [he] anoints you— the nights (*nakta*) and the dawns (*uṣas*), that is, the days—
at every night and at every day; or rather,
the word *nakta* indicates the evening time, because the Agnihotra exists both in the evening and in the morning."
At all times, or specifically at the times of evening and morning, the sacrificers desire—that is, they long—to perform the sacrifice.
Alternatively, it may mean that the days and nights themselves desire you alone as the Hotṛ;
for since the performance of the ritual is enjoined at specific times, the "desiring" of those times is used figuratively.

In this regard, there is an illustration: "Like milch-cows (*dhenavaḥ*) [going] to their calves (*vatsam na*)— that is, like cows going to their calves in the stalls (*goṣṭheṣu*), which are places of easy passage, or as they naturally move about in the pastures (*svasareṣu*)"—

so too, O Agni, possessor of many boons (*puruvāra*), you who are self-restrained (*saṃyataḥ*) and disciplined, are the pervasive master (*aratiḥ*) of heaven itself, spread far and wide like the celestial realm.
The meaning is that he is pervaded everywhere for the very purpose of bestowing oblations upon the gods residing there.
"Mānuṣā yugā" means the ages (yugas) belonging to humans (mānuṣa), that is, to the sacrificers;
the word *yuga* is indicative of time.
The morning and other pressings;
in all the pressings.
The second case ending is used to express continuous connection.
*Kṣapaḥ* means nights;
"O Agni, you shine everywhere (*āmāsi*) throughout all the nights."

1. *ma*—it did not increase; 2. *tha*—they held him firm; 3. *ma*—for the strength of the body is indeed established; 4. *ka-ja-ṇa-ma*—in all [these cases]; 5. *va*—in the words *mukha*, *śaraṇa*, and *adhikaraṇa*; 6. *ka-ṇa-na-ma*—among humans. Ka. 2: The gods have placed him upon the earth, the one of wondrous deeds, between heaven and earth; like a chariot to be known, Agni of bright luster, who is to be praised among the people like Mitra.

The gods have established him—the one of wondrous deeds, the messenger between heaven and earth—in the wise one, in the realm of the mid-air. Like a chariot, they have set down Agni, who is to be known, whose radiance is bright, and who, like Mitra, is to be praised among the people. 3.

“The gods—the well-known deities, or in common usage, the officiating priests—impel that Agni, who is established and distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, into the *budh* (foundation) of *rajas*—that is, the world consisting of passion; the meaning is: upon the earth, specifically upon the sacrificial altar (*vedi*).
There they impel him intensely.”

They exert themselves to obtain their respective sacrificial offerings. In the case of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), they go toward or intensely devote themselves to Him by means of hymns and so forth.
To the question "In what manner?", he says:

‘Sudaṃsasam’ means of beautiful appearance; ‘divaṃ pṛthivyoḥ’ means of heaven and earth; ‘aratim’ means the lord, the one who goes, or the pervader; ‘vedyam’ means that which is to be known, or the wealth consisting of knowledge;
‘tasmai hitam’ means beneficial for that.
"Like a chariot":
just as people resort to a chariot for the sake of attaining their desired goal, so it is here;
or rather, the object of knowledge (vedya) should be understood as being like a chariot in that it serves as the means for attainment.
"Agni, who possesses bright luster and radiant color, like a 'friend' (*mitra*) who accomplishes one's purpose,
or rather like the Sun;
he who is 'to be praised' (*praśastya*) with excellence 'among the dwellings' (*kṣitiṣu*), that is, upon the sacrificial grounds or among human beings."
Thus they prepared the fire of such great power.
They have placed him, being sprinkled in his own home within the mid-air, like the moon of brilliant luster at the gateway— him who is the winged lord of the earth,
the observer with his showers, like a protector of the path, extending over both races of beings.

Him, growing in his own space, resplendent like the moon, they have placed within his own house at the gateway—the Lord of the Earth, who observes with his eyes, following both races as one protects his path.

‘They have placed, or they place, him who is more worthy of praise—him who, in the *rajas* (the intermediate space), sprinkles rain-water from all sides, or who is being poured with clarified butter and other offerings upon the *vedi* (altar) on the earth;
him whom they have established in his own door, in the solitary house, the sacrificial hall.
Of what nature is he?’
"Like the moon, exceedingly radiant.
"Moon" is a name for gold;
[it means] like gold, possessing beautiful luster.
Later, in the state of full growth, [he is] "pṛṇyaḥ," the one who goes further than the sky and the intermediate space;
"akṣabhiḥ," with his own members consisting of flames; "citayantam," making himself known; like "pātho na pāyum," a protector of the path.
Like water, it is a protector.
"I have pervaded both the Heaven and Earth, the two non-born mothers of all.
The sense is that, by abiding upon the earth as the support for the oblation, it has ascended toward the heavenly world in order to deliver the sacrificial offering.
They establish the sacred fire in such a manner.
1. Like a friend who is not a friend; like a friend who is not a friend. 2. Being consecrated. 3. In the forest.

He is the Hotṛ; may he encompass the entire sacrifice. Men honor him with oblations and with song. With golden jaws, flickering among the growing plants, like the sky with its stars, he illuminates the two worlds. He is the Hotṛ; may he encompass the entire sacrifice. Men honor him with oblations and with song. With golden jaws, flickering among the growing plants, like the sky with its stars, he illuminates the two worlds. 5.
May that Agni, acting as the *hotṛ*—the performer of the oblation—be present throughout the entire *adhvara*, the sacrifice.
Men honor that very Agni with offerings (*havyaiḥ*) and with song (*girā*);
the root *ṛñj* here signifies the act of propitiating or honoring.

*Hiriśipraḥ*: one whose helmet is golden, or whose jaw is of a seizing nature; for another mantra states, “The golden *śiprās* are spread over his heads” (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 5.54.11). *Jarbhurat*: he who blazes amidst the growing plants or the increasing flames.
Being invited, he shall go to the sacrifice;
this is a word ending in a śatṛ suffix. Or rather, the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
The growing herbs flicker repeatedly, burning with their flames.
Like the stars across the sky and the intermediate space, they make the two worlds, heaven and earth, conscious.
The meaning is that it pervades the world and the intermediate space with flames and sparks.

Being kindled for our well-being, O wealthy one, bestowing riches upon us, shine forth! Bring hither to us the two worlds, O Agni, for our prosperity; O divine one, accept the oblations of man for the feast. He, being kindled for our well-being, bestowing wealth, shine forth among us! Bring hither to us the two worlds for our prosperity; O divine Agni, accept the oblations of man for the feast.
O Agni, such as you are, be for our well-being—
*svasti* being a name for non-destruction— and for our security (*kṣema*).

O wealthy one, bestowing upon us abundant wealth—whether it be riches or the kind of wealth that increases ever higher—granting it fully and being well-kindled by us, shine forth! Or rather, "revat" may be an adverbial modifier:
shine so as to provide wealth, or shine in such a manner.
Being thus disposed, make both *rodasī*—heaven and earth—conducive for us, for our well-being, and for beautiful fruit;
that is, make both worlds bestowers of enjoyment.
For what purpose? That is now stated:
O divine Agni, [convey] the oblations (*havyā*) belonging to me, the human sacrificer, for the sake of enjoyment (*vītaye*) by the gods— that is to say,
for the purpose of performing the repeated sacrifices and so forth.

Give us, O Agni, great gifts; give us thousands. Like doors, open up strength for us to hear [the call]; prosper us. Make heaven and earth favorable through our sacred prayer (*brahman*). Like the bright sun, may the Dawns flash forth their light. Give us, O Agni, great gifts; give us thousands. Like doors, open up strength for us to hear [the call]; prosper us. Make heaven and earth favorable through our sacred prayer (*brahman*). Like the bright sun, may the Dawns flash forth their light.
1. Let it be—let it pervade.
O Agni, grant us great and abundant wealth consisting of cattle, horses, and other such specific riches;
likewise, grant us those numbered in the thousands, such as sons, servants, and so forth.
This is a form of the root *dadāti* in the Vedic *luṅ* tense;
due to the division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).
For the sake of hearing, for the sake of scattering, [grant] *vāja*—that is, food—as if it were the doors; that is, even the door-panels of that [house].
[The word] *na* has the sense of "also.
Open them; that is, unbar them.
The meaning is "impel.
Alternatively, it is like doors;
he clarifies the means for attaining that [state].
For that purpose, make Heaven and Earth favorable to us through the exalted *brahman*— that is, through ritual action (*karman*)— and direct them toward us;
do this like the Sun (*svar*),
for just as he illuminates the world, so should you.
The dawns, appearing at the time of daybreak, illuminate you, the bright and radiant one, as they shine forth in every direction;
for indeed, at the time of dawn, the fires are kindled.

Being kindled in succession after the lovely nights of dawn, may he shine like the sun with his ruddy luster. Through the invocations of Manu, Agni—performer of the fair sacrifice, king of the people, and the welcome guest—shines for the sake of the living man. 8. Being kindled; after the lovely nights of dawn; like the sun; may he shine; with his ruddy luster; through the invocations; Agni; of Manu; performer of the fair sacrifice; king; of the people; the guest; welcome; for the sake of the living man. 8.
That Agni, being kindled and ignited in accordance with the *uṣas* (dawns)—which are the cause of delight—shines like the sun (*sūrya*) with his ruddy, radiant, and glowing luster.
That Agni [is honored] by the *hotrās* (invocations) of the human *hotṛ* priest;
"hotrā" is a name for speech.

Being praised with hymns that serve as the means for the *homa* sacrifice, he—being of beautiful sacrifice (*svadhvara*), the shining king and lord of the people (*viśām rājā*)—becomes a guest (*atithi*) who is worthy of worship like a guest, moving gracefully (*cāru*) for the sake of the mortal sacrificer (*āyu*).

Thus, O Agni, our ancient prayer has swelled among the immortals who dwell in the high heavens, like a human cow yielding milk for the singer within the sacred enclosures—by her own power, a hundredfold, manifold, and nourishing. Thus, O Agni, our ancient prayer has swelled among the immortals who dwell in the high heavens, like a human cow yielding milk for the singer within the sacred enclosures—by her own power, a hundredfold, manifold, and nourishing.

O Agni, you who exist from of old (*pūrvya*), among the *amṛta* gods of vast splendor (*bṛhadiveṣu*), our human thought (*dhīḥ*)—whether it be our intellect, praise, or ritual action—satisfies (*pīpāya*) you in this very way.
Or rather, may our human thought satisfy you among men;
likewise, may your own thought, milking like a cow, yield for the singer (*kārave*) in the sacrificial assemblies (*vṛjaneṣu*).
Like a milch-cow that yields milk— this is an elided simile (luptopamā)—

she herself, by her own self, when there is a desire for wealth, yields a hundredfold— that is, an immeasurable number— and a manifold form, a collection of riches consisting of various forms such as cattle, horses, and so forth.

1. By means of the meanings of the words *kha*, *ja*, *va*, and *na*, the particles beginning with *pra* (prādayaḥ) function according to their specific senses. 2. [The word] *jha-jha-ma* refers to us humans (*asmān*).
O Agni, through our horse we seek great heroic power, or through our sacred prayer (*brahman*) we would distinguish ourselves above all people.
May our pair of horses shine forth, invincible, over the five tribes like the sun.

O Agni, through our horse or through our sacred prayer (*brahman*), may we surpass all people in heroic power. May our pair of horses shine high above the tribes like the sun, difficult to overcome. 10.
O Agni, may we, the sacrificers, through the horse— meaning either by means of a horse skilled in running,
or by the word *vā* (or) implying "or"—
and by the *brahman*, that is, by the fire maintained by you, surpass and distinguish ourselves above the people who do not favor us.
The agentive suffix is used here in the sense of the object.
Alternatively: by means of the horse given by you, may we manifest—that is, make known—our great heroic power (*suvīrya*).

For that purpose, may our "fivefold" wealth—referring to the five classes of people among the four *varṇas* with the *Niṣādas* as the fifth—shine forth intensely (*uccā*) and abundantly; may that invincible, paired wealth, unsurpassed by others, shine like the sun (*svarṇa*), blazing exceedingly.
Or perhaps this [hymn] is useless;
may that one be our praiseworthy awakening, O Victorious One, in whom the well-born are impelled like the sun— O Agni,
toward whom the prize-winners go for the sacrifice, you who shine brightly in your own dwelling among your eternal offspring.

Be thou for us, O Victorious One, worthy of praise—thou in whom the nobly born shine like the sun, unto whose sacrifice the prize-winners approach, O Agni, while thou art shining brightly in thine own home among our constant offspring.

O Agni, O vanquisher of enemies, O you who are born of power, you who are worthy of praise—be mindful of our hymns and the like; "be" (*bodhi*) means "awaken" (*budhyasva*). To the question "Of which [Agni]? he says:
"In whom"—in that Agni—"the well-born," those of noble birth, the singers, the praisers, and the officiating priests "send forth," that is, they offer their hymns.

Furthermore, O Agni, [protect] this sacrifice, which is worthy of worship, for those sacrificers who possess the *vājina*— that is, the food characterized by oblations— when their own biological son (*aurasa-putra*) has become the cause;
or rather, [protect it] so that it may shine forth in him.

Just as a father shines in his son’s house, so too [the god] "shining" (adīdivāṃsam)—that is, blazing—in "his own" (sve), meaning in his own sacrificial hall at the place of the Savanīya and other offerings, they "approach" (upayanti) him with oblations, hymns, and so forth.
"May he be aware" (sa bodhi) is the syntactical connection.
O Jātavedas, O Agni, may we both—the singers of praise and the Sun—abide in your protection.
Grant us wealth that is excellent, most radiant, abundant, rich in progeny, and blessed with noble offspring.

O Jātavedas, may we both—thou and thy praisers—be under thy protection, O Agni, as is Sūrya. Grant us wealth, riches that are most brilliant, abundant, accompanied by progeny, and blessed with good offspring. 12.

O *jātavedas*, knower of all that is born, O Agni, may both— the officiating priests who praise you and the wise sacrificers who are like the sun— both of us, being under the protection of your shelter (*śarman*) as a means to happiness,
become yours; or rather, may we abide in your protection.

And you, for the sake of our dwelling (*avasvaḥ*), grant us—bestow upon us—such wealth: distinguished riches such as cattle and other property; that which is most delightful to many people (*puruṣandrasya*); abundant (*bhūyasaḥ*) and accompanied by much gold; possessed of progeny (*prajāvataḥ*), provided with servants and the like, or sufficient for the enjoyment of sons and others; and consisting of excellent offspring (*svapatyasya*). Grant this kind of wealth to us!
You are able to give.

The wise ones who bestow upon their praisers a gift consisting of cattle, gold, horses, and beautiful ornaments—lead both us and them toward wealth; may we, possessing brave sons, sing aloud at the distribution of booty.

O Agni, those wise patrons who bestow upon the singers a gift preeminent in cattle, adorned with gold ornaments—lead both us and them forward to great wealth! May we, blessed with heroic sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 13.
The thirteen [verses] beginning with “ye stotṛbhyaḥ” have been explained.

The third hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "samiddho agniḥ," is by Gṛtsamada and is addressed to Agni Narāśaṃsa—the fire so named because he is to be praised (śaṃsaniya) by men (naraiḥ), that is, by the officiating priests (ṛtvigbhiḥ). Being possessed of beautiful flames (svarciḥ), he goes toward each of his own abodes (dhāmāni)—the places that are the receptacles for oblations and the manifestations of his splendor—making them manifest through his own greatness. He goes toward each of the three shining heavens (tisro divaḥ) and the worlds, such as the earth.
The intention is that he sustains the earth, illuminates the intermediate space, and reaches the heaven by means of the sacrificial offerings.
Alternatively, since each of the worlds possesses a triad, the expression "three heavens" is not contradictory;

this is supported by Vedic mantras such as "Three are the heavens, three the earths" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.54.5) and by Brāhmaṇa texts such as "These three worlds are indeed threefold" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 2.17).

Thus, O Ghee, at the head—the summit—of the sacrifice, while being poured out at the time of the oblation, may you, sprinkling the offering with a focused mind, moistening it and making it radiant, manifest the gods perfectly and completely for the sake of the sacrifice.
The meaning is "may he satisfy.
Being praised by us with the mind, O Agni, sacrifice today for us before the human [sacrificer], as did Indra of old.
Bring hither the unshakable host of the Maruts; O men, worship Indra who sits upon the sacrificial grass.

3 | Praised, O Agni, with a mind free from malice, sacrifice for us today to the gods before those of men; bring hither the unshakable host of the Maruts. O men, worship Indra who sits upon the sacred grass. ||3||

O Agni, you who have been firmly established by us, being pressed out with a mind devoted to us—or rather, with the intention of sacrificing to the gods—having become fit for sacrifice, you, the ancient Hotṛ among men, shall sacrifice to the gods on our behalf this very day; indeed, you yourself perform the sacrifice.
As such a sacrificer, do you summon them. Whom? (The gods.)
The host of the Maruts;
the unshakable and imperturbable Indra, who is inseparable from them—
or rather, Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
Immediately thereafter, O men: leaders and officiating priests, worship—that is, honor—that Indra who sits upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
O divine sacrificial grass, you who are increasing, rich in heroes, well-spread, and bringing great wealth upon this altar;
sit here, O Vasus, anointed with clarified butter, all you gods, Ādityas, worthy of sacrifice!

O Vasus, O Viśve Devas, O Ādityas worthy of sacrifice, sit upon this divine, spreading, increasing, and heroic sacred grass, strewn upon the altar for the sake of wealth, well-supported and anointed with ghee. ||4||

O God, you who possess this [sacrifice], increase it—making it rich in heroes (producing excellent warriors), well-sustained, well-filled, and extensive, being strewn by our officiating priests—for the sake of wealth.
For what purpose?
For the sake of riches.
In the phrase *vasyāṃ vedī vedya*,
there is the designation *pragṛhya* for the locative sense.
In the *saṃhitā*, the substitution of *yaṇ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Sit upon this sacrificial grass (barhis), which is made smooth by ghee and clarified butter. Who?
O Vasus, those who bear that name.
O all you gods!
O Ādityas!
O you who are worthy of sacrifice—sit down upon this sacrificial grass (*barhis*); the meaning is: "sit down upon this *barhis*."

1. *na-ma-ntribhiḥ*. 2. Having stood at *kha-jha-ṇa-na-vā*. May the divine Doors, being invoked, open themselves wide; may they, easy of access, be approached with salutations. Expansive and undecaying, may they spread themselves out, purifying their glorious and heroic luster. May they open themselves wide; being invoked, the divine Doors, easy of access, [be approached] with salutations. Expansive, may they spread themselves out; undecaying, purifying their glorious and heroic luster. 5.
The goddesses of the doors are the deities presiding over the doors; let them open wide, that is, let them be separated and remain with their covers removed. Of what nature are they?
"Urviyā" means "urvyo," that is, "mahatyaḥ" (the great ones). "Namobhiḥ" means with hymns accompanied by prostrations.
Being praised; "suprāyaṇāḥ" means they are to be traversed very well and with great excellence;
"īḍyāḥ" means the gods are to be invoked; "viśrayantām" means let them spread out.

Furthermore, may the goddesses—who are expansive (*vyacasvatīḥ*), meaning possessing pervasiveness; who are undecaying (*ajūryāḥ*), meaning unassailable or unborn; and who purify and bring about for the sacrificer a fair complexion (*varṇaṃ*), meaning a praiseworthy and excellent form endowed with noble sons and the like, as well as glory (*yaśasaṃ*)—spread themselves wide and become especially renowned.

May the two well-performing ones, Dawn and Night, who have grown great for us from of old, like two weaving women, rejoicing as they weave the extended thread—the two who, moving together, are the beautiful forms of the sacrifice, yielding milk and rich in nourishment. sādhu | apāṃsi | sanatā | naḥ | ukṣite | upāsānaktā | vyayā-iva | raṇvite | tantum | tatam | saṃvayantī | samīcī | yajñasya | peśaḥ | sudughe | payasvatī || 6 ||
"Excellent, excellent are our deeds, our actions, which have been nourished and honored by this eternal (*sanātana*) hymn and so forth, characterized by an uninterrupted flow of activity.
Alternatively,
there exists a word *sana* ending in a case-suffix that signifies "ancient."
The first dual ending of that [word] is *-au*, which becomes *-ā* [by sandhi].
The meaning is "in the eternal" (*sanātane*) or "in the permanent" (*nitye*). According to this interpretation, [the two forms] are the sprinklers (*ukṣite*) of the fruit.
The past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) has an active sense when used with a transitive verb.

Upāsānaktā—the two deities of day and night—are like two weavers skilled in weaving, delightful (raṇvitā) as they are resonant with sound, or moving toward one another. Weaving together the extended, widespread thread—which stands in the place of the sacrificial thread—that is, the sacrifice; or weaving it forth in a wonderful way, they are the two originators. Moving together (samīcī), properly engaged and mutually favorable, for what purpose do they weave?
The ellipsis is: "in order to fashion the form (peśas) of the sacrifice being performed."
The meaning is that one should cause [the sacrificer] to perform the sacrifice by following the sequence of its constituent parts;
for sacrifices are extended by means of day and night. "Sudughe" means those two who well milk forth fruit; "paryasvatī" means those two who possess water.
Indeed, rain arises from day and night;
thus, the meaning is: "O deities of day and night, being of great power, may you carry out our sacrifice."

The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first, the most wise, shall sacrifice with straightness; more beautiful in their splendor, they worship the gods according to the seasons, anointing [the sacrifice] at the navel of the earth upon the three ridges. (7) The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first, the most wise, shall sacrifice with straightness; more beautiful in their splendor, they worship the gods according to the seasons, anointing [the sacrifice] at the navel of the earth upon the three ridges. (7)
1. [The syllables] *ka*, *kṣata*, *na*, *ma*, and *tadavayavān* in sequence;
*ma*, *a*, *1*, *sū*, *3*; the second Aṣṭaka, 17; *daivyā*.
The divine fire is that which exists in heaven.

From that heavenly fire were born the two Hotṛs, the invokers of the gods, or rather the two fires who accomplish the oblation—the terrestrial and the atmospheric. They are the first to be worshipped, the most wise, the most beautiful, the two gods who, by means of the Ṛc, the sacred verse, worship and honor [the deities] properly, straightly, and without deficiency.

Sacrificing to the gods at the proper seasons, at those respective times and places, the two gods [the sacrificers] anointed [the sacrificial butter] upon the navel of the earth—that is, on the *uttaravedi*—and over the three elevated regions, such as the *gārhapatya* hearth and others, in a uniform manner.
The augment *ḍa* is applied after the root *añj*.

May Sarasvatī, who perfects our inspired thought, and the goddess Iḷā, and Bhāratī, who prevails over all— may these three goddesses, by their own inherent power, sit upon this sacred grass and protect us with a flawless refuge.

Sarasvatī, who perfects our prayer; the goddess Iḷā; and Bhāratī, the all-surpassing—may these three goddesses, by their own inherent power, sit upon this sacred grass and protect us with an unbroken shelter. 8.

May Sarasvatī— the goddess by this name— who perfects (*sādhayantī*) our thought (*dhiyam*) or our sacrifice (*yāgam*), and likewise the goddess Ilā and Bhāratī, who is "all-conquering" (*viśvatūrtiḥ*)— that is, whose power extends to all objects of sense— may these three goddesses protect (*pāntu*) this sacrificial grass (*barhiḥ*) and the sacrifice itself so that it remains unimpaired (*acchidram*), by means of *svadhā*, that is, through our oblation.
Having done what?
Having approached—that is, having resorted to—the sacrificial hall as a refuge;
or alternatively:
By means of their own inherent power, may they sit upon this sacred grass at this sacrifice; having entered our refuge, the home, may they protect it so that it remains free from flaw.
Now, the ninth verse, "piśaṅgarūpaḥ," is the *yājyā* for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ.
This is because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "piśaṅgarūpaḥ subharo vayodhāḥ prathamabhājaṃ yaśasaṃ vayodhām" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
The text is as follows:
Tawny-hued, easy to support, bestowing vital strength, the hero is born through obedience, one who loves the gods.
May Tvaṣṭṛ release the navel for us—the offspring—and then let the goal of the gods be attained.

Of tawny form, easy to support, bestowing vital strength, the hero is born with prompt obedience, longing for the gods. May Tvaṣṭṛ release the bond for us; may the purpose of the gods reach its goal. 9.

One who is tawny-hued (*piśaṅgarūpaḥ*), gold-colored (*suvarṇavarṇaḥ*), or multiform (*nānārūpaḥ*); one who is easily maintained (*subharaḥ*), a performer of beautiful sacrifices (*śobhanayajñaḥ*), or one who possesses beautiful ornaments (*śobhanabharaṇaḥ*); a bestower or supporter of food (*vayodhāḥ*); swift in his qualities (*śruṣṭī*); a hero (*vīraḥ*) who impels in various ways; one who desires the gods (*devakāmaḥ*)—such a son (*putraḥ*) is born or may be born through the grace of Tvaṣṭṛ.

And may that Tvaṣṭṛ, the deity of this name, release (*vi syatu*) for us (*asme*) the "navel" (*nābhi*), meaning the progeny (*prajā*) consisting of sons and so forth, which binds the lineage; that is to say, may he grant it to us.
Moreover, let the food (pāthaḥ) belonging to the gods also come to us; that is, let it go to us. The particle *api* is connected with the verb; the meaning is "let it go."

1. According to manuscripts M, V, and P, [the words] *yaṣṭavyau* (should be sacrificed) are to be read first. 2. According to manuscripts K, Jha, Jha-1, Ma, and Y, the word *yajantī* means "worshipping. 3. According to manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ṇa, Dha, Na, Va, Sarasvatī is the name of this goddess, as is Bhāratī. 4. In manuscript Ta, the ninth reading is as follows. 5. In manuscripts Jha-1, Ṇa, Ta, Tha, Na, and Va, it is *tādṛśaḥ* (such); in manuscript Ka, it is *īdṛśaḥ* (like this). 2–3. [The verse reads: "May the Lord of the Forest, bestowing [gifts], stand near; may he prepare the oblation with his insights. May the divine immolator lead the threefold-anointed offering to the gods for the delight of the people."

The Lord of the Forest has released [the victim]; let Agni stand nearby and prepare the oblation. May the divine immolator, knowing well, lead the offering—thrice-anointed—to the gods with prayers. ||10||
May Vanaspati—the sacrificial post, which is also a fire bearing this name—standing near us, grant permission for our rite and remain present by our side.
And may Agni, the fire that serves as the support for cooking, thoroughly prepare the oblation in the form of the animal through various ritual acts and specific means of cooking;
that is to say, he cooks the oblation so that it is free from undercooked or overcooked portions.
Furthermore, *daivyaḥ* refers to Agni, who is connected to the gods (*deva-sambandhin*) and serves as the locus for the oblation; he is the *śamitā*, the preparer of the sacrificial offering.
Alternatively, *daivyaḥ śamitā* may refer to that specific fire known by the name Śamitṛ.
"It is heard in scripture: 'Agni indeed is the immolator among the gods. (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 2.1.4).
O sacrificers, for your sake, I invoke Agni.
Of what sort is he? He who is of noble birth (*sudyonmānam*), who shines brightly (*sudyotamānam*), who is well-praised (*suvṛktim*) or well-adorned with freedom from sins,
who is the guest (*atithim*) of the people (*viśām*)— that is, always worthy of worship like a guest— and who possesses excellent sacrificial food characterized by beautiful oblations (*suprayasam*).
Furthermore, Jātavedas—the knower of all that is born—is the divine Agni who, like Mitra or like a friend, or like Āditya, becomes one who is to be cherished (didhiṣāyyaḥ), that is, one who sustains.
Where? It is said: among the *jana* (people), from humans up to the gods—that is, among those ranging from men to the deities.
The meaning is that he became their preserver.

Worshipping him in the gathering place of the waters, the Bhr̥gus have established him as the two-fold sustainer of the living world. May this Agni, the messenger of the gods with his swift horses, surpass all beings in greatness. *imaṃ vidhanto apāṃ sadhasthe dvidādadhurbhṛgavo viśviāyoḥ | eṣa viśvānyabhyastu bhūmā devānāmagniraratirjīrāśvaḥ || 2 ||* Worshipping him in the gathering place of the waters, the Bhr̥gus have established him as the two-fold sustainer of the living world. May this Agni, the messenger of the gods with his swift horses, surpass all beings in greatness.
This is the form of the root *dadhāti* in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense.
May this Agni, by his abundance, overcome—that is, surpass—all other classes of beings who are hostile to us.
Of what nature is he?
He is the lord (*arati*) of the gods.
Among them, Aruṇaśīla is swift toward our sacrifice;
likewise, Jīrāśva has rapid horses.

The gods established Agni among the human clans as their beloved, like those seeking to dwell [establish] Mitra. He has illumined the longing nights, he the descendant of Dakṣa, who dwells in the house of the donor. Agni: the gods; among the human; clans; the beloved; they established; seeking to dwell; like; Mitra; he; has illumined; the longing; nights; he; the descendant of Dakṣa; who; in the house; of the donor.
The gods (*devāsaḥ*), while ascending toward heaven (*kṣedhyantaḥ*), formerly established (*dhuḥ*) Agni—the beloved one who gratifies the gods (*priyam*)—among the human clans (*mānuṣīṣu viśvi*).
Therein is an illustration:
like those ascending [to establish] a friend (*mitram na*).
Just as men going toward wealth establish a dear friend as a companion for the protection of their own home, so it is here.

That very Agni who was established by the gods for the sake of the sacrificer who has offered the oblation (*dāsvat*), and who has been placed (*āhita*) in his own sacrificial hall (*dame*), he—the capable one (*dākṣavyaḥ*), the supporter or giver—shines forth (*dīdayat*) on all nights (*ūrmyāḥ*), throughout every night, or indeed illuminates them entirely.
Or: he causes all nights to shine.

1. In the two places [denoted by] *ka* and *ma*, there is *tāyaḥ*, which is *tāyamānam*; this is a Vedic form (*chāndasaṃ rūpam*). Alternatively, "twofold" (*dvitā*) means that by way of duality (*dvitvena*), they established the lightning-spirit in the atmosphere, or among the officiating priests for the sake of sacrifice; whereas in the two places of earth (*kṣiti*) and atmosphere (*antarikṣa*), it is *astāyamānam*.
This is a Vedic form (*chāndasa*).

Or rather: "Twofold" (*dvitā*) means by way of duality; they have placed or sustained him in the atmosphere for the sake of sacrifice, or among the officiating priests, by means of the lightning-form.
His own delightful nourishment is his own abundance; for he is the skillful one who, being urged forward, exerts himself.
He who, bearing his tongue among the plants, shakes it like a swift horse that has been urged on, tossing its tail.

His growth is delightful like that of his own [offspring]; his appearance is beautiful when he, the skillful one, is urged forward. He who has spread out his tongue among the plants shakes it like a chariot-horse tossing its tail.
The nourishment (*puṣṭi*) of this Agni is the growth of his body; it is delightful (*raṇvā*), meaning either charming or accompanied by sound.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
it is like one's own nourishment.

Just as in the world one's own nourishment (*puṣṭi*) is delightful (*raṇvā*) to oneself, so it is here; or rather, the nourishment related to this Agni—which pertains to the sacrificer—is delightful for the sake of his own Agni’s nourishment. Furthermore, the very manifestation (*saṃdṛṣṭi*), the appearance of this Agni as he advances, spreads out, and desires to burn—wishing to consume the fuel—is also delightful.
The fire which, among the plants and in the pieces of wood, has spread its tongue— that is, its flame;
"tongue" is used in the singular to denote the class—
spreads its flames here and there, distributing them.
The meaning is that it causes to tremble.
The augment *iṭ* is applied because [the root] *hṛ*, being treated as ending in *luK*, is prescribed [by Pāṇini 7.4.65] for the meanings of verbal roots and so forth;
due to its connection with this [augment], there is no *anighāta* (lack of accentuation).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as a chariot-horse, a racer fit for a chariot, shakes off the flies—that is, the hairs which are the means of warding off stinging insects—so too does this fire shake its flames.
One crosses over the swelling of this very fire.

When the devourers of wood, shouting aloud, brought to me that which was monstrous—like a colorless form to those with keen sight—he shone forth with wondrous splendor; he who had grown old suddenly became young again.

When those who praise me as the wood-eater proclaimed my greatness, he fashioned for himself a color like that of the eager ones. He has shone with brilliant light among the flames; though he was aged, he became young again in an instant.
Whatever greatness (*abhvam*) belongs to him—that is, my own greatness—the *vanadaḥ* are those who bestow or enjoy it;
or alternatively, the *vanadaḥ* are those who roar loudly, namely the praisers (*stotāraḥ*).
The word *ava* expresses the sense of "intense" (*bhṛśa*).
From the root *chad* preceded by that [prefix], there is the suffix *kvip*. By the rule "*avāpyoḥ*", there is the elision of the vowel *a*.
They praise him from all sides, without end.
That Agni, for the *uśij*—for the officiating priests who desire our form—measured out his own corresponding color, that is, his own likeness;
it is not a matter of literal sound-meaning.
And regarding the produced [fire]:

when the offerings of clarified butter and other substances—which are beautiful in their various forms—are the cause, that fire is perceived through its variegated luster, its golden color, and its radiance. Furthermore, that very fire which, having grown old and its flames having subsided, becomes again and again (*muhuḥ*) "joined" (*ā-yuvā*)—that is, a mixer or youthful in appearance—becomes manifest once more through contact with clarified butter and other substances.
1. Or rather, it is like that which belongs to this Agni;

or rather, it is like the delightful [state] pertaining to the sacrificer for the sake of nourishment belonging to this Agni—that delightful [state] for the sake of nourishment belonging to this Agni is like that.

(Variants *kha* and *ga*: Or rather, it is like the delightful [state] pertaining to the sacrificer for the sake of nourishment belonging to this Agni—that delightful [state] for the sake of nourishment belonging to this Agni is like that.)
2. From *kha*, *na*, *jha*, *tha*, and *dakṣuḥ*.
3. *ba* is caused to fall (*nipātitaḥ*).
4. From *ka*, *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, *ca*, and *yataḥ*.

5. [The letters] kha, ga, ca, and ṇa possess sound. 6. Like that (ta): He who, as if thirsting for the woods, shines like water; he has roared like one seeking his goal on a path. With a blackened track, glowing and delightful, he is perceived like the sky when it is remembered through the clouds. 6. He who, as if thirsting for the woods, shines like water; he has roared like one seeking his goal on a path. With a blackened track, glowing and delightful, he is perceived like the sky when it is remembered through the clouds.

The fire which, like one parched with thirst (*tatṛṣāṇaḥ*), as if thirsty, *ā bhāti*— that is, it shines forth or illuminates— the various forests (*vanā vanāni*), meaning the multitudes of trees; this is the sense of "resounding" (*svaramāṇa*).
The meaning is "it burns.
Alternatively, it shines in every forest (*vana-vane*).
Furthermore, like water (*vāṇam*) [flowing] along a downward path (*pathā*), it moves here and there in that same manner.
Like a horse that draws a chariot, he *svānīt*, i.e., makes a sound;
or rather, there is a substitution of *sau* for the word *ratha*.
Just as a chariot moving along the path of battle rattles, so does he.
Furthermore, being black-pathed, black-trailed, burning, and delightful—
being thus, he is known;
that is to say, he shines forth.
Like the sky, smiling— that is, shining— by means of the *nabhas* (the stars);
or rather, like the celestial realm (*dyuloka*), smiling— that is, appearing beautiful— by means of the various regions of the atmosphere (*antarikṣa*).
Just as the directions of the sky are known when they are blue in color, so too is the path known when it has become black through one's own movement;
the meaning is that it becomes manifest.

He who has stood up on three [feet], burning toward the broad earth, moves like a beast that is self-guided and without a herdsman; Agni, the radiant one, heating the dry woods, with his blackened tracks, has made the earth savory. 7. He who has stood up on three [feet], burning toward the broad earth, moves like a beast that is self-guided and without a herdsman; Agni, the radiant one, heating the dry woods, with his blackened tracks, has made the earth savory.
The fire which has stood forth, which stands in various ways and pervades the entire universe;
likewise, that fire [which pervades] the broad, expansive earth in its entirety.
And he who becomes *abhidakṣat*, that is, increasing by way of being directed toward [the goal].
Both are also negated because of their connection with the word "mine" (mama).
That Agni is like an animal;
just as a born animal moves according to its own will, so he, moving by himself (*svayu*), is without a herdsman (*agopāḥ*)—
meaning he is devoid of a controller.
Thus he goes.
Doing what?

Being radiant with excellent luster, and having blackened—that is, having caused the burning and painful thorns and such—to be consumed by his heat, he intensely relishes, as it were, the juices residing in the trees upon the earth.
It burns dry or sapless trees, shrubs, and so forth that are spread out.

Now has this prayer been recited for you at the third assembly, under the protection of your ancient help. O Agni, grant us abundant wealth consisting of many heroes, great food, strength, and offspring. Now, for your ancient aid, this hymn has been recited at the third assembly. O Agni, grant us wealth that brings together heroes, vast, full of food, strength, and noble progeny.
1. Like one thirsty, as if hungry; 2. likewise, for the sake of success; 3. shining (in the variants kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha); 4. as soon as born; 5. devoid of a cowherd.

O Agni, when there is the recollection—upon remembering—that ancient aid (*avasaḥ*) belonging to you, which was performed at the former time of sacrifice, then by that memory, even now, at the third *vidatha*, that is, at the third pressing of the sacrifice.

Or rather, among the various rites connected with the *prātaranuvāka*—specifically within the third rite consisting of the *āgneya*, *aupāsana*, and *āśvina* offerings—you recite (*śaṃsi*), that is, we recite, the *manma*, the meditative hymn of praise.

O Agni, you too grant to us (*asme*) a great (*bṛhantam*) and abundant (*kṣumantam*) food (*vājam*) characterized by such qualities—an offering accompanied by heroes (*saṃyadvīram*), as well as wealth (*rayim*) consisting of good progeny (*svapatyam*). Grant these to us.
O Agni, just as those Gṛtsamadas have overcome the secret places and reached the lower regions,
so may you grant that vital strength to our patrons and to the singer— one that brings noble heroes and overcomes the malicious.

As by you, O Agni, the Gṛtsamadas, winning [the prize] in secret, may they overcome their neighbors—so may they be; rich in heroic sons, subduing their adversaries. Grant that vital strength to the patrons and to the singer alike. 9.
O Agni, through you as their protector, the Gṛtsamadas— the seers who enjoy [the wealth] according to the Vedic rule (chāndasa)— desiring to win,
have spoken these words in the third person (parokṣya) regarding themselves:

"May they overcome, that is, master, those specific riches which are hidden in the cave (guhā), meaning those means of cessation (uparamaṇa-sādhana) existing within the cave, or those excellent riches existing in the highest place."

They should bring [them] under their own control; or else, they should overcome the hidden enemies—those wicked ones who exist as "uparas," meaning those who act with superiority (adhikatvena). They should subdue them.
The meaning is "act in such a manner.
Of what kind [are they]? They are *suvīrāsaḥ*, endowed with excellent sons and so forth.

"Abhimātisahah": one who endures those who act with hostility, such as enemies, evildoers, and the like; furthermore, [he is for] "the wise," that is, the intelligent sacrificers, and "for the one who praises."
The singular number is used by way of transposition.

O performer of the sacrifice through word, bestow upon the praisers—or indeed upon the wise patrons who are the sacrificers and upon the chanting singer—that well-known, abundant food (vayas) which is your excellent favor (sumati). Grant it! Grant it! Grant it!
The fifth hymn, beginning with "hotājaniṣṭa," consists of five verses; it is dedicated to Soma, is measured in the Ānuṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to Agni.
It is cataloged under the heading "hotā... ānuṣṭubham.
Its application is at the commencement of the sacrifice, during the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina Śastra.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Hotṛ has been born as Agni" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13). On the twenty-fourth day as well, this very same [verse] is the Ājya: "On the twenty-fourth day, the Hotṛ has been born as the Ājya" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.2).
On the second day of the Ābhilāvika sacrifice, this very same [verse] is the *ājya* [laud];
for [the rule] "The *ājya* of the second [day is performed] with the Caturviṃśa [stoma]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.6) has extended this by analogy.
The conscious Hotṛ has been born as a father for the protection of the fathers;
may we be able to offer that wealth which is to be directly known, O powerful ones, to Yama.

The Hotṛ has been born, the conscious one, as a father for the sake of aid to the fathers; may we be able to bring forth that wealth which is to be known through sacrifice, O possessors of strength, [and reach] Yama. 1.
The Hotṛ—the performer of the oblation, the conscious one, the inspirer, and the protector—of our sacrifice, such an Agni has been born.
For what purpose? For the sake of the Pitṛs—the protectors, that is, the sacrificers.
The dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
For their protection and preservation,

and we ourselves, being possessed of *vāja*— that is, food characterized by oblations— may we be able to obtain that wealth (*vasu*) which is most worthy of worship (*prayakṣam*), which is to be won (*jenyam*), and which is to be controlled (*yamam*).
"May we be capable"— this is the sense of the ellipsis.
Or rather, "vājinaḥ" refers to the ignorant; we are able to effect their restraint (*yama*).
"Prayakṣam jenyam vasu" is a comparison for wealth;
it is like the aforementioned kind of riches.
Just as we are able to obstruct it, so too [is it].

1. [The reading] "kṣima-chāndasaṃ bhajantaḥ" does not exist in the manuscripts jha, jha, ṇa, ma, and va. 2. [The reading] "parokṣeṇa" is found in the manuscripts jha, jha, ṇa, ma, and va. 3. [The reading] "na-ta-yamitavyam" is found in the manuscripts ka and kha; [the reading] "ṇa-1-ta-tha-va-yametavyam" is found in the manuscripts ka, kha, ṇa, 1, ta, tha, and va.
In him, the leader of the sacrifice, in whom the seven rays are extended— the eighth being the divine one— Pota impels all that, as he does for Manu.
In whom seven rays are extended, he who leads the sacrifice; like Manu, the divine eighth one, as Potṛ, he promotes all that. 2.

In that Agni who is the leader of the sacrifice (*yajña*), the fulfiller of the ritual (*yāga*), seven rays—the *hotraka* priests who are metaphorically designated as rays because they are associated with them—are extended on all sides, pervaded by their respective duties. He is the *pota*, the purifier, the priest of the gods, or the fire assuming the office of the *potr* priest; like a human *pota*, he performs his divine function.
The sacrifice is divine.

Connected with that, he is the eighth; connected with the eight oblations, he—being himself the eighth together with the seven *hotṛ*s—*invati*, i.e., pervades, that entire multitude of duties to be performed.
Alternatively, there is a change of gender in the word "that" (*tad*);
the connection is "he is the *potṛ*."
Having become the eighth together with the seven Hotṛ-priests, one should perform that sacrifice.
Whether he has run forth or has proclaimed these prayers, he indeed knows that;
he has encompassed all poetic wisdom as a felly surrounds the spokes.
He has sped forth when he has proclaimed the sacred words (*brahmāṇi*) after him; he has encompassed all poetic insights (*kāvyā*), just as the felly encompasses the wheel. 3.
In the preceding mantra, it was stated that he himself carries out the sacrifice, just like the *hotṛ* priest and others.
Here, however, he says that he himself carries it out by abiding in the form of each respective [priest]:

"Or (*vā*), indeed (*oṃ*), having aimed at (*anu*) this sacrifice (*enaṃ yajñam*), whatever oblation (*haviḥ*) and so forth he maintains (*dadhanve*), he does so in the form of the *adhvaryu* priest and others."
Those sacred hymns (*brahmāṇi*) consisting of weapons and so forth, which the Hotṛ and others have recited or are reciting—
in this context, the word *anu* should be joined [with *avocan*].
All that is indeed *veru*, truly powerful.
He himself desires or knows [them];
this Agni [knows] all, every one of the *kāvyā*—
the *kāvyā* being the wise, the insightful officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
He encompasses the actions connected with that;
he brings them under his own control;
the meaning is that he pervades them.
The illustration is "pervasion" (vyāpti). Just as the rim—the outer encircling circle—and the wheel—the component of a chariot—pervade [their respective objects] in their entirety, so it is here.
For together with the pure one, the pure Praśāstṛ has been born through ritual wisdom;
knowing his firm ordinances, he ascends along them as if climbing a tree.
Together with the pure one, he is pure; the Praśāstṛ has won through his mental power. Knowing his firm laws, he ascends like a climbing plant. 4.
