The eighth hymn consists of six verses beginning with "vājayanta iva. Since there is no mention of the word *ha* following the Soma oblation, the seer is Gṛtsamada, the seer who beheld this Maṇḍala.
Agni is the deity;
because of the word "hi," the meter is Gāyatrī;
the others are Anuṣṭubh.
It is listed in the Anukramaṇī as: “*vājayanaś cīvanyānuṣṭubh*.
Its application is stated to be as the third hymn in both the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*, specifically for the final verse of this [hymn].

Like one seeking booty, now praise the yoking of the chariots of Agni—of him who is most glorious and bountiful. 1. Like one seeking booty, now indeed praise the yoking of the chariots of Agni—of him who is most glorious and bountiful. 1.

O inner self, quickly praise the yokes and the horses of Agni—of what kind of Agni? Of him whose fame is most excellent, of him whose glory has increased. [The possessive suffix] expressing the sense of possession is elided. Praise the yokes of such a one, the bestower of the fruit of the sacrifice. Or rather, "O Hotṛ" is an address. An illustration for the praise: "The hymns have magnified Atri, Manu, and Agni the self-ruling; they have bestowed all splendors upon them. (5) Atri. Anu. Svarājyam. Agnim. Ukthāni. Vavṛdhuḥ. Viśvāḥ. Adhi. Śriyaḥ. Dhe. (5)
The devourer of enemies or of those lacking knowledge, the self-ruling one who shines by himself— having sought him as their goal,
they have increased, indeed do increase, the hymns and the ritual recitations for Agni.
And that Agni maintains all glories within himself.

Through the protection of Agni, Indra, Soma, and the gods, may we remain unharmed and be united; may we overcome those who attack us. 6. Of Agni, of Indra, of Soma, through the protections of the gods, may we, being unhurt, be united; may we prevail over those who strive against us. 6.
Desiring to prosper and being unharmed by anyone, may we be united with the protections (*ūtibhiḥ*)—the aids—of Agni, Indra, Soma, and the other gods;
may we be joined with them.
Thus protected, may we overcome those who attack us, the enemies who desire battle for themselves.

From the word *pṛtanā*, when the suffix *kyac* is applied, there is the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule "the elision of the vowels in *kavi*, *adhvara*, and *pṛtana* occurs before the suffix *kyac*."
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness within the heart,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the fourfold goals of human existence.

Thus ends the fifth chapter of the second book in the *Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa*, a commentary on the *Ṛgvedasaṃhitā* composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
1. Sovereignty over the vowels *ga*, *jha*, *ḷ*, and *ma*. 2. They have increased by *na*, *va*, and *vā*.
3. By means of that which exceeds the *ka*, *ja*, *jha*, *jha*, *ḷ*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *ma*, and *sāyaṇa*.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
The ninth hymn, beginning with the verse "ni hotā," is the seer Gṛtsamada's own composition, as indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry "ni hotā.
Since no specific meter is mentioned, it is Triṣṭubh.
According to the general rules regarding the Maṇḍala and other divisions, its deity is Agni.
The application (*viniyoga*) of this [hymn] is in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*, within the *ṛc* addressed to Agni and in the *triṣṭubh* metre.
This is prescribed in the section beginning with "Now, of this" (*athaitasyāḥ*) in the Sūtra: "The hymn beginning with 'ni hotā hotṛpadane'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.13).
The first two verses are applied during the *agnipraṇayana* (the leading forth of the fire).
In the section beginning with "On the fifth full moon," it is stated in the sūtra: "'ni hotā hotṛpadane'—these two [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.17).
The Hotṛ, knowing his place on the Hotṛ’s seat, has sat down—resplendent, shining, and most skillful;
Agni, whose wisdom protects the unviolated vows, the most excellent, the bringer of thousands, with his pure tongue.

As the Hotṛ priest, knowing [the rite], resplendent, shining, and most skillful, he has sat down upon the seat of the Hotṛ. He whose wisdom is unfailing and whose vows are inviolable—O Bull, O Agni, showerer of desired fruits, you become our messenger for the purpose of summoning the gods to our sacrifice.
You alone be our protector from afar, our savior, and our guardian in times of distress.
Furthermore, O Vasu, be the one who brings us wealth— that is, the leader who leads riches toward us— by means of our foremost [prayer],
never failing and shining brightly.
"Dīdayati" means "shining"; it is an action-word meaning "being resplendent. You, [shining], [be] for us, for our offspring—that is, for our son—and for our lineage.
He is called *tanaḥ* because he extends (*tanoti*) and spreads out the lineage; thus, he is the grandson.
In him [Agni] is the *gopāḥ*, the protector, of our *tanūḥ*, our bodies.
And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "Agni indeed is the protector (*gopā*) of the gods; they entrust Agni himself as a protector on all sides for their own sake and for that of the sacrificer" (AiB 1.28).
And you, being such, be our protector—be aware, take heed!
Let us serve you in your highest birth, O Agni; let us serve you with hymns of praise in your lower dwelling-place.
From whatever womb you have arisen, we sacrifice to that; into you, when well-kindled, they have poured the oblations.

Let us worship thee in thy highest birth, O Agni; let us worship with hymns in thy lower dwelling-place. From whatever womb thou hast arisen, we sacrifice unto that; into thee, when well-kindled, they have offered oblations.
O Agni, to you who abide in that most excellent *janman*—
the celestial realm, so called because it is the place of birth where one is born and manifests— we shall pay homage; we shall serve you with hymns of praise.
To you, who abide in the lower dwelling place—the intermediate space beneath the world of heaven—we shall offer worship with hymns; we shall serve you.
From that womb, that place in the form of the earth, from which you have risen up and manifested yourself, I honor that region of the earth.
For there, in you who are kindled by fuel-sticks, the Adhvaryus and others offer oblations such as the sacrificial cakes.
This is the form of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
O Agni, most skilled in sacrifice, perform the offering with the oblation; with readiness, accept the gift and the wealth!
For you indeed are the lord of riches among treasures; you are the inspirer of bright luster.

O Agni, you who are most skilled in sacrifice, worship with the oblation; graciously accept the gift and the wealth offered. For you indeed are the lord of riches among all treasures; you are the inspirer of brilliant splendor. 4.
O Agni, you who are the most excellent sacrificer (*yajīyān*), the most worthy of worship, perform the sacrifice with the offered oblation (*havis*) that has been presented; unite the gods with it.
Bestow the gift (*deṣṇa*)—that which is to be given—and the nourishment (*rādhas*), for *śruṣṭī* is a name for swiftness.
Quickly praise [the gods]!
Before the gods, say, "This is sweeter, this is sweeter.
Or rather, being one who acts swiftly through obedience (*śruṣṭī*), praise the gift (*deṣṇa*)—the wealth (*rādhas*) to be given—and speak with us as your foremost [object], meaning: "Bestow it!"
He demonstrates the power of his generosity:
"Among riches—that is, among wealths—you are indeed the lord of riches (rayipati), the lord of the highest wealth.
Alternatively, in the phrase "lord of riches" (rayīṇāṃ rayipatiḥ), one instance of the word *rayi* is a restatement (anuvāda).
You are the *manotā*, the inspirer or knower, of our bright and radiant speech—that is, of our hymn of praise;
or alternatively, you are the *manotā* [of the sacrificial victim].
1. One who rains down the desired fruit.
2. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa: for the sake of the deity; Va: for the purpose of summoning the deity. 3. Jha: Be a protector.
Second Aṣṭaka, Hymn 33:
Both thy treasures, O Wondrous One, do not diminish day by day as thou art born.
O Agni, make the singer possessed of food; make him the lord of wealth consisting of noble offspring.

Both of these of yours, O Wondrous One, do not diminish day by day—the wealth that arises for you. O Agni, make the singer possessed of food; make him the lord of wealth consisting of good offspring. 5.
O wondrous and beautiful Agni, both kinds of wealth belonging to you—celestial and terrestrial—are yours as you are born day after day at the time of the Agnihotra.
The suffix *yat* is applied after the words beginning with *vasu*, provided that the sense is "having tasted" (*āsvādita*). (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.30.4)
Such twofold wealth *never perishes* nor diminishes.
Regarding the existence of this twofold wealth, there is a Vedic mantra: "For you, O Agni, rule over the celestial, and you rule over the terrestrial" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.144.6).
Therefore, make *this sacrificer*, who is your praiser performing your hymn of praise, *possessed of food* or possessed of fame; that is, make him so.
Furthermore, make him the lord and master of wealth consisting of excellent offspring.
On the day before the Sākamedha festival, three offerings (iṣṭis) are to be performed at each of the three pressings.
In the first offering, for Agni Anīkavat, the invitatory verse is "With his army-host" (senānīkena).

Thus it is sūtra-ed in the section beginning with "Then the Sākamedhas" (tataḥ sākamedhāḥ): "With his army-host, O benevolent one, toward us" (senānīkena suvidatro asme; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.18).
May the very gracious one with his host of armies be our protector; may he, the most noble victor among the gods, grant us well-being.
O Agni, undeceived guardian and our protector from afar, shine upon us with splendor and wealth.
With this face of yours, O Agni, most gracious to us, best at sacrificing among the gods, bring the gods hither for our welfare.
As an undeceived guardian and our protector from afar, O Agni, shine upon us with splendor and with wealth. 6.
O Agni, such as you are, being joined with this face of yours, be well-disposed toward us—meaning one who is true to his promise or possesses good wealth;
be the worshiper of the gods through the offering of oblations to them, the most excellent sacrificer, the undeceivable, and the protector of the gods.

Moreover, O protector from afar, you who are our savior and guardian from calamities, shine forth for our well-being—shine with splendor and shine with wealth—shine everywhere with security; shine everywhere with security.

The tenth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "johutraḥ," is composed by Gṛtsamada, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to Agni, as indicated by the heading "johutraḥ. The application (viniyoga) of this hymn has been stated together with the preceding one.

1. When Agni is kindled by man at the place of libation (iḷā), like a father, he is the first to be invoked. Clothed in splendor, immortal, discerning, the one who belongs to mortals, seeking glory—that is the prize-winning steed. johūtaḥ | agniḥ | prathamaḥ | pitā'iva | iḷaḥ | pade | manuṣā | yat | sam'iddhaḥ | śriyam | vasānaḥ | amṛtaḥ | vi'caitāḥ | martyejanyaḥ | śravasyaḥ | saḥ | vājī || 1 ||
Summoned by all for the sake of the sacrifice, he is to be offered as an oblation or he himself is to be sacrificed.
It is a form derived either from the root *hve* (to call) or from the root *hu* (to sacrifice).
Such is the first;
for it is recorded in scripture that “Agni is indeed the lowest of the gods” (AiB 1.1).
He is the primary Agni.

Whenever that Agni is kindled by a human sacrificer at the place of *iḷā*—that is, at the location consisting of the *uttaravedi* altar—he becomes like a father to the gods through the delivery of the oblation.
Clothed in splendor—that is, enveloped in radiance—he is immortal, free from the law of death, possessed of various insights, and worthy of renown;
for "renown" (*śravaḥ*) is a name for food.
That which is beneficial for him is the *vājī*, the powerful one;
that Agni becomes one who is to be honored by all mortals.
The suffix *kenya* occurs after a verbal root from which the *yaṅ* (intensive) affix has been elided (*yaṅluk*).

May Agni, of wondrous luster, the immortal one who discerns all, hear my invocation with all my songs. Two dark steeds, or two ruddy ones, or even two crimson ones, carry his chariot; the far-reaching Lord has fashioned them for his wheels. śruyāḥ | agniḥ | citrabhānuḥ | havam | me | viśvābhiḥ | gīrbhiḥ | amṛtaḥ | vicetāḥ | śyāvā | ratham | vahataḥ | rohitā | vā | uta | aruṣā | aha | cakre | vibhūtraḥ || 2 ||

May that Agni—the immortal, free from the nature of death; the one possessed of distinguished wisdom (*vicaitas*); the one of manifold splendor (*citrabhānu*), whose radiance is diverse or worthy of being sought as a refuge—hear my invocation (*hava*), the hymn of praise being performed with all songs (*viśvābhir gīrbhiḥ*) which serve as the means of laudation. Two dark-colored horses (*śyāvā*) draw his chariot;
or indeed, two red-colored horses (*rohitā*) draw the chariot.
Moreover, the two ruddy, shining, bright-colored horses carry [the chariot].

The selection of colors for the two horses—whether they be red (*rohita*), dark-brown (*śyāva*), or other—is according to one's own will. Indeed, the priest has fashioned the wheel, which is distributed across various places.
The suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *kṛ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).

They generated him, well-born, as the embryo in her who lies supine; Agni became the germ in her of many forms. Even in the narrow place, with his great powers, the wise one dwells unconfined. In her who lies supine, they generated him, the well-born; Agni became the embryo in her of many forms. Even in the narrow place, with his great powers, the wise one dwells unconfined.
1. "Two horses do not pull the chariot" does not exist;
2. "not-horses"; 3. "they do not pull the chariot."

Upon the fire-pan that was turned face upwards—that is, lying on its back—the Adhvaryu and the other priests generated, meaning they produced, the Agni who is "well-purified" (supūta), meaning the fire well-kindled for the sake of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
That Agni [is present] in the *purupeśas*;
*peśas* is a name for form (*rūpa*).
Within the multiform medicinal herbs, he becomes the embryo; by virtue of existing within them, he is like an embryo.
This is the form of the root *bhū* in the *liṅ* (optative) mood.
In *śiriṇā*. It is called *śiriṇā* because living beings perish (*śīryante*) in it; thus, *śiriṇā* refers to the night.
In that [night] as well, [one should recite] with *aktunā*.
The darkness is as if anointed with collyrium;

by that darkness he is neither enveloped nor touched. Therefore, being endowed with splendors—that is, with radiant energies—and being possessed of supreme wisdom (*pracetāḥ*), he dwells, shining brightly.
I sprinkle Agni with the oblation of ghee, him who instructs all beings in their turn—
he who is broad, vast with transverse vigor, most extensive, impetuous, and visible through his foods.

I sprinkle Agni with the oblation of ghee—he who dwells facing all beings, broad and vast with transverse vigor, most expansive, the portion to be known, the one who conquers by force and is most excellent. May we, protected by you, speak like Manu;
with eloquence and the ladle, I repeatedly invoke the perfect Agni, the honey-sweet winner of wealth.

They are to be known. The portion. The one who bestows strength. The most excellent. Those protected by you. Like Manu. May we speak. To the flawless Agni. With the ladle. With eloquence. To him who drinks the honeyed [oblation]. The winner of wealth. I call aloud. 6.
"Vareṇyam" means excellent. "Varam" refers to splendor (*tejas*), so called because by it one wards off enemies.
Being "sahasānaḥ," meaning overpowering the enemies with that [splendor], you should recognize—that is, understand—the "bhāgam," which is the hymn worthy of being honored.
In the case of the benedictive (āśīrliṅ), [the substitution of] *e* occurs by the rule "vānyasya saṃyogādeḥ" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.68).
"tvādātasaḥ":
those to whom you are the messenger are "tvādātasaḥ.
Or alternatively, impelled by you, may we speak like Manu—that is, like Manu—we shall utter a hymn of praise.

By means of the *juhū*—so called because oblations (*hūyate*) are offered into it, referring either to the flame or a specific sacrificial vessel—I, through my speech (*vacasyā*), that is, through praise, [worship] Agni, who is *anūna*, meaning complete; who is *madhupṛc*, meaning one who unites the sacrificer with "honey," that is, the fruit of the ritual action; and who is *dhanasā*, a distributor of wealth.
O Hero, O Indra, destroyer of enemies, those many waters which you caused to swell—
those waters that were encompassed, held back, and overwhelmed by Ahi, the cloud, or by Vṛtra.
Then, from that mountain, you released—indeed, poured forth—the vast waters.

Increasing through the *uktha* hymns and *śastra* recitations, you struck down the Dāsa, the one who destroys all prosperity; even though he was *amartya*, considering himself to be immortal and free from the law of death, you shattered that Asura so that his face was turned downward.
(The root *bhid* means "to split apart.")
The form [is] in the *laṅ* tense with the suffix *sip*:

"O Hero, in those hymns (*uktha*) wherein you have delighted, O Indra, and in the Rudra-like chants (*stoma*), these [waters] flow forth for you alone—those in which you take pleasure—just as the bright ones rush toward Vāyu. (3) In the hymns, O Hero, in those wherein you have delighted, O Indra, and in the Rudra-like chants; for you alone these [waters] flow forth—those in which you take pleasure—just as the bright ones rush toward Vāyu. (3)
O heroic Indra, in those hymns (*uktha*) and in the *śastra* recitations performed by the *hotṛ* and other priests— namely, the *rudriya* ones;
"rudriya" means bliss— and in those which serve as the means for attaining that bliss.
Or rather, the Rudras are the praisers;
for their sake, in the hymns (*stoma*) of the chanters (*udgātṛ*),
you quickly take pleasure (*cākan*), that is, you desire the praises.
This is a form derived from the roots *kamati* or *kanati* with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix.

In those praises consisting of hymns (*stotra*) and recitations (*śastra*), you become *mandasānaḥ*, that is, rejoicing; these very *śubhrāḥ*, shining praises, flow forth—*pra sisrate*—for your sake alone, toward you who are coming to our sacrifice, O Vāyu. They do not flow for the sake of being merely requested.

Now, therefore, serve them! Increasing your brilliant [power], holding the brilliant thunderbolt in your arms—you, O Indra, being brilliant and having grown strong among us—may you conquer the Dāsa clans with the help of Sūrya. 4. Brilliant; now; your; brilliant; increasing; brilliant; thunderbolt; in the two arms; holding; brilliant; you; O Indra; having grown strong; among us; the Dāsa; clans; with Sūrya; may you conquer. 4.

O Indra, increasing your beautiful and splendid strength with hymns, we quickly place—that is, we take up—your beautiful and radiant weapon, the thunderbolt (*vajra*), within your two arms. For it is well known that when praised, Indra took up the thunderbolt for the slaying of the Asuras; thus, we take up this weapon. Increasing through our hymns, growing great, and endowed with splendor, you, O Shubhra, [subdue] our Dāsa subjects—the Asura progeny who cause destruction—by means of Sūrya, the excellent impeller.

For the weapon impels you, saying, "Fight! Thus, with the thunderbolt placed within your arms, overcome [the enemy]—be invincible (*sahya*). The form *sahyas* is derived from the root *sah* (to endure/overcome) in the potential mood (*liṅ*), with the substitution of the active voice (*parasmaipada*) for the middle voice.

Him who was placed in the cave, the secret one, hidden within the waters, the deceptive one dwelling there; and him who had stayed and propped up the waters and the sky—the Dragon, O Hero, you slew with your valor. 5. In the cave, placed, secret, hidden in the waters, encompassed; the deceptive one, dwelling; and also the waters and the sky, having propped them up—you slew the Dragon, O Hero, with your valor. 5.
1. Thus empowered;
[there is] none.
2. By means of such forms as *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *va*, and so forth.

O Hero Indra, [that which was] placed in a secret place, deposited in a cave, therefore hidden (guhya), unmanifest, concealed (gūḍha), deeply hidden, and veiled— here, although the single meaning is that of concealment, the repetition is intended to demonstrate the abundance of that concealment;
for in the case of repetition, there is indeed a greater significance.

Just as one might say, "O, how beautiful! O, how beautiful!"—so you struck with your heroic power and the thunderbolt that deceptive, illusory Asura who was dwelling there, who was causing harm, and who, by his own strength, had propped up both the waters and the sky; you struck that serpent-like Asura, whether he be a cloud or a visible being, with your prowess and might.
This is the form of the root *han*, meaning "to strike" or "to go," in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense.
Now let us praise those ancient, great deeds of yours, O Indra, and let us praise your recent exploits as well.
Let us praise the thunderbolt yearning in your arms; let us praise your two bay steeds, the banners of the sun.
I praise your ancient great deeds, O Indra; and let me now praise your recent exploits. I praise the eager thunderbolt held in your arms; I praise your two bay steeds, the banners of the sun.
O Indra, we now quickly praise your ancient, primordial, and great deeds;
and furthermore, we praise the deeds performed in the present.
We praise the thunderbolt, blazing and desiring the wide space, within your two arms.
Furthermore, we praise the two bay horses named Hari, the indicators of the sun—the excellent impeller or the one of great heroism—or of Indra, who is of the nature of the sun.
The root *pṛñ* means "to praise.

According to the rule *tiṅāṃ tiṅo bhavanti*, the third person plural ending is replaced by the second person singular form. By the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.

O Indra, the two bay steeds, seeking booty, have indeed brought forth for you that unassailable, resonant sound which distills clarity; the earth has spread out in all directions, and even the mountain seemed about to flow away.

O Indra, your two bay steeds, seeking booty, have raised a roar that resounds like clarified butter; at once the earth has spread itself out, and even the mountain, though wishing to flee, has stood still. 7.
O Indra, they two, seeking prize-winning strength, exert their speed.
The suffix *ṇic* is applied [to the root] according to the rule "he causes to do" (*karoti*).

"Those two," meaning your two horses named Hari, "who cause to flow" (cyāvayitārau) the "clarified butter" (ghṛtaśrutam)—that is, the water of clarified butter—[and who possess] the "resonant sound" (svāram), the thunder of the clouds, [which is] "well" (su) and "swift" (kṣipram), and which is "unassailable" (asvāryam).
The root *svar* has the sense of making sound;
it is a single-rooted word (ekadhātu), just like in the expression "he cooks the food" (*pākam pacati*).
This is the form in the *laṅ* [tense].
Level and even on all sides, or rather, level from every direction, it spread out wide.
Having heard the thundering, it became known that "rain shall fall upon me.
Likewise, even the mountain-like cloud, as if about to flow—meaning, moving here and there for the sake of its color—reposed.
This is the form of the root *ram* in the *laṅ* tense.
1. *ka* is a single element (*dhātu*); *ca* is a single element; *jha* is a single-syllabled element; *jha1* is a single element; *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, and *na* are a single element.
The mountain (*parvata*) has roared, bellowing with its mothers as it rises up.
Strengthening their voice from afar across the boundary, they have spread wide the blast impelled by Indra.

The mountain-like steed, never flagging, has stepped forth together with his mothers, bellowing. Far away on the distant shore, they increase their voice; spreading it abroad, they have set down the blast impelled by Indra. 8.
Unfailing, not negligent, and attentive toward the rain-giver, the cloud (parvata) settled down in the sky;
bellowing together with his mothers—
the intermediate waters— he strode forth and moved hither and thither.
In the word *kramate*, the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) occurs frequently in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), according to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi."

Increasing—the singers or the Maruts making prosperous through hymns—the voice of the intermediate region (mādhyamikā vāk) which stands in the distant, far-reaching atmosphere; impelled by Indra, that voice which utters sound within the *dhamani* (the windpipe), they spread it forth extensively.
Indra, with his flashing bolts, struck down Vṛtra, the wielder of magic who lay across the great river;
at the roar of this bull and from his thunderbolt, the two worlds, heaven and earth, trembled in fear.
Indra struck down Vṛtra, the illusionist who lay across the great river; at the roar of this bull’s thunderbolt, the two worlds, trembling in fear, quaked apart. 9.

The mighty Indra [struck] Vṛtra, the illusory Asura, who was lying upon—that is, reclining on—the *sindhu*. The term *sindhu* refers to the cloud because it moves hither and thither, flowing; or alternatively, it refers to water.
Having taken possession of that, he lay upon Vṛtra;
Vṛtra is the cloud, so called because it "envelops" (vṛṇoti) the sky. Him he "thrust forth," that is, he struck him down.
At the roar of this bull Indra, as he uttered his cry, the two worlds—Heaven and Earth—trembled with fear upon encountering the thunderbolt.
The word *kanikradat* is derived [as a nipāta] by the rule beginning with "dādharṣi dādharti."
The thunderbolt of this Ṛbhu roared aloud when he, being human, utterly consumed the non-human;
he brought down the magical powers of the guileful Dānava as he drank the pressed soma.

He roared aloud; the thunderbolt of this bull [is] superhuman, since he, though human, has consumed [the enemy]; he brought down the magical powers of the guileful Dānava while drinking of the pressed juice. 10.
The vajra of this Indra, the showerer of desires, roared loudly; when? To this he replies:
when it was non-human, that is, devoid of humans.

Or rather, thinking "I am not human," Indra—the benefactor of men (*mānuṣa*), or alternatively, the wise one—should utterly consume (*nijūrvāt*) that Asura; that is to say, he should seek to slay him.
*Jarvate* is a form in the *leṭ* mood from the verbal root meaning "to injure."
Having drunk the pressed soma that was extracted from the *māyin*, the illusory Dānava. 40.
Vṛtra is the son of Dānu, as seen in such passages as "Dānu lies" (adānuḥ śaye).
Of that Vṛtra, the son, [Indra] "brought down" (ni apādayat)—that is, he cast down or struck down—his "māyās," meaning his deceptions.
Drink, drink the Soma, O heroic Indra! Let the exhilarating pressed juices delight you;
filling your flanks, let them cause you to swell. Thus pressed, the draught has helped Indra.
Drink, drink! O Indra, O hero, drink the Soma! Let the exhilarating pressed juices delight you. Filling your two flanks, let them cause you to swell. Thus has the pressed Paura helped Indra. 11.
O heroic and powerful Indra, drink, drink the pressed and excellent Soma; indeed, drink it.
This repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
May these pressed Somas, which have been extracted and are intoxicating, gladden you—may they exhilarate you.
The root *mad* is used in the sense of praising and so forth;
the *parasmaipada* ending occurs here by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
May those two flanks of your belly, filling them both, cause you to increase;
thus, in this manner, the pressed Soma, poured forth as a filler for the belly, has satisfied you, O Indra.
*avate* is the form of the root meaning "to satisfy" in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
O Indra, may we wise ones win your favor through inspired thought, moving according to the Eternal Law; seeking your aid, we meditate upon your praise so that we may be recipients of your wealth.

O Indra, we have come to you; may we, the inspired singers, win the prayer through our devotion to Truth. Moving forward in search of help, we meditate upon your praise. May we be present at the giving of your wealth. 12.
"O Indra, we, the wise and intelligent, have placed our hope in you—specifically, in your heart.
This word *api* is used here in the sense of an inquisitive question:
'What do we abide in your heart?'"
"By the path of Truth— Truth being the fruit of action—
we, desiring that [fruit], serving you by means of the rite called *paricaraṇa* (service), may we win— that is, fully enjoy— the *dhi* (the ritual act) performed with you as its object."
The roots *van* and *paṇ* mean "to serve" (*saṃbhaktau*).
In the benedictive mood (*āśīrliṅ*), the suffix *aṅ* is applied according to the rule "in the benedictive, *aṅ* [is added] after [roots ending in vowels]. Thus, the form is *vanyāt*.

Furthermore: "Desiring protection from you, we, being constrained (*avasyavaḥ*), meditate upon—that is, we place within you—the 'praśasti,' which is praise (*śaṃsanam*); that is, the excellent praise, the hymn (*stotram*)."
Therefore, may we now become worthy recipients for the giving—that is, the bestowing—of your wealth.
May we be yours, O Indra, those who, seeking your aid, increase your strength;
grant us, O God, that most powerful wealth which we desire, consisting of heroic sons.

May we be yours, O Indra—those who, seeking your aid and desiring protection, increase your strength. Grant us that most powerful wealth, O God, which we desire; grant us riches accompanied by heroic sons. 13.

1. The syllables *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *a*, *ṇa*, *la*, *na*, *ma*, *va* constitute the [first] group of words. 2. *Jha* (jha¹) means "drink, drink" (*piba piba*). 3. *Kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *ma*, *laḍi*. 4. *Kha*, *ga*, *ga* (ga¹) signify "excellent praise"; *ca* signifies "excellent instruction. 5. *Ka*, *jha*, *ma* signify "those who have become worthy vessels.
O Indra, by your aid—that is, by your protection through guidance—[protect us].
This is the form of the root *av* in the sense of "attaining," with the suffix *ktin*.
O Lord, those who, desiring your protection and longing for you, increase the *ūrj*—the food characterized by the oblation—may we become such as they, remaining under your control.
O radiant Indra, may we desire that wealth which is splendid, most powerful through its fitness for giving and enjoyment, or indeed, that which most thoroughly withers the enemies.
It is the form of the root *kan*, meaning "to shine," in the imperative (*loṭ*) after the elision of the suffix.
Grant us—that is, give to us—such wealth as that which is accompanied by heroic sons and grandsons.
Bestow abundance, bestow friendship upon us; O Indra, bestow upon us the host of Maruts, and those who, being of one mind and rejoicing, drink the first draught along with the Vāyus.

Bestow wealth; bestow destruction [of foes]; bestow wealth. Grant us a friend, O Indra; grant us the host of Maruts. And those who, being of one accord and rejoicing, the Vāyus, drink first the leading draught.
O Indra, grant us a dwelling.
A *kṣaya* is a house, where people dwell and reside;
give that to us.
Likewise, grant us a friend and a companion.
There is no loss of accent (anighāta) because it constitutes a different sentence.
Grant us, for our sake, the *śardhaḥ*—the strength belonging to the Maruts, the divine hosts.
By this, the arrival of the Maruts is also entreated.

Those Maruts who are *sajoṣasaḥ*—delighting together—and *mandasānāḥ*—rejoicing—who, being *vāyavaḥ*—those who go toward the sacrifice—*pra pānti*—drink with excellence the *agraṇītim*—the Soma that is led forward—of them [is] the *śardhaḥ*; such is the syntactical connection.
Or rather, you bestow strength upon those winds which drink the Soma as it is being led forward.
The plural number in "vāyavaḥ" is used for the sake of honor,
for Vāyu indeed drinks the first portion of the Soma.

O Indra, among those who have gladdened you, drink the soma so that you may satisfy it and ward off malice; O son of strength, as a deliverer, you have increased us and the heavens with your lofty hymns.

Let them come; indeed, being exhilarated among them, drink the Soma to your satisfaction. O Indra, do not harm us; O deliverer, you have caused the heaven to grow with great hymns of praise through these noble sons. 15.
O Indra, those Maruts among whom you become exhilarated—rejoicing as their companions—let those Maruts quickly partake of the Soma; let them consume it.
"It" is used for emphasis.
"Druhat" is a form derived from the root *dṛh* (to be firm).
Strengthening yourself, drink—consume—this *soma* which is satisfying and satiating.
O *tarutra*, the destroyer of enemies, O Indra, together with the powerful *arkas* (the Maruts who are worthy of praise), accompanied by them;
[the particle] *ā* is used in the sense of "and."
By that [means], having well and truly protected us and you with cattle, sons, and so forth, as well as by our protection, you have caused us to reach heaven.
Or rather: those Soma-libations in which you become exhilarated and rejoicing—may those Somas go to you.
The remainder is as before.
1. Kha, ga, tena; jha₁, ṇa, ta, tha, na, va, te tava.
2. Ma, tava, te. 3. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ṇa₁, dānabhāgāyārhatayā; jha₁, dānāya bhogāya vārhatayā; tha, na, dānābhāgāyārhatayā.
4. [The suffixes] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ṇa¹, tha, na, and those ending in -mat; as well as jha¹, manda, and sāna, are called matup. 5.
Kha, ga, ṇa, and ta are used in the sense of "like" (iva); jha¹ is used in the sense of "and" (ca); tha is used in the sense of "or" (vā). 6.
Ka, jha, and pa are used with words such as *paśu* and *puroḍāśa*; ma is used with words such as *puroḍāśa*.

7. By the protection (*pālanena*) of *ka*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *va*, and *pa*; by the protection (*pālanena*) of *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, and *asman* (us); by the drinking of Soma (*somapānena*) of *jha1*; [and] *ma* protects (*pālayate*) not (*na*). Ṛgveda 2.6.16:

"O Overcomer (*tarutra*), those great ones indeed who have sought to win thy favor with hymns (*ukthebhiḥ*), they who are spreading the sacred grass (*barhiḥ*) with nourishing power, being aided by thee, O Indra, have attained booty (*vāja*). bṛhantaḥ | it | nu | ye | te | tarutra | ukthebhiḥ | vā | sumnam | ā'vivāsān | stṛṇānāsaḥ | barhiḥ | pustya'vat | tvā'ūtāḥ | it | indra | vājam | agman || 16 ||
O Indra, you who are the savior in times of distress, may men serve you—the bringer of bliss—with hymns and sacred teachings, seeking to win your favor.
The augment *aṭ* is applied before the suffix *laṭ* after the root *vi-vāsati*.

Indeed, O Vāyu, those men of yours quickly and without delay become great and mighty. (The word *vā* is a filler. Furthermore, those who serve you by spreading the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon the altar—being protected by you—they go toward the food (*vāja*) accompanied by a dwelling (*pastya*).

O Hero, rejoicing indeed among the fierce ones at the Trikadruka sacrifices, drink the Soma, O Indra! Like one with a beard at the onset of evening, coming with delight, come with your two bay steeds to the drinking of the pressed juice. 17. Among the fierce ones; indeed; O Hero; rejoicing; at the Trikadrukas; drink; the Soma; O Indra; like one with a beard; at the onset of evening; coming with delight; come; with your two bay steeds; to the drinking; of the pressed juice. 17.

O powerful hero Indra, being exhilarated at the Trikadruka days—those pressing days of the sacrifice consisting of Jyotiṣṭoma, Gaurīvīta, Āyus, and others, characterized by many hymns and recitations—drink the Soma offering.
Then, being gratified and pleased by the drinking of the Soma, wipe away the Soma from your beard as you did at the Pradoṣa ceremony.
The root *dhṛ* means "to shake.
This is the form of the root in the *śatṛ* (present participle) suffix after the elision of the *yaṅ* (intensive) affix.
Again and again shaking [the vessel], for the sake of the drinking—that is, the consumption—of the pressed and freshly extracted [Soma], go forth, being yoked with the two bay horses.

Take to yourself, O Hero, that power wherewith you rent Vṛtra asunder—the Dānu, the son of Urṇavābha. You disclosed the light for the Ārya; the Dasyu was cast down by you, O Indra, as he lay enveloped in darkness. 18. Take to yourself... power... Hero... wherewith... Vṛtra... rent asunder... Dānu... son of Urṇavābha... disclosed... light... for the Ārya... enveloped... was cast down... Dasyu... Indra. 18.
O heroic Indra, you who possess power, take up and maintain such strength as that.

In the present tense (*laṭ*) of the root *dhā*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap* by the rule "there is diversely [elision] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). Because of the rule "in the Veda, both ways," the suffix *thās* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*; consequently, the augment *iṭ* is added.
With his own strength, he shattered Vṛtra, the son of Dānu, who was like a spider (*ūrṇavābha*).
A spider is a specific kind of insect; one that is made of wool is called *aurṇavābha*.
Just as [one might crush] such a thing, he split him apart.
Alternatively, *aurṇaḥ* refers to the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*).
"Resembling that" means similar to it.
Therefore, because of the destruction of that which consists of darkness, [it leads] to desirable actions.
1. Kha-ṇa-ta-tha-āpadvistāraka; Ga-tāraka | 2. Jha¹-iditi; 3. Ka-kha-ga-ca-jha¹-ṇa¹-danoḥ | 4. Kha-ūrṇanābhaḥ; Ga-kūrṇanābhiḥ | Ṇa-ta-tha-kumbhanābhiḥ | 5.
Ma-aurṇavaḥ | For the people who perform [the rites], for Kutsa, or for the royal seer, you have uncovered—opened up—the light-making Āditya.
That Dasyu, the destroyer of actions, namely Vṛtra, has sat down on your left side; he remains utterly subdued and oppressed by you on your left flank.
May those who cross over all enemies and Dasyus with your aids, like Aryans, be victorious for us; you, O Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, delivered Viśvarūpa to us, as you did for Trita against Sāsya.

May we be victorious! With your aids, crossing over all rivalries, you subdued for us the Dasyus, the Arya's enemies; you brought under our control that Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, for Sāsya and Trita. 19.

May we recognize those men and may we serve them—those who, by means of your protections, cross over all contending rivals and all tribes that cause harm; and who, through noble conduct, subdue the Dasyus, the destroyers.
Bring that [power] under our control for us.
What is that?
Regarding that, he says: "You subdued the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the Asura named Viśvarūpa."
‘The root *radh* [is used] in the sense of coming under one’s control.’
You brought [him] under control;
or rather,
you slew that Asura.
The root *radh* is used in the senses of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) and "accomplishment" (*saṃrāddhi*). The augment *num* is applied by the rule *radhijabhor aci*.
The fact that Indra slew the son of Tvaṣṭṛ has been explained at great length in the Taittirīyaka Saṃhitā (2.5.1.1) in the passage beginning, “Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Furthermore, for the sake of maintaining his friendship, you brought Vaśa to Trita on the great path.
Or rather: may we, being protected by you, become prosperous; and may we, contending with those who oppose us, cross over and surpass both the progeny and the Dasyus.
The root *san* meaning "to increase" is udātta on its first syllable, as in:
"yathā sanema mitrāvaruṇā sanantaḥ" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.52.1).
If it is transitive (*sakarmaka*), it is udātta on its middle syllable.
"May we win the prize through thee" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.61.4).
*Tarantaḥ*: [from] the root *tṛ* in the sense of "floating" or "crossing"; this is the form in the present participle (*śatṛ*).
If it is a word denoting a name, it is accented on the final syllable;
for example: *taranta iva maṃhanā* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.61.10).
Increasing through the pressed, exhilarating soma of Trita, Indra—accompanied by the Aṅgirases—struck down Arbuda; like the sun its wheel, he shattered his stronghold.
Of this pressed, exhilarating [Soma], Trita’s—growing strong, he cast down Arbuda; like the sun [beating] the wheel of a steed, Indra, accompanied by the Aṅgirases, split Vala. 20.

Indra, increasing through the soma, growing great, gave Arbuda— the cloud (so called because it gives water, *ambhūni*)— to Trita, who was exhilarated by this intoxicating juice, pressed by the presser, having crossed over the darkness. The change of the anusvāra to *r* is Vedic.
Or rather,
he struck down that asura named Arbuda;
for in the root *stu* meaning "to injure," when used with the *laṅ* and *tip* suffixes, there is an elision of the *vikaraṇa* by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi."
When the suffix *guṇa* has been applied, there is the elision of the *ti* by the rule beginning with *halṅyābhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal*.
He utterly destroyed him.

In such passages as, “Thou didst trample the great Arbuda under thy foot” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.51.6), the slaying of Arbuda is clearly stated. Furthermore, Indra, accompanied by the Aṅgirases (*aṅgirasvān*), brandished his thunderbolt for the purpose of slaying the Asuras.
Like the sun;
just as the sun impels the wheel, so does the Ṛgveda.
It is like that.
Or rather, because the Sun, by conquering the Asuras, did not turn back his own chariot wheel;
here, the negative particle *na* has a prohibitive sense.
He was unable to turn back that force; he shattered the lord of the Paṇis, the Asura, and struck him with the thunderbolt.
Or rather, for the chariot of Sūrya was formerly two-wheeled, and one wheel of it was taken away by Indra.
In the word *sūryaḥ*, the form *su* is used for the genitive singular by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
He caused that one wheel belonging to the Sun, which had been struck down, to roll away;
he made it revolve for the purpose of slaying the Rakshasas,
and with that wheel, he struck Vala.
In the sense of destruction.

In the midday pressings (*mādhyandina-savana*) of the multi-day sacrificial sessions (*ahargaṇa*), which are characterized by their being extended (*tāyamāna-rūpa*), there is for the *acchāvāka* priest a hymn known as the "Daily Recitation" (*aharahaḥ-śasya*), namely the hymn beginning with "As if from both sides" (*abhitaṣṭeva*).
The verse "Now indeed, [O Indra], of thee... (*nūṃnaṃ mā te*) is to be recited at its conclusion.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The last [verse] is 'Now indeed, that of thee' at the end" (*nūṃnaṃ sā ta ityantamuttamam*; Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).

Surely that wealthy sacrificial gift of yours, O Indra, shall yield its boon to the singer; bestow it upon those who praise you. May fortune not fail us; may we, possessing excellent heroes, attain great knowledge in the assembly.

Surely, O Indra, may that wealthy sacrificial gift yield a boon for you in return to the singer; grant it to those who praise you, do not withhold it. May Bhaga be ours; may we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 21.
O Indra, that *dakṣiṇā*—
so called because it produces skill (*dakṣa*) and energy (*utsāha*)—

which belongs to you, O bountiful one (*maghavan*), rich in wealth, may she now indeed yield for the singer, for the praiser, the desired object of excellence; that is to say, she now milks it forth, she brings it to fulfillment.
Grant such a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to us, who are your praisers;
moreover, O Bhaga, you who are worthy of being honored, do not withhold it.
[The form *māti dhruk* is derived from the root *dah* (in the sense of giving) in the *luṅ* tense, with the elision of the suffix *cli* according to the rule *mantre ghasa* etc.]
"Do not give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to others, bypassing us;
the meaning is that after first giving to us, it should be given to others afterwards.
Or else: "Do not burn (*dhak*), do not consume our desires."
The meaning is: "Fulfill [our desires] by bestowing the fruits that are expected.

Being "well-heroic" (*suvīrāḥ*), that is, possessing excellent sons and grandsons, may we, in this assembly (*vidathe*), speak—that is, utter—a vast (*bṛhat*) and abundant hymn of praise directed toward you.

In this regard, one should consult the *Nirukta* (1.7), which, having introduced the subject with "That milk for you," explains: "A hero (*vīraḥ*) is so called from *vīryam* (valor), or from *veti* (to overcome), signifying one who performs transcendent deeds, or from *vīrayati* (to act like a hero)."
In the second section (anuvāka), there are eleven hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "yo jātaḥ," is composed by Gṛtsamada, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to Indra.
In the *saṃsava* [rite], one should recite the hymn "yo jāta eva" before the *nivid*-insertion in the *niṣkevalya* [śastra].
This is prescribed in the section beginning with "yadi paryāyān" in the sūtra: "‘yo jāta eva’ in the *niṣkevalya*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.6).
On the third day of the *ābhiplavika* [six-day period], "yo jāta eva" is the *nivid*-insertion in the *niṣkevalya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “For the third [pressing], the Mādhyandina [Hotṛ] recites ‘yo jāta eva’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).
At the Mādhyandina pressing of the Viśvajit sacrifice, the Maitrāvaruṇa should recite the Sāman-hymn beginning with ‘yo jātaḥ’ before the original hymn in his own Śastra.
This is stated in the section beginning with ‘viśvajito’smi naraḥ’: “‘satrā madaso yo jāta evābhūrikaḥ’—these are the Sāman-hymns” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).
This is the placement of the *nivid* in the *niṣkevalya* [śastra] of the *agniṣṭoma*.
It is prescribed in the section beginning with "syenājirābhyām" in the Sūtra: "He who recited 'tiṣṭhā harī'... (with the variants *ṇa*, *tha*, *ma*, and *āvartayat*).
2. In the versions ṇa and tha, the phrase “he split with the thunderbolt” (*vajreṇābhinat*) is absent; in the versions kha, ga, ma, and tena, it reads “he split with that thunderbolt.
3. In the version ka, it reads *dhanavatī dhanavate*; in the versions jha, ma, va, and sā, it reads *dhanavatī sā dakṣiṇā dhanavatī dhanavate*.
4. In the versions ka, kha, ga, jha, ma, and va, it reads *sūktaṃ śaṃsyeta*; in jhā¹, it reads *śaṃsat*; in the versions ṇa, tha, and na, it reads *na śaṃsyeta*.

5. According to Ca, Jha₁, Ṇa, Tha, and Ma, it is the *mādhyandina*; according to Na and Va, it is in the *mādhyandina*. 6. According to Ka and Jha, it is *aninni*; according to Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa₁, and Ta, it is *ni* in *atiṣu*; according to Jha₁, it is *ni* in *atiṣu*; according to Ṇa, Tha, and Na, it is *ni* in *aniṣu*; according to Ta and Va, it is *ni* in *abhiṣu*; and according to Ma, it is *atini*.
[The rule] "He is born indeed" refers to the *mādhyandina* (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.7).
The hymn beginning with "yo jāta eva" is for the Mahānāmnya and Niskevalya [Śastras].
It is recorded in the section on the "Ūru" [Sāmans] in the Sūtra: "vane na vā yo nyadhāyi cākan yo jāta eva prathamo manasvān" (Ai. Ā. 5.3.1).
Regarding this, a legend is told in the Bṛhaddevatā: "Having united his self through austerity, he assumed a great form belonging to Indra."
In a mere moment, he was seen in the heavens, in the sky, and here on earth.
Thinking him to be Indra, the two Daityas of terrible prowess,
Yuni and Cumuri, both armed with weapons, rushed toward him.

Having understood their disposition and that they intended to commit an evil act, he recited the mantras dedicated to Indra from the hymn "yo jātaḥ" for the sake of the ritual. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.66–68)
Others, however, describe it differently:
it is said that in ancient times Indra and the other gods attended the sacrifice of Vainya;
Gṛtsamada also came there and sat among the assembly members (*sadasya*).
The Daityas gathered there with the intent to slay Indra.
Seeing them, Indra departed from the sacrifice in the form of Gṛtsamada.
And that Gṛtsamada, having been honored by the son of Vena (Pṛthu), went out from the sacrificial enclosure.
Seeing that ṛṣi departing and thinking, "This one is indeed Indra," the asuras surrounded him.
He replied to them with this hymn: "I am not Indra; rather, he who is endowed with such qualities is [Indra]."
Others, however, relate it thus:
Knowing that Indra had entered Gṛtsamada’s sacrifice alone, the Asuras surrounded him.
That Indra, having emerged from the sacrificial enclosure in the form of Gṛtsamada, went to heaven.

Then the Asuras, seeing that Indra was delayed, entered [the sacrificial hall] and, having seen Gṛtsamada, realized: "Gṛtsamada had already departed; this one, however, is Indra, who remains here in the form of Gṛtsamada at our sacrifice. They seized him.
He replied to them with this hymn, "I am not Indra," and so forth.
This very meaning is elaborated upon in the Mahābhārata.
He who, as soon as born, the first mindful god, surpassed the gods by his wisdom;
at whose breath the two worlds trembled through the greatness of his manly power—he, O people, is Indra.
He who, as soon as born, was the first mindful god, who by his wisdom surpassed the gods;
at whose breath the two worlds trembled through the greatness of his manly power—he, O people, is Indra. 1.
Gṛtsamada says:

O people, O Asuras! Even while being born, he was the first among the gods, the preeminent one; being wise, the foremost of the intelligent, and radiant as a god, he, by means of his own power (*kratu*)—characterized by the slaying of Vṛtra and other such deeds—surpassed all the gods at the sacrifice and encompassed them as their protector.
The root *bhū* is used in the sense of "adornment" (*alaṃkāra*).
It belongs to the *bhū-ādi* class; this is the form in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense.
Or rather, he surpassed, overcame, and transcended all other dualities.
In this view, the suffix *kvasu* [is applied] by [Pāṇini 3.2.107]; there is a prohibition of the *it*-augment by [Pāṇini 1.2.14], "before a suffix marked with *kit*."
At the very breath and strength of Indra’s body, the two worlds, heaven and earth, trembled with fear.
The root *bhyas* is used in the sense of "fear";
it is anudātta.
The etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*) state that *bhyas* is used in the senses of "fear" and "trembling" (Nirukta 3.21).
They trembled or shook;
for thus says another mantra: "These two great ones, O Citta, tremble with fear before your wrath" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.80.11).
That Indra, endowed with the greatness (*mahnā*) of his own strength (*nṛmṇa*) characterized by his army—I am not he.

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "He who, as soon as he was born, being wise, surpassed, encompassed, or overcame with his power—the *kratu* being his action—the gods; he by whose strength even heaven and earth were afraid, through the greatness of his manly vigor (*nṛmṇa*), that one, O people, is Indra. This is a pleasing etymological explanation connected to this meaning (Nirukta 10.10).
1. *ca-jha* 1–*ṇa* 1–*mādhyaṃdinaḥ*; *tha-na-ma-va* in the *Mādhyaṃdina* [recension]. 2. In *jha* 1–*ṇa-ta-tha-na-va*, the word “*eva*” is absent.
3. *ka-jha-ṇa-ta-tha-na-ma-va*: by way of being protected (*rakṣatvena*); in *jha* 1: by way of being preserved (*rakṣyatvena*).

4. In this view (kha-ga), *kya* is substituted by *vyatyaya*; in this view (ṇa-ta-tha), *kasa* is substituted by *vyatyaya* in the suffix; in this view (ma), *sa* is substituted by *vyatyaya* for the root *pavati*.
5. [The forms] *jāta* are derived from kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ṇa 1-tatha-na-va.

He who struck down the trembling earth, who set the agitated mountains at rest, who measured out the vast mid-air, and who propped up the sky—he, O people, is Indra. 2. He who [struck down] the earth while it was trembling; he who [set] the mountains while they were agitated; he who measured out the mid-air more widely; he who propped up the sky—he, O people, is Indra. 2.
O people, that Indra who struck down the trembling, moving earth and made it firm with pebbles and other materials—[he is Indra].
‘The root dṛh means to grow strong.’
And he who restrained the agitated mountains, which were moving here and there and possessed of wings, having bound them, established them each in their own place.
He caused to rest (*aramṇāt*).
[The root] *ram* [is used] in the sense of "sporting. The suffix *śrā* is applied to the causative form (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) of this root, with the addition of the *vyathi* augment.
And he who measured out—that is, fashioned and made extensive—the exceedingly vast and widest atmosphere;
and who propped up the sky, making it firm and supporting it.
The verbal root *stambh* meaning "to obstruct" is a Vedic (sautra) root.
"This very one is Indra; it is not I."

He who, having slain the serpent, set the seven rivers free; he who drove out the cattle by opening the enclosure of Vala; he who generated fire between two stones; he who prevails in battles—he, O people, is Indra. (3) He who, having slain the serpent, released the seven rivers; he who drove forth the cows by breaking open the stronghold of Vala; he who produced fire within the two pressing-stones; he who is victorious in conflicts—he, O people, is Indra. (3)
He who, having slain the serpent Ahi—that is, having performed the slaying of the cloud—caused the seven rivers, the waters characterized by flowing, to flow;
or alternatively, he caused the seven principal rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, to flow.
The root *sravaṇe* (to flow) begins with *ṛ*.
It belongs to the *ṛy-ādi* group.
And he drove out— that is, led forth— the cows that had been hidden by Vala, the one named Vala, an asura, through his stratagem consisting of the obstruction of the fire.
*Apadhā*: From the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *apa*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*) according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.3.106 (*ātaścopasarge*).
The form of the ablative case ending is replaced by *ā* according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 7.1.39 (*supāṃ suluk...*).
And that which is between the two stones:
the *aśman* is the cloud, for it pervades (*aśnute*) and fills the intermediate space;
[it refers to] two clouds of extreme density.
Within [the fire-drill], in its midst, he generated— that is, brought forth— the lightning-fire;
and he who [is present] in the *samadas*—
for *samadaḥ* refers to battle, as the lives of the warriors are consumed therein.
Among them, he becomes unrestrained.
For it is a form derived from the root *vṛṇakti*, meaning "to injure," with the suffix *kvip*.
"He is Indra, not I."

He by whom all these moving things were made, who cast the Dāsa race down into the depths; he who, like a gambler winning the stake, seized the prosperities of the enemy—he, O people, is Indra. By whom these, all moving things, were made; who cast the Dāsa race down into the depths; he who, like a gambler winning, took the stake—the prosperities of the enemy—he, O people, is Indra. (4)
1. He made [the letters] kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, ṇa, 1, ta, tha, na, ma, and va obstructed by the pillar (stambha).
2. [The letters] jha, ṇa, tha, na, and va were obstructed. 3. Ca is in Prasravaṇa; ṇa, 1, ta, tha, na, and va are in Śravaṇa.
4. *Saṃvṛk*: he who gathers together (*saṃvṛṇakti*) and destroys his enemies is *saṃvṛk*.
By that Indra, all these perishable worlds (*bhuvanāni*), these various things (*viśvā vyacanā*), were made—that is, they were rendered firm.
And he who made the *dāsa*—the dark-skinned [class], such as the Śūdra and others;
or alternatively, the *dāsa* as one who oppresses—the lowly *asura*, hidden in a cave, that is, in a secret place or in hell. He made him so.
The form [of *kṛ*] in the *luṅ* tense is derived by the elision (*luk*) of *cli* according to the rule “*mantre ghasa*” and so forth.
Having conquered the target, the mark.
‘ji jaye’ (the root *ji* in the sense of victory).
Why [is there] the substitution of *k* for the letter following the reduplication? [It is] by the rule ‘sanalliṭojeḥ’.
The long vowel is Vedic.
He has conquered;
he who is the purpose of the enemy.
In the singular number, the substitution of *yaṇ* is a Vedic usage.
He seizes the flourishing and prosperous possessions of the enemy.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a dog.
One who kills deer with dogs is a *śvaghnī*, a hunter;
just as a hunter seizes a deer he wishes to capture, so it is in this case.
When they ask, "Where is that terrible one? or "He is not here," he, the noble one whose strength is nourishment, destroys them with his power; place your faith in him, for he, O people, is Indra.

Whom they ask, "Where is he?"—of him they say, "He is terrible," and yet they say of him, "He does not exist. He destroys the prosperity of the enemy like a reaper cutting stalks of grain. Place your trust in him; he, O people, is Indra. 5.
People, not seeing him—the terrible slayer of enemies—used to ask, "Where is he?
[asking], "Where does that Indra abide?"
She lies there.
By the rule "so'ci lope cedādapūraṇam," when the *s* is elided, *guṇa* [substitution] occurs.
Thinking that he does not abide anywhere, people say of this Indra, "This Indra does not exist.
And so says a mantra: "Some indeed say, 'Indra does not exist'" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.100.3).
The particle *īm* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).
That Indra,
being truly like one who causes agitation (vijahva),
utterly destroys (ā mināti) the prosperities— the wealth consisting of cattle, horses, and so forth that nourish— the enemy's possessions.
The root *mī* is used in the sense of "to injure" (*hiṃsā*).
According to the rule “*mīnāter nigame*,” there is a shortening of the vowel.
Therefore, place faith in this Indra;
have confidence here that "this Indra exists.
Even though he is not specifically perceived by us, nevertheless, have confidence that he exists.
Thus, he is Indra, endowed with such greatness that it must be distinguished [from others]; "I am not he."

He who is the impeller of the wealthy man, who [is the impeller] of the needy, who [is the impeller] of the priest who lacks means and is a singer; he who is the protector of the one who has set the pressing-stones in motion and has pressed the soma—he, O people, is Indra, the fair-cheeked one.

He who is the impeller of the wealthy, he who is [the helper] of the lean, he who is [the protector] of the Brahmin, of the one who does not seek wealth, of the singer, and of him who has yoked the pressing-stones; he who is the protector of the one who has pressed the Soma, O fair-cheeked one—he, O people, is Indra. 6.
1. Kha, ga, ṇa, pha: *viśvā viśvāni*; ca: *viśvāni*. 2. Kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, pha: *jighṛkṣantam*; ṇa, ta, tha, na, va: *jighṛkṣatam*. 3. Kha, ga, ca, jha: *mantraiḥ*; jha, ta, tha, va: *mantre*.
4. Endowed with the greatness of the definitive determination [of the letters] kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, ṇa, 1, tha, na, va;
he who belongs to *radhas*.
[The root] *radh* is used in the senses of "injury" (*hiṃsā*) and "accomplishment" (*saṃrāddhi*).
He becomes an impeller of wealth for the prosperous;
and he is an impeller for the emaciated, the poor, and the one who is suffering. [The term] *naṣṭa* refers to those devoid of wealth, sacrifice, austerity, sovereignty, and fame.
Of one who is begging;
of the root *kṛ* (to do) or *kīrt* (to proclaim); or of one who praises.
"He is the impeller of the riches of *brahman* and the *brāhmaṇa*;

he who, being *suśipra*—having beautiful jaws or a beautiful head—is *yuktaprācchaḥ*, with his mouth raised for the purpose of pressing; he who becomes the protector and guardian of the sacrificer who has pressed the *soma* (*sutasoma*)—he alone is Indra, not I.
If the word *brahman* were to retain its own accent, it would have the acute accent on its first syllable, as in: *brahma vanvāno ajaraṃ suvīram* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.8.2).
But this [word *indra*] is recited with the acute accent on the final syllable; therefore, there is no other [form] here.
He whose horses, whose cows, whose villages, and whose chariots are all his own;
he who generated the sun and the dawn, he who is the leader of the waters—he, O people, is Indra.

7 | He whose horses are in every direction, whose cattle, whose villages, and whose chariots are all his; he who brought forth the sun and the dawn, he who is the leader of the waters—he, O people, is Indra. 7 |||
In whose direction—that is, in whose instruction and governance—there abide horses, being secure;
in whose instruction abide cows;
and in whose instruction abide the villages.

The *grāma*s are those who seize [the enemy] here; they are the people of the countryside (*janapada*). He under whose command all the chariots (*ratha*) move—He who, having slain Vṛtra, brought forth the sun, that is, caused it to be born.
And he who is the generator of the Dawn;
likewise, the mantra says: "The one of great deeds generated the Sun and the Dawn" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.32.8).
And he who, by means of splitting the clouds, is the leader and impeller of the waters—he is Indra; such is well known.
He whom the two contending armies, both the distant and the near enemies, invoke;
though they have mounted the same chariot, they call upon him separately—he, O people, is Indra.

The two contending armies, pressing together, call out to one another from the far side and the near side; both sides, having mounted the same chariot, invoke [the gods] separately. He, O people, is Indra. 8.
The two armies—the human and the divine—which are crying out, making a sound, and which, as they encounter and join one another, invoke Indra variously for the sake of their own protection;
whom both kinds of enemies, the superior and the inferior, call upon;
those two chariot-warriors, having mounted that same common chariot comparable to Indra’s, invoke him separately and individually.

Alternatively, Indra and Agni—who are equal in that they have mounted the same chariot—are invoked separately by the sacrificers for the sake of the sacrifice; of those two, one says, "I am that Indra, not he.
1. *ma-ya*: of the emaciated (*kṛśasya*).
2. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ṇa-1-tha-na*: both invoke; *jha-1*: they invoke in both ways.

Without whom people do not conquer, whom those engaged in battle invoke for protection; he who has become the counterpart of the universe, he who is the shaker of the unshakable—he, O people, is Indra. 9. Without whom people do not conquer, whom those engaged in battle invoke for protection; he who has become the counterpart of the universe, he who is the shaker of the unshakable—he, O people, is Indra. 9.
Since, O people, without him men do not conquer— that is, they do not attain victory—
therefore, while engaged in battle, men invoke that Indra for protection,
for their own preservation; he who has become the likeness, the representative, of the entire world.
And he who is the "shaker of the immovable"—the shaker of mountains and other things that are "acyuta," meaning devoid of decay—that is Indra; this and more is well known.

He who slew the many who were committing great sin and acting with arrogance; he who does not grant a hearing to the defiant man; he who is the slayer of the Dasyu—he, O people, is Indra. He who [slew] the many who were committing great sin and acting without restraint; he who slew the cruel one; he who does not yield to the defiant man who seeks a hearing; he who is the slayer of the Dasyu—he, O people, is Indra.

With that weapon called *śarva*, which destroys enemies (*śrṇāti śatrūn*), he struck down those many people— countless and numerous— who had committed great sin, who were thoughtless, who did not know themselves, or who did not honor Indra.
This is the form of the perfect tense (liṭ) of the root *han*.

And he who does not grant—that is, does not bestow—upon a person who is arrogant, who exerts effort, and who lacks self-knowledge, that deed which is worthy of being heard and worthy of being undertaken with effort.
The root *dhā* (from *dhā-dāne*, belonging to the *juhotyādi* class) is used in the sense of giving in sequence.

The initial syllable is unaccented (*anudātta*) according to the rules "the first of reduplicated forms" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*) and "when followed by a *tiṅ* ending with an acute accent" (*tiṅi codāttavati*), resulting in the suppression of the accent of the verbal prefix (*gati*).
And he who is the slayer, the destroyer, of the *dasyu*—the enemy who oppresses—he is Indra; the rest is as explained previously.

He who discovered Śambara dwelling in the mountains in the fortieth autumn; he who slew the dragon Ahi as he displayed his prowess—the Dānu lying there—he, O people, is Indra. (11) He who [discovered] Śambara, dwelling in the mountains, in the fortieth autumn; he who slew the dragon Ahi as he was displaying his might—the Dānu lying there—he, O people, is Indra. (11)

He who, in the fortieth autumn—that is, in the fortieth year—found Śambara, the deceptive Asura of that name, dwelling in the mountains; having remained hidden for many years out of fear of Indra, living in mountain caves;
and having found him, [he slew him] as he was exerting his power.
The elision of the *sakāra* occurs by the rules "kartuḥ kyaṅ ca salopaśca" and "ojaso'psaraso nityam" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.11 and 2).
"He, Indra, struck—that is, slew—the serpent who was exerting his strength, the Dānu, the Dānava, and the lying Śambara, the Ura; it was not I."

He who, the bull with seven rays, the mighty one, let loose the seven rivers to flow; he who, thunderbolt in arm, struck down Rauhina as he was ascending to heaven—he, O people, is Indra. 12. He who, the bull with seven rays, the mighty one, let loose the seven rivers to flow; he who, thunderbolt in arm, struck down Rauhina as he was ascending to heaven—he, O people, is Indra. 12.

"He who is *Saptaraśmi*—he whose rays are seven in number, namely the rain-clouds (*parjanya*). And those rays are indeed mentioned in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (1.9.4–5): 'The boars, self-powerful, of wide splendor, the showerers, the heat-givers, the household-sacrificers—these and these other rain-clouds, the seven *aśmididriya*, rain upon the earth with showers. He is the "bull" (*vṛṣabha*), the showerer; "mighty" (*tuviṣmān*), meaning possessed of growth or strength. He "released for flowing" (*avasṛjat*) the "seven rivers," that is, the waters which have the nature of flowing. He has set them loose.
Or rather, he created the seven principal rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā;
and being "Vajrabāhu" (the one with the thunderbolt-armed), he "sphurat"—that is, struck—Rauhiṇa, the Asura who was ascending to "dyām," the heaven.
The root *sphur* means "to throb" or "to quiver";
it belongs to the *tudādi* class.

Even Heaven and Earth bow down before him; even the mountains tremble at his might. He who is the drinker of Soma, the one established [in power], whose arms bear the thunderbolt, whose hand holds the thunderbolt—he, O people, is Indra. 13. Even Heaven and Earth bow down before him; even the mountains tremble at his might. He who is the drinker of Soma, the one established [in power], whose arms bear the thunderbolt, whose hand holds the thunderbolt—he, O people, is Indra. 13.
To this Indra, [O] Heaven and Earth!
The dual number is used because of mutual dependence, as in the Vedic verse: "Of Mitra and Varuṇa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.66.1).
These two bow down of their own accord.
The root *nam* means "to bow" or "to be inclined.

In the case of the reflexive (karmakartṛ) construction, there is a prohibition of the suffix *yak* by the rule: "In the case of the roots *duh*, *stun*, and *nam*, the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* are prohibited."
Moreover, even the mountains tremble with fear from the *śuṣma*, the strength, of this Indra.
He is the drinker of Soma, the protector of Soma, and is firmly established by all;
or rather, he possesses firm limbs even compared to other gods.
"He who has arms like a vajra, whose arms are truly like a vajra,
and who holds a vajra in his hand— that one is Indra," and so forth, as is well known.

"He who protects—that is, guards—the sacrificer who presses the soma;
and he who [protects] him who cooks the sacrificial offerings such as the *puroḍāśa*; and he who [acts] for the sake of aid (*ūtī*)."
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is a long vowel of the same quality as the preceding sound for the dative case.
Weapons [are for] the protection of the voice.
1. *jha-ma-samaraśmayaḥ*.
2. *tha-yaḥ*: He who protects—that is, guards—the one who praises (*śaṃsantam*) and the one who exerts himself in praise (*śaśamānam*);
he for whom the sacred formulation (*brahma*), the hymn of praise (*stotra*), is the means of increase, that is, the cause of his growth.
Likewise, he for whom Soma is the cause of growth,
and for whom this our gift (rādhas)— consisting of sacrificial cakes and the like— is here the means of prosperity,
that one is Indra; thus it is well known.
O Indra, you who indeed shatter even the firm stronghold for the one who presses and cooks [the oblation], you are truly a friend to us.
May we, ever dear to you, O Indra, and possessed of heroic sons, proclaim our wisdom at the assembly.

O you who, for the one who presses the juice and for the one who cooks the oblation, even from afar shatter the enemy’s wealth—you indeed are truly real. O Indra, may we always be dear to you, and with brave sons, may we proclaim our wisdom at the assembly. 15.
