1. To her who has become our abode: O Indra, the householders—distributing the nourishment, the wealth given by you which sustains them, among their own offspring, making divisions such as "this much for him" and "that much for her"—remain, dwelling each in his own home.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Just as people distribute and bestow wealth (*rayi*)— which is capable of supporting and sustaining— to a guest who is approaching their home, so too does the world,

performing works such as the building of bridges and embankments (*asinvan*), consume with its teeth (*daṃṣṭraiḥ*) the food— that is, water— which has come from the protective heaven (*pituḥ divaḥ*), as well as the plants that are produced from it.

Or rather: "Unsatiated" (*asinvan*), meaning not being appeased, he eats with his "fangs"—that is, with flames in the form of teeth—the food characterized by the oblation belonging to the "protector" (*pituḥ*), namely the sacrificer.
The rest, beginning with "he who made them," is established [as previously explained].
You made the earth a vessel for the sky, you who cleared the paths for the flowing rivers;
as the gods brought you forth with hymns like a prize-winning steed with water, so may you, O God, be worthy of our praise.

Then you made the earth meet with the sky, O slayer of Ahi, who cleared the paths for the rivers; as such, the gods have generated you, a god, with hymns like waters for a prize-winning steed—you are worthy of praise. 5.
O Indra, furthermore, you made the earth—which was trembling—firm for the shining sun, and you rendered it beautiful to behold.
The word *viśve* is established as an indeclinable (*nipāta*) by virtue of ending in the suffix *ca*.
And you, who cleared the paths—the routes—of the *dhautī* rivers, the flowing streams;
that is to say, you made them fit for travel.
The root *ric* is used in the sense of "purging.
In the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense, the suffix is *sip*;
its elision occurs by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisy apṛktaṃ hal*.
O Indra, slayer of Ahi, worthy of being praised, the gods—the singers of praise—have generated and magnified you, such a god, with hymns of praise (*stomaiḥ*).
Therein lies this illustration:
like [strengthening] a vigorous horse with water.
Just as they cause a spirited horse to grow with water and fodder, so it is in this case.
By the rule beginning with "padannomās," there is the substitution of "udan" for "udaka."
The remainder is established.

You who have milked the food, the gift, and the nourishment—both moist and dry, and full of sweetness—you have established that treasure with Vivasvat; you alone rule over all, and you are worthy of praise.

You who provide nourishment and increase, from the moist you have milked the dry and the honey-sweet; you have established the auspicious dwelling for Vivasvat. You alone rule over all; therefore, you are worthy of praise. 6.
O Indra, you who bestow enjoyment— that which is enjoyed, such as food and the like— upon the sacrificers, you grant it to them.
The root *day* (daya) is used in the sense of giving, moving, protecting, winter, and seizing;
it is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Furthermore, you bestow wealth or strength that causes growth;
likewise, from a moist stalk, you have milked out—that is, produced—the dry, non-moist rice and other grains, endowed with sweet sap.
In the periphrastic perfect (liṭ) of the root *duh*, the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule regarding roots beginning with *ṛ*.
O such as you are, while Vivasvat performs service for you—that is, while he acts as the sacrificer—you establish, you place down, a treasure-trove, a seat of wealth.
What more need be said?
Being the one and only lord of the entire world, you alone rule as its master.
In the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), [the root] *īś*;
by the rule "after *īś*, *sa*," there is the augment *iṭ*.
The verse beginning with "saḥ" and so forth is established.

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Jha, 1, Ṇa, Ta, Na, and Va, it reads "asyaitāvat" (of this much). 2. In the manuscripts Ka, Jha, and Ma, it is "apramiḍram" (unmeasured). 3. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, and Ca, it is "arecayaḥ" (without movement). 4. In manuscript Kha, it is "kāṣṭhāt" (from wood). 5. In the manuscripts Ka, Jha, Ṇa, 1, and Ma, it is "madhurasaupetam" (endowed with sweet flavor).

You who have established upon the gift the flowering plants and their productions according to the cosmic law (*dharma*), and you who have spread out the unequalled, bright, and wide-reaching lightnings of heaven on every side—he, you are worthy of praise. You who have established upon the gift the flowering plants and their productions according to the cosmic law, and you who have spread out the unequalled, bright, and wide-reaching lightnings of heaven on every side—he, you are worthy of praise.

O Indra, you who [rule] over the flowering plants, those already in flower, the germinating seeds, those already sprouted, and those currently being produced—the protectors and supporters—upon the gift.
The field of giving (*dānakṣetra*) is that wherein beings are addressed and [their merit] is measured;
it is formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇe*).
In that field, you established and deposited all characteristics through your action;

and you, O Indra, for whom ten times a hundred bay horses (*harayaḥ*) exist for the purpose of drawing [the chariot]— known for that sake as a cause of happiness— belonging to that one, shining Sūrya of heaven, who is alone or preeminent.
And thus says the Vedic mantra: "Indra moves in manifold forms through his powers of illusion (māyā), for his bay horses are yoked by hundreds and tens" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.47.18).
Moreover, he who is the "Ādya," the one upon whom everyone everywhere depends for sustenance—according to the Śruti: "Neither those who eat nor those who do not eat have mastery over him."
And since you have protected the sacrificer who impels the hymns of praise;
furthermore, for Dabhīti, in a prison free from ropes—meaning devoid of cords—you [subdued] the Dasyus, those who cause destruction.
(Dabhīti was indeed a certain person by name.)
For that purpose, you have indeed destroyed the ocean.
In the word *ubhateḥ*, the suffix *śnam* is substituted for *aṅ* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*) in the *laṅ* tense;
the elision of the *mip* ending is according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*;
and the absence of the augment *aṭ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Furthermore, *suprābhyaḥ* means "easily approachable by all";
it belongs to the *tudādi* class and is marked with a circumflex accent (*svarita*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that it is praiseworthy because you cause his wealth to reach the worshippers. *Sahasvataḥ* means "of the powerful one. *Jātūṣṭhirasya* refers to a certain person of this name.
His vigor is his food; he has indeed found it. Or rather, the construction is as follows:

*jātuṣṭiḥ* means "at all times" (*jātu kadācit sarvadā*) [the one] who finds the vigor—characterized by the oblation—which pertains to the ritual acts such as sacrifice, belonging to him who is steadfast (*sthirasya*) and powerful (*sahasvataḥ*). Thus is the connection.
Whatever other deeds there are, all those you have performed;
as such, you are worthy of praise, to be extolled by all.
You brought rest to Sarapa, for the sake of Turvīti and Vṛttra, and you brought forth the son.
You raised up the outcaste who was lying low; you made the blind and the lame hear—worthy of praise are you.

You brought rest; you brought swift action; for Taraya and Kam, and for Turviti and Vṛtti, you brought forth the pressed juice. You raised up the outcast who was lowly; you brought fame to the blind and the lame. Such are you—you are worthy of praise. 12.

O Indra, you made those waters—those whose activity is swift—to flow easily for the crossing; you sported with them. Furthermore, for Turvīti—a certain royal seer—and for Vṛtrī as well, and for Vayya by name, you caused Suti, Prasthara, and Nābhānediṣṭha to cross. For those two, having seen a great river filled with water, were unable to cross; they both were rescued by you. You led Parāvṛj—whoever he was, so called because he "shuns" (vṛk) or burns away sins on all sides—who was submerged in water and was lowly, upward. Moreover, you led up another who was lame, making him no longer lame by granting him sight. What were you doing? Excellently proclaiming yourself, making yourself famous. Thus is the connection of the words "you led up. The rest is established.
O Vasu, prepare for us that wealth to be given; great is the abundance of your riches.
O Indra, whatever wondrous thing you have for the sake of glory day after day, may we, with brave sons, proclaim it loudly at the assembly.

O Vasu, prepare for us that wealth to be given as a gift; great is your abundance of riches, O Indra, which is wondrous and sought after for glory day by day. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.

O *Vasu*, the dweller of all, O possessor of wealth, O *Indra*, bestow that wealth (*rādhas*) upon us, your worshippers, for the sake of giving—this is an elliptical expression meaning "and for the sake of enjoyment. Grant it; the sense is: "Unite us with it. The root *arth* (in the sense of "to request") belongs to the *curādi* class, is *adanta*, and is *ātmanepada*. That abundant (*bahu*) and plentiful (*prabhūta*) treasure (*vasavyam*)—*vasavya* is derived from *vasu* with the suffix *yat* in the sense of identity (as per the rule *vasv-āditvāt svārthiko yat*)—such great wealth indeed exists, which is wonderful (*citram*) and worthy of admiration (*cāyanīyam*), day after day (*anu dyūn*). The accusative case is used here according to the rule *kālādhvanoḥ...*. "May you desire what is to be enjoyed (*śravasyāḥ*)"—since the root *śravas* has the sense of "to eat" (*annarṇātiṇyarthatvāt*), it is *akarmaka* (intransitive), just as in the expression "he weeps" (*rodati*). True; there are two objects here: the object of reference (*uddeśyakarma*) and the object to be enjoined (*vidheyakarma*). It is the object to be enjoined; [the verb] becomes transitive (*sakarmaka*) by virtue of the object of reference.

1. Kha reads *advayaḥ*; Na reads *ādyayaḥ*; Jha reads *apedyaḥ*; Ṇa reads *ābhyaḥ*. 2. Ka reads *pra* in the sense of excellence (*prakaryeṇa*); Ma reads *prava*(ka)*thaṃ*. 3. Kha reads *antarbhāvitaṇyarthatvāt*; Pha reads *antarbhāvitaṇyarthāt*; Ma reads *antararṇyarthatvāt*.
It will occur,
as illustrated in the Bhāṣya [on Pāṇini 3.1.8] with the example *māṇavakaṃ putrīyati* ("he treats the boy as a son").
According to the Vedic rule, the suffix *kyac* is applied after the word *dhruva* when expressing a desire for another.
The form [is derived] from that ending with the addition of *lekhyāt*.
Being virtuous, possessing excellent sons and grandsons, may we, in this triple sacrifice (*tridatha*), speak forth vast and abundant speech, such as hymns and the like.
The third hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "Adhvaryavo bharata," is by Gṛtsamada, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and addressed to Indra.
It is cataloged as "Adhvaryavo dvādaśa. The application of this hymn is determined by its internal indicative marks (liṅga).
In the first round of the Atirātra sacrifice, the offering verse for the Hotṛ's recitation is "O Adhvaryus!
and the invitatory verse is "O Adhvaryus, bring Soma for Indra" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4). This is how it is formulated in the Sūtra.

O Adhvaryus, bring the Soma for Indra; pour out the intoxicating food with the stones. For the hero desires his drink at all times; offer it to the bull, for he indeed longs for this. O Adhvaryus! Bring! To Indra! Soma!
With the stones—which burn like a tree—bring this Soma toward the high altar for that Indra who desires it, who is subject to its power, and who longs for the Soma.
This Indra deserves the drinking, the sipping, of this soma.
O Adhvaryus, he who struck down Dabhīka, who drove out the cattle, and who indeed split Vala asunder—
for that Indra, like the wind in the mid-air, clothe him with Soma-offerings as one clothes oneself with worn garments.
O Adhvaryus! Him who struck down Dabhīka, who drove out the cattle and cast Vala away—clothe that Indra with Soma-offerings in the mid-air, as one wraps a swift steed in garments. 3.

O Adhvaryus, that Indra who [slew] Dabhīka—Dabhīka is the name of an Asura who causes fear by rending those who offer libations—he slew that Asura; and he who drove out the cows confined by the Asura Vala, and then indeed opened up (apa-avṛṇot) that very Vala—the meaning is that he struck him down. Regarding the root *vṛ* (to cover/open) in the *luṅ* tense: "O Adhvaryus, that Indra who [slew] Adhma"—Adhma is so called because he devours (*abhāti*) the host of living beings.

Alternatively, *aśva* refers to a certain Asura who pervades everything through his own unimpaired splendor (*akṣute svatejasi*); he [Indra] struck down that Asura thoroughly (*su*) and completely (*su*).
He who struck down the inauspicious *śuṣṇa*, the demon who could not be dried up by anyone; and he who, having rendered that demon *vyaṃsa*—meaning deprived of his shoulders—struck him down;

and he who, with his splendor, pervading the world, struck down the demon *Namuci*, whose name signifies this very [pervasion]. Regarding Namuci, the *Taittirīyaka* elaborates upon his slaughter in a series of statements beginning with "He did not seize the demon Namuci" and ending with "He caused his head to fall off with foam" (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 1.7.1.5–6).

Likewise, there is a mantra: "With the foam of the waters, Indra struck off the head of Namuci" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.14.13). To that Indra who slew the Asura named Rudhrikā, offer—yea, offer—the *andhas*, the foods characterized by oblations.

O Adhvaryus, he who shattered the hundred fortresses of Śambara as if with a stone in the early morning; Indra, who scattered the hundred thousand followers of Vṛcīna—bring the Soma to him! 6. O Adhvaryus, he who split the hundred citadels of Śambara like a stone against the eastern [forts]; Indra, who cast down the hundred thousand of Vṛcīna—bring the Soma to him! 6.
O Adhvaryus, that Indra who shattered the many ancient hundred fortresses of the illusory Asura Śambara with his thunderbolt, which was like a stone; and that Indra [who likewise struck] Vṛcīna...
The root *varc* is used in the sense of "to shine.
The suffix *ini*, which is prescribed by the rule *gameḥ iniḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.446), occurs here because it is taught with a plural marker.
Alternatively, this is a conventional name (*nāman*).
He struck down—that is, simultaneously cast to the ground—the hundred, the thousand, these countless heroes of that Asura.
Thus says a Vedic verse: "Together you slew the hundred and the thousand irresistible heroes of the Asura Varcin" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.99.5).
Therefore, bring the Soma to this Indra.
O Adhvaryus, he who, having slain [the foe], cast down a hundred and a thousand in the lap of the earth—he, the son of Kutsa, the descendant of Atithigva, chose the heroes; bring Soma for him!
O Adhvaryus! He who struck down a hundred and a thousand in the lap of the earth—having slain the heroes of Kutsa, Āyu, and Atithigva, he has cast them down; bring the Soma to him! 7.
O Adhvaryus, that Indra who, having previously slain his enemies, cast down a hundred thousand Asuras into the lap— that is, the bosom— of the earth, striking them down one by one;
furthermore, [he who protected] Kutsa, the royal seer of this name, and Āyu, the royal seer Pauruvasa.
He struck down the three heroes of Atithigva Divodāsa— namely Śuṣṇa and the other Asuras who were their adversaries and challengers.
For the root *vṛj* signifies the act of harming.
He slew [the demons].
And thus says a Vedic mantra: "You protected Kutsa in the slaying of Śuṣṇa, and you helped Atithigva against Śambara" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.51.6).
To such an Indra, bring the Soma.
1. Furthermore, that asura called Tama does not exist.

O Adhvaryus, O leaders of men, whatever you desire, bring that to Indra by carrying it with speed; O performers of sacrifice, offer the Soma, purified by the hands, to the renowned Indra. O Adhvaryus, O leaders of men (*naraḥ*), whatever you desire to obtain—[the verb *kāmayādhve* is derived from *kam*, with the addition of the suffix *lyap*]—by carrying [the offering] with speed (*śruṣṭī*) to Indra, you shall attain (*naśatha*) that desired fruit. To the renowned Indra, who is famous in the world, bring (*bharata*) the Soma purified by the hands (*garbhastipūtam*) through cleansing, milking, and other rites, toward the northern altar. Then, O Adhvaryus who perform the sacrifice (*yajyavaḥ*), offer (*juhota*) the brought Soma to Indra; cast it into the fire.

O Adhvaryus, perform for him what is easy to do; pour out the Soma that has been purified in the wood-vessel. Being pleased, he longs for that which is pressed by your hands; offer the intoxicating Soma to Indra. O Adhvaryus! Perform (*kartana*) for this [Indra] what is easy to do (*śruṣṭi*). "Perform" is from the root *kṛ* in the imperative; the suffix is elided according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, and *tan* is substituted for *ta* according to *tasanasanathanāśca*. Because it is a vocative, it is not subject to the *nighāta* accent. Furthermore, pour out (*unnayadhvam*) the Soma that has been purified (*nipūtam*)—cleansed by swelling—in the "wood," meaning in the water, or rather, in the "wood," i.e., in the cup (*camasa*) made from it, having been purified by the ten-stranded filter (*daśāpavitra*). Being pleased (*juṣāṇaḥ*), that Indra longs (*vāvaśe*) for the Soma pressed by your hands (*hastyaṃ*). From the root *vaś* (to desire); the form is derived from the present tense with the suffix *yac* elided, and the middle voice is used by metrical license (*vyatyaya*), with the *t* dropped according to *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu*. Offer (*juhota*) this intoxicating (*madiraṃ*) Soma to Indra; throw it into the fire by means of Indra.

O Adhvaryus, fill up with milk this Indra, the enjoyer, who is inclined toward us through the Soma-offerings, just as one fills the udder of a cow. I know his secret; he has perceived me as one desiring to give more, even though I am the worshipper. adhvaryavaḥ | payasā | ūrdhvaḥ | yathā | goḥ | somabhiḥ | im | pṛṇata | bhojam | indram | veda | aham | asya | nibhṛtam | me | etat | ditsantam | bhūyaḥ | yajataḥ | ciketa ||10||
1. *ka-na-ma-kāmayādhve* means "you desire.
2. *kha-ga-jha-jha-va-māñna*; *ka-ca-ja-ṇa-ṇa-ya-ta-pha-ma-āñna*; *ta-māñnadohanābhiḥ*.
O *adhvaryus*, just as the udder of a cow is full of milk, even so, with Soma juices (*somebhiḥ*), fill (*pṛṇata*) this *indra*, the giver and protector of the fruit (*bhojam*).
"I alone know this secret, hidden nature of my own Soma which is the means to bliss"—thus it was not previously told to another; nevertheless, I speak it to you.
Indra, the one who performs the sacrifice, has taken great notice of the sacrificer who desires to bestow the flowing Soma.
Saying this:
[the root] *du-dāj* means "to give";
[the suffix] *san* is used in the sense of desire.
In the form *sani bhīmādhu*, there is the substitution of *is* for the vowel *ā*.

Here, by the rule "elision of the reduplicated syllable" (*atra lopo'bhyāsasya*), the reduplication is elided. Then, by the rule "before an affix beginning with *s* that has an ārdhadhātuka designation," the *s* [of the suffix] becomes *t*.
I shall now proclaim the great and true deeds of this Great One, the truthful acts of Truth.
At the Trikadruka rites, he drank of this pressed juice; in its exhilaration, Indra slew the dragon.
Now indeed I shall proclaim the great, true deeds of this great and true one. At the Trikadruka rites, Indra drank of the pressed soma; in its exhilaration, he slew the serpent Ahi.
Gṛtsamada says:
"Of this great, powerful Indra, whose resolve is true, I shall today proclaim with excellence his true, that is, real, and great deeds—the actions to be described in this hymn.
The root *vac* means "to speak."

While the rule "luṅ-laṅ-liṭaḥ" (the aorist, imperfect, and perfect suffixes are used in the Veda) is in effect, regarding the aorist (luṅ), there is the rule: "aṅ is substituted for [the affixes] after as, vyath, and vyadha. There is also the rule: "um is substituted for vac.
"Gha" is a well-known technical term.
Which ones are they?

They are said to be the days of the *ābhiplavika* [six-day] period, such as those characterized by the *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus* *trikadruka* days. Indra drank the pressed Soma that had been extracted;
then, of this [Soma] that had been drunk...

Just as they construct sacrificial halls with specific measurements, such as being thirty-six steps long and sloping toward the east, so too did Indra measure out the rivers and the worlds, making them flow toward the east with precise dimensions; he fashioned them specifically and, moreover,
pierced the outlets of the rivers with his thunderbolt, digging them open.
The root *tṛd* means "to injure" and "to disregard. It belongs to the *rudhādi* class.
[Present tense] *laṅ*.
And thus says the mantra: "Indra, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, dug out the channels" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.33.6).

Likewise, "by long paths"—meaning by routes to be traversed over a great length of time—he "easily" (vṛthā) created those rivers without effort. Thus, the purpose [of the mantra] is established as "of Soma."

Having brandished all his weapons against the surrounding host of Dabhīti when the fire was kindled, Indra, in the exhilaration of Soma, released him [from bondage] with cattle, horses, and chariots; those deeds he performed.

Having driven forward and surrounded them, he burnt all the weapons of Dabhīti in the kindled fire. He united [the people] with cattle, horses, and chariots; these things Indra accomplished in the intoxication of Soma. 4.
It is said that in ancient times, the asuras such as Cumuri and Dhuni besieged and surrounded the city of Dabhīti; from that city, Indra rescued him—this is the story. "He" refers to Indra.
Dabhīti was also the name of a certain king.
In the word *pravohan*,
[the *u*] becomes *o* by the rule "for the vowel *au* of the roots *sah* and *vah*, there is *o*."

Having seized those Asuras who were excessively carrying that Dabhīti along the middle path, he burnt—indeed, utterly consumed—their entire (*viśvam*) weaponry in the blazing fire, the radiant Vahni; [the form *adhāk* is derived from the root *dah* with the suffix *cli* in the *liṅ* mood, where by the rule *mantra-ghasa-* etc., there is elision of the *cli* suffix.]
Afterwards, he joined that Dabhīti together with cattle, horses, and chariots;
this much from the Soma section is established.

Regarding the *sūktamukhā* of the *maruvatīya* [section] in the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) named *atimūrti*, it is prescribed in the section titled "Atimūrti" in the *Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (9.8): "He has restrained that great roaring river. (*sa īṃ mahīṃ dhunimetoraramṇāt*).
He stilled that great roaring river; he, not swimming, brought those who were swimming safely across.
Having emerged from the water, they stood forth with riches. Indra performed these deeds in the exhilaration of Soma.

He brought that great roaring river to a halt as it flowed; he caused it to flow across without his bathing in it. Having bathed, they stood forth in prosperity through riches. Indra performed these deeds in the exhilaration of Soma. ||5||
That Indra [drives] this great,
mighty *dhuni*— the river Paruṣṇī is called *dhuni* because it shakes away the evils of those who praise him—
from its course.
Even in the absence of the word *īśvara*, the suffix *tosun* [and *na*] is applied [according to Pāṇini 3.4.13].

He caused the sages to rest—that is, he calmed them; the meaning is that he made the great river shallow with little water. Then Indra brought them across in safety—that is, by means of security—to those who were unable to swim, even though they were otherwise capable of crossing.
"Those great seers, having bathed and crossed that river, set forth—meaning they departed—toward that wealth which they were seeking.
The rest is self-evident."

1. With the *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ṇa*, *va*, and many syllables to be traversed over time; with his greatness, he caused the tearful Sindhu to flow. With his thunderbolt, Indra crushed the wagon of Uṣas. O Vibṛśvan, in the exhilaration of Soma, Indra performed those deeds with swift steeds against the sluggish. He caused the tearful Sindhu to flow by his greatness. With his thunderbolt, he crushed the wagon of Uṣas. O Vibṛśvan, in the exhilaration of Soma, Indra performed those deeds with swift steeds against the sluggish.
That Indra, by his own greatness, released the eastward-flowing Sindhu with its rising waters;
he turned it toward the north.
In Vedic literature, the word *sindhu* is masculine in gender.
At the very rising of the Dawn, he crushed— that is, ground to powder— the wagon with his thunderbolt. This will be clearly stated in the verse "Even the daughter of Heaven" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.30.9).
Doing what? Piercing—that is, specifically breaking apart—the slow, sluggish, and weak armies with swift armies;
"he crushed" is the syntactic connection.
The root *ovr* is used in the sense of cutting (*chedane*). In the present participle (*śatṛ*), there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.15 (*grahijyādinā*).
The remainder is clear.

Knowing [the way], he rose up from the hiding place of the crafty ones, becoming manifest in the distance. Śroṇa stood up and stepped forth; Indra performed those deeds in the exhilaration of Soma. 7. He, the knowing one, rising up from the concealment of the crafty ones, became manifest in the far distance. Śroṇa stood firm and strode forth; Indra performed those [deeds] in the intoxication of Soma. 7.
It is said that in ancient times, certain maidens, upon seeing Jigyuṣmūrti—who was devoid of eyes and devoid of feet—rushed toward him.
Thereupon, that seer, having praised Indra, obtained both eyes and feet;
this very fact he expresses [in the following verse].
Knowing the concealment—the hiding or disappearance—of the young maidens, the seer Parāvṛj, becoming manifest and visible to all, rose up.
Śroṇa, who was formerly lame, now, through the grace of Indra, with his knees shining, stood up toward those maidens.
He who was formerly blind now looked out clearly upon them due to the recovery of his sight.
He gazed especially upon those maidens;
Indra performed these very deeds.

Praised by the Aṅgirases, he shattered Vala; he tore apart the firm bolts of the mountain. He released their artificial obstructions; those deeds Indra performed in the intoxication of Soma. 8. He shattered Vala, being praised by the Aṅgirases; he split apart the firm bolts of the mountain. He released their artificial obstructions; those [deeds] Indra performed in the exhilaration of Soma. 8.
Praised and extolled by the Aṅgirases, that Indra split Vala— the Asura named Vala—
and likewise opened wide the bolted doors of the mountain that obstructed the cattle— doors made firm with stones. He explains this very point as follows:
Among these mountains, he opened the embankments that had been constructed artificially, the obstructions, and the closed gates;
the rest has already been explained.
1. [The verses] beginning with *ka* and *jha* are for the *viśvambhājātavedas*.
In the *aikāha* sacrifice named *atimūrti*, when it is performed as a *nikkevalya*, this verse "With sleep... (*svapnena*) serves as the *sūktamukhīyā*.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "With the words 'With sleep,' 'Having approached,' 'Cumuri,' and 'Dhuni,' these are the *sūktamukhīyās*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.8).
In sleep you overpowered Cumuri and Dhuni; you struck down the Dasyu and protected Dabhīti.
Even Rambhi found the golden treasure here; Indra performed these deeds in the exhilaration of Soma.
With sleep, you overpowered and slew Cumuri and Dhuni; you destroyed the Dasyu and protected Dabhīti. Even the pillar found gold there; these things Indra did in the intoxication of Soma. 9.
As such, you struck down—that is, killed—the two Asuras named Cumuri and Dhuni, who were destroyers of all; you did so by inducing them to long sleep through slumber.
Then, you protected Dabhīti, the royal seer, as he was fighting with those two.
And thus says the mantra-text: "You [struck down] the Dasyu Cumuri..."
They chose the house of Aditi.
O sacrificers, for you— for the sake of the great, existing gods, and especially for Indra, the most excellent among them—
[the fire] is kindled like a vessel.
The prefix *vi-* has the sense of "shining" (*vevārtha*).
I offer (*prabharāmi*) the oblation (*haviḥ*) into the shining fire (*vevāgnau*);
thereafter, I perform a beautiful hymn (*suṣṭutim*), a praise that brings well-being (*śambhanām*).
*Bhara* is derived from the root *bhṛñ*, meaning "to support" (*bharaṇe*); because it ends in the suffix *-ñit*, it is conjugated in both voices (*ubhayapada*).
This is the form in the present tense (*laṭ*).

We invoke—that is, we call upon—that Indra who is the thunderbolt, who is worthy of being invoked with the thunderbolt, who causes all things to age, yet himself does not age; who is firmly established, sprinkled with Soma, ancient, eternal, ever-youthful; such an Indra we invoke for our protection and for his own gratification.

Without whomsoever this great Indra, nothing whatsoever exists; in him all heroic powers are gathered together. In his belly he bears Soma, in his body great strength, in his hand the thunderbolt, and in his head wisdom. From whomsoever—Indra—from the great one, without whom—nothing at all—exists; in him all heroic powers are gathered together. In his belly [he bears] Soma; in his body, great strength; in his hand, he bears the thunderbolt; in his head, wisdom.
From the great, from the vast, from that Indra—who is there that does not find [him]? Not even this moving world; the meaning is that there is none at all.
The two combinations *vna* and *veti* mean "and"; *va* means "or," while *vca* and *vcit* have the sense of "also"; *vna* signifies negation;
however, the reading *vaikapayam* is traditional.
Regarding the meaning already stated, there is a mantra: "Nothing whatsoever flows forth apart from Indra" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.69.6).
Or rather, what is this entire world (*jagat*) apart from Indra?
It means nothing small—that is, nothing insignificant.
Why is this said?
In that Indra, all—meaning every—heroic power, that is, capacity, is exceedingly accumulated; it remains fully gathered.
Furthermore, Indra bears—that is, carries—within his own belly, his own stomach, the pressed Soma, the Soma juice.
Moreover, O slender one, he bears within his own entire body strength, power, and majesty;
he bears the thunderbolt as his weapon in his hand;
and he bears creative wisdom in his head.
There is no *nighāta* (elision of accent) due to the occurrence of two different *vṛtti*s; or, due to the division of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), there is an absence of *nighāta*.
[The word] *śīrṣaṇi*.
"In the Vedic language, [the suffix] vśīrṣan [is used]."

Neither the two worlds can encompass thy power, nor the oceans, O Indra, nor the mountains thy chariot. No one reaches thy thunderbolt when thou fliest with thy swift steeds over many leagues. Neither the two worlds can encompass thy power, nor the oceans, O Indra, nor the mountains thy chariot. No one reaches thy thunderbolt when thou fliest with thy swift steeds over many leagues.
O Indra, that which is yours—your own *indriya*, your strength—is not surpassed by the two worlds, nor by heaven and earth; it is not to be surpassed.
The suffix *kvun* is applied according to the rule *kvun śilpisaṃjñayor apūrvacvāt*;
it is *svarita* (circumflex) by the rule *udāttasvaritayoḥ*.
Moreover, you are not to be overcome by the oceans or the mountains; no man whatsoever can seize your weapon,
the thunderbolt.
He does not seek to overwhelm them with contempt.
‘Aśru-vyāsaḥ’: the *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of transposition.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: whenever, at the time of your world-conquest for the purpose of slaying the Asuras, you travel—going—for many *yojanas*, then in that place your strength and so forth are not to be disregarded.
All bring forth their will to him, the worshipful, the bold, the bull who follows them.
As a bull, sacrifice with oblations, O most wise one; drink the Soma, O Indra, with your bull-like radiance.

For all indeed bring forth their mental power to him, the worshipful, the bold, the bull who follows after them. As a bull, sacrifice with the oblation, O most wise one; drink the Soma, O Indra, with your bull-like luster. 4.

To that Indra—who is the sacrificer; to whom all people belong; who is worthy of sacrifice by all; who is unassailable, having the nature of overcoming enemies; who is a bull, raining down desires; who is peerless among those who possess praise and other virtues; to such an Indra, they indeed bring forth *kratu*, the ritual action characterized by sacrifice and the like;
that is, they offer it up. The meaning is that they present it.
They support [him].
Because it occurs at the beginning of a word, there is no elision of the *hi*.
Since this is so, therefore he is a bull (*vṛṣan*), capable of pouring out the Soma juice, and most wise (*viduṣṭara*).
The substitution of a semivowel (saṃprasāraṇa) after the word *vidut* is also Vedic;
furthermore, according to the rule "of *jñā*, *abhi-tras*, *sighas*, and *sīnām*," there is the substitution of *t* for *s* in the Saṃhitā.
"Knowing this, worship that Indra with an oblation.
Now, having addressed Indra, he says:
"O Indra, drink the Soma together with Bhānu—the blazing fire who rains down desires—acting as a bull [who showers them]."
The vessel of the bull flows forth as a wave of honey, for the bull to drink.
The two bull-like Adhvaryu priests and the bull-like pressing-stones press the bull Soma for the bull [Indra].

The treasure-chest of the bull flows forth; the wave of honey flows for the bull whose food is the bull, that he may drink. The two bulls, the Adhvaryus, and the pressing-stones, which have the bull as their source, press the bull Soma for the bull [Indra]. ||5||

O Indra, the wave—the essence and the vessel of the sweet, exhilarating Soma, which rains down the fruit of the non-showering one—flows forth as it impels those who perform the rites and those who drink it.
The root *pav* means "to go";
it is marked with the anudātta accent.
For what purpose?
He is called "one for whom food increases strength" because he possesses foods that increase strength;
for such a bull, Indra—the showerer of desires—for the sake of drinking (*apātave*), [the soma] flows (*pavate*). This is the syntactical connection.

Furthermore, the two *adhvaryus*—the *adhvaryu* and the *pratiprasthātṛ*—who are "non-seeders" (*avṛṣaṇā*) [in the sense of being incapable of discharging the soma-juice], and the "seeds" (*vṛṣabhāsaḥ*), that is, the rain-giving "stones" (*adrayaḥ*), the pressing-granites, press out the "seed," the Soma—the bestower (*setṛ*) of fruits such as heaven—for you, the "bull" (*vṛṣabhāya*), the most excellent among the gods. They press it out for you.

In the present tense (laṭ) of the root *śru*, the suffix *śru* is substituted for the verbal characteristic (*vikaraṇa*) by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (Pāṇini 2.4.73). Then, by the rule "adbhyastāt" (Pāṇini 7.1.4), the substitution of *śn* for *śi* occurs.
1. In the manuscripts jha and ma, the word “rasaḥ” is absent. 2. In the manuscripts ka, jha, and ma, the terms are vṛṣabha and ṛṣaka.

Thy thunderbolt is a bull, and thy chariot is a bull; thy two bay steeds are bulls, and thy weapons are bulls. O Bull, thou art the lord of the exhilarating draught; O Indra, satisfy thyself with the bull-like Soma. Thy thunderbolt is a bull, and thy chariot is a bull; thy two bay steeds are bulls, and thy weapons are bulls. O Bull, thou art the lord of the exhilarating draught; O Indra, satisfy thyself with the bull-like Soma. "O Bull, O Indra, who showers down desires—thy thunderbolt is a bull, a showerer of desires. Likewise, thy chariot is a bull. Thy two bay steeds named Haris are bulls, showerers [of strength]. Therein, even thy weapons other than the thunderbolt are bulls. Of the 'vṛṣṇaḥ', the showering, intoxicating Soma, thou alone 'īśiṣe', art the master. O Indra, with the 'vṛṣabhasya', the showering Soma, 'tṛṇuhi', be satisfied. [The root] *tṛp* means 'to please'. It belongs to the *svādi* class. Although it is read among the roots beginning with *kṣudh* (Pāṇini 8.4.39) as *tṛpnoti*, nevertheless, because all rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there is no prohibition of the substitution of *ṇ* here."

Like a ship in battle, I approach you with prayer, O you who desire the hymn, seeking you at the libations, O bold one. Will you not surely take heed of this our speech? May Indra, the supreme, hear us; we sprinkle him with wealth as if with water. I approach you with prayer at the libations—O bold one (*dādhrṣi*), you who are the subduer of enemies—I reach you through the hymn (*brahman*) at the three pressings. You who desire the hymn, like a ship that is being boarded, I approach you with prayer at the three libations. Furthermore, may Indra surely and fully take heed of this speech, this statement characterized by praise. We sprinkle Indra—the supreme, like a reservoir of water—with wealth, as if with water. *Note on grammar:* "Dādhrṣi" means "you who are the subduer of enemies. "Vacasyuvam" is derived from *vacas-yu*, meaning "desiring the hymn"; the suffix *-yu* is replaced by *-u* according to Pāṇini’s rules for stems beginning with *tan*. "Nivodhipat" is from the root *budh* (to perceive); the form is in the subjunctive (*leṭ*) with the suffix *-sip* added irregularly. Due to its connection with *kuvid*, it is not subject to the usual accentual suppression (*anudātta*). "Sicāmahe" is from the root *sic* (to pour); the augment *num* is absent because the rule regarding augments is not always mandatory.

Before distress comes upon us, turn toward us, as a cow, swelling with milk, turns toward her calf in the meadow. O Śatakratu, may we once more be united with your gracious favors; like bulls with their mates, may we be joined together. Before distress comes upon us, turn toward us, as a cow, swelling with milk, turns toward her calf in the meadow. O Śatakratu, may we once more be united with your gracious favors; like bulls with their mates, may we be joined together.
1. *ka-jha-ma-dadhr-piḥ* | 2.
*ka-jha-prāpnomi yomi?* | O Indra, from the confinement caused by enemies, from that confinement, turn us back toward [safety] before it is too late.
The meaning is: "Act in such a way that distress does not touch us.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"as a cow [does not abandon] her calf."
Just as a cow that has been nourished by eating grass turns away from hunger and other ailments, so it is here.
O Śatakratu, may we, through your *sumatibhiḥ*—your excellent hymns directed toward you—thoroughly pervade you (*su nasīmahi*), even if only once (*sakṛt sakṛd api*).
In this regard, there is an illustration: [the cow].
Like bulls— just as young stallions are covered by their mates, so too [are they].
Surely, O Indra, may that wealthy sacrificial gift yield a boon for you, for the singer; bestow it upon the praisers.
Let not fortune fail us. May we, blessed with brave sons, proclaim our greatness at the assembly.

Surely, O Indra, may that wealthy sacrificial gift yield its boon to you for the singer; bestow it upon those who praise you, do not withhold it. May Bhaga grant us fortune; may we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 10.
"Surely she is that one"—thus it is explained.
‘Tad asmai’: this is the sixth hymn, consisting of nine verses, addressed to Indra and concerning fragrance (*gandha*).
Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: ‘Tad asmai... ending with two *triṣṭubhs*’.
Two other verses are *triṣṭubhs*; the remainder are *jagatīs*.
In the second round (*paryāya*) of the Atirātra sacrifice, the hymn "tad asmai" is used for the Acchāvāka's recitation (*śastra*).
This is established in the section titled "Atirātre paryāyāṇām" in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra (6.4): "The *yājyā* [verse] is 'tad asmai navyam adya pitre... yasya jajñāna indraḥ'."
Sing praise to him as you did for Aṅgiras, when his surging strengths rise up and strike out;
when, in the exhilaration of Soma, he, the conqueror, has shattered all the encompassing cow-pens and cast down the firmly established fortresses.

Sing to him, the one who belongs to the Aṅgirases, like the rivers; for his impetuous powers rise up when he seeks to fly forth, when he with force has shattered all the encompassing cow-pens that were firmly established in the exhilaration of Soma.
Gṛtsamada says:
O singers, praise this Indra with a new, ever-fresh hymn such as that, whose back is unassailed, just as the Aṅgirases did.
For from the moment of his birth, his vital powers (*śuṣmāḥ*)—the splendors that wither his enemies—were as they were of old.
In the Vedic language, the suffix *thāla* is used in the sense of "like" (*iva*) according to the rule *pratnapūrvaviśvamāt chandasi*.
The ancient things, as if from of old, rise up; they emerge.
The root *īr* means "to go.
It is anudātta (unaccented).
According to the rule “tiṅi codāttavati,” there is nighāta (elision of the accent) of the verb of motion.
*vat* means because; *viśvā* means all; *gotrā* refers to the clouds—so called because they protect (*trāyante*) or preserve (*rakṣanti*) the cows, which are the waters;
*parīvṛtā* means those obstructed or encompassed by Vṛtra.
In all cases, the *sup* case endings are replaced by *dā*.
When the exhilaration (*mada*) of Soma had arisen, he suddenly, by his power (*sahasā*), drove forth—that is, he opened—the clouds that were *daṃhitāni*, made firm by him;
the meaning is that by bursting the clouds, he impelled the waters.
Or rather, [he drove forth] all (*viśvā*) the *gotrā*, the enclosures (*parīvṛtā*) seized by the Asura Vala and confined within the mountain clefts.
The suffix *tra* is applied in the sense of a collection according to the rule *initrakañyacaśca*.
He drove herds of cows together with the Sahamas;
therefore, he caused the *balāṅgiras* to go;
therefore, "one should worship"—such is the connection.
*airayat*: [this is] the form of the causative (*pyanta*) of the root *īr* (meaning "to go") in the *laṅ* tense.
Just as there is no injury due to its connection with that.
1. *Jha-ta-tha*: “From the distress caused by enemies,” this does not exist. 2. *Ṇa-na*: “O you who were brought back by enemies. 3. *Ga-tha-ma*: “By the asura Vṛtra.”

May he be present—he who, measuring out his vigor for the first time, surpassed [all others] by his greatness; the hero who, in battles, clothed his body and by his majesty set his heads against the sky. May he be present. He indeed was he who, measuring out his strength for the primordial support, surpassed all in his greatness; the hero who, in the contests, enveloped his own body and by his might set his heads toward the heavens. 2.
May that Indra be;
that is to say, may he increase.
That Indra, while fashioning—that is, creating—*ojas*, brilliance, and strength, [acts] for the first, primordial sustenance (*dhāyase*).
‘At the drinking of the Soma,’ he increased—that is, he magnified—the greatness [of Indra].
The *ś* [ending] occurs by transposition (*vyatyaya*) from the root *tṛ*;
and because it is [thus] displaced, it does not lose its accent (*anighāta*).
Indra, the hero who shatters his enemies, who in battles (*yutsu*) enveloped his own body with armor,
that Indra by his own greatness (*mahinā*) fastened the heavens upon his heads— that is, he bore them upon his head.

Then you performed your first great heroic deed; at the beginning of this [world], you moved forward with sacred power and vital energies. Shaken loose by the chariot drawn by tawny horses, the swift streams flow forth together and separately. Then you performed your first great heroic deed; at the beginning of this [world], you moved forward with sacred power and vital energies. Shaken loose by the chariot drawn by tawny horses, the swift streams flow forth together and separately.
Moreover, O Indra, you first—that is, primarily—performed that heroic power (*vīrya*).
What was it?

By means of *brahman*—that is, by means of praise consisting of Vedic utterances as the instrument of laudation—you, before this very person who is being praised, raised up (*airayaḥ*) that *śuṣma*, the strength that withers enemies.

The *jīrayaḥ*—the wearers away, the destroyers, the Asuras—having been cast down by you, who stand upon your chariot drawn by tawny horses (*haryaśva*), fall from their own positions; being thus displaced, they gather together in a common direction, yet, separated from one another by fear, they flee in various directions with great speed.
The root *sṛ* means "to go";
it belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class.
By the rule "in the Veda [the substitution] is manifold," the *i*-substitution occurs for the reduplication.
In *sādhyak*, the substitution of *sadhi* for *saha* occurs according to the rule "of *saha*, [the substitute is] *sadhi*.

Because of the specific grammatical prescription (*nipātana*) that the final syllables of *adi* and *sādhya* are udātta, the *yaṇ* vowel [in *sādhyak*] becomes svarita by the rule "of an udātta and a svarita."

Then he, who by his might became the lord of all beings, grew great through his own inherent power; then the bearer [of the sacrifice] overspread heaven and earth with light, and he utterly dispelled the thick darkness. 4. Then he, who by his might became the lord of all beings, grew great through his own inherent power; then the bearer [of the sacrifice] overspread heaven and earth with light, and he utterly dispelled the thick darkness. 4.
1. By the leather of the *ja* and *na*; by the *jha* year. 2.
In *jha₁*, *ṇa-ta-tha-na-va* and ‘by you’ (*tvayā*) do not exist.
3. In *ka-kha-ga-ca-ja-jha-ṇa-ṇa-na-pha-ba*, they are joined (*abhiyuktāḥ*); in *jha₁*, they are joined (*yuktāḥ*).

Moreover, whether he be aged, with limbs fully developed, or ancient—that Indra who, by his majesty and strength, having surpassed all worlds and all people, acts as a sovereign lord, making himself the overlord of all;

or rather, making the other gods, such as Agni and others, the lords of their respective worlds—he grew great on every side and became fully expanded. Immediately thereafter, that Indra, the bearer of the worlds, pervaded both heaven and earth (rodasī) with his own light and splendor.
Furthermore, he enveloped the darknesses—those things of the nature of darkness—and the demons who were ill-situated and distressed; spreading and pervading them, he covered them.
The meaning is that he existed having pervaded the entire world.
By his might, he cast down the waters from the eastern mountain toward the west;
he supported the earth that nourishes all, and by his creative power, the year established its abode.

He, strengthening the eastern mountains with his might, turned the waters downward; he held back the floods of the rivers and established the earth as the sustainer of all. By his creative power, the year-stayer supported the firmament.
That Indra [has brought] those who were turned away from here, as if from the presence of his parents, dwelling together in the same seat; bestow fortune upon us.
Make it manifest; bring it near to us; grant a portion for our own body, by which you have honored me.

Like one who has not yet reached maturity, dwelling together with her parents from a common seat, she has approached you; grant her fortune. Bestow upon me a sign; bring it hither to me. Give me a portion for my body, with which you shall honor me.

O Indra, that daughter who, until her death, grows old at home alone with her parents—remaining with her mother and father, devoted to their service, and honoring her husband—[comes] from the common dwelling, the house shared by herself and her parents.
The ablative case is used here by virtue of the rule: "An addition [to the rule for the locative] should be made regarding the locus."
Just as one who has approached the house asks for his share, so too has this hymn been explained: "Surely that [share] is yours."
The seventh hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “prātā rathaḥ,” is addressed to Indra; it was composed by Gālmada, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is dedicated to Indra.
This is indicated by the introductory statement “prātaḥ.
Its application is determined by its internal characteristics (laiṅga).

The chariot has been brought forth; the new one, rich in gain, has been yoked—four-yoked, three-poled, with seven reins, ten wheels, a man as its driver, and heaven as its protector. It has become swift through sacrifices and prayers.

At dawn, the chariot has been harnessed—the new one, the winner, with four poles, three whips, seven reins, and ten fellies; fashioned by Manu, it wins the light of heaven. It has become swift through our sacrifices and prayers. 1.

The *ratha* (chariot) is so called because of its speed; here, the *ratha* is the sacrifice (*yajña*). And it is "new" (*nava*); it is "new" because it is praised (*nūyate*) and celebrated (*ratūyate*) therein—it is possessed of praise. It is "winning" (*sasni*): from the root *snā* meaning "to purify," with the suffix *kin* according to the rule *āṭagamahana*. Thus it is pure. Such a sacrifice was "yoked" (*ayoji*) by us at every "morning" (*prātaḥ*), that is, at the time of dawn. It has "four yokes" (*caturyuga*): the pressing-stones (*grāvan*) are called "yokes" (*yuga*) because they are joined; he of whom there are four such yokes is so described. Or, it refers to the priests beginning with the *adhvaryu*. It has "three whips" (*trikaśaḥ*): he whose three whips are speech in the forms of low, middle, and high pitch is so described. Or, it refers to the three pressings (*savana*). It has "seven reins" (*saptaraśmi*): the meters (*chandas*) are called "reins" (*raśmi*) because they reach and pervade the ritual acts; he whose meters are seven in number, beginning with the *gāyatrī*, is so described. It has "ten oars" (*daśāritra*): the cups (*graha*) are called "oars" (*aritras*) because they protect (*trāyante*) from enemies (*aribhyaḥ*), that is, from sins; he whose cups are ten in number is such. Or, it refers to the *camasādhvaryu* priests. It is "human" (*manuṣya*): beneficial to human beings. It is "heaven-winning" (*svarpā*): the giver of heaven. Such is the sacrifice. By "offerings" (*iṣṭibhiḥ*)—such as the *prāyaṇīya* and *ātithya* rites—and by "thoughts" (*matibhiḥ*), that is, by hymns worthy of meditation, it is "to be urged" (*raṃhyaḥ*), meaning it is to be proclaimed. It "has become" (*abhūt*). Alternatively: "New" (*nava*) means ever-fresh. "Winning" (*sasni*): this is a form derived from the root *man* with reduplication. It is the "giver of desires. The "chariot" (*ratha*) is so called because people delight (*ramante*) in it; it is a vehicle. And at the morning pressing, it was "yoked" (*ayoji*) by the *adhvaryu* for the purpose of drinking Soma. Of what nature is it? It has "four yokes," "three whips"—meaning it possesses three whips—and "seven reins," meaning seven ropes. It has "ten oars," meaning ten wheels. It is "human," meaning beneficial to humans, and "heaven-winning," meaning the bringer of heaven—the chariot of Indra. It is to be attained through offerings (*iṣṭibhiḥ*), that is, sacrifices, and through "thoughts" (*matibhiḥ*), that is, hymns.
He is for this man as the first, he as the second, and also as the third; he is the Hotṛ of mankind. Others have generated him from the womb of another; he, the noble bull, unites with others.
He [is] for him; he [is] sufficient, first, he second, and also third. He is the Hotṛ-priest of Manu; others have generated him from the womb of another. He, the noble bull, unites with others. 2.
That sacrifice, or Soma, was sufficient for this Indra at the first pressing, the morning libation;
it was also sufficient at the second pressing, the midday libation;
and indeed, it was sufficient even at the third pressing, the third libation.
In all these cases, the accusative case ending is applied according to the rule "akālādhvanoḥ."
That sacrifice, or Soma, becomes the Hotṛ-priest for Manu—that is, for the human being—the bearer of the offerings.

Furthermore, while still the embryo of another earth, or of Speech consisting of the Vedas, the other priests [bring forth] Soma. (Ṛgveda 2.10.1) (Note: The variants provided in the footnotes—such as *daśavaktraḥ* vs. *daśavakrāḥ*, *īḍagrayaḥ*, and *traiyātmikāyāḥ*—indicate textual differences among various manuscript traditions.)
They generated the sacrifice, that is, they produced it.

"Vṛṣan" means one who showers desired fruits; "jenyaḥ" means capable of victory. That sacrifice, or Soma, "sacate"—that is, he joins with or associates with—"anyebhiḥ," meaning with other deities such as Indra and the rest.
‘In the case of *samavāya*, [the suffix] is *anudātta*. || *Anudāttet*. ||
I shall now yoke the two bay horses of Indra with a well-spoken hymn, with splendor, and with manly power;
for here there are many inspired singers, and other sacrificers are crying out to you.

Harness the two bay steeds to Indra’s chariot for the sake of coming hither, with well-spoken hymns and splendor, and with manly power. Indeed, let not many sages here restrain you; for other sacrificers also desire you.

Upon the chariot belonging to Indra, I swiftly yoke the two horses named Hari for the sake of easy arrival, by means of a new hymn consisting of Vedic knowledge— a speech not previously composed by others— using the root *yuj* in the sense of "to join. In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the suffix *cli* is replaced by *aṅ* according to the rule *irito vā*.
In this sacrifice, although there are indeed many wise sages who offer hymns of praise,
nevertheless, let other sacrificers who are neither middling nor superior cause you to rejoice most excellently;
that is to say, come to our sacrifice and drink the Soma— this is the intention.
*rurāma*.

From the root *ram*, in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix, there is the shortening of the vowel and lengthening of the reduplicated syllable due to its treatment as if it were a *saṇt* (as per *sanvadbhāva*).
Because there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) here, as there is no connection [between the two parts].
Come, O Indra, with two bay horses, or with four, being urged on;
come with eight or ten for the drinking of the Soma. This [Soma] has been pressed; O bounteous one, do not neglect it.
Come, O Indra, with two bay steeds; come with four; come, being urged on, with six; come with eight, with ten, to drink the Soma! This [Soma] has been pressed, O liberal giver; do not neglect us. 4.
O Indra, being summoned by the Hotṛ-priests, come toward this sacrifice for the sake of drinking Soma with your two bay horses;
or come with four bay horses;
likewise, arrive with six for the drinking of Soma.
The root *pā* means "to drink. By the rule *aco yat*, the suffix *yat* is applied; by the rule *iṃcati*, the vowel *a* is changed to *i*.
Come to drink the Soma with eight horses.
The acute accent of the case-ending is due to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.102: “aṣṭano dīrghāt.”
Come with your ten bay horses!
O Indra—whether you are called Sumakha, Suyajña, or Sudhana—this Soma has been purified for your sake.
Therefore, do not cause harm or injury to this sacrifice. Do not strike it down!
In the *luṅ* [aorist] of the root *kṛ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix by the rule "in mantras, *vama*" etc.;
once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, there is elision of the *mip* ending by the rule "after a consonant, *hal-ḍy-ādi*" etc.
Although Indra has only two bay horses (*harī*), nevertheless, because you know the distinction between their various manifestations (*vibhūti*),
there is no contradiction in the multiplicity of horses.
Come hither with twenty, with thirty, or with forty bay horses yoked;
come, O Indra, with fifty steeds on your noble chariot, urged by the truth, to the drinking of the Soma.
Come hither with twenty, come with thirty; come hither, O Indra, yoking your bay steeds, with forty, with fifty, and with well-yoked chariots—come to the truthful draught of Soma to drink. 5.
O Indra, come toward us with twenty horses for the drinking of Soma—that is, for the Soma which is to be drunk;
come with thirty horses;
or come, yoking yourself with forty bay steeds, toward the drinking of Soma.
Come with your excellent chariots, well-yoked and easy to traverse, with fifty bay horses;
likewise, come for the drinking of Soma with sixty, that is, with sixty in number, or with seventy, that is, with seventy in number.
Borne by eighty, ninety, or even a hundred bay steeds,
this Soma is indeed pressed for you among the Śunahotras, O Indra, out of devotion to you, for your exhilaration.
Come hither with eighty, with ninety, or with a hundred bay horses being borne along! For this Śunahotra here is mine;
may my friendship with Indra—characterized by the sacrificial post—never cease, never be separated at any time.
From the root *yu*, the suffix *sip* is applied by the rule "sid-bahulam";
there is the augment *aṭ*.
May the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) of this Indra—the giving performed by Indra—milk for us, that is, yield our desired fruit.
This is the form [of the verb] *duh* in the optative (*liṅ*).

May we be "in the presence" (*upavartinaḥ*)—that is, in close proximity—to the "arm" (*gabhastau*), meaning the hand, which is "most excellent" (*jyeṣṭhe*), "highly praiseworthy," "in the turn" (*vahaṭhe*), "in the calamity" (*āpadyam*), or "to be chosen" (*varagīye*).
The meaning is: "May we become worthy of being touched by the hand of Indra."

Furthermore, at almost every entry into Indra’s sacrificial hall for the purpose of drinking soma, may we be victorious, that is, conquerors of our enemies. Or alternatively, *prāye-prāye*: a *prāya* is a battle, so called because it is approached (*pra-i*) with intensity by the warriors.
In that battle, may we be victorious, having conquered our enemies.
Surely, O Indra, may that wealthy sacrificial gift yield a boon for you, for the singer;
bestow it upon those who praise you, let there be no neglect toward us. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.

Surely, O Indra, may that wealthy sacrificial gift yield boons for you in return to the singer; bestow gifts upon those who praise you. Let not fortune fail us. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly of the wise. 9.
"Surely, do not [think] 'me'"; thus it is explained.

The eighth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "apāvyasya," is addressed to Indra; it is in the Gāyatrī metre, though some verses are in the Triṣṭubh metre. It is introduced as "apāyi. Its application in the ritual manual (laikhika) is according to the Sūktaviniyoga.
In the second sequence, the *ājyā* for the *hotṛ-śastra* is this verse: "apāyi" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).
O wise ones, [bring] the draught of the soma-pressing for exhilaration, of the nourishing food that has been well-poured;
in which Indra, increasing from of old, has established his dwelling, as have the men who honor the sacred word.

The wise have pressed this juice for exhilaration—the pressed draught of food—in which Indra, increasing from of old, has found his home, and in which the men devoted to sacred prayer likewise find their dwelling.
Of the wise sacrificer who is pressing the Soma, [this is] the connection with the sacrificial food.
The root *prīṅ* means "to satisfy.
[It refers to] those [beings].
This exhilarating drink, characterized by the Soma-mark, has been purified for intoxication;
the meaning is that this food was drunk by Indra.
Alternatively, in the word *apāyi*, the suffix *ciṇ* occurs in the sense of the agent from the root *pā-* (to drink) according to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam*;
and by the rule *chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ*, the *luṅ* tense is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*).
It was drunk for the exhilaration of the Prātikara soma.
The genitive case is used for the object when there is an intention to express something remaining.
Let Indra drink the Soma.
In that ancient food characterized as Soma, having grown and increased from time immemorial, Indra has made his own dwelling, his abode for enjoyment.
Moreover, the leaders of rites, the priests desiring a hymn of praise for Indra, have established their own dwelling therein.
The phrase "this very thing is subject to decay" connects with what precedes it.
1. Of the one who causes delight to *ta*. 2. Of the one who causes delight to *jha₁-ṇa-va*. 3. In the Soma characterized by *ta*. 4. *jha₁-ma-va* established [it].

Intoxicated by this mead, Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, split apart the serpent that encompassed the waters, when, like birds flying toward their nests, he made his way through the enclosures of the rivers.
Exhilarated by this mead, Indra, thunderbolt in hand, rent asunder the dragon who obstructed the waters, so that the swift currents of the rivers flowed forth like birds toward their own sisters. 2.
Of this honeyed [draught].
The genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental.

Intoxicated by this exhilarating Soma, Indra—whose hand is joined with the thunderbolt (*vajra*)—cut asunder, specifically, the serpent Vṛtra, who was like a flood-enveloped obstruction, either surrounded by water or being the very cloud that obstructs the waters.
And another [root] is *chid*,
belonging to the *tud* class;
in the *laṅ* [tense], there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule *grahijyādi*.
When, upon the breaking open [of the channels], the rivers' refreshing waters set forth toward the clear ocean to go there, they began their journey;
therein is the simile:
"like birds."
Just as birds leave their nests,
Indra bestows many unsurpassed and excellent riches upon the mortal— the human sacrificer— who offers oblations.
Moreover, he slays the Asura Vṛtra.
Of what sort is he?
Indra is the one to be praised in the winning of the sun;
*māti* means worshipful devotion.

To the patrons who were contending for the domain of the Sun’s worship—striving against one another, saying, "May I alone first attain the Sun! May I alone first attain the Sun!"—to those men, the friends, you were at that very moment *vatasāyyaḥ*: one to be sought as a refuge, being the means for their attainment; you were *bhṛt* (the supporter) or *abhṛt* (the sustainer). Or rather, [you were so] in the winning of the Sun.
The suffix *ki* occurs after the root *ant* in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
In the battle connected with the Sun, he became one who was to be protected for those contending, that is, those vying with the Sun.
Indra, the god, being praised by mortals, released the sun for him who was pressing the juice;
when the god-granting wealth brought to him a portion, as Etaśa bestows his share.
That god Indra, being praised by the mortal who presses the soma, released the sun for him; when Etaśa, bestowing favor, brought him wealth that destroys the enemy, like a share of the harvest. ||5||
Being praised by Etaśa while himself praising, that shining god Indra bestowed the sun upon the mortal man, the son of Manu, Etaśa, who was performing the pressing of the Soma.
Competing with Etaśa, he surpassed the sun with his wing;
thus says the Vedic hymn: "Indra [delivered] Etaśa, who was contending with the sun, in the fray for the prize" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.61.15).
Because Vetaśa Sauvadhya, acting as a king, desiring to do honor, brought forth—that is, accomplished—for that Indra a hidden speech, or rather, wealth in the form of Soma;
there is a simile for this:
"like a bamboo pole."
Just as a father bears his portion or share to his son, so it is in that manner.
He, for the sake of Kutsa’s charioteer, subdued the insatiable Śuṣṇa and Kuyava;
and Indra shattered the ninety-nine fortresses of Śambara for Divodāsa.
He subdued Śuṣṇa, the swift-conquering Kuyava, for the sake of Kutsa, the charioteer of Sudās; and Indra demolished the nine forts of Śambara and Navavarti for Divodāsa. 6.
The radiant Indra, for Kutsa—the royal sage who acts as his own charioteer—[slew] Śuṣṇa.
"Śuṣṇa" refers to a certain Asura; he is so called because he withers (śoṣayati) everything.
That Śuṣṇa was one who could not be withered by anyone else.
He crushed this Asura named Vka;
*radhyati* means "to bring under control";
he brought him under his power.
Alternatively, the suffix *num* is applied by the rule "radhijabhor aci" to the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *radh*, which means "to injure" and "to accomplish."
Furthermore, that Indra shattered ninety-nine fortresses belonging to Śambara, the Asura, for the sake of Divodāsa, the king of that name.
1. When there is the occurrence of *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *va*, and *sūrya* [in the following sequence].
2. May I alone first attain *Sūrya*: *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ga*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, *va*.
3. For humans (*nṛbhyaḥ*), there is no *ka*, *jha*, *bha*, *ma*, or *va*.
4. He brought the Soma with *ka-jha-jha-ta-va*; he began the Soma with *ṇa-na*; he began the Soma with *tha*; he began the Soma with *ma*. 5.
To this wretched one, *ka-jha-tha-ma-va*; to this wretched one, *jha*. 6. *Ma* [is] the Asura.

O Indra, come for the sake of glory!
By the rule "supām suluk," there is a long vowel of the same quality as the preceding one (pūrvasavarṇadīrgha) for the third case ending.
Seeking strength through the desire for Agni, making you powerful;
or rather, seeking strength through the desire for glory (*śravasyā*), desiring renown.
The causative suffix *ṇic* is also observed after the root *iṣ* (to desire),
as in *aśrāyanto gavyanto vājayantaḥ*. If it were instead a form ending in *kyac*, the word *vājayantaḥ* would have an udātta accent on its final syllable, as in the example *vājayantaḥ śatakratum*.
Being such as we are, we ourselves, by our own mind, shall now bring—that is, convey—to you this hymn of praise.
‘Ahi-gatām’:
not in the sense of "presently."
The bleating ones.

From the root *aś*, in the formation of *kānaci*, even though it is a *liṅ* [optative] suffix, there is the dual *vikaraṇa* due to the rule "there is extensive transposition," and that [suffix] is the *upratyaya*.
May we, having offered oblations with the *khāra* and *śruva* ladles, attain— that is, pervade— the truth that is desired, pertaining to seven generations, extending through seven steps,
and belonging to the unborn deity Pīyu, who knows the gods such as Indra and the rest.
The root *pīy* has the sense of harming as its action.
The slaying of the murderous Asura.
A weapon is that by which enemies are slain.
Homage to that which is not composed of the destruction of those [defilements].
*nanāma*: from the root *ṇamu* in the sense of "bowing" (*prahvatve*); this is the form of the causative (*ṇyanta*) in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense with the suffix *caṅ*.
The vowel is shortened according to the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92).

O powerful hero, O Indra, for you the Gṛtsamadas have here fashioned a hymn worthy of thought.

Regarding this, Yāska says: "Gṛtsamada means 'one who strikes the wise'; *gṛtsa* is a name for one possessed of intelligence, derived from the root *gṛ*, which signifies the act of praising" (Nirukta 9.5).
Such [sages] have thus fashioned—that is, they have composed—for you a hymn that is to be meditated upon.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like those seeking pasture.
Ava:
this form is derived from the root *ava* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *asun*.
Just as men desiring to go desire paths (vayunāni) and prepare them accordingly, so it is;
furthermore, [it is] more recent.
The elision of the genitive case ending is by the rule "supāṃ suluk."

O most recent one, O newest one, may the Gṛtsamadas—desiring to perform a hymn of praise for you with sacred prayer (*brahman*)—obtain *sukṣiti* (a beautiful dwelling), *viṣ* (food), *ūrja* (strength), *sumna* (bliss), and *vaśyu* (submissiveness).
The plural number is used for the single Gṛtsamada, and the reference is made in the third person.

1. [The substitution of] *ka*, *jha*, *na*, *ma*, or *va* occurs for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when [the suffix] *jha* follows the nominal stem; [the substitution of] *ṇa* occurs for a nominal stem ending in *āp*. 2.
And [the substitution of] *va* occurs for *vayam*.

Surely that wealthy sacrificial gift of yours, O Indra, shall yield a boon for the singer; bestow favor upon those who praise you, do not withhold it. May Bhaga grant us prosperity; may we, blessed with noble sons, offer great praise in the assembly. nūnam | sā | te | prati | varam | jaritre | duhīyat | indra | dakṣiṇā | maghonī | śikṣa | stotṛbhyaḥ | mā | ati | dhṛk | bhagaḥ | naḥ | bṛhat | dema | vidathe | suvīrāḥ || 9 ||
"Surely she is yours," [said] Siddhārthā.
The ninth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “vayaṃ te vayaḥ,” is in the Gāthī-Aṣṭadha metre, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and addressed to Indra.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry: “vayaṃ te.
The specific application of this hymn should be determined from its internal indicative marks (liṅga).

O Indra, know us as your own; we bring forth our strength for you, like those seeking booty bring their chariot. Praising you with inspired thought, we meditate upon you, desiring to win the favor of a hero such as you. You are indeed the lord of the one who offers oblations and the protector of the one who gives.
By virtue of the grammatical rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*) stating "prasita-skambhita-stambhita," the vowel *ī* is replaced by *u*.
You are the warder-off of oppressors; moreover, you are the one who possesses abundant wisdom for that praiser— your action consists in the pacification of such calamities as these—
for he who shall honor you with oblations and serve you with sacrificial offerings.
May that Indra, our youthfully invoked friend, be auspicious to us as a protector, O heroes— he who, for his protection,
favors him who praises, him who prays, him who cooks, and him who lauds.

May that Indra, our youthful friend, be one who is easily invoked; may he be the auspicious protector of men, he who, with his aid, takes pleasure in the one who recites, the one who praises, the one who cooks the oblation, and the one who sings hymns. 3.

He who is the separator, the youth among those who sacrifice, the pacifier of the fruit, the one to be invoked by the chanters, the one to be offered oblations, the friend who has become a companion, the auspicious one who brings happiness—that Indra [is the lord] of men.

The guna [substitution] in the case of *nṛ* before the suffix *ām* is Vedic; or, since the instruction regarding augments is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), there is the absence of *vaṭ* in the case of *nara* before *ām*.
He becomes the protector and guardian of us who lead the ritual action—
of him who praises the weapons and of him who is praising them.
‘In the leaping motion of a hare.’
[He protects] one performing rituals, cooking sacrificial offerings such as the *puroḍāśa*, and chanting with *sāmans*—performing the *stotra*.

Because a distinction has been established here between the *stotra* and the *śastra* based on their being accomplished through chanted and non-chanted mantras respectively, they are mentioned separately.
In this way, may he protect (*vūtī*) the sacrificer by means of weaving (*ūyā*) and preserve him (*gṛṇeṣat*).
From the root *nī* (to lead), the suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule *sibbahulam*;
the augment *aṭ* is added; and by the rule *tiṅi codāttavati*, the verb *gati* (leading) receives the *nighāta* (elision of accent).
One should cause [beings] to reach the further shore of karmas.
I praise that Indra, I laud him, in whom they have grown strong in the past and in whom they have found firm support;
may he, being implored, fulfill the desire for wealth in the prayerful man, the new-born Āyu.

I praise him—*ūm*!—Indra; I sing his praises, he in whom they have grown strong in the past and in whom they have found firm support. May he, being entreated, fulfill the desire for wealth of the one who offers prayer, the newest of living men. 4.
I praise that very Indra; I laud him. Likewise, I extol that Indra; I proclaim him.
In both cases, there is a transposition of the grammatical person.
In this Indra, the worshippers have long since increased him;
they have grown strong and have indeed subdued and slain their enemies.
The root *śad* is used in the sense of cutting (*śātane*).
In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable according to the rule *tujādīnām*.

Knowing [our needs] and being entreated by the praisers, may that Indra fulfill—the desire for wealth—the longing of the one who offers prayers, of the one who seeks praise, or of the new mortal sacrificer; may he satisfy it by bestowing the fruits of his wish.

1. Kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, ṇa, 1, ta, tha, na, va—[the hymn] is supported by the sky. 2. Ta, tha—[you are] the pacifier; you are one whose action is not formless. 3. Kha, ga, ṇa, ta, tha—the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth. 4. Jha₁—there is a distinction based on the division between that which is sung (*pragīta*) and that which is not sung (*apragīta*). 5. Ka, kha, ga, jha, ṇa, ṇa, 1, ta, tha, na, ma, ba—thus we [are]. 6. Jha₁, ta, tha, va—causing to reach. (Ṛgveda 2.11)

Delighting in the hymns of the Aṅgirases, Indra strengthened their prayer; seeking a path, the peerless one, plundering the dawns with the sun, while praising, has shattered even the ancient strongholds of Aśva. He, delighting in the hymns of the Aṅgirases, strengthened their prayer; Indra, seeking a path, plundering the dawns with the sun, while praising, has shattered even the ancient strongholds of Aśva.
Having taken pleasure in the hymns and recitations belonging to the Aṅgirases.
The form *juṣāte* is the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) of the root *juṣ*, meaning "to please" or "to serve."
Serving them, Indra, seeking a path for the Aṅgirases who had spread it out with their wings, impelled and urged on their *brahman*—their hymn of praise—by granting their desires.

In the case of the root *vṛdh* (meaning "to increase"), there is the elision (*ślu*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) in the present tense (*laṭ*), according to the rule "there is diversely [elision] in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
He paid attention.
Furthermore, being praised with hymns (*stava*) by the *stotra*s, he was robbing away—that is, taking away—the *uṣas* (dawns) by means of the sun, who has become his own self;
for when the sun has risen, the dawns disappear.
Such was that Indra;
"Aśva" refers to a certain Asura who pervades (*aśnute*) the entire world by his own splendor.
He [Indra] shattered—that is, terrified and weakened—the ancient, primordial, and age-old powers of that [Asura].

That god, renowned by the name Indra, has arisen upright for the sake of man as the most difficult to overcome. The self-dependent one, victorious over Arśāśana, brought down the beloved head of the Dāsa. He, indeed, the famous Indra by name, the god, has become erect for the sake of man, most difficult to overcome. The self-dependent one, victorious over Arśāśana, brought down the head of the Dāsa.

The radiant god, renowned and glorious, for that very reason most difficult to surpass and pre-eminently beautiful to behold—that Indra—stood upright for the sake of man’s desire; he became intent, with face turned upward, upon the granting of wishes.
The word *nāma* is used in the sense of well-known;
*ha* is a particle for filling out the meter.
This is said:
Indra—the conqueror of enemies, self-dependent, and powerful—cast down, that is, caused to fall, the beloved head of the Dāsa, the Asura named Arśāsan, who was oppressing the world.
The *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *hṛ* with the augment *āgama*: *ahṛṣata*.
*hṛ-habhaiḥ*.

That Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the breaker of forts, drove asunder the Dāsa women of dark origin. He generated for Manu both the earth and the waters; he ever strengthened the praise of the sacrificer. 7. He, the slayer of Vṛtra, Indra, the breaker of forts, drove asunder the Dāsa women of dark origin. He generated for Manu both the earth and the waters; he ever strengthened the praise of the sacrificer. 7.

Vṛtrahā, the slayer of Vṛtra; Purandara, the shatterer of the cities of Śambara—that Indra drove away (vya-irayat) and dispersed the Asura armies, those of low birth born from a dark womb, who were the destroyers of others. Furthermore, for the sake of Manu, he [placed] the earth and the waters facing northward.

O Adhvaryu, bring and prepare the Soma for Indra. For what kind of Indra? For the *viśvajit*, the conqueror of all. He elaborates on this very point: for the *dhanajit*, the conqueror of his enemies' wealth through victory over them; for the *svarjit*, the conqueror and sovereign of heaven; for the *satrājit*, who is habitually victorious (*satrā* = continuously) or the conqueror of the great; for the *nṛjit*, the conqueror of men and leaders; for the *urvarājit*, the conqueror of the *urvarā*—the earth known as the source of all crops; for the *aśvajit*, the conqueror by force of cattle that have been carried away; for the *abjit*, the conqueror of the waters that were obstructed by Vṛtra; for the sake of sacrifice, for the one worthy of sacrifice—for such Indra, bring the *haryata* Soma. [The root] *harya* means "to move" and "to desire. By the rule beginning with *bhṛmṛdṛśi*, the suffix *atac* is applied to form the object. Thus, the syntactical connection is: "bring the Soma which is desirable or longed for."

To the conqueror, to the one who is to be conquered, to the one who is not deceived, to the invincible, to the subduer, to the ordainer, to the one of mighty stride, to the bearer of oblations, to the one of irresistible power, to the all-conquering Indra— to him speak your homage.

To the Overcomer, to the Conqueror, to the one who acts without guile, to the invincible, to the Subduer, to the Ordainer, to the one of mighty stride, to the bearer of oblations, to the one of irresistible power, to the ever-conquering—proclaim homage to Indra! 2.

To the Overcomer, the conqueror of all, the one who overcomes by his power, the breaker of the Asuras, the winner; [the suffix *u* is added to the root *van* (to win) with the suffix *yat*. To the distributor of the wealth of enemies; to the invincible; [the past participle suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object; the absence of *ut*-vṛddhi is Vedic.
