To the one not overcome by enemies; to the subduer, the all-enduring, the Ordainer, the arranger of everything; to the one of mighty roar, the full-necked; or [alternatively, from the root *gṛ* (to sound), with the *ki* suffix added in the sense of the object according to Uṇādi rules: to the one to be praised by many, the loud ones; to the bearer, the carrier of all; to the one of difficult approach, because he is hard for others to overcome, the one difficult to harm; to the ever-conquering, the perpetual overcomer, or the overcomer of the great—to such an Indra, O singers, speak a hymn preceded by the word "namas" (salutation). [From the root *brū* in the *luṅ* tense, *brūvo vaciḥ*; the substitution *aṅ* occurs by the rule *asyativaktikhyātibhyo’ṅ*; the *um* augment is added by *vaca um*; then the *guṇa* change occurs. Speak! O you who praise, do you say this.

Victorious in battle, devourer of men, subduer of people, he has grown according to your pleasure; the conqueror who strikes down Vṛtra has been sent among the tribes. I shall proclaim the heroic deeds performed by Indra.

Conqueror of enemies; devourer of men; subduer of the people; the disperser; you; according to; our desire; strengthened; slayer of Vṛtra; victorious; honored among the clans; of Indra—let me proclaim his heroic deeds. 3.
Satrāsahaḥ, the overcomer of many; Janabhakṣaḥ, the bestower of desires upon the people—the sacrificers—or rather, he who is to be shared in by them through such bestowal;
Janasahaḥ, the overcomer of powerful men; Vyavanaḥ, the one who causes enemies to flee from his own chariot;
Yuyudhānaḥ, the warrior; increased (ukṣitaḥ) according to joy—that is, sprinkled with soma.

*Vṛtracyaḥ*: he who destroys *vṛtra*; that is, he who destroys the enemy who is sought after (*abhīṣṭa*). Alternatively, *vṛtra* refers to the enemy because he turns toward [the foe] again and again, coming face-to-face;
he who strikes (*cinoti*) him is *vṛtracyaḥ*.

The root *ci* has the meaning of "injury. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "He who deprives a sharer of his share, indeed injures him; if he does not injure him [directly], then he injures his son, or his grandson—thus he injures him" (AiB 2.7).
He is the conqueror (*sahuriḥ*).

Jasi-sahorinu: 1. *ka-ma-vardha* for the sake of honoring; *kha-ga-ṇa-dhanānāṃ* for the sake of honoring wealth; *jha-vardha* for the sake of honoring; *jha1-vadhabhajanāya*; *ṇa-ta-tha-na-vardha* for the sake of honoring; *va-vardha* for the sake of honoring. 2. *kha-ga-ṇa-tha-satrāsāhe*.
3. *tha-ma-satrāsāhe*: this is the suffix *uri*. He becomes one who has overcome his enemies and has attained (*āritaḥ*) a position among the people (*vikṣu*) as a protector (*prajāsu*).
I shall proclaim—the deeds, the heroic powers such as the slaying of Vṛtra and others—of such an Indra.
He is the unyielding bull, the bestower of strength, the increaser, the profound, the lofty, whose wisdom is unattainable by others.
The impeller of the weak, the loosener, the firm, the path-maker, Indra, the performer of good sacrifices, generated the light of heaven at the dawns.

4. Without a follower; the bull; the one who bestows strength; the increaser; the profound; the lofty; whose wisdom is unattainable by others; the impeller of the weak; the loosener; the firm; the broad; Indra; the performer of good sacrifices; he has generated the dawns and the light of heaven. 4.

"Without a follower. One who gives after [another] is a *anuda*; by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136), the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the agent. He for whom that does not exist is thus described. The meaning is that there is no one equal to him in the distribution of abundant wealth. Therefore, O Bull (*vṛṣabha*), Indra, bestow upon us the most excellent riches, the insight of skill, prosperity, good fortune, the nourishment of wealth, the safety of our bodies—or of ourselves—and the excellence of our speech and our days.
O Indra, bestow upon us the most excellent riches, the insight of skill, prosperity, and good fortune; grant us abundance of wealth, safety for our bodies, mastery over our speech, and fair days.
O Indra, bestow upon us and establish for us the most excellent and supreme riches and treasures;
[bestow] wealth in the state of skillfulness.
Bestow upon us the wisdom and renown that enable the performance of ritual acts.
Grant us good fortune—that is, the possession of beautiful wealth—or auspicious prosperity. Bestow upon us the nourishment and abundance of riches granted by you.
"Tanūnām" means "of the ignorant. Alternatively, "tanvaḥ" refers to sons, because the family is extended (*tāyate*) by them;
the suffix *up* is added to the root *tan* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
Bestow upon them safety and non-violence;
likewise, bestow sweetness upon our speech,
and bestow long life and auspiciousness upon our days.
Those days on which Indra and the other gods are worshipped are "auspicious days" (sudināni);
the state of being such is "auspiciousness" (sudinatvam).
The eleventh hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with “trikadrukeṣu,” is addressed to Indra and belongs to the Gārhamedha.
According to the *Agniprakramaṇikā*: “In the *trikadruka* [hymn], there are four *kapra* [verses]; it is in the *atiśakvara* meter, or the last verse may be in the *agniṣṭoma* [meter].
The first verse is heard in the *aṣṭicchandas* [meter] and consists of five syllables.
The remaining five-syllable verses are *atiśakvarī*s,
or alternatively, they are *anyāprī*s.
When sixteen [verses] are heard, there is the triplet beginning with "at trikadrukeṣu."

It is stated in the Sūtra: "At the Trikadruka sacrifices, [the Hotṛ] should recite the two triplets beginning with *mahiṣo yavāśiram* and *pro asmai puroratham*, which are in the Gāyatrī and Anuṣṭubh meters respectively" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.2).
On the day when no dispute is permitted, the first verse of the *pratipad* for the *marutvatīya* [śastra] is “*trikadrukeṣu*.

This is prescribed in the section beginning with “On the tenth day” in the Sūtra: “In place of the verse ‘*ā tvā rathaṃ yathotaye*’, [one uses] ‘*trikadrukeṣu mahiṣo yavāśiram*’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.12).
On the middle day of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, this is the first verse of the *marutvatīya*.

Regarding the statement, "We shall now declare its specific features," it is formulated in the [Āśvalāyana] Śrautasūtra (10.10) in the section [on the *viśeṣas*]: "The verse beginning with 'In the Trikadrukas, the buffalo [drank] the barley-mash' is the introductory hymn (*pratipad*) for the Marutvatīya [śastra]."
In the Mahāvrata sacrifice as well, at the midday pressing, there is a triplet for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin as the *stotriya*:
"The buffalo at the Trikadruka rites [drinks] the barley-mash" (*trikadrukeṣu mahiṣo yavāśiram*); thus it is prescribed in the Sūtra (AiĀ 5.1).
At the Trikadruka festivals, the mighty and powerful one drank the barley-mash mixed with Soma; having drunk it, he drove away all hatreds according to his will.
That Soma-drop, being mortal, exhilarated the divine Indra—the mortal god—so that he might perform great deeds; indeed, the vast and wide one has performed them for him.

At the Trikadruka festivals, the mighty buffalo, possessing abundant strength, drank his fill of the Soma mixed with barley-gruel, pressed by Viṣṇu. He drank as much as he desired; it exhilarated him for the sake of performing great deeds. Truly, that great and wide god, the true Indu, has ever accompanied this true Indra. 1.
1. The accomplishment of one's purpose;
2. excellence in that regard. Gṛtsamada says:
The great lord of the earth, worthy of worship, possessed of abundant vigor and great strength, the protector of men.
The root *tṛp* means "to satisfy" or "to please. It belongs to the *tudādi* class.
Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rules governing augments, there is an absence of the augment *num*.
Indra, being satisfied at the Trikadruka days—those pressing-days named Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus—drank the pressed soma mixed with *yavāśira*, that is, mixed with barley-meal.
In the case of the root *śrī* preceded by the prefix *ā*, when the suffix *krip* is applied, there is the substitution of *śiras* as seen in examples such as *apastṛdhethām*.
He drank that Soma together with Viṣṇu;
he drank it according to his desire, just as he had previously willed and just as he had desired that Soma.
‘Vaśa’ means ‘desired. The absence of the elision of the *śap* suffix is due to the rule ‘bahulaṃ chandasi’ (Pāṇini 2.4.73).
The great Soma, drunk, has exhilarated this great Indra with its brilliance, having spread it wide;
for what purpose?
To perform the great deed characterized by the slaying of Vṛtra and so forth.
The true drop, the god, shining at the libation—the true Soma—[reaches] Indra, who desires the true god Soma as he exists according to reality;
*saśrat* means "to pervade";
let him pervade [him].

Then, radiant with splendor, he overcame Krivi by his might in battle; he opened asunder the two worlds, Rodasī, at his birth, and grew great. He placed one [portion] within his belly and released the other; the god, having faith, drank of the god, the true Indu, of Indra the true. Then, radiant with splendor, he overcame Krivi by his might in battle; he opened asunder the two worlds, Rodasī, at his birth, and grew great. He placed one [portion] within his belly and released the other; the god, having faith, drank of the god, the true Indu, of Indra the true.
Furthermore, after the drinking of the Soma, the radiant Indra, by means of his power and strength, overcame the Asura named Krivi in battle;
moreover, that Indra filled the two worlds, heaven and earth, with his own splendor on all sides.
Thus, by the greatness—that is, the power—of this Soma that has been drunk, he has grown forth;
or rather, by the greatness—the deadly force—of this Krivi Asura, he filled the two worlds, heaven and earth.
That Indra, having divided the Soma into two parts, placed one portion within his own belly.
This latter portion was left over for the gods; he set it aside.
By this it is meant that one half belongs to Indra and the other half to the other gods.
Thus says the Taittirīyaka: “Just as Indra [received] half of these, therefore Indra is the most abundant among the deities” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.8.3).

Born together with wisdom, you have grown up together with vigor; grown together with heroic deeds, you are the overcomer of enemies, the observer of all people. You are the giver of desirable wealth to the one who praises you; may that true Soma-drop satisfy the god Indra, the true one, for the sake of the pressed juice. Born together with wisdom, you have grown up together with vigor; grown together with heroic deeds, you are the overcomer of enemies, the observer of all people. You are the giver of desirable wealth to the one who praises you; may that true Soma-drop satisfy the god Indra, the true one, for the sake of the pressed juice.
1. The power of frequent practice (*tathā-bahula-bala*). 2. The characteristic of being worthy of honor (*mānanīyatva*) and so forth. 3. Even more than others (*adhamanyebhyaḥ*).
Whether by what deed or by wisdom, you were born together with [them]; together with power and strength, you have willed to carry all.
In the case of the root *vah* followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*), the augment *ām* does not occur in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) because it is a mantra.

Furthermore, you have grown great together with your heroic exploits—such as the slaying of enemies—and through your prowess; you are the subduer of *mṛdhaḥ*, meaning either harmful beings or battles.
(The genitive case is prohibited here by the rule *na lokāvyaya*).

The connection of the words is as follows: he who is the overcomer of those [enemies], whose path is free from wandering, the one who specifically beholds both the doers of merit and the doers of demerit—being a giver of wealth (*vasu*) that is effective, desirable, and worthy of prayer, you have indeed bestowed it upon the sacrificer who offers praise and performs hymns.
The use of the third person pronoun "him" (*enam*) is an indirect reference and serves to establish the fact of the matter.

O Indra, O dancer, you performed that noble deed for the first time, worthy of being proclaimed throughout heaven—the work accomplished by the power of the god when he sent forth life and released the waters. He became superior to all through his might; the Lord of a Hundred Powers found nourishment and found the waters.

That manly deed of yours, O Indra, O Dancer, was the first to be proclaimed in heaven—a deed worthy of praise—when by the might of the god you released the life-force, letting the waters flow; then everything that was godless was overcome by your power. May the Lord of a Hundred Powers find us strength; may he find us nourishment. 4.
O Indra, you who cause all to dance, [grant] that which is foremost, extensive, and beneficial for men.

Yāska says that *prathamam* means "extended. That work of yours, performed by you at the very beginning of time, shall be your *apah*—your deed—which is to be proclaimed, to be spoken of with excellence, in the sky, in the heavenly world;
that is to say, it is to be praised.
What is that?
By wounding—that is, by harming—the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of this victorious Asura, you did cause the waters—that is, the waters obstructed by him—to flow forth;
such is the connection [of the meaning] that this deed is to be proclaimed.
The indirect description remains:
that Indra, by his *ojas*—his power—overcame the all-pervading, godless, darkness-like Asura.
Furthermore, may Indra, the performer of a hundred rites (*śatakratu*), grant us strength (*ūrja*).
And knowing the food characterized by the oblation.
The root *vid* is used in the sense of "obtaining.
It takes the *śap* suffix; the augment *āṬ* is added before the *laṭ* [present tense] ending.

In the third Anuvāka, there are ten hymns (*sūktas*). Among them, this first hymn consists of nineteen verses (*ṛcas*) and is composed by Gharma. Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: “In the [hymn] beginning with *gaṇānām*, there are nineteen [verses]; it is addressed to Bṛhaspati; however, fifteen [verses] have the characteristics of being addressed to Bṛhaspati, while the other two are *triṣṭubh*s.”
The fifteenth and the nineteenth [verses] are *triṣṭubh*s;
the remaining ones are *jagatī*s. Those in which the word "Bṛhaspati" is heard are addressed to Bṛhaspati (*bārhaspatyāḥ*).
The remaining [verses] belong to Brāhmaṇaspati.
This hymn is used at the Pravargya and Abhiṣava rites;
it is prescribed in the section titled "Sṛṣṭodaka" in the Sūtra: "gaṇānāṃ tvā prathaśca yasya" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.6).
1. There is no "ṇa-ta-tha-ma" meaning "accompanied by an elder. 2. And "ma" means "one who has committed evil.
3. "tha" means "continuously."

4. The indirect indication (parokṣanirdeśa) of *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *ṇa* 1, *na*, and *va* is the most excellent (*variṣṭha*); the indirect indication of *jha* and *jha* 1 is the best (*vāśiṣṭa*); the indirect indication of *ca*, *ta*, and *tha* is not distinguished (*aviśiṣṭa*).
5. In *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *ta*, and *tha*, the letter *ca* does not exist. 6. In *ga*, *ṇa*, *ṇa* 1, *na*, and *la*, there is the augment *āṭ* in the *leṭ* tense.
7. Only at the non-pressing [of Soma].

We invoke you, the Lord of the hosts, the sage among sages, possessed of the highest renown, the supreme king, the priest, O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati); hearing us, sit upon your seat with your protections. gaṇānām | tvā | gaṇapatim | havāmahe | kavim | kavīnām | upamaśravastamam | jyeṣṭharājam | brahmaṇam | brahmaṇaḥ | pate | ā | naḥ | śṛṇvan | ūtibhiḥ | sīda | sādanam || 1 ||
O Brahmaṇaspati, O Lord of this prayer (brahman) or of this powerful rite, O protector, [we praise] the lord of hosts—the master of the groups consisting of the gods and others;
the seer among seers, those who possess beautiful vision;
the one of most exalted fame.

*Upamā* (simile) is so called because something else is compared (*upamīyate*) to it. He whose fame (*śravaḥ*) is the object of comparison for all ignorant beings is thus described; one who possesses such fame in the highest degree is *upamaśravastamaḥ*.
The word *upamā* is derived from the root *mā* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*).
By the rule *ātaścopasarge*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
The shortening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñāchandasoḥ*.
O Jyeṣṭharāja! "Jyeṣṭha" means most excellent; among them, we invoke you—the one who shines, the Lord of the sacred hymns (brahmaṇām)—in this ritual act. We call upon you.

Furthermore, hearing our hymns of praise (*stutīḥ*), do thou sit down (*sīda*)—that is, take thy seat—in the dwelling (*sādanam*), so called because things sit (*sīdanti*) within it; that is, in the sacrificial hall (*yajñagṛha*). Do thou sit down with thy protections (*ūtībhiḥ*), which serve as the means of preservation.

Even the gods, O Bṛhaspati, who are immortal and wise, have attained their sacrificial portion from you; like the Dawn, like the Sun with his light, you are the great progenitor of all sacred prayers (brahmans). devāścit te asurya pracetasaḥ bṛhaspate yajñiyaṃ bhāgamānaśuḥ | uṣā iva sūryo jyotiṣā maho viśvepā it janitā brahmaṇām asi || 2 || Even the gods, O Bṛhaspati, who are immortal and wise, have attained their sacrificial portion from you; like the Dawn, like the Sun with his light, you are the great progenitor of all sacred prayers.
O Vāyu, slayers of the Asuras! O Bṛhaspati, most wise one—those gods of yours, possessed of supreme knowledge, have indeed obtained their share which is worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*).
Or rather, "most wise" (*pracetasaḥ*) may be taken as an epithet of Bṛhaspati himself;
thus it should be construed as: "those gods belonging to you, who possess supreme knowledge."
Or rather, "pracetasaḥ" [is used];
there is a change of case-ending.
While you, the wise one (pracetasi), exist, the gods have obtained their sacrificial portion.
Because he drives away the Asuras who create obstacles to ritual action by means of the Rakṣoghna hymns recited over water;
for it is heard in scripture: "Verily, one does not find [the goal] without hearing" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 1.13).
Like the Sun, who is great and worthy of honor through his light and splendor, as if with his rays...
The rays of the Dawn.
The suffix *rak* is applied by the rule beginning with "sphāyitañca."
Just as he produces rays of light, so too is Vasiṣṭha the progenitor—the very creator—of all the Vedas and of all the mantras.
The elision of the suffix *ṇi* occurs by virtue of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) in the word "janitā" as used in a mantra.
1. Ka, kha, ga, jha, na, ma, and mahar are the names. 2. Among those who dwell in the "ma" [state], supreme splendor is the dawn (uṣas). 3. Ma refers to the Brāhmaṇas.

O Bṛhaspati, you ascend the three-seated chariot of the *ṛta*, which dispels the waters and the darkness, radiant with light— terrible, crushing the enemies, slaying the *rakṣases*, cleaving the cow-pens, and finding the sun.

O Bṛhaspati, you mount the radiant chariot of Cosmic Order—triple-seated, warding off injury, dispelling darkness, formidable, deceiving the enemies, slaying the Rākṣasas, cleaving the cow-pens, and finding the light of heaven. 3.
O Bṛhaspati, [ward off] the injury;
[ward off] from all sides the injury, the evil-natured demon.
Alternatively, [it is derived from] the root *rap* or *lap*, meaning "articulate speech," with the suffix *kip*.

Having dispelled with your splendor the darkness of those who revile and slander you, you mount— meaning, you ascend upon— that radiant chariot which possesses light, which brings about the *ṛta* (the sacrifice), which is formidable and terrifying to enemies, and which crushes adversaries; indeed, you mount that chariot which slays the *rakṣases*, which cleaves the clouds (or the mountain-castles), and which wins the heavenly realm.
With wise counsels I lead [thee]; thou protectest the people—Thee, the protector of the distressed, we invoke.

O Lord of protection, the advocate who is well-disposed toward us; O Bṛhaspati, strike down those who revile the gods! Let not the evil-doers attain the highest bliss. We invoke thee, the protector of the distressed, the advocate who is well-disposed toward us. O Bṛhaspati, strike down those who revile the gods! Let not the evil-doers attain the highest bliss.

O Bṛhaspati, we invoke you—our protector, the one who carries us across from calamities, or rather, the one who, through protection (*avas*), delivers us from misfortune; the guardian of our bodies, of our limbs, or of our sons and kin; the advocate who speaks for us with partiality; and you who desire us, those who offer oblations—to you we call in this rite. Furthermore, strike down and destroy the revilers of the gods, the Asuras.
May the enemies—those of evil course, wicked conduct, and corrupt intellect—not lose, that is, not deprive us of, our *uttara* (superior) *sumna* (happiness).

Through you, O Lord of Prayer, who cause us to prosper, may we receive the desirable wealth of men. Those enemies of ours who are far away, those who are near, and those who attack—crush them all, O Anaprās! Through you, O Lord of Prayer, who cause us to prosper, may we receive the desirable wealth of men. Those enemies of ours who are far away, those who are near, and those who attack—crush them all, O Anaprās! (9)
O Brahmaṇaspati, by means of you—the excellent increaser—we [attain] desirable riches, O men.
The vowel *ā* is the substitute for the fourth case plural by the rule "supām suluk."
From human donors, may we receive; may we take.
The ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule "āṅo do'nāsyaviharaṇe" (Pāṇini 1.3.20).
Those enemies who are far away in distant lands, and those enemies who are close at hand, who overcome us—those who are devoid of offspring and destitute of action—crush them, destroy those enemies!
[The root] *jabhi* means "to destroy";
it belongs to the *curādi* class.

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "O Brahmaṇaspati, through you, our excellent prosperer, may we obtain from men those desirable riches which are far away, deep down, or near at hand—those 'rātayaḥ,' which mean either those whose action is non-giving or those whose wisdom is non-giving; crush them, O Anaprasa! 'Apra' is a name for form" (Nirukta 3.16).

Through you, O Bṛhaspati, we meditate upon the highest vital power—with you as our fulfilling, all-sustaining ally. Let not those of evil intent or malicious desire prevail over us; through our hymns of praise, may we cross over to prosperity. 10. Through you, O Bṛhaspati, we meditate upon the highest vital power—with you as our fulfilling, all-sustaining ally. Let not those of evil intent or malicious desire prevail over us; through our hymns of praise, may we cross over to prosperity.
1. One who speaks excessively with *ka*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *ma*, and *ba*; one who speaks even more excessively with *kha*, *ga*, *va*, *ṇa*, and *abhi*.
2. In the case of *ka*, *jha*, *la*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, and *va*, the suffix ‘*tvā*’ does not exist.
[M. 2. A. 3. Sū. 23] Second Aṣṭaka, 93.
O Bṛhaspati, with the ploughshare.
The root *pṛ* is used in the senses of protecting and filling. The suffix *kin* is applied according to the rule *āṭagamahan*.
The substitution of *yaṇ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

With him who fulfills desires, who bestows rain, who is pure, who is our companion, and who is the cause of our offerings, we offer the most excellent food characterized by oblations. We maintain this.
The root *dhrī* means "to hold" (*dhāraṇe*).
It is superior to [the root] *div*.
May the man who speaks ill, who is deserving of ill speech, who seeks to harm, and who desires to deceive us—may he not have power over us;
may he not be our master.
The root *īś* means "to rule" (*aiśvarye*).
The augment *yaṅ* is applied according to the rules for the *leṭ* mood.
Being endowed with excellent praise through our thoughts and hymns, may we cross over and flourish exceedingly.
The bull, who never retreats, who goes to the battle, who has scorched the enemy and is victorious in the hosts;
you are the true one, O Brahmaṇaspati, the avenger of debts, the subduer even of the fierce and the impetuous.

Without a rival, a bull, a wanderer, to the invocation, a smelter of the enemy in battles, you are the conqueror; you are true, the exactor of debts, O Brahmaṇaspati, the subduer even of the fierce one who exults in his strength. 11.
O Brahmanaspati, you who are *anānuda*.
One who gives after [another] is called *anuda*;
one who does not do so is *anānuda*.
The meaning is that he is devoid of any other giver;
for this very reason, he is the "bull" (vṛṣabha), the showerer of desires in the sacrifice.
By the rule *āṅi yuddhe* (Pāṇini 3.2.73), the suffix *upa* is applied and there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
He went to that battle; he is one who goes.
In the word *āṭagamahana*, the suffix *kin* is applied.
Because it functions as a gender marker (*liṅga*), there is a prohibition of the genitive case in the expression *āhavam*.
He makes his enemy known and, being thoroughly heated himself, becomes the ultimate tormentor of that enemy.
Because it ends in a suffix marked with *ṇ*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prohibited. The substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "nisastapatāvanāsevane" (Pāṇini 8.3.102).
The accent of the prefix *gati* is determined by the rule "tādau ca niti... (Pāṇini 6.2.50).
In battles and conflicts, you are the victorious one, the overcomer of enemies.
You are such as this: true, possessing true prowess, or possessing true wisdom. You are the remover of debt, the one who drives away what is owed.
The root *yu* is used in the senses of "mixing" and "not mixing.

When it is in its causative form (*ṇyanta*) and reduced by *kvip*, the *ṇi* suffix is elided; then, by the rule "the elision of *v* and *y* occurs before a consonant," there is the elision of the *v*.
Furthermore, you are the subduer—the one who pacifies—even the fierce and powerful, the one who crushes the joy of the stubborn, the lustful, and even the atheist.

He who, with an ungodly mind, seeks to harm us, thinking himself fierce and desiring to kill those under your command—O Bṛhaspati, let his weapon not reach us; strike down the wrath of that arrogant one who acts with evil intent.

Whosoever offends with a godless mind, thinking himself fierce and seeking to strike down our hymns—O Bṛhaspati, let his deadly weapon not reach us; subdue the wrath of that arrogant one who follows evil ways.
That person who injures or harms us with a mind that is godless—disregarding the gods—or characterized by demonic conduct; |||

The word *uṣṭra* is derived as a nipāta (irregularly formed) according to the rule: "After the root *vas*, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied, and there is the substitution of *iṣ* for *vas*. Thus it is established.
And whatever fierce man of evil mind, thinking highly of himself and considering himself great, [attacks] the reciter of the *śāsa* and *uktha*,
or our own hope (*āśaṃsā*),
or the reciters of the *śāsa*s— [the word] "fierce" (*ugra*) should be construed with "of the instructors" (*śāstṝṇām*).
He seeks to kill us; he desires to slay us.
In the case of the root *han* with the suffix *san*, there is lengthening according to the rule "añ-jan-gam-ām sani."
O Bṛhaspati, let there be the weapon of that [enemy]. A "weapon" (vadha) is so called because one is struck (*vadhya*) by it;
[let it be directed] at us (*naḥ*), meaning toward ourselves.
1. You are tamed by *ka*, *jha*, *ta*, *tha*, *ma*, and *da*.
1. [You are] distinguished by the conduct of the asuras through *kha*, *ga*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *la*, *ma*, and *a*.
2. A man [is characterized] by *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *pha*, and *ya*.

1. There is no [augment] for *ka*, *jha*, *ma*, *śā*; [the augment] *m* is not [added] after *jha*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, *śā*, or *p*. [The root] *pṛcī* means "to join. It takes the *śnu* suffix. By transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is the augment *am*. Because of the rule "when *ca* and others are elided," there is no *nighāta* (elision of accent). By transposition, it is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). Furthermore, we have subdued (*ni-karma*) the wrath (*manyu*)—whether it be anger or knowledge—of the one who is far from the gods (*durevasya*), whose mind is wicked (*duṣṭamanasya*), who is arrogant (*śardhataḥ*) and powerful; or rather, of him who acts with impetuous force (*vega*) due to evil intent. We have subdued it by our own grace.

To be invoked in battles, to be approached with homage, he who goes among the spoils of war, the winner of wealth after wealth—Bṛhaspati has driven away all the hostile plotters and enemies, as if with chariots. 13. In battles, to be invoked; by homage, to be approached; going among the spoils; the winner of wealth after wealth—all those enemies, the malicious plotters, Bṛhaspati has driven away, as if with chariots. 13.
He, Bṛhaspati, is to be invoked by warriors in battles—that is, in conflicts—for the sake of self-protection; he is to be approached with homage, meaning he is to be approached with reverence by all.
Furthermore, he is one who goes to the contests, being disposed to go to battles for the sake of protection;
likewise, he is the winner, the distributor, and the giver of wealth after wealth.
Because of its infinitude, the application of the genitive case is prohibited.

Likewise, the noble lord Bṛhaspati "vivavaha," that is, he especially weakened or shattered "all" (viśvāḥ) "mṛdhaḥ"—meaning all the attacking, injurious armies—"like chariots," as if [shattering] the enemy's chariots with speed in battle.
Or, the word *iva* may have the sense of "and";
thus, he also shattered their chariots.
The suffix *liṭ* is used in the sense of the *luṅ* (aorist) tense.

With your most piercing heat, burn the demons who have set you, whose valor is manifest, to shame! Make that deed of yours visible which is worthy of praise; O Bṛhaspati, destroy those who surround us with evil. With your most piercing heat, burn the demons who have set you, whose valor is manifest, to shame! Make that deed of yours visible which is worthy of praise; O Bṛhaspati, destroy those who surround us with evil. (14)

O Bṛhaspati, with your most sharpened—that is, exceedingly sharp—and scorching—that is, tormenting—weapon, burn—that is, cause pain to—the Rākṣasas. Connect the meaning as follows: "Burn those Rākṣasas who have made you, whose valor has been witnessed in battles, an object of censure. Make manifest now that valor of yours which was previously worthy of praise by all and which existed [within you].
And by that vigor, O Paripara, "vi ardya"—strike down specifically those reviling, censuring Asuras.
In the Bārhaspatya [rite], the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the oblation belongs to the Ātreya family.

It is prescribed in the section beginning with "Pradānānām" in the Sūtra: "O Bṛhaspati, when the enemy exceeds his due, may our words be attended by glory" (*Bṛhaspate ati yadaryo arhāttamściyā upa vācaḥ sacante*, Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7).
This very same verse serves as the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*) in the Aśvina-śastra.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "The verse *bṛhaspate ati yadaryo arhāt* is the concluding verse" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.5).

O Bṛhaspati, that which belongs to the noble one, which deserves it—splendid, radiant, and full of wisdom among the people; that which shines forth with power, O you who are born of the Eternal Order (Ṛta)—bestow that wonderful wealth upon us. 15 O Bṛhaspati, that which the noble one deserves, which shines forth splendidly and full of wisdom among the people, and which glows with might, O you born of the Eternal Order—that wondrous wealth, bestow it upon us. 15
1. For the purpose of protecting the vowels *ka*, *jha*, and *ma*.
2. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *ma*—these belong to you (*te tava*); *jha₁*—by that (*tena*). 3. And it is formulated (*sūtritam*) by *ta* and *tha*.

O Bṛhaspati, born of the chosen [sacrificial] seat, may I, as the most excellent Brahmin, bring all desires and honor that splendor which is the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). [The root *vṛh* is used here in the sense of honoring.
"I" [is used] in the sense of honoring.
The augment *letyā* [is applied].

Among the people, among the Brāhmaṇas, that *brahmavarcasa*—which is auspicious, endowed with splendor, possessed of vigor, and filled with knowledge—shines forth, that is, it blazes intensely; and by its power (*śavasā*), it illuminates the people who depend upon it.
The root *dīdayati* means "to shine.
He causes it to shine.
Place—that is, deposit—within us that wonderful (*citram*), praiseworthy (*cāyanīyam*), and desirable (*vat*) wealth (*draviṇam*) which consists of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

Or rather: even though you have granted wealth that is exceedingly difficult to obtain, it shines forth as a means for accomplishing deeds among those people who offer hymns of praise to you; and since that wealth, through its power (*śavas*), illuminates its own locus with abundance for us—grant us such wealth.

And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "With the verse, 'O Bṛhaspati, that which you have surpassed, O worthy one' (RV 2.23.15), one desiring splendor and desiring Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should conclude [the recitation]. For one who surpasses others is indeed worthy of Vedic luster; [the word] *cumat* means 'shining forth,' for Vedic luster shines forth as it were; [the word] *vibhāti* means 'it shines intensely,' for Vedic luster shines intensely as it were; [the word] *dīdāya* means 'it has shone,' for Vedic luster has shone as it were; [with the words] 'bestow upon us that wonderful wealth' (*draviṇam... citram*), for Vedic luster is indeed wonderful; thus one becomes possessed of Vedic luster and possessed of the glory of Brahman" (Ai. Prā. 4.11). 31.
Do not deliver us to the thieves who, dwelling in the place of malice, have awakened as enemies among our foods.
They deceive the gods; the three [groups] do not know the *sāman* before their hearts, O Bṛhaspati.

Not [us], O Bṛhaspati! Not those who are thieves, who pursue malice at every step, enemies who are greedy for food and plot against the gods; they do not know the threefold fortress of the Sāman in their hearts. 16.
O Bṛhaspati, deliver us from thieves; do not give us over to them. "Thieves" (stenāḥ) means robbers;
do not surrender us to them.
He shows them:

"And those who are thieves, haters, delighting excessively (*nirāmiṇaḥ*) in the place of injury to living beings (*prāṇadrohasya pade*), being enemies (*vṛpayaḥ*) and harmful (*hiṃsakāḥ*), they long for (*abhijāgratuḥ*)—that is, desire intensely—their own wealth belonging to others.
[The root] *gṛdh* is used in the sense of longing.
This is the form in the *liṭ* (perfect tense).
And "ye" refers to those gods who are "vitrayaḥ," meaning they perform "vi-vrī"—that is, they specifically exclude (*vi-varjana*).
The verbal root *vrī* signifies exclusion (*varjana*).

"One who, knowing thus, accepts the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), does not indeed injure the sacrificial fee" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.5.1). Since this is seen as a statement for the purpose of excluding one [person], it serves the purpose of excluding the other as well. They bear that in their own hearts or they offer it into their hearts;
that is to say, they think, "We shall not perform the sacrifices and praises of the gods."
"May they not give us to them"—this is the connection.
Those men who are of the *sāman*, consisting of the *sāman*, beyond, further beyond, other than evil-doing—that *sāman* which is unassailable.
Indeed, the *sāman* is the slayer of the Rakṣases.
They do not know; they do not understand.
But do not deliver us, who know you alone as the *sāman* that accomplishes everything, to the thieves.
For from all the moving worlds, the seer has extracted you, the *sāman*, from every *sāman*.
He, the knower of debts, the Lord of Prayer, the slayer of the deceitful, is the upholder of the great cosmic order.

For Tvaṣṭṛ, the seer, fashioned you from all the moving worlds, you who are the master of every sacred song. He, the knower of debts, the Lord of Prayer, the slayer of the deceitful, is the upholder of the great cosmic order. 17. From all the moving worlds; indeed; for you; from around; Tvaṣṭṛ; fashioned; from every sacred song; the seer; he; the knower of debts; of the debt; the Lord of Prayer; the slayer of the deceitful; of the great; of the cosmic order; the upholder. 17.
1. Ka, kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, ṇa, tha, na, ma, va: this is the form of *brahmavarcasa*. 2.
Ka, kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, ṇa, na, va: this is to be seen by all; for the other [initiate], it is to be seen by me alone.
3. Ka, kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, ṇa, na, ma, va: this accomplishes everything.
O Brahmanaspati! Tvaṣṭṛ, Prajāpati, has indeed begotten you—superior to all worlds, that is, superior to all classes of beings.
Therefore, you are the seer (kavi) of every single *sāman*.
[The root] *ku* means "to sound."
The suffix *ip* is applied by the rule "aca hraḥ."
You are the one who utters [the praise], the agent.
Or rather, Tvaṣṭṛ, the seer (kavi) who has transcendent vision, has generated you through the *māra* of every single *sāman*.

Furthermore, that Brahmaṇaspati is the supporter (*dhartā*) of the great (*mahaḥ*) *ṛta*, the sacrifice; he is the "debt-collector" (*ṛṇacit*), so called because he gathers the debt—the desire for praise—just as one collects a debt from the sacrificer who maintains it.

Furthermore, he becomes the one who drives away and separates himself from debt—that is, from debt which is of the nature of evil—and he becomes the slayer of the Asura Droghu, the malicious one who acts with hostility.
When you, O Aṅgiras, released the mountain from its body and let loose the sphere of light,
O Bṛhaspati, with Indra as your ally, you unbarred the ocean that was enveloped in darkness.

The truth: For the sake of glory, the mountain opened wide; you released the herd of cows, O Aṅgiras. With Indra as your ally, O Bṛhaspati, you pushed open the ocean that was encompassed by darkness. 18.
O Aṅgiras, O Bṛhaspati, the mountain that was the obstructer of the cows and presided over by Vala opened its gates for the sake of your glory;
then, whenever you [sought] the herd.
The suffix *tra* is applied in the sense of a collection [of things] according to the rule *ini-kaṭaka-yacaś-ca*.

At that time, you released—that is, you drove out—the herd of cows; joined by Indra as your ally, you overturned—that is, you turned completely face-down—the ocean of waters, which was the cloud that had been enveloped and overwhelmed by the darkness of the demon Vṛtra.
O Lord of Prayer, be the uniter of this hymn and prosper our offspring.
All that which the gods protect is auspicious; may we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.
O Lord of Prayer, be the uniter of this well-spoken hymn; prosper our offspring. All that the gods favor is auspicious. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 19.

O Brahmanaspati, Lord of the sacred word (brahman), Sovereign of hymns, you who are the guide and controller of this world—be mindful of this well-spoken hymn addressed to Brahmanaspati; take heed of it!
Strengthen our progeny, characterized by sons, grandsons, and the like.
The word *jīva* means "for the sake of pleasing";
it is a form in the imperative mood (*loṭ*).
Delight [us]. Since gods such as you protect and guard, all that universe becomes auspicious and well-being.
Therefore, being possessed of excellent heroes—meaning having noble sons and grandsons—in this sacrificial assembly (*vidatha*), may we speak forth this great and most excellent hymn of praise.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the second book in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial authority of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.

1. *Ka-kha-ga-gha-ṇa-jha-jha-la-ṇa-la-ta-tha-na-ma-va*: O Brahmanaspati, you who are the supporter (*dhartā*) and sustainer (*dhāraka*) of the great and vast *ṛta* (cosmic order) and sacrifice (*yajña*), [be present] for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
2. *Ta-tha-sādhāraṇaṃ tvām*; *ma-sādhāraṇatvam*: You who are common to all; [I seek] the state of being uncommon [to others].
3. *Ka-jha-ṇa-ta-tha-na-ma-va-tvam*: You who are [the essence of] *ka*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, and *va*.

4. When *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ḷ*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, *va* [occur], then at that time; 5. [The one] characterized by sons, grandsons, and so forth, [indicated by] *kha*, *ṇa*, *pu*, *tra*, *pau*, *trā*, etc.; [the one] characterized by sons, grandsons, and so forth, [indicated by] *ga*, *jha*, *ḷ*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *na*, *va*, *pu*, *tra*, *pau*, *trā*, etc.;
6. By the minister named *ka-jha-sāya*.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now, the seventh [section] is explained, preceded by the [specification of] the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), deities (*devatā*), and applications (*viniyoga*).
In the third anuvāka of the second maṇḍala of Gṛtsamada, there are ten hymns (*sūkta*);
among them, one hymn is a grammatical exposition (*vyākaraṇa*).
“Semām” is the second hymn, consisting of sixteen verses. Regarding this, it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “Semām: sixteen verses; the twelfth is a Triṣṭubh, and it is addressed to Indra.
The seer (ṛṣi) is Gṛtsamada, the seer who perceived this Maṇḍala.
The twelfth and sixteenth verses are *triṣṭubh*s;
the remaining fourteen are *jagatī*s.
Since it is stated, "It belongs to Brāhmaṇaspati," these first three hymns belong to Brāhmaṇaspati according to the technical definition beginning with "tulā."
The twelfth verse of this hymn has Indra as its deity;
by the word "and" (ca), it is also addressed to Bṛhaspati.
Its general application has already been stated previously.
This should be understood especially from the indicative mark [of the mantra]:
"From this time forth, know this; we shall worship you with a new and great song, O Lord.
So that our liberal friend Bṛhaspati may grant us protection, may he further our prayer."

He is that Brahmaṇaspati who, by his *ojas*— that is, by his strength— thoroughly bent down (*vy anamat*), causing them to bow low, those things such as the Rākṣasas which were "not to be bent" (*ananvāni*).
"And furthermore, that Brahmaṇaspati [acts] with *manu*, that is, with *manyu* or anger."
"Manyu [is derived] from the root man, which has the sense of shining, or the sense of anger, or the sense of killing," says Yāska (Nirukta 10.29).
"Śambarāṇi. This refers to the clouds. "Vi adadaiḥ": he split them open for the purpose of raining.
This form is derived from the root *dṛ* in the sense of "tearing," with the *yaṅ*-luṅ suffix applied, followed by the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense ending.
Immediately after that, he "caused to fall" (prācyāvayat)—that is, brought forth with great force—the "unfallen" (acyutā) waters which remained motionless within the cloud;
the meaning is that he made them emerge from the cloud.

Likewise, he [brought] "toward" (ā) the "wealthy" (vasumantaṃ)—meaning possessing the wealth of cows in the form of water—"mountain" (parvataṃ), which was a mass of rock placed by the Asura named Vala at the mouth of the cave for the purpose of blocking it. And [the word] "ca" (and) implies "toward" (abhimukhyena).

The word *ca* has the sense of *ced* (if). If, however, it were intended in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), then by the rule "when joined with *ca*, *vā*, or *ha*, the first [word] is [accented]," the preceding indeclinable would have the acute accent on its first syllable,
while this [word *ca*] itself would be entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*).
But for the sake of the meaning, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule "nipātair yadyadīhantā" is established.
"Vi-aviśat" means he enters specifically;
the meaning is that at that time, he obtained that wealth in the form of cattle.
For that which is the most divine among the gods, the strong ones, having seized him, spoke with low voices;
he drove forth [the cattle], he split Vala with his sacred prayer, he concealed the darkness, and he made the light of heaven visible.

That—unto the most divine among the gods—he went. Eating the firm things, he ate them; the solid things, he shattered. He drove forth the cows; he split Vala with his sacred word (brahman). He concealed the darkness; he made the light of heaven visible. "Svar"—thus [he said] "Svar. 3.
"Among the gods, such as Indra and others, to the most divine one (*devatamāya*), who is pre-eminently endowed with qualities such as generosity."
The dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
The "deed" (*katvam*)—the action to be performed—of such a Lord of Prayer (*brahmaṇaspati*) is this:
what is it? It is said:
"devouring" (*aśnan*) the "firm things," such as mountains and the like.
The root *śranth* is used in the senses of releasing and rejoicing.
By his power, things that were loose became firm;
likewise, trees and other objects that were unsteady (*avīḷitā*) became steady (*vīḷitāni*), being supported and made firm.
Regarding this, Yāska states: "The roots *vīḷayati* and *vīḷayati* both have the sense of supporting. (Nirukta 5.16).
"O toothless one, you have become soft;
the toothless one has the nature and action of being soft.
Moreover, that Brahmaṇaspati has driven out the cows seized by force."
The root *aj* is used in the senses of "going" and "throwing."
He caused the gods to rise up;
likewise, by means of his own mantra, he shattered—that is, destroyed through the power of the mantra—the *asura* named Bala, who was the obstructor of all.
Immediately thereafter, he dispelled the darkness (*tamas*) produced by Bala.
The root *guhū* means "to conceal."
He made his own heart hidden;
immediately thereafter, he caused the sun—the heavenly light—to be seen, making it manifest by dispelling the darkness.
The eye has the function of seeing.
Brahmaṇaspati has pierced with might the stone-mouthed well, a stream of honey;
all have drunk from that very spring, and together they have poured out the abundant fountain.

The stone-mouthed well, the fountain of the Lord of Prayer, which he pierced with his might—the one that pours forth honey—into it all have drunk who behold the light; you have poured out much from the water-bearing spring all at once.
1. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ja, ṇa, ṇa, na, pha, and va are firm.
*Brahmaṇaspati* is the Lord, the protector of *brahman*, that is, of the sacred mantra; he is the deity who possesses a mouth as firm as stone (*aśmavat*).
Yāska says: "Possessing stones (*aśanavat*), that is, possessing flowing water" (*Nirukta* 10.13).
The meaning of this is: "one who is destructive and overflowing.

[He is] such that his water-stream (*udakadhārā*) is a giver of honey (*madhudhāra*). From that well (*avata*), which is situated and spread out (*tataṃ vistṛtam*), he overcame (*abhy atṛṇat*) that cloud by means of his vigor (*ojasā*), that is, by his strength.
The root *tṛd* is used in the senses of "injuring" and "making a sound."
The meaning is that he struck [the cloud] for the purpose of raining.
All those very clouds are the "regions of heaven" (*svardeśaḥ*);
*svaḥ* refers to the sun (*āditya*).
The rays, which are its relatives and beholders, drink—meaning they consume—the water of the rain during the summer season;
it is said that they drink that very [water] because they drink the water of the rain through the cloud.
And those rays, during the rainy season, have poured out together, simultaneously, much from the cloud, which is full of sprinkling (*utsam*), watery (*udriṇam*), and full of water.
The meaning is that they sprinkle even more than what was drunk during the hot season—specifically, a thousand times as much.

Ancient indeed are those wondrous worlds, which have come into being; through months and autumns, they have opened wide their doors for you. Moving with independent effort, each in its own direction, Brahmaṇaspati has established these ordinances of wisdom. sanā | tā | kā | cit | bhuvanā | bhavītvā | mādbhiḥ | śaradbhiḥ | duraḥ | varanta | vaḥ | aryatantā | carataḥ | anyad'anyad | it | yā | cakāra | vayunā | brahmaṇaḥ | patiḥ || 5 ||

O you who are being officiated as priests (*ṛtvij*), for your sake (*yuṣmad-arthaṃ*), those various eternal (*sanā-tanāni*) sacred formulations (*brahmāṇi*) of Brahmaṇaspati, [and] the worlds (*bhuvanāni*) of the worlds—
here the genitive case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*—
the doors (*duraḥ*) of the waters (*bhuvanām udakānām*) that are to come into being (*bhavyānām*), [we have fashioned] with the months (*mādbhiḥ*).

By the rule beginning with *‘pahna’* and so forth, the substitution of *māsa-* for the word *māsa-* occurs; the application of *t* [as a substitute] is desired by the rule *‘svatavasmāsoṣāṃ ca ta iṣyate’* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.48.2). Thus, the form *māstvam* is established.
"By autumns and years they open" means that at that time, for the purpose of raining, they open the doors of the clouds;
what, then, are those?
Brahmaṇaspati [knows] those various insights.
This is knowledge.
He produced—that is, he created—the various forms of knowledge concerning mantras.

Immediately thereafter, both [the heaven and the earth], being effortless (*ayatantau*)—that is, exerting no effort—move about and enjoy each other's respective domains: the two worlds, namely heaven (*dyauḥ*) and earth (*pṛthivī*). Heaven is the divine water, while earth is the terrestrial food characterized by the oblation; thus, through mutual exchange, they move about and consume one another.
The root *car* is used in the senses of moving and eating.

Those who, seeking it, have found that treasure of the Paṇis, hidden most deeply in the cave—they, being wise, having discerned the falsehoods, returned; from where they had come, they went forth again toward their dwelling. abhinakṣantaḥ | abhi | ye | tam | ānuśuḥ | nidhim | paṇīnām | paramam | guhā | hitam | te | vidvāṃsaḥ | praticakṣya | anṛtā | punaḥ | yataḥ | u | āyan | tat | ut | īyuḥ | āviśam || 6 ||

When the herd of cows had been carried off by the Paṇi Asuras, Saramā, the divine dog, discovered the location of the Paṇis. Then the Aṅgirases, created by Brahmaṇaspati, reached that place; having seen the herd of cows and the illusions (māyā) constructed by the Paṇis, they burned down the dwelling-place of the Asuras with fire produced from their own hands and returned.
This very event is expressed in the Ṛgvedic verse:
"The Aṅgirases who were approaching, going towards [them] from all sides..."
This treasure, consisting of a multitude of cows, is the supreme wealth for merchants.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental.

The wise ones, the Aṅgirases, having perceived the falsehoods— the illusions created by the Asuras— which had been placed and hidden in the cave by the Paṇis, attained them; they exerted themselves to enter and pervade [the cave], and from whatever place they had departed,
they went back to that very place and rose up again, attaining it with excellence.
The truth-abiding sages, having beheld the falsehoods, have returned again from the great paths;
they [found] the fire fanned by their two arms upon the stone—there is no one who can obstruct it, for they have abandoned that which is not to be harmed.

The upholders of *ṛta*, having perceived the falsehoods, have returned from there; the sages have stood upon the paths of the great. With their two arms, they [have kindled] the fire blown into being upon the stone; indeed, no one is a stranger to him, for they have abandoned that [falsehood]. 7.
The *ṛtāvānaḥ*—
*ṛta* is a name for truth;

those possessing it, the *kavayaḥ*, the far-seeing and omniscient *Aṅgirasaḥ*, having perceived (*praticakṣya*) the falsehoods (*anṛtāni*) in the manner previously described, have come back again (*ājigamivaḥ*) from this place (*ataḥ*) and have stood firm (*ā tasthuḥ*) upon the great paths (*mahaḥ pathaḥ*).
And standing there, they indeed cast—the fire produced by churning and kindled by their arms and hands—upon the stone, the rocky heap that was the dwelling place of the Paṇis, in order to burn it;
for previously, that fire, the "araṇaḥ" (the one who causes restlessness through burning), did not exist there at all.
The meaning is that, having generated the non-existent fire by their own power, they scattered it there.
With his swift bow, whose string is truth, Brahmaṇaspati desires this; with that bow he reaches his mark.
Excellent are his arrows with which he shoots—the eyes of the man-beholder, whose source is the ear, are visible.

With his straight shaft, with his swift arrow, the Lord of Prayer reaches whatever he desires. Excellent are his arrows with which he shoots; they are visible to the man-beholder, for their origin is in the ear.

By means of that bow which has *ṛta* (cosmic order) as its very string—that bow which is swift, a launcher of arrows, and serves as a support—the divine *Brahmaṇaspati*, the protector of *brahman* (the sacred word or mantra), attains and pervades extensively whatever object he desires within that sphere.
The *parasmaipada* ending is used when the sense is "he reaches" (*aśnoti*).
The arrows of that bow are virtuous and effective; with those arrows, Brahmaṇaspati shoots—that is, he hurls—at the Rākṣasas and others.
Of what nature are they? They are "nṛcakṣasaḥ," meaning they behold men.
This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

For the omniscient Brahmaṇaspati, they were born for seeing—that is, for perception and knowledge—as "ear-born" (*karṇayoni*), meaning either arrows made of the sense-organ of hearing (*śrotrendriya*) which are to be grasped [by it], or arrows fashioned to the ear.
The sense is that one accomplishes everything by means of the mantra of Brahmaṇaspati alone.

1. O Brahmaṇaspati, those created by you—ka, jha, ña, ṇa, ta, dha, ma, va, he—are Brahmaṇaspati; kha, ga, pha, yaḥ are Brahmaṇaspati; na, he—O Brahmaṇaspati, those created by you. He is the one who leads forward, he is the one who arranges, he is the domestic priest, he is well-praised; he is Brahmaṇaspati in battle.
When the wise one brings forth booty through his thought, the sun, the son of Aditi, shines with its heat as it pleases.

He is the one who brings together; he is the one who disperses. He is the domestic priest; he is the well-praised one. He is the Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati) in battle. When he, the skillful one, wins booty through his inspired thought, then the sun shines forth freely upon the glowing [world]. 9.

That Purohita, established here in front by the gods, is Brahmaṇaspati; he is the *sanya*, the one who unites those who are divided through sacred hymns. He alone is the *vinaya*, the various leader and also the separator of those who have come together. Likewise, he is *suṣṭuta*, well-praised by the singers of praise.
Likewise, in battle—that is, in combat—he manifests for the sake of favoring his worshippers; this is the ellipsis.
"When" (yat) means when he is visible (cākṣmaḥ).
It is derived from either the root *caṣṭi* (to look) or *kṣamate* (to endure).

The Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), the seer of all or the endurer of all, brings forth—*vāja*, food; *matī*, that which is to be meditated upon, the praiseworthy; and *dhana*, wealth—for the sake of his worshippers. He bears it and nourishes it for their increase.
Immediately thereafter (*ādita*), the Sun, the burner, shines effortlessly;
this word "effortlessly" implies the absence of exertion.
He blazes and shines without effort;
the meaning is that, because the sacrifice has been accomplished through the wealth granted by Brahmaṇaspati, he exists merely consuming the oblations himself alone.
O Bṛhaspati, the all-pervading Lord, the first possessor of wisdom, your well-known and successful gifts are these:
the acquisitions of the desirable, powerful one, by which both classes of people enjoy their share.

Pervasive, powerful, and foremost, the gains of Bṛhaspati are rich in wisdom and worthy of attainment; these are the acquisitions of the prize-winning Vainya, by which both classes of people—the clans—enjoy their sustenance. 10.

These [gifts] are all-pervading and abundant, powerful and mature, foremost and preeminent; they belong to Bṛhaspati, the protector of the great mantra, who possesses wisdom, who is endowed with excellence, and who bestows rain—[gifts that are] truly most gracious.
The root *vid* means "to find.
[The suffix] *katr* is applied after *su-vid*. (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.388)
They are to be well-obtained;
Yāska states, "wealth is that which is easily found" (Nirukta 7.9).
They are to be won (rādhyā), meaning they are to be properly accomplished.
That is to say, "those which are to be obtained.
These pleasant things, these riches, belong to the desirable, food-possessing Vājina, the Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati).
The genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
These have been given by Brahmaṇaspati.

By means of this [gift], both kinds of people—namely, the two types of persons, both the singers of praise and the sacrificers, or alternatively, both gods and humans—the settled *viśaḥ* (clans/people) enjoy and obtain their enjoyments.
The meaning is that all of that has been bestowed by Brahmaṇaspati.
He who is all-pervading in the lower realm, the great and exultant one, has carried you as a host;
that god has spread himself wide against the gods, for he, Brahmaṇaspati, encompasses them all.

He who, all-pervading, in the lower realm, is the great joy of the host; as the mighty one, you have carried us across. That god has spread himself wide against the gods; indeed, he, Brahmaṇaspati, encompasses them all. 11.

In every way (*viśvathā*), that is, in all manners, he is the pervasive (*vibhu*) one; the spreader (*vyāsaḥ*); the wound-healer (*vraṇaḥ*); or the one to be praised (*vyaḥ*); [he is] Brahmaṇaspati, who dwells in the lowly (*vcare*) enclosure (*vrajane*)—that is, in the strength that causes exclusion, meaning in the weak—and who [protects] the great (*mahām*).
The elision of phonemes is according to Vedic usage.
He desires to carry (*vavakṣita*), by means of his own power (*vśavasā*), the praiser who is of both kinds; that is to say, he carries him at all times.
This form belongs to the root *vah* with the desiderative suffix (*san*), in the perfect tense (*liṭ*);
it denotes a male descendant.
That god, endowed with qualities such as generosity, acting as the representative of all the gods toward the gods, spreads far upon the wide path—that is to say, he becomes extensive in fame.
Because it is so, therefore he exists as one who encompasses and surpasses all those various classes of beings. (The word *iti* is to be supplied at the end.)
The universe is true; O Maghavans, yours alone is it. Men violate your ordinance.
Come hither, O Indra and Brahmaṇaspati, to our invocation; like two yoked steeds seeking food, come to us.

The universe, truth, and the two Maghavans—your divine ordinance, even the seer himself, does not violate. O Indra and Brahmaṇaspati, come toward our oblation and our food like two yoked steeds eager for the prize. 12.
He is *maghavān* (the possessor of wealth); *magha* is a name for wealth.
O Indra and Brahmaṇaspati, you two who possess that wealth, you have indeed separated everything; all praise unto you both is true, according to reality.
The meaning is that whatever collection of qualities is set forth through praise, all of that exists in you both; it is not superimposed.
Thus, the two-word combination "na" and "iti" [is used].
Alternatively, there is a single compound [reading] according to the traditional transmission of teachers, just as in the case of the word "iva" with the preceding word.

And the plants, as well as the waters— this is an elliptical expression meaning that all the elements indicated by these do not violate, that is, they do not harm, your (vām) vow, which is your activity (vrata).
The root *mī* is used in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*);
it belongs to the *kaiyādika* class.
According to the rule "the short vowel occurs in the *nigama* [Vedic] usage of *mīnāti*," there is a shortening of the vowel.
O Indra and Brahmaṇaspati, come toward our oblation; that is to say, approach it.
Come hither.
The root *jigāti* has the sense of "going";
it belongs to the *juhoty-ādi* class.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"With a yoke, like two spirited horses.
Just as two spirited, vigorous horses yoked to a chariot go quickly of their own accord toward fodder and grass, so too [the meaning is]: "Come quickly in that same manner."
In the word *yujeva*, the vowel *ā* is the substitute for the nominative dual ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39);
for if it were the instrumental case, the case-ending would be acute by the rule *sāvekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.168).

And the draft-animals, free from disease, listen; the eloquent man, fit for the assembly, brings forth wealth with his thoughts. Firmly hating [the enemy], following his own will, consuming the debt, he is indeed the prize-winner in the encounter—Brahmaṇaspati.

And indeed, the swift steeds listen to the prayer; the eloquent one, fit for the assembly, brings forth hymns and wealth. He who is firm against those who hate, who collects the debt according to his will—he is truly the powerful Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati). 13.

Furthermore, the swift-moving, rapid-goers, the steeds of Bṛhaspati—those who carry the sacred prayer (*brahman*)—listen; they listen in due order to the hymn of praise performed by us. Or rather, [they listen] to that which has been fashioned by Bṛhaspati. (Note:
*kha-ga-gha-1-rūpajālam* refers to a collection of forms;
*kha-ga-jha-ṇa-ga-1-ta-tha-na-ma-va-ekapadyam* indicates these words form a single metrical line.)
They listen to the instruction given;
therefore, let them cause him to reach our sacrifice—this is the ellipsis. *Sabheya* means one who is proficient in the assembly.
The suffix *ṭha* is applied [after a word] in the sense of "in the Veda" (*cchandasi*).
The wise one—the Adhvaryu or the Hotṛ priest—with inspired thought, that is, with a hymn worthy of contemplation.
The long vowel of the same quality as the preceding [vowel] occurs by the rule "supām suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
He brings— that is, he procures— the riches characterized by oblations for that Brahmaṇaspati;
or rather, through his hymn of praise, he brings— that is, he sustains and nourishes— the riches.
Therefore, he is "vbīludveṣāḥ": Brahmaṇaspati is such because he hates (dveṣṭi) the firm (bīḷūn), that is, the Rākṣasas and others; [and] "vaśā" [is used] for the sake of the cow (vaśāyāḥ).
The elision [of the case-ending] occurs by the rule "supāṃ suluk" (Pāṇini 7.1.39),
and the preservation of the original form occurs by the rule "ṛtyakaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.128).

The remaining portion [of the sentence] is: "We, as sacrificers, must give what is to be given in the form of portions (*avadāna*); you, in turn, become the receiver. Furthermore, the nature of the *avadāna* as a debt is clearly known from the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā*: "One is born with three debts: through studentship (*brahmacarya*) to the seers," and so forth.
Alternatively, *anu* signifies conformity (*ānuguṇya*).
It should be understood that she (*vaśā*) becomes one who takes on the conformity to *vaśa*, that is, to desire or longing.
The particle *ha* indicates well-known fact.
Indeed, he (*saḥ*), Brahmaṇaspati, [is present] in the conflict (*samithe*).
The *samidh* is the sacrifice (*yajña*), because in it the gods come together (*saṃyanti*) and meet (*saṃgacchante*) through the oblations (*āhutibhiḥ*).
In that [sacrifice], the *vājī* is one who possesses food (*annavān*);
therefore, the meaning is that the wise man becomes a receiver (*ādātā*).

The true wrath of Brahmaṇaspati arose according to his will, as he was about to perform a great deed. He who drove forth the cows distributed them throughout heaven; like a vast stream, he became distinct through his power. Brahmaṇaspati’s: arose; according to his will; true; wrath; great; deed; performing; who; cows; drove forth; he; to heaven; and; distributed; like a vast; stream; by power; became; distinct. 14.

The wrath (*manyu*)—the means of thought (*manana-sādhana*), that is, the *mantra* or anger—of Brahmaṇaspati, who was about to perform a great deed, became true (*satya*), that is, unfailing (*avitatha*), according to his will (*yathākāma*).
The meaning is: he acts exactly as he desires.
That Brahmaṇaspati drove forth (*udājat*), that is, caused to rise up, the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis.

The meaning is that he brought them out from the cave. He, Brahmaṇaspati, for the sake of *div*, that is, for the heavenly world and the gods residing there, divided those cows; he made them distributed.
And that herd of cows was like a vast expanse of earth,
or like a great hymn of praise.
‘Rīṅ’ [is used] in the sense of flowing.

Just as the currents of the Ganges and other rivers, being divided, flow toward low-lying regions, so too did she, by her own power (*vaśasā*), go to dwell in various separate temples of the gods, wandering from one to another.

O Lord of Prayer, may we ever be masters of well-governed wealth that brings vigor; grant us heroic sons among our heroes, since you, as the sovereign lord of prayer, heed my invocation. 15. O Lord of Prayer! Of well-governed wealth! Evermore! Of riches! May we be! Masters! Of that which brings vigor! Among heroes! Heroes! Bestow upon! Us! You! Since! Being the sovereign lord! Of prayer! You heed! My! Invocation! 15.

O Brahmaṇaspati, Lord of Mantras, may we be masters (rathyāḥ)—that is, possessors of chariots—at all times (viśvahā), throughout all days, over the wealth (rāyaḥ) that is well-restrained (suyamasya), excellent (suṣṭhu), endowed with vitality (vayasvataḥ), and accompanied by food (annayuktasya). May we be the sovereign lords (adhipatayaḥ). Those who possess chariots are called rathyāḥ.
1. Kha-ga-anu means in sequence; ṇa-anu means in sequence. 2. Ka-ca-jha-ṇa-tha-ma-va is like a hymn of praise (stuti).
3. Ka-ca-jha-ta-tha-ma-va is in the hearing (śravaṇa).
The vowel *ī* in *īvanipau* is an affix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*), according to the rule *chandasīvanipau*.

Furthermore, *naḥ* means "for us"; *vīreṣu* means "among our sons," those born of heroic power; *vīrān* means "sons"; and *tvam upa pṛṇdhi* means "you, bestow upon them"—that is, make them endowed with [heroic power], produce them.
The root *pṛcī* signifies "to join together" (*saṃparke*).
Belonging to the *raudhādi* class [of roots].
"May we obtain even grandsons"—this is the sense.
*Īśānaḥ*: you, the lord of all; *brahmaṇā*.
O you who possess various names! You desire my invocation—my call characterized by praise—along with the oblation characterized as food;
for the root *vī* is used in the senses of "motion," "procreation," "beauty," "eating," and "devouring."
Therefore, what I have said means "do it.
O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), be the controller of this hymn and prosper our offspring.
All that which the gods protect is auspicious; may we, possessing brave sons, proclaim this aloud at the assembly.
O Lord of Prayer, be the controller of this well-spoken hymn; prosper our progeny. All that which the gods favor is auspicious. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 16.
O *Brahmaṇaspati*, you who are the controller and ruler of the entire world, [be the master] of this hymn—this very hymn.
(The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative because of the rule: "The mention of the action must be made," whereby the object becomes a recipient.
*Bodhi*: be aware; take heed.
O Buddhas, quicken—that is, impel—our offspring and our sons;
here the root *jivi* has the sense of "pleasing," yet it functions in the sense of "impelling" because verbal roots can have multiple meanings.
And whatever is auspicious and beneficial that all the gods protect, quicken all that auspiciousness as well—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

And we, being endowed with excellent heroes—sons, grandsons, and so forth—shall speak, shall utter a vast and mature hymn of praise at the *vidatha*. A *vidatha* is a sacrifice, for it is therein that one knows the gods; it is in that sacrifice that we shall speak.
The third hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "indhānaḥ," is in the Gāyatrī meter; however, this [third verse] is in the Jagatī meter and is addressed to Brāhmaṇaspati.
Thus it has been enumerated: "indhānaḥ pañca jāgataṃ tu" (five verses beginning with indhānaḥ, but the [third] is in Jagatī).

The application [of the mantra] is indicated by its characteristic marks (*laiṅgika-viniyoga*). "Kindling the fire, he shall overcome those who attack; having performed the sacred prayer (*brahman*), may he hear the offered oblation.
He who is known through his offspring spreads abroad—he whom Brahmaṇaspati makes his ally."

1 | He who kindles the fire shall conquer those who seek to conquer him; he who has offered prayers and presented oblations shall hear [the gods]. From this world, with that which is born, he overcomes what is known; he whom Brahmaṇaspati makes his companion advances far beyond. || 1 ||

Kindling Agni—that is, enkindling the fire for the purpose of the sacrifice of Brahmaṇaspati—the sacrificer shall conquer (vanavat), that is, strike down (hiṃsyāt), the enemies who seek to harm or inflict injury. Regarding the word *vanuṣyat*, Yāska states: "The root *vanuṣ* has the sense of 'to kill'.
The particle *it* is used here in the sense of *ca* (and).
"Kṛtabrahmā": he by whom the *brahman*—that is, the hymn of praise (*stotra*)—has been performed; thus he is so called.
"Rātahavya": [he by whom the oblation has been offered].
The oblation (*havya*) has been offered and given by the sacrificer (*havīyan*);
being thus, he who hears (*śṛṇuvat*) increases.
[The root] *duśri* means "to move" and "to increase."
This is the form [of the verb] in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix derived from this root with the causative (*ṇic*) affix.
Likewise, the sacrificer, by means of his born son, "far surpasses" (*atisarsṛte*)—that is, he goes far beyond—the "born," i.e., the produced, grandson of himself.
The meaning is that even by beholding his grandson, he may live for a long time.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by way of transposition from the root *dhū* (to shake) in the sense of "to purify.
The meaning is that he whom Brahmaṇaspati makes his "companion" (*yujam*)—that is, his friend—by accepting his hymns and oblations, becomes equal to him.
1. kha-ma-prajvālayan | 2. ka-jha-1-ta-ma—*vanuṣyati* is a verb whose action is to injure. 3. ca-tha—the word *caḍi* does not exist. 4. ta-tha—produced.
Through his heroes he has won heroes; nourished by cattle, he has spread his wealth like a flame.
May he increase both the offspring and the descendants of him whom Brahmaṇaspati makes his ally.

With heroes he shall conquer the attacking warriors; with cattle he shall extend his wealth and lead it forth. His offspring and his progeny increase, whomever the Lord of Prayer makes his ally. || 2 ||
That sacrificer, by means of his own heroic sons, shall conquer—indeed, he shall strike down—the heroic sons of the enemy who seek to harm him;
moreover, he shall extend—that is, he shall cause to spread and increase—his wealth together with cattle.
This form [prāpayat] is derived from the root *prath* in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix.
Likewise, he awakens by himself, that is, by his own self;
the meaning is that his knowledge becomes independent of anything else.
Furthermore, for that sacrificer, *tokaṃ* means "son" and *tanayaṃ*—the case ending being indeclinable—means "grandson."
The son and his offspring increase and become fully grown;
or rather, Brahmanaspati causes the child, the son, the grandson, and the great-grandson to grow.
The root *vṛdh* should be understood as having the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it.
One of these two.
Like the surging flood of a river, like a roaring bull, he rushes impetuously with might;
like the spreading flame of Agni, he cannot be turned back—whomever Brahmaṇaspati makes his ally.

Like the surging flood of the Sindhu, impetuous and fierce, he strikes like a bull; with his might he seeks to overcome [all]. Like the spreading flame of Agni, he cannot be turned back—whomever Brahmaṇaspati makes his ally. 3.

The Sindhu is a river characterized by its flowing; just as a rushing torrent (*kṣodaḥ*) breaks through a crumbling bank (*kṣudhyamānam kūlam*), so too does the *śimīvān*—for *śimī* is a name for action—the sacrificer, joined with the ritual activity that constitutes the service of Brahmaṇaspati, desire (*vaṣṭi*) to slay with his might (*ojasā*) and strength (*balena*) the attacking (*ṛghāyataḥ*) and harming enemies, desiring them on all sides. [The root] *vaś* [is used] in the sense of "desire."
This is another illustration:
"Like a bull, he strikes down the strikers; the oxen have their testicles crushed and are rendered powerless.
Just as a bull capable of impregnation, being full of vigor, overcomes other oxen, so too does he overcome his enemies—this is the meaning.
Moreover, this [light] is like the *prasiti* of fire;
*prasiti* means a flame, that by which one is *prasīyate*, i.e., bound—
[the root] *ṣiñ* meaning "to bind."
The suffix *kin* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
Just as the flame of a fire whose spread has been obstructed cannot be stopped or turned back, even so it is not possible at all to restrain or turn this back.
The word *aha* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
The suffix *taven* is applied to the root *vṛ*, with the causative meaning (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) inherent within it, or to the root *vṛt*, in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*).
Or anything else.
For him flow the celestial waters from all sides; as the first among the heroes, he goes forth for the sake of the cattle.
Whomever Brahmaṇaspati makes his ally, that one strikes with unassailable and irresistible might.
For him flow the celestial waters, unceasing; as the first among warriors, he goes forth for the cattle. With undiminished vigor, he strikes with might whomever he makes his ally, O Brahmanaspati. 4.
1. *ma-ra-yiṃ-dhanaṃ*.
2. *jha-ṇa-ta-tha-na-tathā*.
Ṛgveda 2.14.
For that sacrificer, the divine waters—those existing in heaven, characterized by rain—flow, move, and reach him, being unattached and unrestrained.
Therefore, it has the form of a lamp-wick.
Likewise, that sacrificer,
accompanied by *satvānaḥ*— those who are effective achievers and attendants— goes first, being prior to other sacrificers, into the cattle;
the meaning is that he obtains wealth such as cows and so forth.
Furthermore, *anibhṛṣṭatavipī*:
*tavipī* is a name for strength. Being one whose *tavipī*, that is, strength, is *anibhṛṣṭā*, meaning not crushed or overcome by enemies, he thus slays his enemies with *ojasā*, that is, with power.

Therefore, all the roaring rivers have made their way; they have provided many flawless shelters. Fortunate, he prospers in the favor of the gods, whomever Brahmaṇaspati makes his ally. (5) For him indeed, all the roaring rivers have made their way; they have provided many flawless shelters. Fortunate, he prospers in the favor of the gods, whomever Brahmaṇaspati makes his ally. (5)
Therefore, for that very sacrificer, all the rivers—all those characterized by flowing—shake themselves;
that is to say, they flow forth for the sake of accomplishing his desired fruit.
Likewise, they bestow, and are maintained for him alone, many and abundant protections (*śarma*), which are flawless and without defect, being continuous.
Alternatively, "śarma" is a name for a house;
many dwellings free from defects are maintained.
Being "subhagaḥ," one who possesses beautiful wealth, and dwelling in the "sumne" (bliss) of the gods—that is, in the happiness bestowed by the gods—he "edhate," meaning he prospers and increases.
The remainder is clear.
The fourth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with “Ṛjuḥ,” is the seer Gṛtsamada’s; it is composed in the Jāgata meter and is addressed to Brāhmaṇaspati.
Thus it is enumerated: “Ṛjuścutukam. Its ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.

The upright singer shall prevail over the one who assails him; the seeker of the gods shall overcome the one who does not seek the gods. The well-aided man shall prevail in battles; the sacrificer shall divide the food of the non-sacrificing enemy. The upright one indeed; the singer; shall conquer; the assailant. The seeker of the gods indeed; shall overcome; the one who does not seek the gods. The well-aided one indeed; shall conquer; in battles; the invincible. The sacrificer indeed; shall divide; the food; of the non-sacrificing enemy.
*Ṛjuḥ* means straight or indeed endowed with uprightness.
Alternatively, *ṛñjati* is a term for the act of adorning;
thus, he is the very one who adorns the hymns. *Śaṃsaḥ* is the praiser, the singer of *Brahmaṇaspati*. May he *vanavat*—that is, may he conquer or strike down—the *vanuṣyataḥ*, the harming enemies.
This is the form of the act of removing forest-dwellers.

Likewise, one who desires for himself the godly Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), who is divine and endowed with virtues such as generosity, should overcome—that is, surpass—the ungodly person who is the opposite of him.
This form consists of eight limbs.
Likewise, *suprāvīḥ*.
From the root *ava* in the sense of protection (*styarthāt*), the suffix *ī* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules.

May he, the one who thoroughly and pre-eminently satisfies Brahmaṇaspati, [be victorious] in battles, in conflicts, in combats—[he who is] like a forest, difficult to cross over, impossible to overcome. (Note: Regarding the variants:
1. ṇa reads *sodakāḥ*; kha, ga, tha read *sādakāḥ*; ma reads *sādaraḥ*. 2. jha₁ reads *sa tādṛśaḥ*; ta and tha read *etādṛśaḥ*.)
He should strike [them].

Likewise, he should sacrifice; having sacrificed with an oblation to Brahmaṇaspati, he should "threefoldly allot"—that is, specifically distribute—the enjoyment, the means of pleasure, of those who do not sacrifice between the two types of sacrificers. This is the meaning.

Sacrifice, O hero; understand the one who intends [the rite]; make our mind auspicious for the conquest of Vṛtra. Prepare the oblation so that you may be fortunate; we choose the protection of Brahmaṇaspati. Sacrifice, O hero; understand the one who intends [the rite]; make our mind auspicious for the conquest of Vṛtra. Prepare the oblation so that you may be fortunate; we choose the protection of Brahmaṇaspati.
The seer instructs his own man:
"O *vīra*, especially impelling the hymns, O friend, worship *Brahmaṇaspati*; honor him with praise.
[Worship] those who move as swiftly as thought, the destroyers."
Or rather, against the enemies who are challenging you, *pravihi*—go forth pre-eminently for the sake of battle.
