The root *vī* is used in the sense of "going" and so forth;
the short vowel is a Vedic (chāndasa) irregularity.
In the *vṛtratūrya*—in the battle that serves as the cause for the destruction of the *vṛtras*, the obstructing enemies—make even that mind auspicious and courageous;
through the grace of Brahmaṇaspati, victory will surely follow.
Likewise, prepare and offer the oblation, such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other offerings, to Brahmaṇaspati.
Just as you are fortunate, possessing beautiful wealth, so may you be.
In the case of *alaṃṭi*, there is the augment *aṭ*.
That is to say, through the sacrifice to Brahmaṇaspati, you shall become possessed of splendid wealth.
Moreover, we choose—that is, we pray for—the protection (avaḥ) of Brahmaṇaspati; we seek it directly.

He indeed, with his people, he with his clan, he with his lineage, he with his sons, wins booty and wealth with his men—he who, with a mind full of faith, seeks to win over Brahmaṇaspati, the Father of the gods, with an oblation. He indeed, with his people; he with his clan; he with his lineage; he with his sons, wins booty and wealth with his men—he who, with a mind full of faith, seeks to win over Brahmaṇaspati, the Father of the gods, with an oblation.

That sacrificer who, possessing a mind full of faith— that is, one whose mind is characterized by faith— worships with an oblation such as cooked rice or sacrificial cake the Lord of Prayer (*Brahmaṇaspati*), the protector of the gods; he alone, that very sacrificer, brings forth or gathers for himself *vāja*, food, through all living beings and the entire world.
He alone, with his people, his offspring, and his own kinsmen, brings forth strength (*vāja*). He alone, with his sons—his own progeny—brings forth strength.
Likewise, with men—leaders and other attendants—he brings forth, or maintains, or accomplishes various riches (*dhana*).
This means that for the sacrificer who has worshipped Brahmaṇaspati, people from all sides become providers of food and wealth.

Whosoever has offered to him oblations rich in clarified butter—him Brahmaṇaspati leads forward. He delivers him from distress and protects him from harm; even here, the wonderful one, who creates wide space, makes room for him even from danger. yaḥ asmai havyairghṛtavadbhiradhvaraṃ tam prācā nayati brahmaṇaspatiḥ | uruṣyatīmaṃhaso rakṣati riṣa iho cidasmā urukridadbhutaḥ || 4 || He who has performed the sacrifice for him with oblations accompanied by clarified butter—him Brahmaṇaspati leads forward. He delivers him from distress and protects him from injury; even in this world, the wonderful one, who provides wide space, makes room for him.
1. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ṇa, ta, tha, na, va are assigned; jha and ma are assigned. He who is the sacrificer—for this Brahmaṇaspati.
Because the object [of the action] is treated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) due to the rule "the term *kriyā* must be included," the dative case is employed.
One worships this Brahmaṇaspati with oblations (*havya*) consisting of clarified butter (*ājya*), which includes both the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).
[The root] *viṣ* means "to arrange" (*vidhāna*);
it belongs to the *nau-dādi* class.
This is recited among the duties of service.
Brahmaṇaspati leads that sacrificer forward by a straight path directed eastward; he causes him to attain excellent fruit.
Moreover, he delivers (uruṣyati) him from distress—that is, he protects him.
Yāska states: "The root *uruṣyati* has the sense of protecting."

Likewise, he protects from enemies, such as those who would harm him; even from distress, that is, from those who obstruct the truth or possess false knowledge. Or rather, having approached even to kill, he protects [them].
Moreover, for this sacrificer, the wonderful one— this is indeed great—
is the teacher-like, great Brahmaṇaspati, the wide-maker, the performer of vast and extensive benefit.

The fifth hymn, consisting of seventeen verses beginning with "imā giraḥ," belongs to Kūrma, the son of Gṛtsamada, or to Gṛtsamada himself; it is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter and has Āditya as its deity.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "imā giras—Tvasū Kūrma, the son of Gṛtsamada, [praises] Āditya.
The application of this hymn is determined by its internal characteristics (liṅga).
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to the deity Āditya, the verse "imā giraḥ" is the invitatory formula (*anuvākyā*) for the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).
This is recorded in the section on Agni-Soma in the sūtra: "imā gira ādityebhyo ghṛtastṛta ādityama uravo gabhīrāḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).

These songs, dripping with clarity, I offer with the ladle to the Ādityas, the radiant kings. May Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, the many-born Varuṇa, Dakṣa, and Aṃśa hear us. These songs, dripping with clarity, I offer with the ladle to the Ādityas, the radiant kings. May Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, the many-born Varuṇa, Dakṣa, and Aṃśa hear us.

To the Ādityas—the sons of Aditi, the kings, the radiant ones, or the lords such as Mitra and the others—I offer these songs, characterized by praise, which drip with clarified butter (*ghṛtastṛḥ*), meaning they flow with *ghṛta* or pour forth *ghṛta*. With the *juhū*—this being a name for speech—I offer them; that is, I present them or perform them by means of the organ of speech at all times, eternally.
Alternatively, I offer the oblations in the form of speech—dropping clarified butter as if from a *juhū* ladle—and renounce them for the sake of the Ādityas.

Furthermore, the fact that mantras are the cause for the flowing of milk and other substances is clearly stated in the *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* (2.10): "Whatever one studies, by that he performs an act of milk [and so forth].
May Mitra and the others individually hear those songs of ours.
And these are clearly enumerated in the *Taittirīya* [Āraṇyaka], beginning with "Eight sons of Aditi": "Mitra, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Aṃśu, Bhaga, Indra, and Vivasvat—these they are" (Tai. Ā.
1.13.3). Mitra is the protector from death (*pramīti*);
or rather, he is affectionate toward all.
He is Aryaman because he restrains (*yacchati*) and holds back (*niyacchati*) enemies.
Bhaga is the god who is to be honored (*bhajanīya*).
*Tuvi* is a name for "much."
He has manifested for the sake of bestowing grace upon many lands;
this is a specific epithet of Varuṇa.
He is called Varuṇa because he wards off evil.
"Dakṣa" means capable;
this is an adjective qualifying Aṃśa. Let each of these listen individually.
For the very same animal mentioned previously, "imaṃ stomam" is the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the omentum offering (*vapā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "imaṃ stomaṃ sakratavo me adya... trīṃrata dhūn" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
1. "ṇa-ta" constitutes one [syllable]. 2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, jha, and ṇa, the phrase "I give" (prayacchāmi) is absent; likewise in 1, tha, na, and va. 3.
In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, and ṇa, it is by means of that which stands in place of *ju* and *hra*.
4. In ṇa-1-tha-ma, "adakṣaḥ samarthaḥ" (inexpert, capable) does not exist.
5. In ka-jha-ma, it is [the word] aṃśuḥ.
6. In kṣa-1-ta-tha-na-ma-va, it is the *yājyā* of the *vapāyāga* (oblation of the omentum); in ṇa, it is the *yājyā* of the *vapāyāga*.

May Mitra, Aryaman, and Varuṇa, together with the Ṛtus, graciously accept this hymn of mine today—the Ādityas, who are pure, purified by the stream, free from crookedness, blameless, and unharmed. imaṃ stomam sa'ṛtavo me adya mitro aryamā varuṇo jupanta | ādityāsaḥ śucayo dhārapūtā avṛjinā anavadyā ariṣṭāḥ || 2 ||
O Mitra and the others— those of equal deeds or equal wisdom— may they now graciously accept and enjoy this our hymn of praise today. Of what nature are they?
The Ādityas are the sons of Aditi;
they are pure, shining, and purified as if by streams of water— the meaning is that they are stainless.
*vavṛjināḥ*: from the root *vraj* in the sense of "avoiding" (*varjane*). The meaning is "those who avoid [harm]," that is, those who favor all beings.
Free from fault means being devoid of blame, reproach, and evil;
most excellent means being unharmed by anyone.
For that same animal sacrifice, "Then the Ādityas... is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) for the oblation;
the sūtra has already been cited previously.

Those Ādityas—broad, profound, undeceived, seeking to harm, many-eyed—behold within both the crooked and the straight; for these kings, everything, even the most distant, is near at hand. 3. Those Ādityas: broad, profound, undeceived, seeking to harm, many-eyed; they behold within; the crooked; and also the straight; everything; for the kings; even the most distant; is near. 3.
O Ādityas, sons of Aditi,
you are wide-ruling, great,
and profound, endowed with depth.
Being unassailable, meaning not harmed by enemies, they are *vdipsantaḥ*, desiring to deceive or to injure their enemies.
Regarding the root *dambh* in the sense of "deceiving":

from this root, with the suffix *san* in the sense of desire (*icchā*), there is the substitution of *i* for *dh* in the form *dambh-i-iccha* according to Pāṇini 7.4.56 (*sanīvantardha*), in the alternative where the augment *iṭ* is absent.
This is established by Pāṇini 1.2.10 (*dambher grahaṇasya jātivācakatvāt siddham*), which provides for the suffix *san*.
When a *kit* suffix follows, there is the elision of a nasal.
Likewise, "bhūryakṣāḥ" refers to those who possess many (*bhūrīṇi*) or numerous (*bahūni*) eyes (*akṣīṇi*, *cakṣūṃṣi*);
or it means those of great splendor (*bahutejasaḥ*).
The compound suffix *pac* is applied by the rule "bahuvrīhau sakthyakṣṇoḥ... [Pāṇini 5.4.113].

Such Ādityas, dwelling within the hearts of living beings as their inner impellers, behold—that is, they know—the crooked, meaning sins, and also the straight, meaning meritorious deeds, performed by living beings.

Even those things that are most distant, situated in far-off places, they see; indeed, all visible things are near them, being close to the sovereign rulers who are the primordial source. This is the sense.
By the rule "elision of the initial [consonant] is frequent" (*kādilopo bahulam*), there is elision of the initial *ka-* of the word *antika*.
In the *sāmidhenī* verses and the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, there are two *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the Āditya sacrifice beginning with "dhārayantaḥ.
For this very reason, they are also used in the Āditya sacrifice qualified by the epithets "bhuvat" and "bhuvanapati.

Accordingly, it is stated in the section on the *dīkṣaṇīyā* in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] beginning with 'dhārayanta ādityāso jagatsthāḥ'—these same two [are used] for the sacrifices to Bhuvat and Bhuvat, or to the Lords of the World" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.2).
1. In the manuscripts ṇa, ta, tha, ma, and 'me, [the word] does not exist. 2. In the manuscript ga, it is *ṇa* and *dabhitum*.
3. In the manuscript jha, it is *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, and *dve*.

Upholding [the world], the Ādityas, the gods who dwell in the moving and the stationary, are the guardians of the entire universe; they are far-sighted, protecting their divine power, upholders of cosmic order (ṛta), and collectors of debts. 4. Upholding; the Ādityas; the moving; the stationary; the gods; of the entire; of the universe; the guardians; far-sighted; protecting; their divine power; upholders of cosmic order; collecting; debts. 4.
The world consists of both the moving (*jaṅgama*) and the stationary (*sthāvara*).
The suffix *asun* occurs after the root *sthā* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed.

Sustaining and establishing these two kinds of created beings, the gods—endowed with qualities such as generosity—are the guardians and protectors of the entire world, the whole universe; they are those whose thoughts, actions, or knowledges are far-reaching.
The rule "anyeṣām api dṛśyate" [Pāṇini 6.3.137] prescribes the lengthening of the vowel in the preceding member.
"Sūrya" refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*). By that term, the waters, which are the cause of those breaths, are indicated.

And the fact that water is the cause of that [life-force] is clearly stated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "The vital breath consists of water" (Chā. Up. 6.5.4). An *asura* is a cloud (*megha*), so called because it gives (*dadāti*) water (*asu*). Those who protect the water existing there, within the clouds, are the *rakṣamāṇāḥ*.
At that time, they were protecting [the world] by bringing about rain.
From the word *asura*, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule "in the Vedic language, when denoting existence."
Those who possess truth, or those who possess reality, or those who possess sacrifice.
The suffix *vanip* is applied in the sense of possession according to the rule *chandasīvanipau*;
as before, there is lengthening of the vowel.
The debts that ought to be paid by the singers to others are being cleared away as they are accumulated and discharged.
The root *ci* in the sense of "motion" (*gati*) belongs to the *bhūvādi* class and is marked with an *anudātta* accent.
The ellipsis is: "May those of such distinguished qualities and great majesty come under our control."

May I know this protection of yours, O Ādityas—O Aryaman, that which is truly blissful even in the midst of fear. Under your guidance, O Mitra and Varuṇa, may I avoid all difficulties, just as a daughter-in-law avoids her mother-in-law. 5. vidyām | ādityāḥ | avasaḥ | vaḥ | asya | yat | aryaman | bhaye | ā | cit | mayobhu | yuṣmākam | mitrāvaruṇā | praṇītau | pari | śvaśreva | duritāni | vṛjyām || 5 ||
O Ādityas, sons of Aditi, this favor of yours belongs to you.
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
May I obtain this protective vidyā;
when fear from rākṣasas and others has arisen, may there be that protection which belongs to you—
the word *ca* (cic) is used in the sense of "and."
"May I obtain this which brings bliss (*mayobhu*) and is the producer of bliss (*mayaḥ*); such is the connection [of the words].

O Āryaman, O Mitra and Varuṇa, when your guidance—that is, your well-disposed leading—is directed toward us, may I avoid, that is, abandon, misfortunes (*duritāni*), which are like pits or uneven ground unfit for standing upon, just as one avoids the feet of a mother-in-law (*śvaśrūṇīva*)."
The root *vṛj* means "to avoid" or "to exclude.
According to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).

For easy to travel indeed is your path, O Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa; it is smooth-flowing and straight. By that path, O Ādityas, speak for us and grant us protection that is difficult to overcome. 6. For easy to travel indeed is your path, O Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa; it is smooth-flowing and straight. By that path, O Ādityas, speak for us and grant us protection that is difficult to overcome. 6.
1. *Mārakṣaṇam* is a protective spell (*vidyā*).
O *arthaman*, *mitra*, and *varuṇa*: *vaḥ* means "of you"; *sugaḥ* means "easily traversable"; and *ṛkṣaraḥ* refers to "thorns," as they cause one to stumble (*ṛcchati*).
"Free from that," "good," "an adept," or "excellent"—such a path, distinguished by these qualities, "exists" (asti) indeed. Therefore, the ellipsis is: "by that path, lead us to what is auspicious."
O Ādityas, speak for us—utter words of advocacy with partiality toward us.
Moreover, grant us that happiness (*śarma*) which is difficult to overcome—that is, impossible to destroy.
[The root *dāṇ* means "to give."]
In the word *śapi*, the substitution of *ya* occurs according to the rule "pā-ghrā-... and so forth.
"May Aditi, the daughter of royalty, and Aryaman protect us from hatred by easy paths.
May we, possessing many heroes, remain unharmed under the high protection of Mitra and Varuṇa."

7 | They uphold the three celestial luminaries; they are golden, pure, purified by their stream; they have sleepless offspring, they are unblinking, undeceived, and far-famed for the sake of the upright mortal. 9 | They uphold the three celestial luminaries; they are golden, pure, purified by their stream; they have sleepless offspring, they are unblinking, undeceived, and far-famed for the sake of the upright mortal. 9 | They maintain the three divine realms of light; they are golden-hued, radiant, and purified by their own flow. Having progeny that never slumber, they are unwinking, inviolable, and possess wide renown for the sake of the upright mortal. 9 | They maintain the three divine realms of light; they are golden-hued, radiant, and purified by their own flow. Having progeny that never slumber, they are unwinking, inviolable, and possess wide renown for the sake of the upright mortal. 9 |
The Ādityas, holding fast the three luminous realms— the three shining, radiant, celestial regions as if they were divine—
did so for the sake of the upright mortal, that is, for the human being who is straightforward, in order to accomplish his enjoyment.
Of what sort are the Ādityas?
They are golden (*hiraṇyayāḥ*), meaning made of gold, with all their limbs adorned with gold; or else, they are those whose appearance is delightful to behold.
"Pure" means shining; "purified by their streams" means stainless, as if washed by a flow of water. "Asvapna-jāḥ" means those in whom sleep has not arisen;
[here] the suffix *su* is used for the nominative plural *jas* according to the rule "supāṃ suluk."
Another says:
"Without their own offspring" means they do not sleep, being free from drowsiness.
Regarding the statement that "the suffix *nañiṅ* [is applied] after *svapiti* and *porṇoti*," this is not the view intended by the author of the *Padapāṭha*.
"Unblinking," meaning free from winking;

"unassailable," meaning unharmed by Asuras and others; "widely praised," meaning worthy of being extolled and lauded by many—such beings, distinguished by these qualities, "maintained [the world]"—this is the syntactical connection.

O Varuṇa, you are the king of all—both those who are gods, O Asura, and those who are mortals. Grant us a hundred autumns to behold; may we attain long lives, well-established and many. 10. You... of all... Varuṇa... are... king... those... and... gods... O Asura... those... and... mortals... a hundred... for us... grant... autumns... to see... may we attain... lives... well-established... many. 10.
O Varuṇa, you are the *asura*, the repeller of enemies, and the king of all— meaning of both those who are the gods, the divine beings, and those who are mortals, human beings subject to death.
Therefore, grant us—give to us—for the sake of seeing clearly for a hundred autumns, that is, for a hundred years.
In the root *rā* meaning "to give," this very [root] takes the ātmanepada endings.
And may we attain—that is, pervade—the life-spans, characterized by a hundred years, which were well-established and properly ordained by the ancient gods.
The form *sudhita*, *vasudhita*, *nemadhita*, *dhivadhita*, and *pīya* are established as irregular (nipātana) forms.
By the rule "the preceding [member] is its own original accent" (*gatiranantaraḥ*), the initial syllable of the prefix retains its original tone. Thus: *pūrvī*.
The substitution of *ḍā* for the third case ending is according to the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39).

In the animal sacrifice dedicated to the deity Āditya, the verse "No gift for the right, no gift for the left" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8)—"They support the three earths; they strike down the malevolent ones"—is the invitatory verse (yājyā) for the oblation.

Neither the right nor the left is distinguished; neither the east, O Ādityas, nor yet the west. Whether by simplicity or by wisdom, O Vasus, may we, led by you, attain the light that is free from fear. 11. Neither the right nor the left is distinguished; neither the east, O Ādityas, nor yet the west. Whether by simplicity or by wisdom, O Vasus, may we, led by you, attain the light that is free from fear. 11.

1. [The words] *ka*, *jha*, *jña*, *la*, *va* are made of gold; *ma*—the word "made of gold" (*hiraṇmayāḥ*) is not present. O Ādityas, the *dakṣiṇā*, the right side, is not discerned by me; the *savya*, the left side, is also not known.
In both cases, the substitution of *su* by *āj* is according to the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
Likewise, it is not even known from what direction it comes from the east;
here, the suffix *ma* is added in the sense of the base itself according to the rule "vibhāṣāgnerdikchriyam."
Moreover, even the rear— the back portion— is not perceived,
because it is shrouded by nocturnal darkness or due to internal ignorance.
The form *paścāt* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātana*) according to the rule *paścātpaścā ca chandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.33).
What need is there for much? Even one who is "to be cooked" (*pākyā*), that is, "one who must be matured" (*pākya*)—even one whose knowledge is not yet fully ripened—[is worthy of honor].
The root *pac* with the prefix *ḍu* means "to cook.
By the rule *ṛhaloṇyat*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied;
this suffix is marked with the svarita accent by the rule *titsvaritam*.
*Dhīrya* refers to one who is timid, being so called because he must be led by a wise person.
The suffix *yat* [is applied] by the rule "in the sense of *bhava*, in Vedic."
Even those who are cowardly.
In both cases, the form ‘iyā’ is substituted [for the case-ending] by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

O Ādityas, you who possess the power to remove darkness, may I—having been led by you from this world and having reached [the goal] by a beautiful path—attain fearlessness and the light, whether it be the solar radiance or the internal light consisting of knowledge.

He who has offered gifts to the kings, to those who follow the cosmic order (ṛtunibhyaḥ), and whom the constant nourishments cause to grow—he, the wealthy one, goes first on his chariot, a giver of riches, highly praised in the assemblies. 12. He who [has offered] to the kings, to those who follow the cosmic order; whom the constant nourishments cause to grow; he, the wealthy one, goes first on his chariot, a giver of riches, highly praised in the assemblies. 12.
The sacrificer who offers oblations such as cooked rice and sacrificial cakes to the *rājabhyaḥ*—the shining ones, the leaders of *ṛta*, that is, of the sacrifice or of truth—the Ādityas;
and whom those nourishing, eternal, and everlasting Ādityas cause to prosper.

That sacrificer, being wealthy, famous as the foremost, and a giver of riches (vasu), being praised by all, goes by means of his chariot—his vehicle—to the *vidadhepus*, that is, to the houses which are to be obtained.

Pure, with good pastures for his waters, undeceived, he dwells there with increased vigor and heroic sons. No one slays him, neither from near nor from afar—he who is under the guidance of the Ādityas. śuciḥ | apaḥ | suyavasā | adabdhaḥ | upa | kṣeti | vṛddhavayāḥ | suvīraḥ | nakiḥ | tam | ghnanti | antitaḥ | na | durāt | yaḥ | ādityānām | bhavati | praṇītau || 13 || Pure, with good pastures for his waters, undeceived, he dwells there with increased vigor and heroic sons. No one slays him, neither from near nor from afar—he who is under the guidance of the Ādityas.

That sacrificer, being *śuci*—shining or pure; *adabdha*—unassailed by rivals; *vṛddhavayas*—possessing abundant food; and *suvīra*—having excellent sons—dwells near *sūyavasa*, excellent pastures, and *apaḥ*, the waters characterized by rain.
The meaning is that he always dwells in the vicinity of well-situated waters.
Likewise, *nakir*—no one at all—*ghnanti*—slays or harms him, whether from *antitaḥ*—from nearby—or from *dūrāt*—from a distant place, even when afflictions have arrived from afar.
In the word *antikasya*, there is elision [of the final syllable] according to the rule: "There is elision of [the letters] beginning with *ka*."

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: that sacrificer who exists—that is, who proceeds—under the *praṇīti*, the excellent guidance or leading, of the Ādityas, the sons of Aditi, such as Mitra and the others.

1. *kṣa* is understood. 2. *ka*, *jha*, *jña*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, *va*: the word *yajñasya* does not exist [in these cases]. 3. *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *ma*, *ya*, *m*. 4. *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *tha*, *ma*, *tasil*-etc.: elision occurs. Ka. 2-15: O Aditi, O Mitra, and O Varuṇa, be gracious; whatever sin we have committed against you, may we attain wide, fearless light. O Indra, let not the long-reaching snares reach us.
O Aditi, Mitra, and Varuṇa, be gracious! Whatever offense we have committed against you, may we attain the broad, fearless light, O Indra; let not the long darknesses reach us. 14.
And furthermore, O Āditi, O Mitra, O Varuṇa!

Because of the rule "an vocative is treated as if non-existent when it precedes [another]," each preceding vocative is considered non-existent; therefore, all [vocatives] possess the acute accent on the first syllable by virtue of the rule Pāṇini 6.1.198, "of a vocative."
May you each individually be gracious; show us mercy—this is the sense of "protecting.
Even though we [have been such], toward you... [we have acted].

O worshipful Ādityas, that magic of yours which is directed against the malevolent, and those snares spread out for the enemy—may we pass beyond them as a charioteer with his chariot; unharmed, may we abide in broad protection.

O worshipful Ādityas, those deceptive snares of yours which are set against the malevolent and turned away from the enemy—may we pass beyond them as a charioteer passes with his chariot; may we remain unharmed within your wide protection. 16.

O you who are worthy of sacrifice (*yajatrāḥ*), O Ādityas, those *māyās* (magical powers) of yours which have been fashioned by those intent on injury (*abhidruhe*)—namely, the Rākṣasas and others—and those snares (*pāśāḥ*) which are spread out (*vivṛttāḥ*) against the enemy (*ripave*); [the root] *vṛt* is used in the sense of "injury" and "knotting. The meaning is that they are extended. May I pass beyond (*ati yeṣam*) those snares and *māyās* with my chariot; that is, may I cross over them. There is an illustration for this: like a man with good horses (*aśvīva*). Just as some person with excellent horses quickly crosses over difficult paths, so too [may I cross]. The root *yeṣ* is used in the sense of "exertion" (*prayatne*). [End of commentary.]
May all these things be appeased by the greatness of this poet Aditi, the self-ruling sovereign;
for he is the god who, being most delightful, is worthy of sacrifice. I beg for the high renown of the abundant Varuṇa.

This [hymn] belongs to the poet, to Āditya, the self-ruling one. May it surpass all things in greatness—he who is the most delightful god for the sacrifice. From the abundant Varuṇa, I beg for a glorious renown.

The sacrificer performs this oblation or hymn of praise for the Seer (Kavi), who possesses far-reaching vision; for Āditya, the son of Aditi; for the Self-Ruler (Svarāj), who shines by himself, or for the Lord Varuṇa—this is the ellipsis. And may he, through his greatness (mahnā)—that is, through the majesty obtained by the grace of Varuṇa—overcome all existing beings that are subject to the second stage of transformation (decay).

The god who is shining, Varuṇa— who is exceedingly delightful (*mandraḥ*), meaning praiseworthy or a source of joy— for the sake of sacrifice for the sacrificer who protects the heavy [burden]— of that abundant sustainer Varuṇa, there is the quality of being entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*) for the whole of the two-word compound, due to the entry of the *anupraveśa* (penetration) of the *sukīr* (well-praised) from the preceding mantra.
"O gods, you who are invincible—unharmed by enemies—forgive us, who have committed offenses, for the sake of our alliance and truth; endure the transgression we have committed."

The Āditya has released them; they flow forth in separate channels. The rivers of Varuṇa go on their way; they do not weary, nor do they slacken. Like birds, they fly swiftly across the expanse of the earth. pra sīm ādityo asṛjad vidhṛtā kṛtaṃ sindhavo varuṇasya yanti | na śrāmyanti na vi muñcanty ete vayo na paptū raghuyā parijman || 4 ||

Like a dam that holds back water, he is the establisher; Āditya, the son of Aditi, Varuṇa, has "pra-asṛjat"—that is, he has excellently emitted—"ṛtam" from all sides, which is truth as the cause of support, or alternatively, the water that is the source of the rivers.
By the rule "aṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ," the vowel *ā* becomes nasalized.
By that truth of Varuṇa, the rivers—the flowing streams—go forth;
they flow onward.
These rivers do not grow weary; they do not reach exhaustion.
"They do not even cease" means they do not become inactive; rather, being untiring, they flow continuously with a single uniform nature.
This very point is expressed as follows:
Like birds in flight, the Raghus— swift-moving like the wind— flew, that is, they moved rapidly,
everywhere across the vast expanse of the earth.
The root *pat* means "to go.
In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) with the suffix *us*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel according to the rule *tanipatyo’cchandasi*.
Due to the status of the substitute being as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), reduplication and other operations apply.
In the word *raghuyā*, the suffix *jas* is replaced by *yā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.

Untie for me, as one unbinds a cord, the path of transgression; may we prosper in the fount of your eternal Law, O Varuṇa. Let not the thread be severed while I weave my prayer; let not the measure of my work be ruined before the time of fulfillment. 5.

O Varuṇa, loosen— that is, make slack and release— the sin (āgas), which is the evil produced by the non-performance of prescribed duties, like a rope or a cord from me. [Loosen] that stream (khām) of yours, full of the waters of cosmic order (ṛtasya).
*Khā* is a name for a river; may we *ṛdhyāma*, that is, obtain it.
Furthermore, may my *tantuḥ*, the continuity of my ritual action (*karma*), which *avayataḥ*—meaning which I am weaving together or extending—not *chedi*, that is, let it not be severed.
The meaning is "without interruption.

Likewise, "before" (purā) the completion of the season—that is, prior to the time of its conclusion—may the "measure" (mātrā), which is the body characterized by its eastern and northern [limbs], "not crumble" (mā śāri); that is, may it not become decayed or impaired.
The root *śṛ* is used in the sense of "injury.
[The form] is in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*) with the suffix *luṅ*.
In the expression *pura ṛtoḥ*, the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāvaḥ*) is maintained according to the rule *ṛtyakaḥ*.

1. *Sva* (the letter *s*) preceded by *ga* (the letter *g*), *ṇa* (the letter *ṇ*), or *pa* (the letter *p*); *ta* (the letter *t*) preceded by *ma* (the letter *m*); *tha* (the letter *th*) followed by *pa* (the letter *p*). 2. *Va* (the letter *v*) when light (*laghu*). 3.
*Sva* (the letter *s*), *ga* (the letter *g*), *ṇa* (the letter *ṇ*), *ta* (the letter *t*), *tha* (the letter *th*), and *ma* (the letter *m*) when not produced by a pause (*avagraha*).
4. *Ma* (the letter *m*) when relaxed (*śithila*).
O Varuṇa, let me go; release me from fear, O Sovereign Lord! Do not hold me fast, but let me go like a calf from its tethering-rope. For without you, I have no power even for the twinkling of an eye.

O Varuṇa, let there be no fear for me; O sovereign lord of the cosmic order (*ṛtá*), look upon me with favor. Release me from [this bond] as one releases a calf from its tether. For apart from you, I have no power even for the blink of an eye.
O Varuṇa, drive away (*apo myakṣa*) that great fear (*abhiyasam*) from me.
O Sovereign (*samrāṭ*), O Righteous One (*ṛtāvaḥ*), O Varuṇa, favor (*anugṛbhāya*) me.
In the Vedic language (chandas), by the rule "śāyaj api," there is the substitution of *śāyac* for *kṣa*;
and by the rule "hyahobhaiḥ," there is the substitution of *bha*.
Moreover: "Just as a milker releases the tethering rope from the calf, so too, O Day, release—unloose—the evil from me."
In Vedic usage, there is the elision (ślu) of the suffix śap.
"Separate [him].

This means that someone other than you—existing in a place far from you—is not even "nimiṣat," that is, not even capable of the twinkling of an eye, the movement of the eyelids; he has no power (īśe) over even that.
The meaning is that you alone are the Lord.
The elision of *t* occurs by the rule "lopas tathordhāt" in non-ātmanepada forms.
O Varuṇa, do not strike us with those weapons of yours that, when discharged, cause harm and afflict the unrighteous.
May we not go forth from the light into exile; release us from our oppressors so that we may live.

O Varuṇa, do not strike us with those weapons of yours which, O Asura, they brandish at the one who commits sin against you in the sacrifice. May we not go to the dwellings beyond the light; rather, loosen our enemies so that we may live. 7.

"O Varuṇa, do not harm us with weapons—that is, with the instruments of slaughter—this is the ellipsis. O Asura, the driver away of evildoers, those weapons of yours which destroy—that is, strike down—the person who commits sin (*enas*) in your sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), that is, the sin produced by the non-performance of prescribed duties; this is how it connects with the preceding clause."
The root *śrī* is used in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*);
it belongs to the *krayādi* group.

Moreover, from the fire existing in the house of light, or from the solar radiance, [the prayer is]: "May we not go to, may we not go to, the dwellings abroad"—that is to say, "May I live for a long time, seeing the sun always remaining in the house."
In the imperative (luṅ) of the root *gam*, there is the elision of the suffix *cl* by the rule "ghama."
Likewise, "for us," for our "living," "well" and "completely" "loosen" (vi-śiśrathaḥ)—that is, separate—our "enemies," the "harassers.
The meaning is: "drive them away."
Homage to you, O Varuṇa, both now and in the past, and even hereafter, O many-born one;
for in you alone, O unassailable one, are our steadfast vows established, as immovable as mountains.
Homage! O Varuṇa, of many births, we would speak to you—both now and hereafter—for in you alone, O invincible one, are established those unshakable laws, as if upon a mountain. 8.
1. By performing what was not prescribed:
O Varuṇa, in former times (*purā*), we spoke the word "namaḥ" to you (*te*), which expresses salutation;
and furthermore (*uta*), even now (*nūnam*) we speak it.
Moreover, O Varuṇa, you who have manifested in many places (tuvijāta), even at a future time we shall utter—the word "namas" (reverence);
why?
Because you are *daḷhabha*, that is, *dudaṃbha*, impossible to deceive or to harm.

By the rule *duro dāśanāśadabhadhyeṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.109), there is the substitution of *u* for the *r* and the substitution of *h* for the initial letter of the following word; the word *kam* is used here as a filler to complete the metrical foot.
For indeed, O Śvāparvata, like a mountain peak, you have taken refuge in—meaning you have relied upon—vows that are unshakable, actions that cannot be displaced by others, and supports [of dharma].
This is the meaning.
Wipe away the debts incurred by me; O King, let me not suffer for what I have not done. There are yet many dawns that have not dawned; O Varuṇa, ordain that we may live through them.

O King Varuṇa, ward off the debts incurred by others; let me not suffer for what another has done. Many dawns have yet to dawn upon us; while we are still alive, O Varuṇa, ordain for us those [dawns] that remain.
O Varuṇa, drive away—drive far off—the debts, those debts incurred by our fathers and others which we ourselves must pay;
send them back.
The root *pū* means "to impel"; the form is in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Now, at this moment, O Supreme One, please discharge the debts incurred by me, those obligations fulfilled by me.
Furthermore, O King, Lord Varuṇa, may I not enjoy—that is, may I not obtain—the wealth acquired by another or earned by another.
If it is asked for what reason, it is said:
"Many more nights have passed—vastly more, even beyond measure;
indeed, they truly remain unbroken.
Even as I was rising in the latter part of the night, reflecting upon my debts while awake, those nights that had dawned seemed to me as if they had not dawned at all."

O Varuṇa, ordain for us, while we are still living, that we may possess the vitality of life at dawn; instruct us thoroughly on all sides—meaning, having cleared our debts, grant us wealth sufficient for our enjoyment.
O Varuṇa, whether it be a rival king or a friend who has spoken of some personal fear to me, or a thief who seeks to harm us, or a wolf— protect us from him!
O King, whoever—whether an ally or a friend—has spoken of danger to me who am afraid, or the thief who seeks to harm us, or the wolf; from him, O Varuṇa, protect us. 10.

O King Varuṇa, my own kin—whether a father or other relative, a friend capable of joining in a journey, or another kinsman sharing the same dwelling—whoever speaks to me, who am fearful by nature, of the danger regarding you that I have seen in a dream;
or likewise, whoever—a thief or a robber, or a wolf, a wild dog—seeks to harm or kill us.
The absence of the augment *iṭ* is due to the optional rule "sanīvantardha";
the substitution of *i* is according to the rule "dambha hucca."
O Varuṇa, therefore protect and guard us from all of that.

1. [The substitution of] *ṇa*, *ta*, and *tha* occurs in many places; [the substitution of] *ma* occurs in certain places. 2. [The substitution of] *ṇa*, *tha*, and *ma* occurs at another time. 3. [The substitution of] *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *ta*, and *tha* occurs for the purpose of deception (*dambhitum*). 4. [The substitution of] *ka*, *jha*, *jha*, *la*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, and *va* serves to complete the meter (*padapūraṇam*).
May I not find lack from Maghavan, the beloved Varuṇa, the giver of much, the one who possesses abundance.
O King, may I not be excluded from well-governed wealth; may we, possessing brave sons, proclaim great [praise] in the assembly.

O Varuṇa, may I not experience the destitution of my dear Maghavan, the giver of much; may I not fall away from the well-governed wealth of my kinsman, O King. May we, possessing heroic sons, offer great oblations at the assembly.

O Varuṇa, may I not be made known as one lacking before the presence of the beloved, the bountiful giver of much wealth, the possessor of riches who is to be invoked—the son and his descendants; rather, may I make myself known, may I announce it, may I cause it to be understood.
O King, because you are a perfect restrainer, may I not stand apart from your protection;
may we, possessing noble sons, remain within the sacrifice or the home and utter a mature hymn of praise.

The seventh hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "dhṛtavratāḥ," belongs to Gṛtsamada Kūrma; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas, composed in the Triṣṭubh metre. Thus it has been enumerated: "dhṛtavratāḥ—seven [verses], dedicated to the Viśvedevas. The application (viniyoga) has already been explained.
O Ādityas, upholders of vows, full of nourishment—may the portion of the secret seers be far from me.
O gods Varuṇa and Mitra, you who hear me, knowing the auspicious [path], I invoke you for protection.

O you of firm vows, O Ādityas, full of vigor, far from me—like a woman who has given birth in secret—cast away my offense! O Varuṇa, Mitra, and you gods who hear me, knowing what is auspicious, I call upon you for protection. 1.

O Ādityas—those of firm vows, performers of sacred rites, sons of Aditi, swift-moving, and worthy of being approached or entreated by all—O Viśve Devas, perform (karta) the removal of my sin (āgaḥ), that which is produced by the non-performance of prescribed duties and the like, in a place far away from me (mat āre).
[The suffix *lu* is elided from the verb root *kṛ* due to Vedic usage;
the substitute *ta* is applied according to the rule *tasanasanathanāśca*.]
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a woman in secret.
A woman in secret is one who gives birth in a place unknown to others, that is, an unfaithful wife.
Just as she, having caused an abortion, abandons it in a distant land, so [is this].

O Varuṇa, Mitra, and O gods, knowing—that is, being aware of—your auspiciousness, the welfare to be brought about by you, I, while you are listening and cognizant through your hearing of the hymns composed for me, call upon you for protection, that is, for the sake of preservation.
O gods, you are wisdom, self-restraint, and vigor; drive away our enemies to a far distance.
As those who have sprinkled us with favor, look upon us with patience; be gracious to us today and be gracious to us hereafter as well.

You, O gods, are our providence; you are our strength. Drive away our enemies to a distance. As our protectors, look upon us with favor; be patient with us today, and show us mercy hereafter as well. 2.
1. There is no [word] meaning "remaining after having separated from the state" for *ka-kha-ga-gha-ña-a-jha-ṇa-ṇa-ta-tha-ma*.
2. *vasuvīrāḥ*: those with excellent sons. 3. *magṛtsamadasya*: of Magṛtsamada.
O gods, you alone are those whose superior intellect (*pramati*) belongs to fathers and others;
likewise, you alone are *ojas*, strength.
Moreover, you are the ones who [overcome] *dveṣāṃsi*—the hating ones, such as Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and so forth.
*Sanutaḥ* means "out of sight"; this is a term for being hidden. In a hidden place, *yuyota* means "separate" or "keep apart."
The root *yu* is used in the senses of "mixing" and "not mixing.
The *śap* suffix is replaced by *blu* according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
As before, there is the substitution of *ta* for that [suffix].

O you who are assailants—those who strike down enemies from all sides—overpower and conquer the foes! On this very day, be gracious to us and grant us happiness; furthermore, at another time, even in the future, continue to be gracious to us.
What indeed can we do for you with a future alliance, or what with a past one, O Vasus?
O Mitra, Varuṇa, Aditi, Indra, and Maruts, grant us well-being!

One of you alone has surpassed many, who, like a father, has instructed me, a gambler. O Gods, let your snares be far away, let misfortunes be far away; do not seize me, as one seizes a bird upon its young. 5.

O gods, among you I alone have greatly increased—indeed, I have extensively committed many sins. If it is asked how I am the only one among us, it is said: because you have instructed me, as a father instructs a son who has gone astray like a gambler, you have indeed taught me.
This is the second-person singular form in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) derived from the root *śās* in the sense of "instructing."
Moreover: "O gods, may your snares be far away from us;
may sins and evils be far away;
[may they not be] upon our son."
*Adhi*: expressive of the sense of the locative case.
While the son is looking on, do not seize—do not capture—the father who is present, like a hunter seizing a bird.
"May there be no fear for us from the Lord of Beings," thus [he said].

Turn toward us this day, O worshipful ones; being brought [as an offering], may I enter into your heart. O gods, protect us from the devouring wolf; protect us, O worshipful ones, from the pit that has been dug. arvāñcaḥ | adya | bhavata | yajatrāḥ | ā | vaḥ | hārdi | bharyamānaḥ | vyayeyam | ādhavam | naḥ | devāḥ | nijuraḥ | vṛkasya | ādhavam | kṛtāt | avapadaḥ | yajatrāḥ ||6||
O you gods who are worthy of worship, be turned toward us this very day;
may I, being afraid, reach your heart—the protection residing within your hearts—by approaching it directly.
The root *vyaya* is used in the sense of "going" (*gati*);
it belongs to the *bhūvādi* class.
O gods, [protect us] from the bonds of the wolf, the thief, or the wild dog, and from their slayers.
The root *jūr* has the meaning "to injure.
From this, the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule for *saṃpad* and so forth;
the shortening [of the vowel] is Vedic.
"Protect us from the *ādhvar* (sacrificial failure).
Likewise, O worshipful ones (*yajatrāḥ*), protect us from the *ādhvar* from the agent (*kartuḥ*) who brings about the calamities (*avapadaḥ*, i.e., misfortunes)."

O Varuṇa, may I not suffer loss through the wealth of my dear friend, the bounteous giver; O King, may I not fall away from well-governed riches. May the horse, distinguished by such qualities, impel our sacrifice forward.
The meaning is that *ju* is a verbal root (dhātu) found in the Sūtra;
from this causative form (*ṇyantāt*), the word-form is derived in the aorist (*luṅ*) with the suffix *caṅ*.
Likewise, may Viḷā, the first of the three goddesses, and the goddess Iḍā drive the chariot. Bṛhaddivā:
she who shines intensely, being great (bṛhat) and vast (mahat), is Bṛhadivā.
The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ḍvitaḥ ktriḥ*; the vowel *a* of the case-ending is substituted by *i* according to the rule *supāṃ sulukpūrvasavarṇāccheyāḍāḍyāyājālaḥ*.
May such a Bhaga impel us;
and also Rodasī, heaven and earth, the far-sighted Puraṃdhi,
and the god Pūṣan, the protector.
The word *adhas* has the sense of "below."
The meaning is: "May the two lords, the Aśvins, who possess the splendor of the sun—may all these impel our chariot."
And also those two divine, auspicious goddesses, Dawn and Night, who appear alternately and impel all moving creatures—
I praise them, for with my newest speech I would spread forth a threefold age for both that which moves and that which stands upon the earth.

And also these two goddesses, the auspicious ones, the beautiful ones, Night and Dawn, who look upon each other, who stir all living beings—I praise you both, O Earth, with a new song, for you provide the threefold nourishment for both that which moves and that which stands. 5.

Furthermore, indeed, those two well-known goddesses—those who delight in play (*devanaśīle*), who are fortunate (*subhage*, possessing beautiful wealth), and who look at one another (*mithudṛśā*)—namely *Uṣas* and *Naktā*, Dawn and Night—being such as they are, they are the ones who must impel (*apījuvā*) the moving beings (*jagataḥ*) of the world.
Therefore, let them also impel our chariot.
The latter half-verse is addressed directly to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivyau*).
O Earth and Heaven, you two, with most recent, newest, and most excellent speech, [protect] you [and us].
The elision of the third case ending occurs by the rule "supāṃ suluk."
When I offer the oblation, I pour it out.
The middle [note] occurs by way of transposition from the highest.

At that time, I am the one who spreads the underlayer for the stationary—such as rice and other grains—which is my food. "Vaya" is a name for food; I, whose food consists of such sacrificial offerings (*havis*) characterized by herbs, animals, and *soma*, spread the underlayer.
The meaning is that one offers [the food] preceded by the spreading of clarified butter (upastaraṇa) and the sprinkling over it (abhighāraṇa).
The root *sruj* means "to cover.
In the first person plural of the present tense (*laṭ*), there is the Vedic elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
Here, the word *atraṇi* is not [the negative particle] *na*; rather, it is another particle (*nipātāntara*) used as *caṇ* for the purpose of completing the metrical foot.
In the phrase “ṛta iddhātoḥ,” there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) according to the rule “nipātairdyadihanta.”
And may Ahibudhnya, Aja Ekapād, Trita, Ṛbhukṣan, and Savitṛ accept our praise like that of the Uśijs; may the Son of the Waters, the swift impeller, accept it with his thought and his power.

Or indeed, we desire your praise as if we were the Uśijs. May Ahi Budhnya, Aja Ekapād, Trita, R̥bhukṣan, and Savitṛ grant us favor. May the Son of the Waters, the swift impeller, through our prayer, bring us strengthening nourishment.
Moreover, O gods:
as if for the sake of those who desire [you], we two—meaning "we two"—rejoice; we long for, we desire, we seek your praise, you who desire our praise.

The root *vaś* means "to desire. [The suffix] *masi* ends in *i*. 1. The [variant readings] *ṇa*, *tha*, and *ca* do not contain *caḍhi*. 2. *ṇa*, *tha*, and *sāyā*; *ma* has *sayo*. 3. *kha*, *ga*, *jha*, *la*, *ṇa*, and *va* have *apijuvā*. 4. *ma* has *sthāvarasya carasya*. 5. *kha*, *ga*, and *ṇa* have *oṣadhayaśca*. 6. *kha*, *ga*, *jha*, *la*, *ṇa*, *ṇa*, and *va* have *stṛha*. 7. *kha*, *ga*, and *ṇa* have *pūraṇam*; *tha* and *va* have *padapūraṇam*. 8. *kha*, *ga*, *jha*, *la*, and *ṇa* have *masi*. (Ṛgveda 2.17)
There is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) due to the rule *grahijyā* etc.;
there is elision of a phoneme by Vedic license (*chāndasa*);
and furthermore, [there is] Ahirbudhnya.
The atmosphere is increasing;
therein dwells the god named Ahi,
the Unborn One-footed (Aja Ekapād).
He who is not born is "Aja" (the Unborn).
He alone moves, he alone goes; thus he is "Ekapāt" (the One-footed).
The Sun is known by the name Aja Ekapāt.

Trita, the one who has crossed over most completely; Ṛbhukṣan, whose dwelling is wide, whose abode is vast, or rather the one who causes the Ṛbhus to dwell; and Indra, the impeller of all, and Savitṛ, the progenitor of all—may they bestow, grant, and provide *canaḥ*, that is, food, for us.
Likewise, may Āśuheṣas, the swift-moving one, do so.
From the root *hi* in the sense of "going," the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well.
Such is *apāṃ napāt*, Agni, who stands in the place of the grandson of the waters.
Since non-dual herbs and trees are born [from the waters], and this Agni is born from the herbs and trees, they possess the status of being his grandsons.
And he becomes pleased through prayer, praise, and *śami*— *śami* being a name for ritual action— the remainder of the sense being that he is gratified by the performance of the sacrificial rite.

Or rather, through our devotion (*dhi*) characterized by service and through our ritual action (*karman*), O Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), you who desire *ṛta*— that is, the sacrifice (*yajña*)— for yourselves, and who desire to bestow it, [grant] *śam*, meaning happiness, for that purpose, on account of this speech (*vacas*).
One who speaks is *vacas*: the praiser; [derived from] the root *as* (to speak).

O Heaven and Earth, may you two be my protectors—my guardians and preservers. From you two, from whom food arises most excellently and abundantly—this is the implication—now these two, Heaven and Earth, have been praised by the singers stationed here and there; and for you two, I, desiring wealth, [pray] for the great [boon].
The reversal of the division.
With a great hymn of praise, I place [him] before me; I honor him.
Do not let the secret malice of the mortal deceive us; do not deliver us over to these calamities.
Do not abandon us; know us with a favorable mind, for we desire that from you with a devoted heart.

Let not the secret deceptions of the living foe harm us; do not deliver us over to these calamities. Do not let us be parted from you by distress; find for us that which brings happiness. With a benevolent mind, we entreat you for this.

O Indra and Tvaṣṭṛ, do not strike us with the secret, hidden, and unperceivable deceptions (*māyā*)—in the form of injury—of the human being who has become our enemy. This is an elliptical expression; [the meaning is] "may they not harm us by day or by night."
Likewise: "from these misfortunes for us. *Śuna* is a name for happiness; *duḥśunā* means misfortune (*ducchunā*).
Do not surrender yourself to the power of these enemy armies that cause suffering; do not be led into their control.
Yāska states: "The root *radh* is used in the sense of coming under control. [Elsewhere it is stated: "*Radh* is used in the senses of injury and success.
From this root, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and in the aorist (*luṅ*) with the reduplication (*caṅ*), this form is derived.
Moreover: "O Lord, let not our true friendships be severed from you; do not cause them to be separated.
Rather, O Blessed One, with a mind that desires our happiness, recognize—that is, know—that friendship of ours."
The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative because the object [of the action] functions as the recipient (saṃpradāna), according to the rule: "The term 'action' (kriyā) must be supplied."
We entreat you, such as you are—that is, we implore you for the desired fruit.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is elision (luk) of the case-ending following the word *tat*.
With a mind free from malice, bring hither with readiness the milch-cow who yields her milk, the swelling, the inexhaustible;
with swift-footedness and splendor, O you invoked by many, I urge you forward every day like a prize-winning steed.

Without malice, with your mind, bring hither the willing gift—the milch-cow yielding her full udder, inexhaustible. With your feet, you who are swift and possessed of splendor and vigor, I impel you, O you who are invoked by many, at all times. 3.
O Indra, O Tvaṣṭṛ, being without malice and with an unangered mind, milk [the cow] that yields obedience which is pleasant, productive, overflowing, increased, and full.
The root *pyai* means "to grow.
[In the formation of the word *pīna*,] the suffix *kasu* is applied after the perfect tense (*liṭ*). By the rule "liṅaḍoḍośca," there is the substitution of *pī* for the root vowel.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ugitaśca"; the vowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule "vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam";
and the retroflex *ṣ* is applied by the rule "śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca."
Bring hither—that is, cause to arrive before us—the cow, the milch-cow, who is such that her limbs are unattached and never fail;

moreover, O Puruhūta Indra, invoked by many, Tvaṣṭṛ has fashioned you with swift, pervasive movements of the feet, and with speech I impel you, the vigorous one, full of speed, on every single day with my hymns of praise.
The root *hi* is used in the senses of going and increasing.
1. In the manuscripts *ka*, *jha*, *jña*, 1, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, *tra*, and *‘asya’*, [the word] does not exist.
2. From *ka*, *a*, *jña*, *ta*, *tha*, *ma*, *tra*, and *śatrusenābhyah*: *no’smān*; in *kha*, *ga*, “*śatrusenābhyah*” does not exist; in *jha*, 1, *na*, and *ṇa*: *no’smān*.
In the *paranīmaya* sacrifices, before the *gṛhapati*, one should sacrifice to *rākā* and *sinīvālī*.
In that context, for the Rākā sacrifice, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses begin with "rākām aham" and so forth.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are 'rākām aham', 'sinīvāli', and 'kuhūm aham'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.10).
Likewise, these same two are also the *dhāyyā* verses in the Agnimāruta [section].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Regarding 'rākām aham', there are two [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).
"I invoke Rākā, who is easily summoned, with a beautiful hymn; may she, the fortunate one, hear us and take notice of us herself.
May she sew together our wounds with a needle that does not break, and may she grant us a heroic son, a giver of a hundred, worthy of praise."

I invoke Rākā, who is easily invoked, with a beautiful hymn of praise. May she, the fortunate one, hear us; may she take notice of us by herself. May she sew together our works with a needle that never breaks, and may she grant us a praiseworthy hero-son who bestows a hundredfold wealth. 4.
The full moon of the Paurṇamāsī is Rākā;
that goddess, named Svāhā, who makes the invocation successful, I invoke with a beautiful hymn of praise.
From the word *suṣṭhu*, the third case singular ending [is replaced] by the vowel *ī* through the rule *supāṃ suluk*, which substitutes a phoneme homogeneous with the preceding [vowel].
And may that auspicious lady, possessed of beautiful wealth, hear our invocation.
Having heard it, may she herself—by her own self—be aware; may she understand our intention.
And having understood it, may she sew together—may she extend—the work, characterized by the procreation of a son, with a needle-like, uninterrupted, and unbroken mind of grace.
Just as cloth and other items remain for a long time when sewn with a needle, so may he do this.
And having done so, may he grant a son who is heroic, valiant, a giver of a hundredfold, possessed of much wealth, a liberal giver, praiseworthy, and worthy of hymns.
O Rākā, those benevolent thoughts of yours which are well-fashioned, by which you bestow riches upon the donor—
approach us today with a gracious mind, O auspicious one, granting us thousandfold prosperity.

O Rākā, those gracious thoughts of thine which are beautiful in form, by which thou grantest riches to the donor—with those, well-disposed toward us today, come hither, O blessed one, bestowing thousandfold prosperity. 5.
O Goddess Rākā, those beautiful thoughts of yours—those excellent insights by which you bestow and grant riches and treasures to the donor who has offered oblations—come now with those very thoughts;
being well-disposed and of auspicious mind, approach us.
The *śap* suffix is elided due to the Vedic (*chāndasa*) irregularity of the root *gam*.
The nasal is dropped by the rule beginning with "anudāttopadeśa...". Because of the status of "asiddhavadatrābhāt," the elision of *hi* does not take effect.
What is she doing?
O fortunate one, O lady of beautiful wealth, she is bestowing—giving—the nourishment of a thousandfold wealth, that is, the increase of riches numbering one thousand.
The root *rā* means "to give.
The suffix *śānac* is used here by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
The substitution of *śru* for the *śap* affix is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
The initial syllable [of the word] *abhyastānām* is udātta according to the rule "the first of reduplicated forms" (*abhyastānāmādiḥ*).
In the sacrifice to Sinīvālī, there are two invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) beginning with "O Sinīvālī";
the sūtra has been cited previously. Among them, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is as follows:

1. O you of beautiful intellects! O Sinīvālī, broad-tressed one, who art the sister of the gods, accept the offered oblation; O goddess, grant us progeny. (6) O Sinīvālī, broad-tressed one, you who are the sister of the gods, accept the offered oblation; O goddess, grant us progeny. (6)
Sinīvālī is the new moon when the moon has not yet appeared.

O Sinīvālī, you who have broad braids, a broad hip, or a broad mass—since you are the sister of the gods, or rather their self-moving sister—do you graciously accept our oblation, the sacrificial offering cast into the fire before us.
Furthermore, O Goddess Sinīvālī, grant us offspring, such as sons and the like, or bestow them upon us.
The meaning is for the sake of the root.
In the word *diha*,
the suffix is the imperative (*loṭ*) with the Vedic elision (*ślu*) of the *śap* affix;
or [it is derived] from the root *diś* in the sense of "bestowing."

To her who has beautiful arms, beautiful fingers, a well-filled womb, and many sons—to that Sinīvālī, the mistress of the people, offer the oblation. (7) To her who has beautiful arms, beautiful fingers, a well-filled womb, and many sons—to that Sinīvālī, the mistress of the people, offer the oblation. (7)
She who is Sinīvālī, with beautiful arms, with beautiful fingers, and who is well-prolific.
The root *pūṅ* is used in the sense of "the production of life.
According to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*, the suffix *manin* is applied.
The accentuation follows the rule for a compound where the final member retains its original (prakṛti) accent when preceded by a root ending in *kṛt*.
Possessing much gold, she is the progenitor of many offspring.
By that same rule [Pāṇini 4.1.78], the suffix *kan* is applied;
then, by [Pāṇini 4.1.7] *vano ra ca*, the suffix *ṅīp* is added. The accentuation follows the rule for the original form of the second member of a compound (*kruduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).
To her, Sinīvālī, the mistress of the house, the protectress of the people.

By the rule *vibhāṣā sapūrvasya*, there is no substitution of *n* for the final syllable of *pati*. Because it belongs to the *ayasmaya*-class, there is an absence of the *jaśtva* change [of *t* to *d*]. By the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam*, the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the initial syllable of the second member of the compound.
O priests and sacrificers, offer, yes, sacrifice the oblation!
In the expression "tasanathanathanāśra," there is the substitution of *tana* [for *tanu*].

Her who is Guhū, Sinīvālī, Rākā, and Sarasvatī—Indrāṇī for our aid, Varuṇāṇī for our well-being. 8. Her who is Guhū; her who is Sinīvālī; her who is Rākā; her who is Sarasvatī—Indrāṇī for our aid; Varuṇāṇī for our well-being. 8.

Here, by the word *guhū*, because of its association with *rākā* and *sinīvālī*, *kuhū* is meant; that *guhū* who is *kuhū*, her I call (*āhe*). In the same way, it should be applied in the subsequent instances as well. I call *Indrāṇī*, the wife of Indra, for the sake of protection (*ūtaye*).
(Note: 1. ka, jha, tha, ma—*svayaṃsāriṇī*)
2. In manuscript Kha, ṇa-1, tha, and 'atra', the phrase "...kuhu rucyate" is absent. 3. In manuscripts Ka, a, jha, ṇa, ta, na, ma, and va, "kuhaḥ" is absent.
4. In manuscript Kha, [the reading is] "āhvayāmi".
She who is Sinīvālī, she who is Rākā, she who is Sarasvatī—those very ones I invoke today. She who is Sinīvālī, she who is Rākā, she who is Sarasvatī—those very ones I invoke today.
(5. kha-tha: "The same should be applied hereafter" does not exist.)
Likewise, I invoke Varuṇānī, the wife of Varuṇa, for well-being and for the destruction of the enemy.
By the rule beginning with "indravaruṇa," the feminine suffix ṅīṣ and the augment āmu are applied.
In the fourth section (anuvāka), there are eleven hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with “ā te pitaḥ,” is the Ṛṣi Gṛtsamada’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Rudra.
It is thus enumerated: “ā te paśnonā raudram.”
In the Rudra-sacrifices such as the Śūlagava, the western direction is to be worshipped with this hymn.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: “With the verses ‘O Rudra, for thee,’ ‘These [offerings], O Rudra,’ ‘Father, these [offerings], O Rudra,’ and ‘To Rudra, whose bow is firm,’ the worship of the directions is performed in all Rudra-sacrifices” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.8.23).
In an animal sacrifice dedicated to the deity Rudra, the verse beginning with “O Father, to thee” is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the oblation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “O Father of the Maruts, may this [oblation] go to you; for the tawny bull, the wise one, stand forth! (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).

Regarding this, Śaunaka says: “Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one who is pure and restrained in speech should offer a caru-oblation with the ‘ā te’ hymn dedicated to Rudra, verse by verse.”
Having first offered oblations of clarified butter and then worshipped Śaṅkara,
he should subsist on the remnants of the sacrificial offering, fasting for one day at a time, remaining unwearied.
"One should recite [this] at the full moon; one conquers and is completely liberated from diseases" (Ṛgvidhāna 1.168–170).
O Father of the Maruts, let our libation reach you; do not deprive us of the sight of the Sun.
May our hero prevail in battle and in peace; O Rudra, may we increase through progeny.
O Father of the Maruts, let your favor come to us; do not deprive us of the sight of the sun. May the hero be gracious toward our horse; O Rudra, may we be propagated with offspring.
O Father of the Maruts, O Rudra, progenitor of the gods known as the Maruts!
By the rule "param api chandasi," because that which follows a genitive case ending behaves like the preceding vocative member, there is acute accent on the first syllable of the entire word.
May that blissful happiness which is yours come to us.
And regarding Rudra’s fatherhood of the Maruts, we have already explained it through the narrative in the verse, "This [is] for the father of the Maruts" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.114.6).
Likewise, do not separate us from the sight of the Sun; do not deprive us of beholding him.

The root *yu* is used in the sense of "mixing" and "not mixing. In the present tense (*laṭ*), there is the substitution of *śru* for the *śap* suffix by Vedic rule; because of the rule "in the Veda, both ways," it is treated as an ārdhadhātuka suffix, and thus, due to the absence of the *ḍit* designation, *guṇa* strengthening occurs.
Against the attacking enemy;
for the Śruti states, "The horse is indeed the swift one" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.8.4).
Our hero—meaning our valiant son and so forth.
May they favor us with security;
or rather, O Hero, may you beg from us—beg from us even though we have committed offenses.
O Rudra, may we be procreated through our offspring, sons, grandsons, and so forth, and may we be abundant.

O Rudra, with those most auspicious healing medicines bestowed by you, may I attain well-being and long life. Drive far away from us all hatred, drive away distress, and scatter our maladies in every direction.

O most auspicious Rudra, may I obtain through the healing medicines bestowed by you a winter free from cold. Drive far away from us hatred, drive away distress, and drive away diseases in all directions. ||2||

1. Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer a portion of black [grain] (*kṛṣṇa*); having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer a single portion of black [grain]; having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer a sacrificial porridge (*caru*); having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer clarified butter (*ghṛta*); having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer a hundredfold portion of black [grain]. 2. Having offered the oblation to *ma*, one should then perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*). 3. *ka-ta-tha-ma-na*-single interval; *jha*- *ma*-single interval; *jha₁*- *ne*-single interval.
4. *jha*-full moon; *jha1*-on the full moon day; *ṇa-na*-full moon.
5. *ṇa-ta-tha*-for indeed, a son.
O Rudra, with these most healing medicines (*bheṣajebhiḥ*) given by you—most exceedingly pleasant ones—may we attain a hundred winters, that is, a hundred years.
In the case of the optative (*liṅ*) of the root *aś*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), according to Vedic usage.
Moreover, from us—from ourselves—drive away, destroy, those who hate us.
Likewise, utterly drive away, destroy, our sin.
Drive away, destroy, the diseases; make them go in various directions, spreading throughout the entire body, and severing them from us, annihilate them.
O Rudra, you are the most excellent among those born, preeminent in glory; O wielder of the thunderbolt, may you be the strongest.
As one who has reached the further shore, grant us well-being; ward off all threats and keep us free from harm.

O Best One! O Rudra! For one who is born, [grant] prosperity; may this darkness of yours depart. O wielder of the thunderbolt among the powerful, carry us across to the further shore of distress. May it be well with us; ward off all assaults of injury. 3.

O Rudra, among all that has been born—that is, within the entire world—you abide as the most excellent and most praiseworthy through your sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Likewise, O Rudra, wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrabāhu*), you are the strongest among the strong, being pre-eminently powerful.
As such, lead us safely across the further shore of sin and distress with well-being (*svasti*).
Likewise, O Vr̥tra-slayer, drive away—separate and dispel—all the fears, that is, all the approaches of evil.
In this instance, there is *ślu*-substitution for the *śap* affix due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Because of the optionality of the designation *apit* in the rule "vā chandasi," when the *ṅit* status is absent, the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs by the rule "aditaśca."
O Rudra, do not harm us with your weapons; do not strike us with your missiles, O Bull, nor with ill-praises or joint invocations.
Raise up our heroes with your healing remedies, for I hear you are the best of physicians among all healers.

O Rudra, let us not provoke you with our prostrations, nor with ill-praises, O Bull, nor with joint invocations. Raise up our heroes with your healing remedies; I hear that among physicians you are the most skilled healer. 4.
O Rudra, let us not obstruct you with our salutations—whether those salutations are performed improperly or are deficient—and let us not provoke your anger; let us not cause you distress.
The root *kudh* means "to be angry.
This form is derived from the present participle (*ṇantāt*) of that root, in the aorist (*luṅi*) with the suffix *caṅ*.
O bull among those who desire, rain down [our] wishes! Do not let us be overcome by ill-praise—that is, by an improper or unseemly hymn of praise.
Likewise, do not let us be provoked to anger by the great invocation of the gods along with the Vimadas and others;
for when one is invoked together with someone superior to oneself, it causes distress.
As such, O Lord, unite our heroic sons with your medicines—your healing herbs—and elevate them to excellence.
O Rudra, I hear of you as the most eminent physician among physicians, the supreme creator of remedies.
As it is also stated in another mantra: "The divine physician first" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.1.2; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 16.5).

1. One hundred and forty-one years. 2. Jha¹: "Vicātayasva" means "separate. "Ahaḥ" means "sin. "Vitara" means "make it go to a far distance. "Amīvāḥ" refers to Rākṣasas. "Vipūcīḥ" means "gone in various directions. Ṇa¹ and Viśvak: 3. Ṇa and Ta do not have "acali.

"He who is invoked with offerings, who is to be praised with oblations and hymns—that Rudra, the soft-bellied, the easily invoked, may he, the fair-cheeked, not deliver us over to this womanish malice. (Ṛgveda 2.33.14) 5. [End of section]

He who is invoked with oblations, who is called upon with offerings—may I win over Rudra with hymns of praise. May he, the soft-hearted and easily invoked, not harm us; may he, the fair-cheeked one, grant us our desire for this prayer. 5.

That Rudra who is invoked—meaning he is summoned and praised—with oblations (havīṃṣi) consisting of offerings such as cooked rice (caru) and sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa), accompanied by invocations characterized by hymns of praise.
The karmic suffix is used in the passive sense by transposition;
the vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa) of the root *hvā* occurs according to the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
I appease that Rudra with hymns and praises; I sever him, I separate him—
my intention is to make him free from anger.

Moreover, O Bull, showerer of desires, having become the bearer away, the remover, and the destroyer of the sin and evil committed by the Vaiśya created by the gods, look with favor upon me, who have committed an offense; forgive me quickly! May you be gracious to me.
The root *kṣamū* means "to endure. In the *laṅ* tense, there is the substitution of *śap* by *plu* according to Vedic usage;
the augment *iṭ* is added because of the rule "there is much [irregularity] in the Vedas" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Rudra, there are three *yājyā* verses beginning with "pra babhrave" for the omentum (*vapā*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and the oblation (*havis*) respectively:
"pra babhrave vṛṣabhāya ścitīce," and so on—these three—and "ā paścātān nāsatyā purastāt" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
To the tawny bull, the radiant one, I offer a great and mighty hymn of praise.
With prostrations we celebrate the flaming one with adorations; we extol the piercing name of Rudra.

To the brown, bull-like, radiant one, I offer a great and lofty hymn of praise. O you who are worthy of homage, we celebrate with prostrations the flaming name of Rudra, the name that is brilliant and awe-inspiring. 8.

To the tawny one (vabhrave), the sustainer of all, or to the tawny-colored bull who showers down desires—or to him who brings about clarity—[we offer praise] to the observer (ścitīce), who bestows excellence.
[The word] *dhitā* means "color";
the suffix *in* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules.
The word *ścitimat* is derived from the root *cit* with the suffix *kin* by the rule "ṛtvig0" etc.

In the singular dative case (*caturthyekavacane*), the vowel *a* is elided by the rule "acaḥ," and lengthening occurs by the rule "cau. The acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending follows from the "udāttanivṛtti-svara" rule.
To Rudra, who is distinguished by such qualities, I offer—indeed, I utter with excellence—a great, magnificent hymn of praise (*suṣṭuti*), a beautiful eulogy.
O singer, [praise him] who is *kalmalīkina*;
this is a name for those that blaze (Nirukta 1.17).
It blazes;

it is called *kalmalīka* because it causes one to perceive (*kalayati*) or removes (*apagamayati*) impurity (*mala*). That which has that [blazing] as its end is *madram*; worship (*namasya*) it with salutations (*namobhiḥ*), that is, with prostrations or with oblations.
And we praise, we celebrate, this blazing splendor of Rudra, the Great God.
The root *gṛ* means "to sound. It belongs to the third class (*tryādi*). It ends in the vowel *i*. It is marked with the mute letter *m*.
"The short vowel is substituted for the roots beginning with *pū*."
With firm limbs, multiform, fierce, and tawny, he has adorned himself with bright golden ornaments.
From Rudra, the lord of this vast world, let not even the sovereignty depart.

With his steadfast limbs, he of many forms, the fierce one, the tawny-hued, has adorned himself with radiant golden ornaments. From Rudra, the lord of this vast world, no one indeed can conceal his divine power. 9.

Endowed with firm, steady, and solid limbs and members; possessing many forms through his eightfold manifestation (*aṣṭamūrti*); fierce, exalted, and radiant; brown-hued or the sustainer (*babhru*), Rudra; he shines (*pipiśe*)—is adorned or blazes—with brilliant, golden, or most delightful ornaments. [The root *piś* means "to divide" or "to adorn"; it is used here in the passive sense, perfect tense. From the Lord (*īśāna*), the Sovereign, the sustainer of this vast world of created beings—from Rudra—[comes] the *asurya*. [From the root *as*, "to throw": *asura* is one who throws; that which is "good" (*sādhu*) in that regard is *asurya*. This *asurya*—meaning power—is never separated from him; it does not depart. [In the verb *yauti*, the *āḍ* augment is applied; the *sip* suffix is used because "the *siP* is frequently elided in the *leṭ* (subjunctive)"].
1. There is no ‘mā’ after the letters ka, jha, ṇa, tha, and va.
2. [The elision occurs] also after the letters ka, jha, ṇa, ta, tha, na, and ma; and after the letter va, [the elision occurs] before a following letter.
(Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya 2.18)

Worthy, you carry arrows and a bow; worthy, you wear the sacrificial, all-formed golden necklace. Worthy, you bestow this entire world as a gift; indeed, O Rudra, there is nothing more powerful than you. Worthy, you carry arrows and a bow; worthy, you wear the sacrificial, all-formed golden necklace. Worthy, you bestow this entire world as a gift; indeed, O Rudra, there is nothing more powerful than you.
O Rudra, you, being indeed worthy and fit, bear—meaning you carry—the arrows and the bow;
likewise, being indeed worthy, you bear the golden necklace (*niṣka*), which is worshipful, worthy of adoration, and possessed of manifold forms;
and likewise, being indeed worthy, [you pervade] this entire universe.
This is a great name.
You take pity upon—that is, you protect—the exceedingly vast world.
[The root] *deṅ* means "to protect."

O Rudra, there is indeed nothing else whatsoever more powerful (*ojīyaḥ*), more vigorous, or more strong than you; that is to say, such a thing simply does not exist. Therefore, the meaning is that you alone should be employed in the aforementioned tasks.
The suffix *vini* is added to the word *ojas* in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*).

Then, the suffix *iṇ* is added in the sense of "exceeding" (*ātiśāyanika*). By the rule "the elision of *vin* and *mat*" (*vinmator luk*), there is elision; by the rule "of *ṭi*" (*ṭeḥ*), there is the elision of the final phoneme.
Upon hearing the unpleasant cry of a deer while on a journey, one should mutter the verse beginning with "Praise the Learned One" (*stuhi śrutam*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "For a deer, [one should recite] 'Praise the Learned One, who sits in the pit, the youthful one'" (*stuhi śrutaṃ gartasadaṃ yuvānam*, Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.10.10).

Praise the famous one, who sits upon the chariot-seat, the youth, fierce like a terrifying beast with a deadly body. O Rudra, being praised, be gracious to the singer; let your missiles strike down someone other than us. 11 Praise! The famous one! Who sits upon the chariot-seat! The youth! Like a beast! Terrifying! With a deadly body! Fierce! Be gracious! To the singer! O Rudra! Being praised! Someone other [than us]! From us! Down! Let [your] missiles strike! 11
O singer, praise Rudra—the famous, widely renowned, and celebrated one. Of what nature is he? He is seated upon his chariot in the *garta* (the seat of the chariot);
there he dwells, ever-youthful, as terrifying as a wild beast, like a fearsome lion.
O Rudra, you who are fierce and preeminent among the destroyers of enemies—being praised by us, may you be gracious and bring happiness to me, your singer.
May your armies strike down and slay anyone other than us.

The youth indeed, toward his father who bows down, O Rudra, approaching with various [forms], you praise him—the giver of much, the lord of the good. Being praised, may you grant us medicines. 12. The youth; indeed; toward the father; bowing down; facing; O Rudra; approaching; of much; the giver; the lord of the good; you praise; being praised; you; medicines; grant; to us. 12.
1. There is no such thing as "progeny" for the letters *ka*, *kha*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ṇa*, *la*, *ma*, *va*, and *'*.
Just as a young boy might address his father who is bowing down and praising him as "O long-lived one, O gentle one," so it is with these.
The word "cit" is used here in the sense of a simile.
O Rudra, I bow down to you as you approach us;
indeed, I am prostrate before you, the giver of abundant wealth and the protector of the virtuous.
In the compound "padhyāvaiśvaryam," the original accent of the preceding member is retained.
O Rudra, I thus praise—that is, I extol—you who have become such as this.
Regarding *mipaḥ*: by the rule "the substitutes for *tiṅ* are [themselves] *tiṅ*s," the substitution of *se* occurs.
And being praised by us, grant and bestow upon us medicines, one after another.
O Maruts, whatever healing remedies are yours,

O tawny one, O bull, you who are renowned— just as a god, O Rudra, you do not fail and do not harm; hear our invocation here, be mindful, and may we, possessing brave sons, sing aloud at the sacrifice for the sake of wealth.
O tawny one, O bull, O you who are observant, so that you, O god, do not grow angry and do not strike us—O Rudra, hear our invocation here! May we, with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 15.
