O tawny one (*babhru*), supporter of the world, O bull (*vṛṣabha*) who showers desires, O perceiving one who knows all— O radiant god Rudra— in whatever manner you do not become angry (*haṇīṣe*) and do not strike [us].
[The root] *haṇīṅ* means "to feel shame," and this [root *han*] is also used in the sense of "to be angry."
Thus, O Rudra, you who hear our invocation, listen to our call; be mindful of us here in this place.
At the sacrifice, or in the assembly, or in the home, being possessed of noble sons, may we utter—that is, recite—your lofty and mature hymn of praise.
The second hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "dhārāvarāḥ," is dedicated to the Maruts and is composed by Gātmada.
The final verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter, while the remaining verses are in the Jagatī meter.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "dhārāvarā: [is] Māruta, ending in Triṣṭubh."
This is the placement of the *nivid* for the Maruts in the *āgnimāruta* litany on the third day of the *pṛṣṭha-abhiplava-ṣaḍaha*.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The *āgnimāruta* [litany] consists of [the verses] 'vaiśvānarāya', 'tripaṇāṃ', 'dhārāvarā marutaḥ', and 'svame prathamo aṅgirāḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.7).
The Maruts, pourers of rain, bold in their might, terrible like wild beasts in their strength, resplendent in their power—
blazing like fires, straight-acting, blowing away the whirlwind— they disclosed the cows.
The Maruts, pourers of rain, possessing bold vigor, like terrifying wild beasts with their might, radiant like fires blazing forth, impetuous and blowing away the storm-dust, have uncovered the cows.
The *dhārāvarāḥ* are those who fill the atmosphere with the burden of water;
or rather, they are the restrainers or shakers of the *dhārāḥ*, that is, the firm things such as trees;
or alternatively, they are the sustainers of the entire world.

Bold and endowed with the power to overcome others, they are therefore as terrifying as lions, like wild beasts. By their own strengths, such as the bestowing of rain and other such acts, they are *arcinaḥ*, honoring the entire world.
Like blazing fires, they were radiant; like glowing flames, they were shining brightly.
The root *śuc* means "to shine.
The suffix *kānac* is applied to the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
[Thus we have] *ṛjīpin*.
*Ṛjīpa* refers to water; those who possess it are *ṛjīpiṇaḥ*. Alternatively, *ṛjīpa* is Soma from which the essence has departed; those joined with that are [the *ṛjīpiṇaḥ*].
For at the third pressing, the Maruts are praised in the Agnimāruta hymn;
and in that context, they press the Soma which has already been pressed in the two previous pressings and has thus lost its essence.
Therefore, they are connected with that [rite].

The Maruts, being thus, blowing the *bhṛmi*—the cloud that wanders about—and driving it hither and thither for the sake of rain, they open up (*apa-avṛṇvata*) the waters contained within it; that is to say, they cause them to flow forth so that they may be seen by all. Alternatively, *bhṛmi* refers to a particular kind of lute.
Blowing and playing that [trumpet], they opened the cow-pens protected by the Asura Vala; they made them free from obstruction, having removed the covering.

1. The seer is Gṛtsamada (according to Kha, Ca, and Ṇa¹). 2. The meters are Jagatīs (according to Kha, Ca, and Ṇa¹); the Maruts are the deity. 3. They are called *gāḥ* because they go (*gacchanti*). 4. [The name] Bhrmiṇā is given by Ka, Jha¹, Ta, Tha, Na, Ma, Va, and Bha.
Like the heavens with their stars, they shine; like the edges of swords, the rain-showers flash forth.
When Rudra begot the Maruts—those gold-breasted ones—from the bull Pṛśni, the bright [seed] was upon her udder.

Like the heavens with their stars, the wearers of rings have become visible; like clouds, the showers of rain have flashed forth, O Maruts, when the bull Rudra was born for you upon the bright udder of Pṛśni, O you who bear golden ornaments upon your chests.
*Stṛbhiḥ*. This is a name for the constellations (*nakṣatra*). As Yāska says: "‘Ṛkṣāḥ’ and ‘stṛbhiḥ’ [are names] of the constellations" (Nirukta 3.20).
Like the heavens by means of the constellations, they shine forth; that is, they become conscious of themselves and make themselves known.
[The root] *cit* is used in the sense of "perception" (*saṃjñāna*).
The meaning is that they shine forth.
Likewise, the Maruts, who devour their enemies (*khādinaḥ*), are recognized by their own ornaments;
or alternatively, *khāda* refers to a bracelet.
Being joined with that, they shine forth; likewise, the word *vṛṣṭayaḥ* (showers) refers to the rain-bringing Maruts,
and this form is derived through grammatical substitution (*nipātana*) as in the case of *dādhry-*.
With the *pṛpatī*s— female deer or mares marked with white spots that are yoked to your chariot— you have reached *pṛkṣa*,
the food characterized by the oblation, [for] the sacrificer who possesses that food.
The suffix *ac* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *arśas-* group.
You go; you proceed.
They have grown strong to provide nourishment for all beings, or always for Mitra, they who grant swift gifts;
with spotted horses, their strength undiminished, they sit at the pole like soaring birds upon their paths.

They have carried all beings forward for nourishment, or always for Mitra, they who grant swift gifts; with spotted horses, possessing inexhaustible food, they are like soaring birds set upon the yoke-poles in their courses.

To the sacrificer who possesses food—namely, oblations characterized as sacrificial offerings—the Maruts bring all those various waters, just as they always bring them to Mitra; the word *vā* has the sense of comparison. They constantly convey [them].
Alternatively, the word *vā* is used for emphasis:
for the sacrificer who has become a friend, when food (*pṛkṣa*) serves as the cause, they bring down the waters of rain.
Of what nature are the Maruts?
*Jīradānavaḥ*: those who give quickly;
*pṛṣadaśvāsaḥ*: those whose horses are provided with white spots (*pṛṣat*), thus described;
*anavabhrādhasaḥ*.
The root *bhraś* means "to fall down.
*Avabhraḥ* means "falling down.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule: "It is also seen elsewhere" (*anyatrāpi dṛśyate*, Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.48).
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound *nāsyavabhra*, by the rule "nañ-subhyām," there is udātta accent on the final syllable of the second member.
Those whose *rādhaḥ*—wealth—is *anavabhram*, meaning free from deficiency (*aṃśana*).
In a *bahuvrīhi*, the original accent of the first member prevails.

Like straight-going horses that move without crookedness, they sit upon the yoke-poles (*dhūrṣadaḥ*)— that is, they are seated or settled within the dense mass of the cloud (*megha*)— amidst those who travel along the paths (*vayuneṣu*).

O Maruts, you who possess the power of kings, come hither with your swift, earth-shaking, and destructive steeds that consume the fuel; like swans going to their own sister-lakes, come, O wrathful ones, for the exhilaration of the honeyed draught.

With blazing brands, with milch-cows, with spotted deer, with swift horses, and with broad [chariots], O Maruts of one mind, come hither like swans to their sister-lakes, for the exhilaration of the sweet mead. 5.
O Maruts, you who are like-minded—having a common intent, a common wrath, or a common splendor—and whose weapons are blazing, [come] with those that kindle, which possess the power to ignite.
From the word *indhana*, the suffix *vanip* is applied in the sense of possession according to the rule "in the Veda, *vanip* and *matup*" (*chandasīvanipau*);
there is an elision of a phoneme [the *n*] by Vedic license.
With "dhenubhiḥ," meaning with those who satisfy; "rpaśādbhiḥ"— *virapśa* is a name for greatness—
meaning with those possessing great vigor.

The *ūtrāṃsi* are the paths of the water-courses; or else, from the roots *rap* and *lap*, meaning "in distinct speech," they are the elevated regions resounding with sound. By means of these *adhvasadbhiḥ*—that is, by the paths that are free from destruction (*adhvaṃsana*).
The clouds are called *panthānaḥ* because they fall and move; come (*ā gantana*) together with such clouds, or indeed along the paths themselves. For what purpose?
For the exhilaration of the honey, that is, for the sake of intoxication from Soma.
Therein is an illustration:
just as *huṃsāsaḥ*, i.e., swans (*haṃsāḥ*), reach their own dwelling places (*khasarāṇi*), so it is here.

1. Possessing *ka*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, and *pṛkṣa*; possessing *jha*, *va*, *pṛkṣa*, and *vatī*. 2. *ca*, *pha*, *bhu*, and *vanā* [constituting] the worlds (*bhuvanāni*). 3. Those who possess inquiry (*praśna*) regarding *ma*. 4. Those of equal age (*vayas*) with *ma*.

O Maruts, you who are of one mind, come to our prayers as to the praises of a swift steed; come to our libations. Make the cow swell with milk at her udder, and fashion for the singer a hymn adorned with strength. ā | naḥ | brahmāṇi | marutaḥ | samanyavaḥ | nūram | na | śaṃsaḥ | savanāni | gantana | aśvāmiva | pipyata | dhenum | ūdhani | kartā | dhiyam | jaritre | vājapeśasam || 6 ||
The Maruts are indeed of like mind and like wrath; come to our prayers—this is their name—and to our offerings, that is, the oblations characterized by the pressed Soma at the libations. Come hither!
The form *gameloṭ* is Vedic; there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*.
By the rule "tasanasanathanāśca," *tasi* is replaced by *tanap*. Precisely because of this, due to the absence of the *ṅit* designation, there is no elision of the nasal (*anunāsikalopa*).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
*vnarāṃ vna vśaṃsaḥ*.
Just as our praise—the hymn worthy of being recited—comes to you, O heroes, so [do you come].
From the word *nara*, the absence of the augment *nuṭ* in the genitive plural occurs because of the rule "the teaching of grammatical elements (*āgama*) is not mandatory.
The word *śaṃsaḥ* ends in the suffix *ghas* and is acutely accented on its first syllable.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," the case ending *ām* is replaced by *su*.
And having approached the cow, may you satisfy the one who offers water; swell like a mare in a contest for a prize.
The meaning is: "Make our strength nourished and capable of its color, just as horses have their limbs made plump.
Moreover, [bestow] upon the singer, the one who hears, that which is characterized by vigor—that is, impelled by foods (*vāja*).
The root *piś* means "to divide" or "to break apart."
Perform the action that is to be done with diligence.
The *śap* suffix of the root *kṛ* is elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
As before, the word *ta* undergoes the substitution of *tab*.

O Maruts, grant us that powerful chariot, a source of refreshment, which brings forth sacred prayer (*brahman*) day after day. Grant nourishment to the singers in our assemblies; grant to the poet skill, wisdom, inviolability, invincibility, and conquering might. tam naḥ dāta maruto vājinam ratham āpānam brahma citayat dive-dive | iṣam stotṛbhyaḥ vṛjaneṣu kārave sunim medhām ariṣṭam dustaram sahaḥ || 7 ||
O Maruts, grant us that son; O Giver, bestow him upon us.
The elision of the *śap* suffix is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
Of what sort?
Swift—possessing food or possessing strength.

When there is your chariot-race, that is, your coming which serves as the cause [for our praise], day by day, it makes known—that is, it reveals—the *brahman*, the hymn of praise, which brings you near and possesses water.
Moreover, bestow and grant to us, your praisers, excellent food;
likewise, [grant it] to the singer in the encounters of battle.
A change in the grammatical construction of the words.
Grant us wisdom, the intelligence for battle, and excellent wealth-giving; grant us strength that is most excellent—unharmed by enemies—and invincible, which enemies are unable to overcome.

When the Maruts, with golden ornaments upon their chests, yoke their horses to the chariots—those bounteous givers, Bhaga included—they cause the cow to swell for the calf among the sisters; they provide great nourishment for the people who offer a hundred oblations. yat | yuñjate | marutaḥ | rukmavakṣasaḥ | aśvān | ratheṣu | bhagaḥ | ā | sudānavaḥ | dhenum | śiśve | svasareṣu | pinvate | janāya | śatahaviṣe | mahīm | iṣam || 8 ||

1. In the manuscripts ṇa, ta, tha, and ma, the word ‘ūdhani’ is absent. 2. In the manuscripts ṇa, ta, tha, and ma, the phrase ‘medhāṃ...ariṣṭaṃ’ is absent; in the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, and pha, it reads ‘yuddhaprajñām’.

When the Maruts— those with golden chests, whose breasts are adorned with shining ornaments, and who are liberal givers— yoke their horses to the chariots, that is, they bring them forward to the place of enjoyment which is worthy of being shared.

At that very moment, for the sacrificer who has offered the oblation (*huta-haviṣka*), they cause great nourishment (*mahiṃ iṣam*)—or rather, the water which is the cause of that nourishment—to swell, to pour forth, and to scatter within their own dwellings (*svasareṣu*).
The root *pinv* means "to sprinkle.
An illustration of this follows:
Like a cow for her calf: just as a cow, having given birth, provides milk for her own calf with her udder full, so too [is this].

O Maruts, whatever mortal enemy seeks to harm us with wolfish intent—O Vasus, protect us from that injury! O Rudras, turn him away with your swift wheeling power; strike down the weapon of the one who curses us. yaḥ | naḥ | marutaḥ | vṛkatāti | martyaḥ | ripuḥ | dhve | vasavaḥ | rakṣata | ripaḥ | vartayat | tarpuṣā | cakriyā | abhi | tam | ava | rudrāḥ | aśasaḥ | hantana | vadhaḥ ||9||
O Maruts, that mortal man who is a *vṛkatāti*—a *vṛka* meaning "one who seizes" (*ādātā*)—is like a wolf. [The word *vṛka* is used here in the sense of] "seizing" (*ādāne*).
The suffix *tāti* is added in its own sense (*svārthika*) according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 5.4.41: *vṛkādyathābhyāṃ tiltātilau ca chandasi*.
Being such, he maintains us as our enemy—that which acts as enmity toward us.
O Vasus, you Maruts who provide dwelling, protect and preserve us from the harmful one.
Having scorched with heat the mortal who has become our enemy, turn him back completely with your power in the form of the words of the Ṛgveda.
The Rudras are the sons of Rudra;
or alternatively, those who run while crying out repeatedly (*rorūyamāṇāḥ*). [They are] of the devourer (*aśasaḥ*).

From the root *aś* in the sense of "eating," the suffix *asi* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules. Of such beings as Rākṣasas, *vadhaḥ* means a weapon that is an instrument of killing. *Avahantana* means "fight back," "separate," or "destroy" without attachment.
From the root *han*, the imperative form *tanap* is used according to the rule *tasan-asanathanāśca*.

Wondrous is that journey of yours, O Maruts, which is made manifest when the female buffalo, the mother-cow, yields her milk; or when, O sons of Rudra, you who are invincible, brought Trita to old age for the sake of the reviler of the one who ages. Wondrous is that journey of yours, O Maruts, which is made manifest when the female buffalo, the mother-cow, yields her milk; or when, O sons of Rudra, you who are invincible, brought Trita to old age for the sake of the reviler of the one who ages. 10.
O Maruts, your wondrous and admirable course is known to all; now he speaks of it as if it were beyond the senses. The word *api* is used here in the sense of what is well-known.
Whenever the Maruts, the bringers of water (*āpayaḥ*), milked the uplifted cloud—the udder connected to the touchable, central speech—they milked it;
the *liṭ* (perfect) ending is Vedic for the root *duh*.
The absence of reduplication is due to the rule: "It should be stated that [this applies] in the Veda."

Or rather, when [the Maruts] committed an injury against Trita—who was being praised and was blameless—for the sake of his reviler, that is, his enemy; the word *nide* means "for the reviler. The root *nid* is used in the sense of "censure" (*kutsā*).
The suffix *kvi* is applied according to the rule *kvi ca*.

At that time, O Maruts—unassailable (*adābhya*) and invincible (*ahiṃsya*), the sons of Rudra (*rudriya*)—you became the means for the decay (*jarāya*), that is, the destruction, of Trita, the seer, as he was being worn away by his attacking enemies.
ka-jha-ma: *asmabhyam* (for us).
2. In the manuscripts ṇa, ta, and tha, the reading "abhito nivartayata" does not exist.
3. In manuscript ka it is "uddhantam"; in kha, ṇa 1, it is "ūdhanam"; in ga and ca, it is "uddhanam"; in ja, ṇa, ta, na, and va, it is "uddhatam".
We invoke the great ones, the Maruts, who move at will, for the offering of the swift-moving Viṣṇu.
We, devoted to sacred prayer, seek from those golden-hued, preeminent ones who possess radiant rays, praiseworthy wealth.

We invoke those great Maruts, who travel with their own power, at the offering of the swift-moving Viṣṇu. We, who possess golden colors, are preeminent, and have extended our sacrificial ladles; seeking to fulfill the sacred word, we implore them for praiseworthy wealth.

O Maruts, you who travel swiftly to this hymn or sacrifice—those great ones of mighty power—we invoke you, you who pervade everywhere in the large vessels and elsewhere, at the offering of the desirable Soma that is to be sought after, when it is being excellently prepared by the chanters. We call upon you.

And call upon those golden-colored (hiraṇyavarṇān)— meaning either of pleasing color or preeminent and worthy of praise— those who are such as these, with sacrificial ladles raised for the sacrifice (yata-sucaḥ), we who are devoted to sacred prayer (brahmaṇyantaḥ). Desiring that prayer (brahma), we beg for wealth (rādhaḥ) that is worthy of praise (śaṃsyam).

They, the first Dawns, have furthered the sacrifice; may they urge us on at the breakings of the night. Like the Dawn, she discloses the dark nights with her ruddy beams, with great, radiant light that abounds in cattle.

They, the first ones worthy of being seen, have carried forth the sacrifice. May they, the Dawns, impel us at their breakings. Like the Dawn, she discloses the dark nights with her ruddy rays; with great, pure, and shining light, she unveils them like a flood of kine. 12.
Those Maruts, the Daśagvas— who,
having attained perfection in ten months, became like the Aṅgirases and, being the first among the Ādityas, performed the sacrifice first— carried the sacrifice upward.
Among the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases who were competing for the ascent to heaven, the Aṅgirases first reached heaven by performing the sacrifice.
And thus it is heard in scripture: "The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases were here in the beginning; they first conquered Agni" (AiB 1.16).
May such as those, at the dawning of the *uṣas*, at the break of day, at the flush of morning, *hinvantu*—may they impel us.
[The root] *hi* means "to go" and "to increase."
As the red dawns uncover [the world] with their shining splendors, so do the beautiful, dark-hued nights.

Just as the dawns reveal [all things], they dispel and drive away the darkness by means of the great, radiant, and shining light consisting of a flood of moving waters—that is, the light called the Sun.
The meaning is that, having slain Vṛtra and others who obstruct the solar orb, they illuminate the entire universe.

Those Rudras have grown strong at the seats of Cosmic Order (Ṛta) with their dark-blue [garments] and ruddy ornaments. Streaming forth like a cloud, they have assumed a most radiant and well-fashioned color on the further shore.

With their dark-blue [horses] and ruddy ornaments, the Rudras have grown strong at the seats of Truth; pouring down rain, they have attained a most radiant and well-fashioned color on the further shore. 13.

The *bhadrās*, the sons of Rudra, those *maruts*, [are accompanied] by *kṣoṇīs*— specific types of lutes (*vīṇā*) known as *vāṇās* that produce sound— and by *aruṇas*, which are hollow tubes (*nālis*).
The particle *na* is used here as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).
Possessing radiant, ruddy-colored forms and adorned with various ornaments, they increase as the bride Speech within the clouds, which are the dwellings—the seats—of *ṛta*, that is, water.

Moreover, moving swiftly and constantly with their own impetuous force (*pāja*), they do not hesitate; thinking intensely of the water from the cloud, they [attain] that which is most bright, providing beautiful delight, and well-formed.
*Peśas* is a name for form.
They possess a beautiful form and complexion, and they maintain a radiant luster.
Seeking that great protection, we praise them with devotion;
as Trita brought hither the Hotṛs for aid, so may he turn the two wheels toward us for our protection.
To them, the great protection for our aid, we indeed sing with reverence; those whom Trita, like the five priests, has brought hither for our desire, turning the swift ones toward us for help.
O Maruts, that great, vast, desirable, and praiseworthy wealth—O Maruts, we, approaching you with prayers for protection, implore it for your aid.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," the case-ending *jas* is replaced by *su*.
With this homage, with this act of salutation, or with this hymn of praise, having approached, we sing—that is, we praise.
The syllable *gha* is for the purpose of filling the meter; in the word *enā*, the third case ending is replaced by *āj* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*;
the particle *ma* denotes conjunction.

Trita, the seer, turned toward himself—toward his own vital breaths—from which he had drawn them forth, those Maruts who are the five *hotṛ*s existing as the five elements such as prāṇa and apāna within the self, and who are therefore the performers of the oblation (*homa*). For the sake of attaining his desired success (*abhiṣṭaye*), by means of the wheel (*cakriyā*)—that is, the navel-wheel—he turned them for protection (*avase*) and for union; he drew back toward himself those vital breaths (*prāṇān*) that had been scattered.

Alternatively, [he turned] those who were equipped with the weapon called the *ṛṣṭi* (the discus/spear) for the sake of gratification through hymns and the like. "We praise them"—this is the connection with what precedes.
*vavarta* is the form [derived] from the root *vṛt* with the desiderative suffix (*ṣyan*), in the aorist (*luṅ*) with the reduplication (*caṅ*).
May that aid of yours, O Maruts, by which you carry R̥dhya across distress and release the one who praises you from reproach, come hither; may your benevolence approach us like a lowing cow.

With that [aid] by which you cause the distressed to cross over the flood, with which you release the worshipper from reproach—that aid of yours, O Maruts, may it come hither; may your favor come swiftly like a well-neighing horse. 15.

O Maruts, by whatever aid you cause the worshipper, the seeker of favor, to cross over distress— that is, to transcend evil; and by whatever aid you release the praiser, the singer, from reproach— that is, from the presence of the reviler, the enemy— O Maruts,
may that aid of yours be directed hitherward toward us.
Likewise, *sumati*: may your auspicious mind, your intellect characterized by grace, like a cow lowing with the sound "haṃbha," go most excellently (*su*) and swiftly (*o*) toward us;
that is to say, may it come toward us in every way.
1. Ma is with those who produce sound.
2. Ka, Ca, Jha, Jha 1, Tha, Ma, Va are called "lutes" (vīṇā); Ṇa 1 is called "elephant" (vāraṇa).
3. Ka, Kha, Ga, Jha, Ṇa, Ṇa 1, Tha, Na, Ma, Va are of the color of dawn (aruṇavarṇa).
4. In the manuscripts jha, ṇa, and jha 1, the word *citayantaḥ* is present.

5. In the manuscripts ka, jha, ṇa, tha, na, ma, va, and jha 1, the term *pūraṇaḥ* (a filler) appears after *padapūraṇaḥ*; in manuscript jha, it simply reads *pūraṇaḥ*. 6. In the manuscripts ka, jha, jha 1, ṇa, tha, na, ma, and va, the phrase *‘avarān mukhyān’* is absent; in manuscripts kha, ga, and ṇa 1, it reads *avarānmukhyān*.
7. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ta, tha, pha are to be repeated.
8. ca, jha, ma—thus. The third hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "upema," is addressed to Gāsmada; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and has Apāṃnapāt as its deity.
And thus it has been introduced: "The Upemo-napatrīya. The application of the hymn is based on its indicative marks (liṅga).
Desiring strength, I have sent forth this speech with eloquence; may he, the eater, accept my songs.
Will the Son of the Waters, the swift-moving one, perhaps fashion them beautifully? For he shall surely take pleasure in them.

Desiring strength, I have sent forth this eloquent speech toward him. May the Son of Waters, who delights in our songs, accept my hymns. Will he, the swift impeller of the waters, make them well-adorned? For he indeed takes pleasure in them. 1.
Desiring strength—that is, desiring food for myself—I release this eloquence, this desire for speech, namely, the desire for praise; I bring it forth, I produce it.
The meaning is: "I have begun to praise the Son of the Waters (Apāṃ Napāt)."
In *sujeṣ*, the *luṅ* suffix is used according to Vedic usage (*chandasaḥ*).
Due to the rule “*liṅsicāvātmanepadeṣu*,” the *sic* suffix has the *kittva* property, which results in the absence of *guṇa*.
And he is the one to be praised by the roaring rivers—the waters situated in the clouds—and he is the swift-goer, moving with rapid speed.
From the root *hi* in the sense of "going," the suffix *manin* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well."
In this state, Vapā is the son of Vnapāt;
he stands in the position of a grandson, for today the plants and trees are born, and from these plants and trees this Agni is born—thus he possesses the status of a grandson.
The deity bearing this name is Giraḥ.
One who praises is *gīḥ*, a singer; for me, his, *kuvit*— that word signifies "much."
May he bestow abundant food; may he grant it, may he provide it—the meaning is that he should give it.
Furthermore, may he make us *supeśasaḥ*, i.e., possessed of beautiful forms or beautiful ornaments.
The suffix *śap* is applied to the root *kṛ* by virtue of its being included in the *dhṛṣi* group.
By the rule "In the case of *kaḥ*, *karat*, *karati*, *kṛti*, and *kṛte*, [the *s* is substituted] except for *anaditeḥ*" (Pāṇini 8.3.50), the *visarjanīya* is replaced by *s*.
For since this god *vjoṣiṣat*—that is, he accepts (*sevate*) our hymns of praise—therefore he should favor us in this manner; such is the meaning.
The root *juṣ* means "to please" and "to serve. [In this form:
there is the addition of the augment *yaṅ*, the suffix *liṅ*, and the personal ending *sip*.
And there is the augment *iṭ*. By the rule “*hi ca*,” there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent).
Let us speak this mantra, well-fashioned from our own heart; may he surely know it.
Apām Napāt, by the greatness of his solar power, has generated all beings as a sovereign lord.
To him we shall speak this well-fashioned mantra from our own heart; perhaps he will take note of it. Apāṃ Napāt, by the greatness of his divine power, the noble one has brought forth all the worlds.
To this god named Apāṃnapāt, let us well and directly recite this mantra, well-fashioned from the heart—that is, from the core of our being;
may he surely know this mantra uttered by us.
The augment *r* is added after *vette*. There is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) by the rule "nipātair yadyadīhantā... [Pāṇini 8.1.30].
If it is asked what the hymn is, it is replied: Varya is the lord known as Apāṃnapāt, the fire of lightning;
he is Vasu, and Asura, the thrower of enemies.

By the greatness—the majesty and vastness—of that power which is his own nature, he brought forth all beings, all the worlds, namely the waters of rain, or rather all classes of living beings, through the production of rain.
1. *Kha-ga-ṇa-ta-tha-ma-viśvā*.
When the *ekadhanā* waters have arrived near the *vasatīvarī* waters for the *apāmārga* ritual, this verse, "samanyā yanti," should be recited.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'samanyā yanty upayanty anyā' at the place of the *tīrtha*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.1).
And in the *Sārasvata* sacrifice, if the *śamyā* should fall into the waters, then the *Apolaptrīya* offering must be performed;
in that case, this very same verse is to be used as the *yājyā*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Some go together, others come together; henceforth, for all [the offerings], it is the same" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 12.6).
Some flow together, others approach; the rivers fill the common expanse. The pure waters stand around that pure, shining Son of the Waters.
Some flow away; others approach. The rivers fill the common reservoir. To him, the pure one, the shining son of the waters, the bright waters stand around—him, Oṃ! || 3 ||
"Other waters" (varṣyā āpaḥ) "come together," that is, they meet with the waters already present on the earth. And "other" waters previously situated there "approach" them.
All those waters, having become rivers (*nadyaḥ*), "fill" (*pṛṇanti*)—that is, they satisfy—the "wide one" (*ūrvaṃ*), the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) located within the ocean.
The root *pṛṇ* means "to satisfy";
it belongs to the Taudādi class.
To him alone, the Son of Waters, pure, stainless, and resplendent, shining brightly.
The root *dīdī* belongs to the Vedic language (*chāndasa*) and has the sense of shining (*dīpti*).

The suffix is *kasu*, which is the reduplicated form of *liṭ*. There is an absence of the augment *iṭ* due to the restrictive rule: "after a monosyllabic root ending in a consonant that is not a guttural or a nasal, [the *iṭ* is absent] when followed by *vasu*."
Due to the statement, "It should be stated that [the rule] is optional in the Veda," there is an absence of reduplication.
Thus, the "impure waters" stand around him, surrounding him;

that is to say, they wait upon him who exists in the form of the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*), perceiving him as the one who produced the unequal [fire] while abiding in the cloud in the form of lightning-fire.
Or rather, other waters called *ekadhanā* come together and join with the *vasatīvarī* waters between the *cātvāla* and the *utkara*.
Other waters called *vasatīvarī* also approach;
they come together and reach a state of oneness.
And these, uniting and accomplishing the sacrifice, become rivers by means of their flow and fill the wide expanse (*ūrva*), and so forth, as is common [in the ritual texts].
For in this way, the scriptural application (*viniyoga*) found in the Brāhmaṇa—"The waters, indeed, contended: 'We shall carry the sacrifice first'" (Ai. Brā. 2.20)—and so forth, is supported.
The youthful waters, being purified, go around him, the youth;
he, shining with bright rays, shines splendidly for us—unassailable, clothed in ghee, within the waters.
To him, the longing young women, being purified, go around—the youth—the waters. He shines richly with his bright, shimmering rays; kindled without fuel, he is clothed in ghee within the waters.

The waters—those not contending, free from pride, like young women adorning themselves for the sake of a bridegroom—have brought that Son of the Waters toward us, as they groom him like a youthful prince.
The root *mṛj* is used in the senses of cleansing and adorning.
They go around, [moving] on all sides: 1.
by means of the letters ṇa, tha, ma, va, and dha;
2. by means of the letters ka, jha, ma, and any other vowel-consonant (varidhi); [alternatively,] by means of kha, ga, and the vowels; or by means of ṇa, tha, na, va, and the vowels.
3. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, jha, 1, ṇa, 1, tha, na, and 'a, the word "prīṇayanti" does not exist.
4. In kha and ga, it is "tvatsādhyaḥ"; in ca, jha, 1, ṇa, 1, tatha, and sva, it is "svasādhyaḥ"; in ṇa, it is "svatsādhyaḥ".
They go; they attain.
He who purifies with clarified butter, whose feet are cleansed by water— *nirnik* being a name for form,

he is of beautiful form— that Agni, the Son of Waters, in the midst of the waters, whether those within the clouds or those in the ocean, shines forth for us (*asme*) with his bright, pure, and stainless flames (*śukebhiḥ śikabhiḥ*), even while remaining without fuel (*anindhah*), so that our food may be richly endowed with wealth (*revat*).
For him, three other women—the divine goddesses—offer food;
for he, like one sent forward, drinks the first milk of the mothers who have borne before.

For him, three other chapters: "The women," "O noble god," "The goddesses," "They desire," "Food," "As if prepared," "Toward," "For," "In the waters," "He," "The first-milk," "He drinks," "Of those who have borne before. 5.
The three goddesses worthy of praise— the divine ones known as Iḷā, Sarasvatī, and Bhāratī—
desire to offer, that is, they sustain, the food called Soma for this god, the Son of the Waters, for his study, [the root] *dhi* meaning "to hold" or "to support.
The word *ghipa* means "in sound."
The root *dhā* begins with *jha*.
By the rule of substitution for the final letter, it becomes *dhyai*.
Since roots have a single meaning, here it carries the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*).
As if made upon the waters, they spread forth; the root *sṛ* means "to go. In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), by the rule *iryo re*, there is the substitution of *re* for *ira*.
The absence of the elision of the initial *u* is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

Because it is so, therefore he—Agni, the Son of Waters (*apāṃ napāt*)—drinks, that is, consumes, the nectar called Soma, which is the essence of the "milk" produced from the preceding [rays] from the presence of Brahman.
The word *hi* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).

Protect the patrons here at the birth of this horse, O subduer of the heavens; guard the wise ones from harm. May the malevolent ones perish before these unassailable fortresses, and may falsehoods vanish away.

At the birth of this horse, protect us here from the sky, from the malicious enemy, and from those who seek to harm us; guard the patrons within the raw fortresses, for the enemies shall not find their way through the unassailable strongholds, nor shall falsehoods prevail.
In this very god named Apāṃnapāt, the birth of the horse occurs;
for the horse was born from the ocean presided over by Apāṃnapāt, having arisen from Uśanas.
What more need be said?
And from this very one, who is well-praised, the birth of this entire world occurs;
for he, abiding in the midst of the clouds, generates the whole world by means of rain.
Such as you are, O Apāṃnapāt, you are the remover of the harmful, the destroyer of the malicious.
Protect—i.e., guard—us, the wise ones who are your praisers, from the contact with the destructive *ripas*.
Within the raw, uncooked, and yet-to-be-filled waters, the non-givers (*arātayas*) do not reach—that is, they do not attain—the invincible god who dwells far beyond.
The verb *naśati* here functions as a verb of reaching or attaining.
The augment *leṭ* is added;
falsehoods and the *rakṣas* demons do not reach those who possess *māyā*.
1. [The letters] ka, ca, jha, ña, ṇa, ma, and ghṛtanirniq; kha, ga, ṇa¹, and ghṛtanirmika.
2. [The letters] ka, kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, ṇa¹, tha, na, ma, va, and dītirūpaḥ. 3. [The letters] tha and śurkaiḥ.
4. There is no filler [of the meter] among *ka*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, *va*, and *hi*.

He whose cow is well-milking in his own home swells with nourishment (*svadhā*) and eats what is substantial; he, the Son of Waters, conquering through strength, shines forth for the sake of bestowing wealth upon the one who worships him within the waters.

In his own home, he whose cow is easy to milk has caused the sacrificial food (*svadhā*) to swell; he eats well-being as his nourishment. That Son of the Waters, increasing strength within the waters, shines forth for the sake of bestowing wealth upon the one who honors him.
He who, as the Son of Waters (Apām Napāt), sits within his own home— the atmosphere— and whose cow,
the voice of the mid-region, is easily milked,
that god causes the self-sustaining rain-water to swell.
In the root *pyai* (meaning "to grow"),
there is the substitution of *pī* by the rule *liṅcaṅośca*.

He who eats—well-being (*subhu*) meaning he truly (*suṣṭhu*) consumes the food characterized by the oblation arising from rain—is the god named Apāṃnapāt. Strengthening—that is, producing strength—he shines forth preeminently for the sake of the sacrificer who serves him within the waters—that is, amidst the waters residing in the clouds—for the granting of wealth.
He who, pure with his divine [nature], abiding by the cosmic order (*ṛta*), shines far and wide with vigor within the waters—
for him, all other beings and the plants are born as offspring through their progeny.

He who, the upholder of cosmic order (*ṛtāvā*), shines far and wide with his pure, divine radiance upon the waters; from him alone do all other beings, the branches, and the plants spring forth through their progeny. ||8||
He who is the Son of Waters (apām napāt), the observer of cosmic order (ṛtāvā)— *ṛta* being a name for water,

meaning he who possesses it or is truthful— and who is unaging (ajasaḥ), whose treasure is hidden, who exists eternally with one form, and who is vast and wide (urviyā) among the waters within the clouds— he shines forth intensely on all sides with his purifying, divine (daivya) splendor.
Of this Apāṃnapāt, all other various worlds—all living beings—are like branches (*vayāṃsi*).
Creepers (*vīrudhaḥ*) and herbs (*oṣadhayaḥ*), together with their own offspring such as flowers and fruits, are born forth from him alone.
The particle *ca* is used for completion.
In the aforementioned *sārasvata-sattra*, for the *caru* offering to Apām Napāt, the verse "apāṃ napādā hi" serves as the invitatory formula (*anu-vākyā*).
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "A *caru* for Apām Naptṛ; 'apāṃ napādā hyasthādupastham'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 12.6).
The Son of the Waters has indeed taken his seat upon the lap of the tongues, standing erect and clothed in lightning.
Carrying his supreme majesty, the swift, golden-hued rivers flow around him.
The Son of the Waters has indeed ascended to the lap of the tongues, standing upright and clothed in lightning. Carrying his supreme majesty, the golden-hued, swift-moving ones go around him. 9.

1. In the manuscripts ṇa, tha, and na, the phrase “by their own” (*svakīyābhiḥ*) is absent; in manuscript ma, it reads “by their own and so forth” (*svakīyādibhiḥ*). 2. In the manuscripts ka, ca, jha, jha₁, ṇa, tha, na, ma, va, and va, the phrase “and completing” (*ca pūraṇaḥ*) is absent.
3. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ṇa, ta, tha, and tha, that which was stated previously [is present].
The fire known as Apāṃnapāt has indeed "stood upon" (ā sthāt)—that is, ascended to—the "lap of the waters," which is the intermediate space (antarikṣa).

Doing what? Standing upright amidst the "tongues" of the waters—that is, the winding-moving waters—blazing upward himself and "clothing" (vasānaḥ), that is, covering, the lightning-flash, the cloud that flashes.
Having taken his stand in the intermediate space, he brought about the raining down.

Carrying his— of that showerer of rain, the lord of waters— most excellent, most praiseworthy greatness and majesty, bringing it everywhere, the great rivers, golden-hued (for this is a name of rivers;
the rivers are golden-colored and free from impurity), flow around on all sides.
The meaning is that the rivers flow as if manifesting his greatness everywhere out of gratitude, thinking: "A great rain has been produced by Apāṃnapāt for our flowing forth."
Golden-hued is he, golden in appearance, the grandson of the golden one; indeed, he is golden-colored.
Having sat down from his golden wombs, those who give gold offer food to him.
He is golden-hued; he is golden in appearance, the Son of the Waters. He indeed, of golden color, having sat down from his golden womb, the givers of gold bestow food upon him. 10.
He, the Son of Waters (Apām Napāt), is golden-formed (*hiraṇyarūpa*).
"Form" (*rūpa*) means that which is formed, namely the body;
thus he has a body made of gold, or a body that is exceedingly beautiful.
Likewise, "of golden appearance" (*hiraṇyasaṃdṛk*):
the sense-faculties are called "appearances" (*saṃdṛś*) because they perceive correctly;
thus, he is one whose sense-faculties are golden, or whose sense-faculties are beneficial and beautiful.
He himself, Apāṃnapāt, is golden-hued—
possessed of a splendor like that of gold—
and being such, having sat down upon his golden womb, that is, his place, he shines forth; this is the sense.
To this such-like *apāṃ napāt*, the sacrificers—givers of gold (*hiraṇyadāḥ*), that is, givers of gold in the form of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)—give food, namely the oblation (*havis*).
Therefore, his banner and his lovely name increase, dear to the grandson of the waters, whom the young maidens kindle together at the meeting; he is golden-hued, and clarified butter is his food.
His countenance and his lovely, secret name increase—the grandson of the waters—whom the young maidens kindle together; verily, his food is golden-colored ghee. 11.
The face—the body in the form of a mass of rays—of this divine *napāt* (grandson) of the waters is beautiful and splendid;
moreover, his name and designation are also beautiful and splendid.
This is because of the etymology: he is called *napāt* because he does not cause to fall (*na pātayati*) nor destroy (*na vināśayati*).
Both of these are secret;
this has a hidden name.
Being concealed within the clouds, it increases.

The young women—the waters, whose nature is to come together—thoroughly kindle and illuminate that Apāṃnapāt, who possesses a golden hue and a splendor equal to gold, right there in yonder atmosphere.
And for this god, ghee—the water characterized by its flowing—is his food to be consumed;
for he is the fire of lightning, which indeed has no other fuel.

To him, the nearest friend among many, let us do service with sacrifices, with reverence, and with oblations. We have smoothed his back; I shall support him with fuel-sticks; I establish him with fires; I praise him all around with hymns. 12. To him, among many, the nearest, for friendship, let us serve with sacrifices, with homage, and with offerings. We have groomed his back; I desire to maintain him with splinters of wood; I sustain him with fires; I laud him on every side with verses. 12.

To him who stands before us, the protector of many gods, the teacher, the friend with whom we share a common renown—to this *Apāṃ Napāt*, let us serve with sacrifices, that is, with the means of worship such as oblations consisting of cooked rice, sacrificial cakes, and the like, and with reverence through prostration;
let us attend upon him. I thoroughly cleanse, purify, or adorn the *sānu*—the elevated ridge—of this *Apāṃ Napāt*.
(The root *mṛj* is used in the sense of purification and decoration.)
There is an optional prohibition of the *nighāta* accent by the rule “*cādilope vibhāṣā*”.
I shall hold and maintain [it] with splinters—that is, with pieces of wood used for shining or polishing.
The root *dhip* means "to sound."
This is also for the purpose of retention (*dhāraṇa*).
Due to its belonging to the *juhoty-ādi* class, there is the elision (*ślu*) of the *śap* suffix. The augment *ad-* is applied to the *mip* ending by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

The word *abhyastānām* is udātta according to the rule "the first [syllable] of reduplicated forms. I place and maintain this [Agni], who exists in the form of the Gārhapatya and other fires, within the oblation characterized by the *havis*;
likewise, with *ṛc*s—that is, with mantras—I praise him from all sides.

He, the bull, has cast his seed into those [waters] as an embryo; he, as a child, sucks them, and they lick him. He, the Son of Waters, of unfading color, here on earth, clothes himself in a body as if it were that of another. He, the bull, has cast his seed into those [waters] as an embryo; he, as a child, sucks them, and they lick him. He, the Son of Waters, of unfading color, here on earth, clothes himself in a body as if it were that of another.

This very god, known as Apāṃnapāt, having become a bull (*vṛṣā*)—a showerer—produced an embryo within those waters, namely the streams of rain from the clouds; the meaning is that he made his own self into the form of an embryo for the purpose of raining.
And having become an embryo, this very one—the intermediate, lightning-like fire (*vaidyuta agni*)—being their child (*śiśu*), drinks them, that is, he consumes those waters residing in the cloud;
for his fuel is water.
The waters lick—that is, they taste—that [fire] which occupies the position of a son;
the root *lih* means "to taste. There is an optional substitution of *tva* due to its inclusion in the *kapilaka*-group.

This very Son of the Waters (Apām Napāt), having descended to the earth with rain, possesses a color that is not faded (*anabhimlātavarṇaḥ*)—that is, the opposite of one whose color is faded, withered, or diminished; being thus truly radiant, he has pervaded (*viveṣa*), that is, has become diffused throughout, this world with a body like that of another.
The word *iva* is used here for emphasis;
[he is] like another earthly fire in his body, characterized by wood as its fuel.
‘*Viplu* means expansion.

Him who stands upon this highest step, the neighing one, shining forever with his rays—the mighty waters, bearing clarified butter as food for their offspring, fly around him of their own accord with their wings. In this highest place, standing, neighing, shining forever with his rays—the mighty waters, bearing clarified butter as food for their offspring, fly around him of their own accord with their wings. (14)
1. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and ṇa are for the purpose of indicating similarity with 1, ta, tha, na, and va.

who has stood, remained, in this supreme, most excellent station characterized by the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); who has shone, been radiant, throughout all days (*viśvahā*) with splendors that are undecaying; [him], the Son of Waters (*apām napāt*), whom the great waters (*yalhīḥ*)—the waters themselves (*svayam*)—surround and encompass with their own forms, which are like rays (*arkaiḥ*), characterized by pervading, and ever-moving.
The root *dī* signifies "going.
The root *dīḍ* means "to perish.
By way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), the parasmaipada ending is used. What are they doing?
To the grandson of the waters, the great-grandson of the waters, they carry forth ghee, carrying food that has milk as its water.
I have come for the sake of the people’s secure dwelling; I have come with a well-fashioned hymn for the sake of the liberal patrons.
All that the gods protect is auspicious; may we, blessed with brave sons, proclaim this aloud at the assembly.

I have attained, O Agni, a secure dwelling for the people; I have attained a well-fashioned hymn for the patrons. All that which the gods favor is auspicious. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 15.
O Agni, I have approached you for a beautiful dwelling;
for what purpose? For the sake of people—namely, our sons and other such folk.
Thus, I have approached with a well-fashioned hymn of praise directed toward you—the sacrificers who possess wealth characterized by oblations.
[The root] *yam* means to cease or rest.
For that reason, whatever is auspicious (*bhadra*) which all the gods protect and preserve—that entire auspiciousness shall be ours.
May we, possessing brave sons and excellent offspring, loudly proclaim—utter—the great and mature hymn of praise at the assembly, at the sacrifice, or in the home.
The fourth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "tubhyam," is by Gātsamada; it is in the Jagatī meter.
Indra and Madhu are the deities of the first verse;
the Maruts and Mādhava are the deities of the second.
On the third [lunar day], Śravaṇā and Śukra;
on the fourth, Agni and Śuci;
on the fifth, Indra and Nabhas.
On the sixth [day], Mitra and Varuṇa, and Nabhasya as well; thus it has been enumerated: "To you belongs the sixfold offering, which is in the Jāgata meter.
On the sixth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), during the seasonal offerings (*ṛtuyāja*), one must be dispatched and sacrifice with *praiṣas* that have the beginnings of *ṛc*-verses.
There, the deities belonging to the first six *praiṣas* are to be removed in succession by means of the sixth day-and-night (*ahorātra*) and so forth.
And thus it is sūtra-ed: beginning with “And after the *ṛtuyājas*” and ending with “‘To thee, being urged, the best [Soma] has flowed for cows and waters’—these twelve” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.1).

For you, being urged on, Vasiṣṭha has driven forth the cows and the waters; the men have milked the stream with their strong arms. Drink, O Indra, Svāhā! The Soma offered at the sacrifice, which rains down rain, from the Hotṛ’s bowl—you who are the first and the lord thereof.

For you, being urged on, Vasiṣṭha milked out the cows and the waters. With the sheepskins and the stones, the men have drawn them forth. Drink, O Indra, Svāhā! The Soma offered and prepared by the rain-maker; drink from the Hotṛ’s cup as the first one who has mastery over it. 1.

O Indra, for you, for your sake, the Soma—being urged and impelled—has clothed himself (*vasiṣṭa*), that is, he has enveloped himself in the products of the cow such as curds and milk which serve as mixing ingredients, as well as in the waters called *vasatīvarī*;
the meaning is that he unites with them.

And the men—the leaders of the sacrifice and the Adhvaryu priests—have milked this Soma with the sheep’s wool filters (*avibhiḥ*) known as the ten-strand strainers (*daśāpavitra*), and with the pressing-stones (*adribhiḥ*). They have caused it to flow forth.
The meaning is that [the Soma] is purified by means of the stones (*grāvan*) and the *daśāpavitra* filter.
O Indra, you who rule over all—[this is for the sake of the birth of the people].
(1) *ca-tha* has the reading *°*; (2) *kha-ca-pha* have *uccārayāma*; *u* is a filler; *ga-ṇa1* have *uccārayāma*; *pūraṇaḥ*; *ka. 2-20*.

You are the Lord of the world; being the first among other gods, existing prior to them, drink that Soma—which has been offered with the utterance of "svāhā" (cast into the fire), and clearly presented with the utterance of "vapaṭ"—from the Hotṛ, that is, from the sacrifice performed by the Hotṛ-priest, drinking it entirely.

United with sacrifices, with spotted deer and spears on your journey, you radiant ones, dear to the fires—having sat upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) of Bharata, O sons of heaven, O heroes, drink the Soma from the Potṛ’s cup! yajñaiḥ saṃmiślāḥ pṛṣatībhirṛṣṭibhiryāman śubhrāso agniṣu priyā uta | āsadya barhirbharatasya sūnavaḥ potrādā somaṃ pibatā divo naraḥ || 2 || United with sacrifices, with spotted deer and spears on your journey, you radiant ones, dear to the fires—having sat upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) of Bharata, O sons of heaven, O heroes, drink the Soma from the Potṛ’s cup!

Those Maruts, joined and united with sacrifices and offerings, stationed upon their chariots—the means of motion—yoked with spotted deer as their own vehicles, are brilliant, shining, and resplendent with their own weapons, the *ṛṣṭi*s;
the word *uta* is used in the sense of "and."

O sons of Bharata, beloved ones, you who are the sons of Rudra—the sustainer of the entire world—and the heroes of heaven, the leaders of the sky and the intermediate space; O Maruts, being such as you are, having sat down upon the strewn sacrificial grass (barhis), drink the Soma from the Potṛ’s cup.
At the third pressing, "agneva naḥ" is the standing *yājyā* of the *neṣṭṛ*.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "agneva naḥ suhavā ā hi gantam indrāviṣṇū pibataṃ madhvo asya" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5).

Come indeed to us, you who are easily invoked; sit down upon the sacred grass and take your delight. Immediately thereafter: O Tvaṣṭṛ, you who possess a beautiful host (sumadraṇaḥ) together with the other gods and the divine wives (janibhiḥ), rejoicing in the *andhas*— that is, the food characterized by Soma (the genitive used in the sense of the accusative)—
be exhilarated and satisfied.

O wise (*vipra*) one, you who are intelligent (*medhāvin*), bring (*āvaha*) the gods (*devān*), such as Indra and others, for the purpose of sacrificing (*yakṣyan*). And sacrifice (*yakṣi*) them; that is, worship (*yaja*) them.
O *hotṛ*, you who are the invoker of the gods, desiring us and being well-disposed toward us, sit down (*niṣīda*) in the three wombs or stations characterized by the *gārhapatya* and the others.
Having sat down, accept with longing the sweet Soma-juice (*somya madhu*), which has been set forth and brought forward to the northern altar for the sake of the oblation.
And having desired [the offering], drink the Soma from the Āgnīdhra, that is, from the Āgnīdhra sacrifice.
And having drunk, satisfy yourself—that is, become satiated—with your own portion, with your respective share.

This very [Soma] is for you, increasing the vigor of your body; from of old, strength and power have been placed within your arms. For you it is pressed, O Maghavan; for you it is brought. Drink of this to your heart's content from the vessel of the Brahmin. 5. This very one is yours, increasing the vigor of your body; might and power have been placed in your arms from ancient times. For you it is pressed, O Maghavan; for you it is brought. You, drink of this to your satisfaction from the vessel of the Brahmin. 5.
O Indra, this Soma is yours; it is for you, the increaser of the vigor (*nṛmṇa*)—that is, the strength—of your very body. "It has been pressed for you" is the connection with what follows later.

In that Soma, from of old in ancient times, power (*sahas*)—characterized by the overcoming of enemies—and vigor (*ojas*), as well as the strength (*bala*) that is the cause of those two, have been placed within you, in your arms and hands. (Note:
there is a change of grammatical gender.
O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, for your sake such Soma has been pressed; it has been extracted by the Adhvaryu priests.
The *hotṛ* has been brought for you, and [the oblation] has been offered upon the *uttaravedi*.
Being satisfied (*tṛpat*), that is, being satiated, drink this *soma* from the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*—that is, from the sacrifice of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*—or rather, drink it directly (*ā*).

Because of the rule "the mention of the action must be made," the object [of the action] becomes a recipient (*saṃpradāna*); therefore, in the word *asya*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.

Be pleased with the sacrifice; take heed of my invocation. Seated there, the Hotṛ priest follows the ancient invocations. O two Kings, the prayer approaches you; come hither! "Understand"—that is, comprehend.

The meaning is that he recites the *śastra*s, such as the *ājya* hymns, in accordance with the *stotra*s performed by the *udgātṛ*s.

Furthermore, the food characterized by Soma (*namaḥ*), which has been turned toward and surrounded by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*s), approaches—that is, reaches—both of you, the two shining ones (*rājānā*).

I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the eighth chapter of the second Aṣṭaka begins.
In the fourth Anuvāka of the second Maṇḍala, the fifth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "Mandasva," is by Gṛtsamada.

In the previous [section], because of the use of the word "tu" in the phrase "But the *ṛtavya* is in the *jagatī*," this [present section] is also a *jagatī* *ṛtavya*.
Among these, the first four verses have Draviṇodās as their deity; the fifth has the Aśvins as its deity, and the sixth has the Ṛbhus.

On the sixth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), during the *ṛtuyāja* offerings, one should perform the ritual by issuing the *praipa* (directions) after adding the *anuṣṭubh* heads to them, and one must sacrifice using those *praipas*.
In that context, after the seven *praipa* formulas beginning with the seventh, the six verses beginning with "mandasva" are to be inserted in sequence;
however, the sūtra has already been cited previously.

Rejoice according to your pleasure in the oblation of the soma-juice, O Adhvaryus! He desires the full ladle; bring this to him, for he is the giver who seeks it. From the Hotṛ’s office, drink the Soma, O Draviṇodas, according to the seasons. Rejoice! From the Hotṛ’s office. *Anu* (after).

*Joṣam* (according to pleasure). *U* is a filler. *Draviṇodas* (the giver of wealth), the bestower of desired fruits—he who indeed beholds [the deity] as the one to be worshipped (*devatātvena iṣṭa*)—for that Draviṇodas, the sweet soma-nectar has been brought forth and offered by the Adhvaryus.
O bestower of wealth, you who possess the sacrificial ladle, drink the Soma together with the seasons known as *ūrja*, from the purifying vessel of the sacrificer.

May thy many steeds be fat, with which thou goest; being uninjured, O Lord of the Forest, take thy strength. O bold one, having been summoned with force, do thou, O Giver of Wealth, drink the Soma from the Neṣṭṛ’s cup according to the seasons. 3. May thy many steeds be fat, with which thou goest; being uninjured, O Lord of the Forest, take thy strength. O bold one, having been summoned with force, do thou, O Giver of Wealth, drink the Soma from the Neṣṭṛ’s cup according to the seasons. 3.
O bestower of wealth, by those steeds with which you are carried and by which you proceed— you being such as Yāska described in Nirukta 8.3 as "many carriers" (*bahvayo voḍhāraḥ*)—
let them come hither and be satisfied.
O Lord of the Forest, O Lord of the woods, not desiring to harm and not injuring, grow firm and become strong.
O bold one, O assailant, having come with vigor and having raised [the vessel], drink the Soma from the Neṣṭṛ’s portion in the wood, together with the Ṛtus known as the Saṃjñas.

He has drunk from the Hotṛ’s cup and also from the Potṛ’s; he has become exhilarated from the Neṣṭṛ’s and has enjoyed the offered food. He who is the giver of wealth, who from the office of the Hotṛ drank the Soma, having drunk it, he was exhilarated;
and whatever [he drank] from the office of the Potṛ, having drunk the Soma, he became intoxicated.

And moreover, having been carried forth from the *vaneṣṭhāt* (the one standing in the wood) as part of the *neṣṭṛ* ritual function, the *vapra*s (the ploughers) have accepted—that is, they have served—the Soma, which is the food of the gods.
He is beneficial to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), who are the bestowers of *draviṇa* (wealth) in the form of oblations (*havir-rūpa*).
For Yāska has stated: "In this context, the *ṛtvij*s are called *draviṇodas*; they are the givers of the oblation, and they produce this [sacrifice]" (Nirukta 8.2).
May such a giver of wealth drink that which is unimpaired, cleansed by the tenfold filter, immortal, the means of attaining immortality—the fourth vessel, the Soma residing in the fourth cup.
