O Agni, accept the fuel;
accept the oblation;
accept the sacred word (brahma), which is beneficial to people (janya).

O Agni, accept with pleasure our excellent hymn of praise (*suṣṭuti*). Furthermore, O *vaso*—you who are the abode of all—desiring the great and all the gods who desire [you], and desiring [them] yourself, cause them to drink the oblation, the Soma in the form of *havis*, together with the rite known as *tapas* and with all the gods.
The sixth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "udu tyam," is composed by Gātsamada; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and has Savitṛ as its deity.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "Udu tyam: eleven [verses], dedicated to Savitṛ.
In the expanded (vyūḍha) ten-night rite (daśarātra), on the sixth day, this hymn is to be recited during the Vaiśvadeva Śastra along with the Sāvitra Nivid.
In the section beginning with "If it is a *vyūha*," it is stated in the aphorism: "'For the sixth [day], 'udu tyam citram' is the *gātsamada*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8).

Up has risen that god Savitṛ for his impelling, having performed that most constant work; as a bearer, he has stood firm. Now indeed he distributes treasure to the gods; then he bestowed wealth upon the one who offers the oblation for well-being. ut | ūṁ iti | syaḥ | devaḥ | savitā | savāya | śaśvattamam | tat | apāḥ | vahniḥ | asthāt | nūnam | devebhyaḥ | vi | hi | dhāti | ratnam | atha | ā | abhajat | vītahotram | svastau || 1 ||
That god Savitṛ, the shining one, has risen—and rises—every day, most constantly, for the sake of *sava*, that is, for the impelling, the setting in motion, or the authorization of the worlds.
Of what nature is Savitṛ? He is *tadapāḥ*: one whose work is that very impelling.
Because [the word] *apaḥ* is listed among the names for ritual acts (*karman*) in [Nirukta 2.1.1]: "The waters are *amaḥ*."
Vahni is the bearer of the worlds.
Furthermore, now indeed, he bestows—that is, grants—treasure, meaning wealth, to the gods who are his praisers;
for "hi" is used as a filler.
Moreover, may he grant a share—that is, make him a partaker—in *svasti*, meaning security and non-destruction, to the sacrificer who offers the beloved sacrifice (*vītihotram*).

Although the word *svasti* is indicated here as a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix (and thus seemingly referring to the word itself), it nevertheless refers to its actual meaning because the sense remains incomplete [if taken literally].
1. [The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to] the oblations (*āhuti*), the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), the Soma, and so forth.

2. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, and ṇa read: "for the sake of permission" (*anujñānāya*). 3. [The variant] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and ṇa read: "the subsequent word *nirdiṣṭa* is [to be understood as] *na*. 6. [The variant] ṣa reads: "the subsequent word *nirdiṣṭa* is [to be understood as] *na*."

For the sake of hearing from all, the God, standing erect with broad hands, stretches forth his arms. Even the waters are submerged within his law; even this wind rests in its circuitous course. viśvasya hi śrutyai deva ūrdhvaḥ pra bāhavā pṛthupāṇiḥ sisarti | ārṣcidasya vrata ā nirmagrā ayaṃ cidvātoṃ ramate parijman || 2 || For the God, rising up, extends his two arms, he of the broad hands, so that all may hear. Even the waters are submerged within his ordinance; even this wind rests in its wandering path.
The radiant god Savitṛ, the broad-handed one who performs great deeds,
being uplifted, extends his two arms for the glory and the well-being of the entire moving world;
even the waters, though devoid of consciousness, remain within his ordinance during the act of his impulsion.
Because it is listed among their names in the Nirukta (2.1.7), "‘vrataṃ karvaram’" [is used].
The word "flow" (*syandante*) is to be supplied. And they are "purifiers" (*punantīḥ*), meaning they thoroughly cleanse the world in the form of the Gaṅgā and other rivers.
We are the wind, and this too is the wind;
like a weaving woman weaving cloth, the night has again enveloped the spread-out light.
The word "again" indicates that she did so in the same manner on the previous day.
Even every wise and intelligent person in the world [finds it difficult] to complete the work that is being done;
for it is listed among its names in the Nirukta (2.1.18) as "that which is to be done by the doer" (*kartuḥ kartavyam*).
Even that which is capable of being done—meaning even when the task has been commenced in the midst of it—[remains uncompleted] until its conclusion.
He has placed [them] apart;
the words "when Savitṛ has ceased" are to be supplied.
Every person, having risen—that is, having abandoned their bed—has stood up.
He rises again to perform the remaining work.
The verb *jahāti* preceded by the prefix *sam-* signifies the abandonment of the bed;
and thus it is heard in scripture: "While lying down he is the Kali age, but upon rising he is the Dvāpara" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.15).

Savitar, the impeller of all, Sūrya, the unceasing Aramati, the shining Deva, has come— he is rising— so much as to say he comes. And he has rent asunder the specific times (kratus), that is, he causes them to be distinguished.
The all-pervading, sovereign, and all-encompassing heat of Agni spreads out in many directions;
the Mother has bestowed the supreme portion upon her son—the very banner of this world impelled by Savitṛ.

To various dwellings, to the homes, to every life-span, the source of Agni’s flame spreads abroad. The Mother has bestowed the most excellent portion upon her son, according to his desire as impelled by Savitṛ. 5.

The abundant radiance of Agni, his fiery splendor, dwelling in the house and present within the home, takes its stand— indeed, presides over— the various dwellings of the sacrificers, which are separate from one another;
it likewise presides over all life and all food,
for "āyus" is listed among the names for food in the Nirukta (2.7.23).

The Mother Dawn, impelled and sent forth by Savitṛ, has assigned to her son Agni his portion—the first, the most excellent, the portion consisting of the Agnihotra and other rites—that is his signal, the indicator.
The desire of all who move about, seeking to conquer from every side, has come together. It has arrived.

The eternal one, having left behind the waters and the transformation, has come according to the ordinance of the divine Savitṛ. He returns again; he who was standing apart, desiring victory, has become the desire of all who move. The eternal one, having left behind the waters and the transformation, has come according to the ordinance of the divine Savitṛ. śaśvān apaḥ vikṛtam hitvā ā agāt anu vratam savituḥ daivyasya ||6|| The eternal one, having abandoned the waters and the transformation, has come in accordance with the law of the divine Savitṛ. ||6||
The warrior desiring victory, having set out for battle, turns back [the enemy]; he causes them to turn back from the presence (*amā*) of all moving beings— that is, of all that walks—
since *amā* is listed among the names for "home" in the Nirukta (3.4.11) with the gloss "in the house."
A desire for home has arisen;
he who is ever devoted to his work, having repeatedly left behind his altered or half-finished tasks, comes back to his home.
All this is born in accordance with the *vrata*—the ritual act known as setting—of the divine Savitṛ, the impeller who dwells in heaven.
1. He is encompassed by *jha* and *ma*. 2. One desiring victory [is encompassed] by *ma*.
By you, even that which was placed in the waters, the desert lands, or the mountains have been spread abroad.
No one violates those forest-like laws of this god Savitṛ.

By thee [is] the benefit to be bestowed; in the waters [is] the portion. Along the desert have they spread out, seeking [thee]. To the woods, to the birds—no one violates these ordinances of this god Savitṛ. 7.
O Savitṛ, by you [is that which is] placed within the waters or in the intermediate space—
for "āpaḥ" is read among the names of the intermediate space in Nirukta 1.3.8—
or in a reservoir; the deer, seeking the watery portion belonging to the waters (*āpya*) in the desert regions and forests devoid of water, have stood all around, taking their positions.
Furthermore, the forests—the trees—have been granted by you as a portion for the birds in the form of dwellings;
no one at all violates or harms those such vows, the ritual acts, of this god Savitṛ.
Having attained his goal in Varuṇa’s womb, quivering and darting at every moment, every Martanda bird has entered its fold like a beast; Savitar, the radiant one, has surveyed all births.

Whatever is to be attained—Varuṇa [has entered] the watery womb; flickering in his unceasing glance, every Martanda bird has gone to its stall like a beast. Savitar has distributed the births one by one, having made them distinct. 8.

Varuṇa bestows upon these creatures that which is attainable by those who go—that is, what is to be won through their journey—and that which is worthy of attainment; he grants them that which is soft, meaning not sharp, but rather pleasant;
and he provides a resting place, a womb, for all living beings at the moment of closing the eyes, that is, at sunset, so that they may find repose.
Because he brings about the departure [of the breath] through the nights of Varuṇa;
*jarbhurāṇaḥ*, moving intensely; *viśvaḥ*, every; *mārtāṇḍaḥ*, the bird produced from each and every dead egg, *ā gāt*, comes hither.
Every *paśuḥ*, beast, has also come to its *vrajam*, stall. *Savitā*, the impeller, has separated *janmāni*, the beings born, in their respective places (*sthaśaḥ*).
He whom Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and Rudra do not violate, nor the unrighteous—
him I invoke for well-being with salutations, the god Savitṛ.
No; he whose law neither Indra, nor Varuṇa, nor Mitra, nor Aryaman, nor Rudra, nor the enemies violate—him, the god Savitṛ, I here invoke for well-being with prostrations. 9.
The ordinance (*vrata*) of that god Savitṛ, known as "impulsion" (*prasava*), Indra does not violate nor does he destroy;
Varuṇa does not violate it;
and Mitra and Aryaman do not violate it.
And Rudra does not diminish [it]; neither the enemies nor the Asuras [can diminish it].
(Note: *ka-ma-va* refers to the reading "in reservoirs of water.")
2. *jha1*—trees and so forth;
3. *ka-jha1-ga-na-tha-na-ma-va*—the Lord (*īśaḥ*); 4. *ga*—that which is to be propitiated. Verse 2.21.
They speak.
The term "minoti" (he measures) is understood as a verbal root; it is connected individually with each [term] through appropriate modification.

I invoke— that is, I praise— for the sake of well-being (*svasti*) and security (*kṣema*), that radiant god Savitṛ, the impeller of all, now with these salutations (*namas*) consisting of oblations in the form of food; for "salutation" (*namaḥ*) is listed among the names of food in the *Nighaṇṭu* (2.7.22).
Seeking fortune, inspired thought, and abundance, may Narāśaṃsa and Grāsa protect us from others.
May we be dear to the god Savitṛ at the gathering of wealth and the attainment of all that is desirable.

Seeking strength, we pray for Bhaga, for wisdom, and for Puraṃdhi; may Narāśaṃsa and Grāsaṃti bring us other [blessings] at the arrival of desirable wealth in its gathering. May we be dear to the god Savitṛ. 10.
Bhaga is that which is to be honored; Dhiyaḥ is that which is to be meditated upon; Purandhi is the supporter of the city, or one of great wisdom—[all these refer to] Savitṛ.
"Purandhi is the one of many thoughts," says Yāska (Nirukta 6.13).
Seeking vigor, they bring forth the vigorous one who possesses strength.
An indeclinable that functions as a case-ending.

May Narāśaṃsa—praiseworthy by men, the lord of the *grāsas*, and the husband of the wives of the gods, or rather the lord of the meters—for it is heard in the Śruti: "The *grāsas* are indeed the meters," and "And let the wives of the gods, the *grāsas*, come" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.46.8)—may Savitṛ protect us as we praise him. May he look upon us.
Furthermore, [may we be dear] to the desirable wealth, riches, and cattle;
for it is heard in scripture: "Cattle indeed are wealth.
On the occasion of arrival (āya), coming together (saṃgatha), and meeting (saṃgamana), may we be dear to the radiant Savitṛ, the impeller.

May that desirable wealth, granted by you from heaven and earth, O Savitṛ, come to us—wealth that brings well-being to the singers, to our kinsman, and to the one who praises you far and wide. For the victorious one, O Savitṛ.

From there, from heaven and from earth, may that desirable wealth granted by you come to us—wealth that shall be a blessing to our singers and a source of prosperity for our kinsman, O Savitṛ of wide renown. 11.

O Savitṛ, may that well-known and desirable wealth (*rādhas*) bestowed by you come to us from heaven (*div*), from the intermediate region (*aṅga*), and from the earth (*pṛthivī*). Furthermore, may that wealth which brings happiness (*śam*) be for the singers, for their kin, and for their offspring; and may it be for me, the singer (*jaritr̥*) of wide renown (*uruśaṃsa*). For "singer" (*jaritā*) and "poet" (*kāru*) are listed among the names for a singer in the *Nighaṇṭu* (3.16.2).
O Savitṛ, restrain that.

The seventh hymn, beginning with “*grāvāṇeva*,” consists of seven verses; it is composed by Gṛtsamada, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to the Aśvins, as indicated by the *Anukramaṇī* entry: “*grāvāṇeva*... [is] the Aśvina [hymn].
Its application is in the *Pravargya* ritual during the *Abhiṣṭava* in the first section (*paṭala*).
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “*grāvāṇeva le dyāvāpṛthivī*” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.6).
This hymn belongs to the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvināśastra. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "With the words 'grāvāṇeva mā satyābhyām,' [he recites] three [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.15).

Like two pressing-stones, you two stir for this very purpose; like two vultures, fly toward the tree that contains the treasure. Like two priests at the rite, chanting hymns of praise; like two messengers, you carry the oblations to many people. Like two pressing-stones, for that very purpose, you two stir; like two vultures, toward the tree containing the treasure. Like two priests at the rite, chanting hymns of praise; like two messengers, the offerings of the people to many places.

The two Aśvins were sent forth against the enemy like two grinding-stones; the word *artha* here has the sense of "toward" or "against," as Yāska states: "The word *artha* [is used] with the root *at*" (Nirukta 1.18).
"Tam arātim" means "that enemy.
"It" is a filler particle.
"Jarethe" means "you two grow old"; [here it means] "you two drive away the enemy."
Or rather, just as two heavy stones, once thrown, move swiftly at that very moment, so do you two cause the one who goes toward each respective object to "grow old"—
that is, to go quickly having been praised;
for the root *jar* signifies the act of praising.
Furthermore: like two vultures, like two birds, come toward the sacrificer who possesses wealth as if toward a tree laden with fruit or a treasure-trove—this is the ellipsis;
[come] to the *vidatha*, that is, to the sacrifice.

Because *vidathaḥ savanam* is listed among the names of sacrifice (*yajña*) [in Nirukta 3.17.5], [the phrase] *ukthaśāsā* means "two reciters of hymns. Like two *brahmāṇau*, that is, like two Brāhmaṇas; like two messengers (*dūtau*) sent by kings among the people (*janyā*) in various regions (*purutrā*); you two are to be honored with offerings (*havyā hātavyau*) by many men.
Here, there is a dual number for the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) in accordance with the object of comparison (*upameya*).

Moving at dawn like two chariot-warriors, like two heroes, like two goats, you two, O twins, move together toward the chosen goal. Like two women adorning their bodies with beauty, like a husband and wife, you who know the sacred seasons, you are present among the people. *prātaryāvāṇā rathyaiva vīrājeva yamā varamā saṃcethe | meneiva tanvāi śubhramāne dampatīva ṛtuvidā janaiṣu || 2 ||* Moving at dawn like two chariot-warriors, like two heroes, like two goats, you two, O twins, move together toward the chosen goal. Like two women adorning their bodies with beauty, like a husband and wife, you who know the sacred seasons, you are present among the people.
Those two Aśvins, who travel at dawn, coming early indeed for the sake of the sacrifice; like two chariot-warriors, heroes brave in their own task;
like two goats, twins joined together;
like two women, shining with their bodies in splendor.

Like a married couple, like husband and wife joined together among the people and the objects of the senses, you two—you who know the seasons and know the ritual—come together toward the one who provides enjoyment.

Like two horns, come first toward us; like two hooves, flickering with your strides. Like two ruddy geese, come hither at dawn; O mighty ones, come like two charioteers! 3. Like two horns, come first toward us; like two hooves, flickering with your strides. Like two ruddy geese, come hither at dawn; O mighty ones, come like two charioteers! 3.

1. O Aśvins, like the two shoulder-blades of a beast, like the two foremost parts of faith, like the two foremost things among the gods, like the two hooves of a horse or similar animal—moving rapidly with your speeds, you who go most swiftly, come toward us, come hither!

Furthermore, O Aśvins, day after day, like two Cakravāka birds, O you who drive away enemies or who are swift in motion, like two chariot-warriors in their chariot, O powerful ones capable in your own work, come hither, come toward us!

Like two ships, ferry us across; like two yokes, like two nave-pieces, like two inner wheels, like two outer wheels—like two dogs that do not quarrel over our bodies, like two jawbones, protect us from falling apart.

Like two boats, ferry us across; like two yokes, like two nave-pieces, like two inner linings, like two outer linings; like two dogs that do not barter away our bodies—like two leather thongs, protect us from falling apart. 4.
O Aśvins, ferry us across our difficulties like two boats across rivers.
Just as the two yokes [secure] a chariot, just as the two nave-boards of a chariot wheel,
just as the two side-boards attached to its sides, or just as the two outer-rim bands [secure] the chariot, so do you ferry us across our difficulties.

Furthermore, like two dogs—just as two dogs protect [their masters] from attackers and ward off injury to their bodies—so may you two be non-injurious (*aripaṇyau*) toward our bodies, that is, our limbs. Like two leather shields (*khagaleva*), which protect against injury to the body, so may you two protect us from *visras*, that is, from old age.
Like two winds, ageless; like two men, O protectors; like two eyes, come from afar!
Like two hands most beneficial to the body, like two feet, lead us toward greater prosperity.

Like two winds, you who are ageless; like two leaders of men, a path; like two eyes with sight—come hither! Like two hands, bestowing welfare upon our bodies; like two feet, lead us toward greater prosperity. 5.

Those two Aśvins are like the two winds, undecaying and impossible for one to age; they are like two rivers in their flow, where the singular number is used due to the interchangeability [of the dual].

May you two go quickly! Like two eyes—the eyes themselves—come hither toward us with your vision. Furthermore, like two hands and like two feet, being most conducive to well-being for our bodies, lead us toward, and bring us, wealth that is more excellent, the very best.
Like two lips, speak to us with sweetness; like two udders, nourish us so that we may live.
Like two nostrils, be the protectors of our bodies; like two ears, be well-hearing for us.
Like two lips, you are honey; may you speak for us. Like two breasts, cause us to swell with life. Like two nostrils, protect our bodies; like two ears, be well-hearing for us. 6.
O Aśvins, having taken your stand upon our mouths like two lips, cause us to swell with life by means of speech that carries sweet flavor;
and furthermore, like two nostrils, become the protectors of our bodies;
and moreover, like two ears, become well-hearing for us.
Like two hands, bestow power upon us; like two tongs, gather the dust-particles for us.
O Aśvins, sharpen these songs of ours directed toward you, as an axe is sharpened on a whetstone.

Like two hands, take hold of power; like two well-aimed archers, strike us together. Like two ploughs, drive us through the realms. O Aśvins, sharpen these songs of ours directed toward you, as an axe is sharpened on a whetstone. 7.

O Aśvins, like two hands, grant us power (*śakti*) by bestowing it upon us completely and directly. Furthermore, like the two worlds (*rodasī*), grant us the regions (*rajāṃsi*)—that is, the places or the waters; for Yāska says, "Water is called *rajas*" (Nirukta 4.19).
O Aśvins, impel us;
furthermore, O Aśvins, sharpen these hymns of praise composed by us—which long for you—just as one sharpens an axe with a whetstone, making them perfectly keen.
These strengthening prayers and hymns of praise the Gṛtsamadas have fashioned for you, O Aśvins.
O Heroes, come hither, well-pleased with them; may we, blessed with brave sons, proclaim this aloud at the assembly.

These strengthening prayers and hymns of praise, the Gṛtsamadas have fashioned for you, O Aśvins. O Heroes, graciously accepting them, come hither. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 8.
O Aśvins, these strengthening prayers—mantras that bring about your growth—and this hymn of praise, the Gṛtsamadas have fashioned for you both.
O leaders, taking great delight in those prayers, come hither to us.
Furthermore, as we, possessing noble sons, shall offer a lofty song of praise to you both at the sacrifice in the assembly.
The eighth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “*somāpūṣaṇā*,” is composed by Gṛtsamada, is in the *triṣṭubh* meter, and has Soma and Pūṣan as its deities.
Thus it is enumerated: “*Somāpūṣaṇā*: six [verses]; [the hymn] is dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan; the latter half-verse is also [dedicated] to Aditi.
Regarding the half-verse “*avatu naḥ... aditiḥ*,” the deity is Aditi.

In the animal sacrifice for Soma and Pūṣan, the first three verses among the oblations of the omentum (*vapā*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and the offering (*havis*) are respectively the invitatory verses (*anu-vākyā*); the following three are the offering verses (*yājyā*).
This is stated in the section beginning with “Agnīṣomau” in the Sūtra: “‘Somāpūṣaṇā jananā rayīṇām’” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).

1. *ka-jha-jha* 1-ṇa-ṇa 1-tha-na-ma-va-madhurasa°. 2. Regarding this [syllable] *ma*: "O Soma and Pūṣan, you two who are the progenitors of riches, the progenitors of heaven, the progenitors of earth; born as the guardians of the entire world, the gods have made you the navel of immortality. (1) Soma and Pūṣan. Progenitors. Of riches. Progenitors. Of heaven. Progenitors. Of earth. Born. Of the entire. World. Guardians. The gods. Made. Of immortality. The navel. (1)
O Soma and Pūṣan, you two are the progenitors of riches (*vrajīṇām*), the progenitors even of heaven (*divaḥ*), and the progenitors of earth (*pṛthivyāḥ*).
Moreover, as soon as you were born (*jātau*), the gods made you the guardians (*gopau*) of the entire world (*viśvasya bhuvanasya*), the navel (*nābhim*)—the cause—of immortality (*amṛtasya*).

May these two gods, as they are being born, take pleasure [in this]; may these two seize the unwelcome darknesses. Through these two, Soma and Pūṣan, Indra generated the cooked milk within the raw cows. These two gods, as they are being born, have been pleased; may these two seize the unwelcome darknesses. Through these two, Soma and Pūṣan, Indra produced the ripe [milk] within the unripe cows.
These two gods, Soma and Pūṣan, shining and being born—just as soon as they were produced—all the gods rejoiced in them;
that is to say, they served them.
Furthermore, these two, Soma and Pūṣan, destroy the darkness that is to be shunned, which belongs to every house.
Furthermore, Indra, together with these two, Soma and Pūṣan, produces (*janat*) the fully ripened milk within the beautiful, swift-moving cows, in the middle of their udders.

O Soma and Pūṣan, you two, O Bulls, quicken that seven-wheeled chariot which measures out the mid-world, which is all-pervading, which revolves in every direction, and which is yoked by the mind—having five reins. Soma and Pūṣan; of the mid-world; the measurer; seven-wheeled; the chariot; all-pervading; revolving in every direction; by the mind; being yoked; it; you two quicken; O Bulls; having five reins.

O *vṛṣaṇā*, the two bulls, the showerers of desires, O Soma and Pūṣan—O Soma and Pūṣan—[open] the *vraja*, the world. Regarding this, Yāska says: “The worlds (*lokāḥ*) are called *rajāṃsi*” (Nirukta 4.19).
[Open] the *vimānam*, the delimiting [space].
The meaning is "all pride.
"Seven-wheeled" means having seven wheels.
The thirteenth month is the seventh season.

According to the Śruti, "There is a thirteenth month" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.3.4). [He is] *vaviśvaminvam*, that which pervades the universe; *viśvasya*, the immeasurable; *vviṣpavṛttam*, revolving everywhere; *viṣvak*, moving in all directions; and *pañcaraśmim*, having five rays—namely, the five seasons, including the two of Hemanta and Śiśira.
1. *ka-jha* is all speech (*sarvavāk*); *jha1* is all beings (*sarvabhūta*); *ṇa-ta-tha-na-va* is all thought (*sarvamata*); *ma* is all tranquility (*sarvata*).
In brief, there are five seasons. And thus it is heard in scripture: "There are twelve months and five seasons, by combining the cold and the dewy seasons" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 1.1).
Yoked by the mind, yoked by mind alone—drive that well-known chariot toward us; you two urge it forward.
One has made his dwelling in heaven, the other upon the high earth, and another in the intermediate space.
May those two bestow upon us an abundance of wealth, rich in boons and rich in food, and may they establish our kinship with them.

One has made his dwelling high in heaven; the other, upon the earth and in the mid-air. May those two release for us an increase of wealth—abounding in desirable things and abundant in food—as a kinsman to us.
Of those two, one, Pūṣan, made his seat—his dwelling place—in the high, lofty heaven, the world of sky;
the other, Soma, made his seat upon the earth in the form of plants, and in the intermediate space in the form of the moon.
O you two, Soma and Pūṣan, [grant us] that which possesses many boons, desirable by many, much-nourishing, of great renown, and the increase of wealth.
The meaning is that wealth consists of cattle.

Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Cattle indeed are the increase of wealth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.6.2). "Asme" means for us; "nābhim" means the cause of all enjoyment; may it be released—that is, bestowed—upon us.
The meaning is "let them both bestow."
One has generated all beings; the other moves along beholding everything.
O Soma and Pūṣan, further my inspired thought; with you two may we conquer all hostile armies.
One has generated all beings; the other moves, beholding everything. O Soma and Pūṣan, may we, through you two, conquer all hostile armies with our swift horse and our inspired thought. 5.
O Soma and Pūṣan, one of you two—Soma—has generated, that is, brought forth, all beings, all existing things;
as it is said in the mantra: "Soma flows on, the progenitor of thoughts" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.96.5).
The other, the second, Pūṣan—the Sun—goes along, beholding, that is, looking upon, the universe.
O you two, Soma and Pūṣan, protect—i.e., guard—my *dhi* (insight); for *dhiḥ* and *śacī* are listed among the names for action (*karman*) in the Nighaṇṭu (2.1.21). Protect!
Moreover, by means of you two as our causes, may we conquer—that is, overcome—all *pṛtanās*, all enemy armies.
May Pūṣan, who possesses all wisdom, quicken our intellect; may Soma, the lord of wealth, bestow upon us riches.
May the divine Aditi grant us swift horses; with brave sons, may we proclaim our great hymn at the assembly.

May Pūṣan quicken our prayer; may Soma, the lord of wealth, bestow all-encompassing riches upon us. May the divine Aditi, who is free from enemies, grant us swift steeds. May we, possessing heroic sons, offer great praise in the assembly.

1. There are indeed twelve [letters]: ka, ca, jha, jña, ṇa, ta, tha, na, va, dva, da, ra. 2. There is no [letter] between tha and ma. 3. There is no [letter] among ṇa, ta, tha, and tā. 4. For the sake of the enjoyment of wealth (*ma-bhogahetu*).
May *pūṣan*, the Āditya, the one who gladdens all (*viśvamanu*), strengthen (*jinvatu*) and satisfy our work (*dhriyam*).
May Soma, the lord of wealth (*rayipati*), bestow (*dhadhātu*) wealth (*rayi*) upon us.
Furthermore, may the radiant goddess Aditi—who is unassailable, meaning she has not been brought into opposition by anyone—protect us.
The rest is self-evident.
The ninth hymn, consisting of twenty-one verses beginning with “vāyo ye te,” is composed by Gārtsamada and is in the *gāyatrī* meter.
Regarding the sixth triplet beginning with “ambitame,” the first two verses are *anuṣṭubh*s and the third is a *bṛhatī*.
The two verses beginning with “vāyo ye te” are dedicated to Vāyu.
The verse beginning with “*śukrasyādha*” belongs to Indra and Vāyu.
For the five *ṛc*s beginning with “*ayaṃ vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā*,” the deities are, in order: Mitra and Varuṇa, the Aśvins, Indra, the Viśve Devās, and Sarasvatī.

As for the verse “*pretāṃ yajñasya*,” because it is prescribed in both the Brāhmaṇa and the Sūtra for the commencement of the rite and is employed as the *dyāvāpṛthivya* *nivid*, its deities are either Heaven and Earth or the *havirdhāna*.
The verse “agniṃ ca havyavāhanam” either has Agni as its deity or is without a specific deity.

Thus it is enumerated: “‘vāyo,’ etc., consists of one [verse] in the Gāyatrī meter; the deities mentioned in the *prauga* [śastra] are [as follows]: the first triplet belongs to Indra and Vāyu; another triplet belongs to Heaven and Earth; the third triplet belongs to the two *havirdhāna* carts; the third *pāda* [of the next verse] belongs to Vāyu; and the two *anuṣṭubh*s and the *bṛhatī* [beginning with] ‘ambitame’ [belong to Agni].
On the second day of the *pṛṣṭha-abhiplava* six-day period, this hymn is used in the *prauga*, with the exception of the other triplet.

Regarding the Vāyavya-trca, the first two verses beginning with “vāyo ye te sahasriṇaḥ” [RV 7.92.1–2] and for the Aindravāyava-trca, the verse “śukrasyādha” [RV 8.101.15] are prescribed by the Sūtra: “‘vāyo ye te sahasriṇaḥ’, ‘tīvrāḥ somāsa ā gahi’, ‘ubhā devā divispṛśā’—these two, ‘śukrasyādha gavāśiraḥ’—one [verse], ‘ayaṃ vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā’—these five triplets” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.6).
On the twenty-fourth day, at the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana), in the Maitrāvaruṇa-śastra, the triplet beginning with “ayaṃ vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā” is known as the *pālahasta* or *unnītra*.
In the section beginning with "The Hotṛ was born in the twenty-fourth," it is sūtra-ed: "This [hymn], O Mitra and Varuṇa, which is far-reaching... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.2).

During the morning pressing on the days of the *ābhiplavika* period, this very triplet is to be inserted as an *āvāpa* in the Maitrāvaruṇa’s *śastra* for the purpose of the *iṣṭoma* consisting of fifteen verses and others, because it is sūtra-ed: "The triplets 'This [hymn], O Mitra and Varuṇa,' and 'O Mitra and Varuṇa, for us... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.5).
The first [verse] is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the Maitrāvaruṇa's recitation.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "For the Maitrāvaruṇa: 'This, O Mitra and Varuṇa' (*ayaṃ vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā*, Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.5).

In the *Gāyatrī* meter, which is suitable for the Morning Litany (*prātaranuvāka*) and the *Āśvina* Śastra, the triplet beginning with "Possessing cattle" (*gomad ū ṣu*, Ṛgveda 1.91.16–18) is prescribed for use.
Because it is stated in the Sūtra: “*gomad pu nāsyeti tṛcāḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.15).
In the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* recitation during the first *paryāya* of the *atirātra*, there is the triplet beginning with “*indro aṅga mahaddhyam*.
This is prescribed in the section titled “*atirātre paryāyāṇām*” as follows: “*indro aṅga mahaddhyam abhi nyūṣu vācam*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
In the Āgrayaṇa [sacrifice], for the Vaiśvadeva oblation, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is "O Viśve Devās...
As it is sūtra-ed in the section on the Āgrayaṇa: "O Viśve Devās, come hither, you who are on earth, the great ones of serpent-like power" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.9).
On the first day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), in the *prauga* litany, the seventh triplet dedicated to Sarasvatī is "O most motherly one, O most riverly one... (*ambitame nadītame*).
In the section beginning with “On the fourth day,” it is sūtra-ed: “‘O most beloved mother, O best of rivers,’ [this] Anuṣṭubh Prauga [is used]” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.11).

In the Vaiśvadeva Śastra of the first Chandoma during the expanded ten-night rite (*vyūḍha-daśarātra*), the triplet for the insertion of the *Nivid* addressed to Heaven and Earth is: “May the two auspicious ones of the sacrifice go forth” (RV 10.13.1–3).

In the section beginning with “Now the Chandomas,” it is sūtra-ed: “‘May the two auspicious ones of the sacrifice go forth; this for the god’s birth’—these are the triplets” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.9).
This triplet of verses is also prescribed for the movement of the *havirdhāna* cart.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "May the two auspicious ones go forth, when the two Yamas strive together over the oblation" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.9; *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 1.29).

O Vāyu, with those thousand chariots which are yours, come hither; bring them along for the drinking of the Soma. O Vāyu, those thousand chariots which are yours—with those, come hither; bringing them along, for the drinking of the Soma.
1. [In the versions] kha, ga, ca, jha, ṇa, ṇa, tha, and na, the word "ṛcānām" does not exist; in ma, it is "ṛcām.
O Vāyu, those thousand chariots belonging to you—those chariots numbering one thousand—with them, being possessed of the teams of horses (niyutvān), come hither for the drinking of Soma.
The sense is that because Vāyu possesses manifold forms, his arrival accompanied by all his manifestations is being prayed for.

O Vāyu, come with your team of horses; this bright [soma] is offered to you. You shall go to the house of the one who presses the juice. 2. O Vāyu, come with your team of horses; this bright [soma] is offered to you. You shall go to the house of the one who presses the juice. 2.
O Vāyu, you who possess the teams; "niyutaḥ" refers to the draft-animals of Vāyu:
yoked with them, come hither!
This bright, shining Soma was offered to you; it was presented and taken up for you.
*yame*: the *luṅ* [suffix] is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
You shall go—you will be the one who goes—to the house of the sacrificer who is pressing the Soma.

O two sovereign rulers, by your very command you are the destroyers of all; you are *ghṛtāsutī*, those for whom clarified butter is the food, as is known from another mantra: "May that greatness of yours belong to you two whose food is clarified butter" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.67.8).
The two Ādityas, the sons of Aditi, the lords of *dānu*— that is, masters (*pati*) of *dānu*, or of the gift (*dāna*) that is to be given,
or of wealth (*dhana*)— those two, Mitra and Varuṇa, attend upon (*sacete*) the sacrificer who is straightforward (*anavahara*), meaning not crooked.
O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, you who are Rudras and lords of men, come to Gormada with your horses for our protection.
O Nāsatyas, rich in cattle, come hither with speed, O Aśvins, Rudras, to our dwellings.
To the protector of men.

O Aśvins, O Nāsatyas—those free from speaking falsehood—O Rudras, you who roar and rush, come by that path, or by means of your chariot; come to the Soma which is to be drunk by men—that is, by the gods—and which is rich in cattle and likewise rich in horses. Come so that it may be full! O Pū! O Ū! (The two syllables *ū* and *pu* signify "fullness").
Neither an outsider nor an insider, O Ṛṣanvant, shall dare to harm me—
the malicious enemy among mortals.
Neither from without nor from within can the malicious enemy, who plots with his wits, prevail against you, O possessors of manly wealth! 8.

O you two who possess the wealth of rain, O bestowers of riches! That wealth which even a distant enemy—an ill-intentioned person unfit for praise—cannot assail; and likewise, that wealth which even a nearby enemy—one characterized by longing and close at hand—cannot assail: that is the wealth to be seized, so the sense is completed.
O Aśvins, you who are worthy of praise, bring hither that wealth which is beautiful to behold, O bounteous ones,
and which finds wide space.
O Aśvins, you who are worthy of praise, bring to us wealth that is visible as golden-hued, O bounteous ones, which finds us room and freedom.

O two Aśvins, you who possess the wisdom-seats and are worthy of praise—bring hither to us that wealth, which is of variegated appearance, which finds wide space, and which bestows cattle. Bring it to us!
O Indra, indeed, you have struck down great fear;
for you are the one who wields the firm thunderbolt.
O Indra, let him indeed drive away this great fear that assails us; for he is the one who stands firm as a showerer of blessings. 10.
1. [The variants] kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ṇa lack *deyasya*; jha-tha-ma-va have *devasya*. 2. jha 1-ṇa-ta-tha-na-va have *yathā*.
Indra, may he overcome (*abhipat*) the great, excessive fear—that which causes fear—and cast it away (*apattucchat*). May he think it away.
For indeed, because he is firm—incapable of being moved by anyone—and all-seeing, beholding the universe.

May Indra be gracious to us; may no evil reach us from behind; may there be prosperity before us for us. (11) And may Indra be gracious to us; may no evil reach us from behind; may there be prosperity before us for us. (11)
May Indra, the possessor of supreme sovereignty, if he is indeed Indra, grant us joy and make us happy.
From behind, from our rear, may evil and misfortune not reach us;
and before us, in front of us, may there be auspiciousness and well-being.

May Indra grant freedom from fear from all directions; may he, the observer of all people, be the conqueror of enemies. 12. Indra—from all directions—around—from all—may he grant—fearlessness—the conqueror—of enemies—the observer of all people. 12.
Viccarṣaṇiḥ: the observer of all things; the conqueror;
the conqueror of enemies and Asuras.
Because it is being woven, there is the absence of visibility.
May Indra, the possessor of supreme sovereignty, grant us fearlessness from all directions and quarters.
The particle *pari* indicates the ablative case (*pañcamī*).

O All-Gods, come hither; hear this my invocation. Sit down upon this sacrificial grass (barhis). 13. O All-Gods, come hither; hear this my invocation. Sit down upon this sacrificial grass (barhis). 13.
O all you gods, come hither;
hear this my invocation;
sit down upon this sacred grass.

Strong for you is this honeyed, exhilarating [Soma] among the Śunahotras; drink it, the desirable one. 14. Strong. For you. Honeyed. This. Among the Śunahotras. Exhilarating. This. Drink. The desirable. 14.

O All-Gods, this Soma—sharp, providing a sharp exhilaration, honeyed, flavorful, and intoxicating—is for you, residing among us, the Gṛtsamadas, the descendants of Śunahotra. Drink this desirable, lovely Soma!

With Indra as their chief, the hosts of Maruts, the gods who bestow wealth upon the city—may all of them hear my invocation! 15 With Indra as their chief, the hosts of Maruts, the gods who bestow wealth upon the city—may all of them hear my invocation! 15.
1. Terrifying in the midst of fear. 2. [The letters] *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *ma*, and ‘*vaḥ*’ are not present.

O *indrajyeṣṭhāḥ*, those who have Indra as their leader; O *marudgaṇāḥ*, you whose form is the host of Maruts; O *pūrātayaḥ*, those for whom the god Pūṣan is the giver of delight (*rati*); O *devāḥ*, shining gods; O *viśve*, all of you—*śruta*, listen to my *havam*, my invocation!
*Indrajyeṣṭhādayaḥ* ending in vocative case (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.23.8).

O most motherly one, O most river-like one, O most divine Sarasvatī! We are, as it were, unpraised; O Mother, make us worthy of praise. 16. O most motherly one, O most river-like one, O most divine Sarasvatī! We are, as it were, unpraised; O Mother, make us worthy of praise. 16.
O most motherly one, best among mothers; O most river-like one, best among rivers; O most divine one, best among goddesses—O Sarasvatī, we are as if unpraised [and lacking wealth].
O Mother Sarasvatī, grant us—that is, make for us—a praiseworthy abundance of wealth;
that is to say, bestow it upon us.

In thee, O goddess Sarasvatī, all lifespans are centered. Rejoice in the offerings of Śunahotra; O goddess, grant us progeny. 17. In thee; all; O Sarasvatī; centered; lifespans; in the goddess; in the offerings of Śunahotra; rejoice; progeny; O goddess; grant; to us. 17.

In you, O goddess Sarasvatī, the radiant one, all— meaning every— *āyūṃṣi*, that is, all forms of knowledge; for *āyus* is listed among the names [of knowledge] in Nirukta 2.7.23 as "the well-spoken word" (*sūtṛtā*)—
are *śritā*, meaning they are rested or supported.

As such, O Goddess Sarasvatī, rejoice in the drinking of Soma among us Gṛtsamadas, the descendants of Śunahotra; that is, be satisfied within our domain. Furthermore, O Goddess, bestow offspring upon us—that is, grant us sons.

O Sarasvatī, rich in nourishment, graciously accept these prayers; for those beloved hymns of Gṛtsamada which they offer to you among the gods, O upholder of Truth. 18. imā | brahma | sarasvati | juṣasva | vājinīvati | yā | te | manma | gṛtsamadāḥ | ṛtāvāri | priyā | deveṣu | juhvatī || 18 ||
O Sarasvatī, rich in steeds, rich in food, observer of cosmic order, and rich in waters, graciously accept—take possession of—these, these very *brahmans* (prayers) and oblations.
Whatever meditations are worthy of thought, which are dear among the gods, or which are dear to you among the gods, those the Gṛtsamadas offer for your sake.
1. O Mother Mahe!

2. There is no *yā* after *ṇa-ta-tha-ma*. We choose you two here today, Agni and the bearer of oblations, the two who bring prosperity to the sacrifice. (19) We choose you two here today, Agni and the bearer of oblations, the two who bring prosperity to the sacrifice. (19)

May the two sacrificial carts (*havirdhāne*), which are the bringers of bliss (*śaṃbhuvā*)—the means of accomplishing happiness—for the sacrifice (*yajñasya yāgasya*), or rather, may Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivyau*) in that form, proceed toward the western part of the high altar (*uttaravedi*). Now, addressed directly: we choose (*ā vṛṇīmahe*) you two alone.
And we invoke Agni, the bearer of oblations;
here, "Agni" is a particle (nipāta).

May Heaven and Earth today present this successful, heaven-reaching sacrifice of ours among the gods. 20. May Heaven and Earth present this successful, heaven-reaching sacrifice of ours among the gods. 20.

Both Heaven and Earth—the two that accomplish the attainment of heaven and other goals—[are reached by] the Kapiñjala bird, who touches the sky, crying out again and again, proclaiming and indicating the matter being born. Like Kaṇva, he sends forth his voice as if [propelling] a boat;
now [the poet] speaks in the direct mode (pratyakṣakṛta).
O bird, O Kapiñjala, may you be auspicious—naturally endowed with well-being—and may you be so.
Furthermore, let no affliction or oppression reach you from any direction whatsoever.
A bird is so called because it is capable of lifting itself up. Crying out loudly, he utters his voice according to its nature, like one who impels speech as if propelling a boat.

"And be a source of auspicious omens, O Śakuni! You are called *sumaṅgala* because you utter words that are exceedingly auspicious, or because you swallow away misfortunes," says Yāska (Nirukta 9.3–4).

May the hawk not strike you down, may the falcon not strike you, nor may the hero armed with arrows find you. Following the direction of your father, O auspicious one, speak what is propitious and offer salutations here.

Let not the falcon strike you down; let not the fair-winged bird seize you; let not the hero armed with arrows, the archer, find you. Crying out toward the direction of your father, may you, most auspicious, speak here words of blessing. 2.
O Śakuni, let not the powerful Śyena, that specific bird, kill you;
nor let the Suparṇa, Garuḍa, the bird, kill you.
Likewise, let not the arrow-bearing hero, the archer who hurls shafts, find you.
Furthermore, toward the southern direction—
the south— let Kaniṛd, repeatedly making sound, being auspicious (sumaṅgala), possessing beautiful blessings, and speaking what is excellent, speak here in our presence; indicate auspiciousness.
Neigh toward the right of our houses, O bird of auspicious omen, speaking blessings!
Let not the thief nor the malevolent man master us; may we, blessed with heroic sons, speak aloud at the assembly.

Neigh, O bird, from the south of our houses, as one most auspicious and a speaker of blessings! Let no thief nor any evil-minded man master us. May we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly. 3.
O bird, O *kapiñjala*, being auspicious (*sumaṅgala*) and a speaker of blessings (*bhadravādī*), cry out—that is, make a sound—from the south, in the southern direction, of our dwellings.
For a bird crying out from the south is indeed an indicator of good fortune.
May the thief, the robber, have no power over us; may he not rule over us.
May even the one who "desires evil"—the one who intends harm—have no power over us.
The final quarter-verse has already been explained.
The hymn beginning with “pradakṣiṇit” is the eleventh, consisting of three verses; it is composed by Gṛtsamada and is in the Jāgata meter.
Thus it is enumerated: “pradakṣiṇi... [is] Jāgata; in the middle [there is] an Aṣṭi-Arvā in the Atiśakarī meter. The second verse is an Aṣṭi-Arvā in the Atiśakarī meter.
The other two [verses] are in the Jagatī metre;
Indra in the form of a Kapiñjala bird is the deity.
Having heard the unpleasant speech of birds, one should mutter the hymn beginning with "pradakṣiṇit."
The Sūtra has already been cited previously.

1. *tathāprabalaḥ* [is] *mā suparṇaḥ*. 2. In manuscripts *ka*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *na*, *ma*, and *tra*, the phrase “*uta... vadhīt*” does not exist; in manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, it is “*uta... vadhīt*”. 3. In manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ṭha*, *na*, *tra*, and *pra*, it is “*prāpayat*”.

4. Moving clockwise, the poets praise him; the son of Śakuntalā speaks forth the vital breaths according to the seasons. Like a singer of Sāmans, he utters both voices; he shines in accordance with both the Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh meters. Moving clockwise, the poets praise him; speaking forth the vital breaths, the son of Śakuntalā [speaks] according to the seasons. He utters both voices like a singer of Sāmans; he shines in accordance with both the Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh meters.
The Kapiñjalas, the sons of Śakuntī,
speaking auspiciously at the proper times, indicating the seasons—
like singers, they praise you by circling to the right; let them address you.
The plural number is used for the sake of honor.
Furthermore, the Sāma-singers utter both voices—the chanted (gāna) and the recited (śrauta)—just as a bird utters both the Gāyatra and the Traiṣṭubha Sāmans;
and he shines forth accordingly.
The meaning is that he performs those things which were not explicitly stated for one who hears [the injunction].

Like a Udgātṛ priest, O bird, you sing the Sāman; like a son of a Brahmin, you recite at all sacrifices. Like a vigorous stallion, having approached the mother-cows, O bird, proclaim auspiciousness for us from every side; O bird, proclaim merit for us from every side. Like a Udgātṛ priest, O bird, you sing the Sāman; like a son of a Brahmin, you recite at all sacrifices. Like a vigorous stallion, having approached the mother-cows, O bird, proclaim auspiciousness for us from every side; O bird, proclaim merit for us from every side.
O Śakuni, O Kapiñjala! Like an Udgātṛ priest, you sing the Sāman; just as the Udgātṛ sings the Sāman, so do you sing—you produce the sound of singing.

Like a son of Brahmā, that is, like a Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest who recites the Śastras during the Savanas, so do you recite at the proper times—you produce the Vedic tone. Like a "vṛṣan," that is, a stallion capable of impregnation.
"Like pregnant mares,
having approached and arrived, you too should speak just as they make a sound.
The remainder is clear.

Speaking, O bird, utter auspicious words; sitting silent, be mindful of our well-being. When you fly up and call out like a cuckoo, may we, with brave sons, speak loudly at the assembly. "Speaking," "you," "O bird," "auspicious," "utter," "silently," "sitting," "be mindful," "of us," "when," "flying up," "you call out," "like a cuckoo," "loudly," "may we speak," "in the assembly," "with brave sons."

1. *tha-ma-śakuniḥ* (the bird *tha-ma*). 2. *ṇa-tha-ma-mānasvanam* (the sound *mānasvana* with *ṇa-tha-ma*). 3. *ṇa-ta-tha-ma-* ‘*tathā tvam*’ does not exist. 4. *ṇa-ta-tha-ma-* ‘*yathā*’ does not exist.

O bird (*vśakune*), O *kapiñjala*, uttering the sound (*vāvadan*) while crying out, speak what is auspicious (*vbhadramā vada*); speak that which is propitious. Sitting in silence (*vtūṣṇīmāsīnaḥ*), you remain silent; awaken (*vcikiddhi*) our good thought (*vsumatim*).
When you fly up and speak, then you "karkarīyatha," meaning you speak like a *karkarī* (a type of musical instrument).
*Karkarī* is a specific kind of lute (*vādyaviśeṣa*).
The rest has been explained previously.
Thus ends the fourth Anuvāka in the second Maṇḍala of the Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa composed by Sāyaṇācārya.
And the second Maṇḍala is completed.
